16000.name: InteractionRequired
16000.title: AADSTS16000: Account isn't in the tenant the app uses (fix)
16000.description: AADSTS16000: the account isn't in the tenant the app uses. Usually a personal account or an uninvited guest. Low attack value. Fix and KQL.
16000.summary: AADSTS16000 means a user signed in with an account that doesn't exist in the tenant the app sent them to, so it can't use that app there. Usually it's a personal Microsoft account, the wrong account in the browser, or an external user who was never added as a guest. It has low attack value. The fix is to sign in with the right account or invite the user.
16000.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InteractionRequired**: User account '{EmailHidden}' from identity provider '{idp}' doesn't exist in tenant '{tenant}' and can't access the application '{appid}'({appName}) in that tenant. This account needs to be added as an external user in the tenant first. Sign out and sign in again with a different Microsoft Entra user account. This error is fairly common when you try to sign in to Microsoft Entra admin center by using personal Microsoft Account and no directory associated with it.

The user proved who they are at their own identity provider. The tenant the app sent them to has no user or guest object for that account, so the sign-in stops there.

The wording is almost the same as [50020](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50020/). Microsoft doesn't document when Entra returns 16000 and when it returns 50020. Our reading: the name `InteractionRequired` suggests 16000 is the variant returned when the user can fix it by signing in again with another account. Treat the causes and fixes of the two codes as the same.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS16000 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **InteractionRequired**: User account '{EmailHidden}' from identity provider '{idp}' doesn't exist in tenant '{tenant}' and can't access the application '{appid}'({appName}) in that tenant. This account needs to be added as an external user in the tenant first. Sign out and sign in again with a different Microsoft Entra user account. This error is fairly common when you try to sign in to Microsoft Entra admin center by using personal Microsoft Account and no directory associated with it.

The user proved who they are at their own identity provider. The tenant the app sent them to has no user or guest object for that account, so the sign-in stops there.

The wording is almost the same as [50020](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50020/). Microsoft doesn't document when Entra returns 16000 and when it returns 50020. Our reading: the name `InteractionRequired` suggests 16000 is the variant returned when the user can fix it by signing in again with another account. Treat the causes and fixes of the two codes as the same.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No, in almost all cases. Microsoft's description names the most common cause itself: a personal Microsoft account used on the Entra admin center. Microsoft's 50020 troubleshooting article explains that case: *"you are connected to the Microsoft Services tenant by default. Within the default tenant, there is no linked directory for performing any actions. This behavior is expected."*

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A personal account (outlook.com, hotmail.com) on an Azure or Entra portal | The user picked the wrong account, or has no directory of their own. Benign. |
| A partner user on one specific app, repeating | The partner was never invited as a guest, or the guest object was deleted. |
| One user who has both a work and a personal account | The browser silently reused the wrong session. Benign. |
| Many users from one other company on one app | The app sends everyone to your tenant (a tenant-specific authority) but expects outside users. App or invitation problem. |

There is no documented attack pattern for 16000. The account has already authenticated at its home, and your tenant refuses it. As far as we can tell, an attacker gains nothing from this error that they didn't already have.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 16000 is logged in. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "16000"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which apps and which home tenants are involved. `HomeTenantId` is documented as *"the tenant identifier of the user initiating the sign in"*, so it tells you which organisation the outside users come from:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "16000"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Sample = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, HomeTenantId, ResourceTenantId
| sort by Users desc
```

We haven't checked this against real data, but the user name may be hidden or empty in these rows, because Microsoft's message template shows `{EmailHidden}`. If `UserPrincipalName` is empty, look at `SignInIdentifier`.

Users who keep failing with 16000 on the same app and never succeed afterwards. These are the ones that need an invitation or an app change, not a retry:

```kusto
let fails =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == "16000"
    | summarize Fails = count(), LastFail = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName;
let successes =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize LastSuccess = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId;
fails
| join kind=leftouter successes on UserPrincipalName, AppId
| where isnull(LastSuccess) or LastSuccess < LastFail
| where Fails >= 3
| project UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, Fails, LastFail
| sort by Fails desc
```

The threshold of 3 is a starting point. If the first query shows most rows in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, run the others against that table too. Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource ID match, so row counts there are not request counts.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS16000?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign out, or open a private browser window, and sign in again with your work account. Microsoft's description says to *"sign in again with a different Microsoft Entra user account"*. If you used a personal Microsoft account on the Azure or Entra portal and you have no directory of your own, you need to create one; Microsoft's 50020 article says *"If you aim to have a directory, you must create an Azure account and a new tenant."* If you are from another organisation, ask the app owner to invite you as a guest.

**For developers:** check which authority your app uses. Microsoft's 50020 article says that with `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<YourTenantNameOrID>` *"users from other organizations can't access the application. You have to add these users as guests in the tenant that's specified in the request."* If the app is meant for any organisation, use `/organizations` (or `/common` if personal accounts are allowed too), and make sure the app registration's supported account types allow it.

**For admins:**
1. External user who needs access: invite them as a guest (B2B). Microsoft's description says the account *"needs to be added as an external user in the tenant first."*
2. Guest that used to work: check whether the guest object was deleted, or whether the home tenant re-created the account. For the second case Microsoft's 50020 article says to reset the guest's redemption status instead of deleting and re-inviting.
3. Give guests a tenant-specific link. Microsoft's redemption article: *"A direct link is tenant-specific. In other words, it includes a tenant ID or verified domain so the guest can be authenticated in your tenant."*
4. Many users from one partner on one app: decide whether that app should accept them at all. If yes, invite them, ideally as a group; if no, the error is doing its job.

50001.name: InvalidResource
50001.title: AADSTS50001 fix: resource disabled or doesn't exist
50001.description: AADSTS50001: the token was for a resource that is disabled or doesn't exist. Usually a wrong resource URL. How it differs from 500011, plus KQL.
50001.summary: AADSTS50001 means an app asked Microsoft Entra ID for a token to a resource (an API) that is disabled or doesn't exist. Usually the resource URL in the app's code or settings is wrong. Users report it in Nintex, Power BI and custom web APIs. It is a configuration error with low attack value. 500011 is the related code for a resource with no service principal in the tenant.
50001.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidResource**: The resource is disabled or doesn't exist. Check your app's code to ensure that you have specified the exact resource URL for the resource you're trying to access.

The **resource** is the API the app wants a token for: Microsoft Graph, SharePoint, or your own web API. Entra ID couldn't use it, because the identifier in the request matches nothing usable, or the resource is switched off.

Users post a message that names the resource and the tenant: *"AADSTS50001: The application named <application name> was not found in the tenant named <tenant ID>."*

**50001 or 500011?** [500011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500011/) is Microsoft's code for a resource with no service principal in the tenant: *"The resource principal named {name} wasn't found in the tenant named {tenant}."* The messages users post for the two look alike. Microsoft's 50001 description adds one cause that 500011 doesn't have: a resource that exists but is **disabled**. Our reading: check the resource URL first for either code. If the resource's service principal exists but is switched off (**Enabled for users to sign-in?** set to No), Microsoft documents that as [500014](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500014/), so look there first. If the missing object is the client app, not the resource, the code is [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/). Our reading is that a disabled client app returns [7000112](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000112/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. A request for a resource that doesn't exist gets nothing back. Users report it in integrations with a wrong or unexpected resource:

- **Nintex for Office 365**: the error appeared when documents were stored on a SharePoint subsite. The reported fix was to store them at the site collection level.
- **A custom web API used from Power BI / Azure**: the resource named in the error was the web service's own domain, which wasn't registered in the tenant. One reply suggested the custom domain setup; a later commenter said that didn't help.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One app, every user, starting at a deployment or settings change | A wrong resource URL or App ID URI in the app's settings. Developer error. |
| An app that worked starts failing for everyone, with no code change | Something changed on the resource side. Check the resource's enterprise app and app registration; if it was switched off, Microsoft documents that case as [500014](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500014/). |
| 50001 naming a resource you don't recognise, from an app or IP you don't recognise | Someone asking your tenant for tokens to an API you never set up. Not a documented detection, but worth a look. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 50001 lands in. Check your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50001"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which client apps fail, and the resource they asked for:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50001"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Resources = make_set(ResourceIdentity, 10),
            ResourceNames = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppName = coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName), AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

When the resource doesn't exist, `ResourceIdentity` and `ResourceDisplayName` may be empty. Microsoft doesn't document this. If so, take the resource name from the error text the user or app received.

Recent changes to apps, to find a resource that was disabled. Microsoft lists **Update service principal** and **Update application** as audit activities. Our assumption: switching off **Enabled for users to sign-in?** or deactivating an app registration is recorded under one of them.

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName in ("Update service principal", "Update application")
| extend Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
         ByUser = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Target, ByUser, Result
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

For app-only rows, check in your workspace that `ResultType` carries `"50001"` and not *"Failure"*. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"50001"`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50001?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this. Send IT the app name and the full error, including the resource name.

**For developers:**
1. Compare the resource URL or scope in your code or settings with the API's identifier. Microsoft's description says to *"ensure that you have specified the exact resource URL for the resource you're trying to access."*
2. For your own API, check that its App ID URI is registered and that the client asks for exactly that value.

**For admins:**
1. Find the resource under **Enterprise applications**. If it isn't there, treat it like [500011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500011/): the resource was never set up in your tenant.
2. Open its **Properties** and check **Enabled for users to sign-in?**. Microsoft: when it is **No**, *"Tokens aren't issued for the application."* Microsoft documents a disabled resource service principal as [500014](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500014/), so if you find it switched off, read that page.
3. Check **App registrations** > **Deactivated applications**. Microsoft says a deactivated app *"immediately stops receiving new access tokens"*, but doesn't say what other apps get when they ask for a token to its API. To undo it, select the app and **Reactivate**.
4. Only re-enable a resource if disabling it was a mistake. Someone may have switched it off on purpose; the third query shows who changed it.

2. For your own API, check that its App ID URI is registered and that the client asks for exactly that value.

**For admins:**
1. Find the resource under **Enterprise applications**. If it isn't there, treat it like [500011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500011/): the resource was never set up in your tenant.
2. Open its **Properties** and check **Enabled for users to sign-in?**. Microsoft: when it is **No**, *"Tokens aren't issued for the application."* Microsoft documents a disabled resource service principal as [500014](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500014/), so if you find it switched off, read that page.
3. Check **App registrations** > **Deactivated applications**. Microsoft says a deactivated app *"immediately stops receiving new access tokens"*, but doesn't say what other apps get when they ask for a token to its API. To undo it, select the app and **Reactivate**.

50011.name: InvalidReplyTo
50011.title: AADSTS50011: Reply URL does not match
50011.description: AADSTS50011: the redirect URI doesn't exactly match the app registration. Usually a config typo; the exact match blocks token theft. With KQL.
50011.summary: AADSTS50011 means the redirect (reply) URI in the sign-in request doesn't exactly match one registered for the application. It is almost always a configuration mistake: http instead of https, a trailing slash, a wrong port. The exact-match rule is also what stops attackers redirecting authorization codes and tokens to their own server.
50011.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidReplyTo**: The reply address is missing, misconfigured, or doesn't match reply addresses configured for the app. As a resolution ensures to add this missing reply address to the Microsoft Entra application or have someone with the permissions to manage your application in Microsoft Entra IF do this for you.

(The wording, including "IF", is Microsoft's.) The troubleshooting article shows the message users see:

> The reply URL does not match the reply URLs configured for the application <GUID>. Make sure the reply URL sent in the request matches one added to your application

For SAML apps, the article names the cause as the `AssertionConsumerServiceURL` in the request not matching the Reply URL configured on the app.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Almost always not. The common causes are small differences between what the app sends and what is registered:

- `http://` vs `https://`
- a trailing slash, or a different path or port
- a new environment (staging, a new hostname) that was never added to the app registration
- a SAML app whose service provider sends a different ACS URL than the one configured

The security point is the control behind the error. Entra ID only sends an authorization code or token to a redirect URI the app owner registered. **If that check were loose, an attacker could send a victim a sign-in link with their own server as the redirect and collect the code or token.** 50011 is that check refusing.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Errors right after a deployment or hostname change | Missing reply URL. Benign. |
| One app, one wrong URI, many users | App misconfiguration. Benign, but users are blocked. |
| One app, **many different** redirect URIs, from one IP or a few users | Someone testing which redirect values the app accepts. Investigate. |
| 50011 for an app ID you don't recognise | Check whether the app is yours at all. See also 700016. |

The probing pattern is **our reasoning** about how an attacker would look for a lax reply URL. Microsoft's troubleshooting article doesn't discuss security implications.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
50011 per app per day, to spot misconfigurations after changes:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == "50011"
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Attempts = count(),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc, Attempts desc
```

Few sources, many attempts against one app:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50011"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            Apps = dcount(AppId),
            AppNames = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
            Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 5),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5)
          by IPAddress
| sort by Attempts desc
```

The sign-in logs don't record the redirect URI that was sent, as far as the documented `SigninLogs` columns show. To see the exact value, use the error page or the request itself (browser developer tools, or the app's own logs). Volume and source are what you can hunt on in the logs.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 50011 is not a Conditional Access result. The request fails on application configuration before a token can be issued.
- Conditional Access doesn't protect against a lax reply URL. If an app registration accepts a redirect URI you don't control, a user who completes sign-in, MFA and device checks still sends the code to that URI. Review the registered reply URLs as part of app hygiene.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50011?
sections.text:
**For the user:** this isn't something you can fix. Report the app name and the time to IT or the app owner.

**For developers and admins:**
1. Read the redirect URI from the failing request and compare it character for character with the app registration (**Authentication** for OIDC/OAuth apps, **Basic SAML configuration** > Reply URL for SAML apps).
2. Add the exact URI the app uses. Don't add a broad or wildcard pattern to make the error go away.
3. Remove reply URLs for environments that no longer exist. A registered URI on a domain you let expire can be taken over and used to receive codes (reasoning, not a Microsoft statement).

sections.heading: Practice the attack side
sections.text: The [Close enough lab](https://brambrinkmeier.com/labs/redirect-prefix/) is a local exercise where a redirect URI check that only compares the start of the string leaks an authorization code.

50013.name: InvalidAssertion
50013.title: AADSTS50013 fix: invalid assertion in on-behalf-of flow
50013.description: AADSTS50013: Entra rejected the token passed as an OBO assertion. A reported cause: the API got a Graph token, not its own. Fix the audience; KQL included.
50013.summary: AADSTS50013 means Entra rejected an assertion, usually the user's access token that a middle-tier API tried to exchange in the on-behalf-of (OBO) flow. Microsoft lists issuer mismatch, expiry and malformed tokens as causes. One reported cause is an API that was handed a token meant for Microsoft Graph instead of for itself. Low attack value; fix the token the API receives.
50013.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidAssertion**: Assertion is invalid because of various reasons - The token issuer doesn't match the API version within its valid time range -expired -malformed - Refresh token in the assertion isn't a primary refresh token. Contact the app developer.

An *assertion* is a token that an app hands to Entra ID as proof of something, and Entra ID refused it. The error comes back as `invalid_grant`, which Microsoft describes as *"some of the authentication material (auth code, refresh token, access token, PKCE challenge) was invalid, unparseable, missing, or otherwise unusable"*.

Most user reports of 50013 come from the **on-behalf-of (OBO) flow**. A client calls your API with an access token. Your API sends that token to Entra ID in the `assertion` parameter and asks for a new token to call another API, often Microsoft Graph. Microsoft's OBO reference sets the rule for that token: *"This token must have an audience (`aud`) claim of the app making this OBO request (the app denoted by the `client-id` field). Applications can't redeem a token for a different app (for example, if a client sends an API a token meant for Microsoft Graph, the API can't redeem it using OBO. It should instead reject the token."*

The message usually carries a reason in brackets. The ones users post:

- *"Assertion failed signature validation. [Reason - Key was found, but use of the key to verify the signature failed.]"*
- *"Assertion failed signature validation. [Reason - The key was not found.]"*

Microsoft doesn't map these reasons to causes. See the table below for what users found.

Don't confuse it with [700024](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700024/). That code is about the **client assertion**, the signed JWT an app uses to prove its own identity. 50013 is about the assertion being exchanged, in OBO the user's token.

sections.text:

> **InvalidAssertion**: Assertion is invalid because of various reasons - The token issuer doesn't match the API version within its valid time range -expired -malformed - Refresh token in the assertion isn't a primary refresh token. Contact the app developer.

Your API sends that token to Entra ID in the `assertion` parameter and asks for a new token to call another API, often Microsoft Graph. Microsoft's OBO reference sets the rule for that token: *"This token must have an audience (`aud`) claim of the app making this OBO request (the app denoted by the `client-id` field). Applications can't redeem a token for a different app (for example, if a client sends an API a token meant for Microsoft Graph, the API can't redeem it using OBO. It should instead reject the token."*

The message usually carries a reason in brackets. The ones users post:

- *"Assertion failed signature validation. [Reason - Key was found, but use of the key to verify the signature failed.]"*
- *"Assertion failed signature validation. [Reason - The key was not found.]"*

Microsoft doesn't map these reasons to causes. See the table below for what users found.

Don't confuse it with [700024](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700024/). That code is about the **client assertion**, the signed JWT an app uses to prove its own identity. 50013 is about the assertion being exchanged, in OBO the user's token.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. It is a developer error in how the app passes tokens around. Microsoft's own text ends with *"Contact the app developer."*

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| "Key was found, but use of the key to verify the signature failed", from a backend calling Graph via OBO | The client sent the API a **Microsoft Graph** token and the API tried to exchange it. In one Q&A thread the frontend requested Graph scopes and the backend passed that token on; the cause wasn't confirmed there. Microsoft says Graph tokens have a *"proprietary format"* and can't be validated like other tokens; our reading is that this is why the signature check fails. |
| "The key was not found", and the token's `kid` only appears in metadata fetched with `?appid=` | The middle-tier app has a **custom signing key**. A user reports exactly this. Microsoft: *"applications with custom signing keys can't be used as middle-tier APIs in the OBO flow. This includes enterprise applications configured for single sign-on."* |
| 50013 that mentions expiry | The client passed an expired access token. Get a fresh one before calling the API. |
| 50013 for one app, starting right after a release | The new version changed which scope the client requests. |
| 50013 from an unfamiliar IP for an app you own, with no successes | Someone is sending tokens your app didn't issue to the token endpoint. Our interpretation: a forged or tampered token would also fail signature validation and land here. Not documented by Microsoft, but worth a look. |

A token with a bad signature gets nothing from Entra ID, so the failure itself grants no access.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table an OBO failure lands in. OBO is a sign-in *"performed by a client app or OS components on behalf of a user"*, which fits the non-interactive log, but we haven't checked. Look in all three:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50013"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which app fails, for which downstream API, and with which reason. We assume `ResultDescription` carries the bracketed reason; Microsoft documents it only as *"the error message or the reason for failure"*:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50013"
| extend Reason = extract(@"Reason - ([^\]]+)", 1, ResultDescription)
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, Reason
| sort by Rows desc
```

50013 for apps that had no successful sign-in in the last 14 days. A starting point for spotting tokens sent to an app from somewhere it doesn't normally run; tune the window to your tenant:

```kusto
let failing =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50013"
    | summarize Fails = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10) by AppId, AppDisplayName;
let working =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct AppId;
failing
| join kind=leftanti working on AppId
| sort by Fails desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"50013"`, not `50013`. Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource match, so row counts there are not request counts.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50013?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report the error, with the time and the Correlation ID, to whoever runs the app.

**For developers:**
1. Decode the token you pass as `assertion` (Microsoft names [jwt.ms](https://jwt.ms) for debugging only). Its `aud` must be **your API's** client ID or App ID URI. If it points at Microsoft Graph (`https://graph.microsoft.com`), the client asked for the wrong token.
2. Expose a scope on your API (App registrations > your API > **Expose an API**) and have the client request that scope, for example `api://<api-client-id>/access_as_user`. The accepted Q&A answer gives these steps; the scope name is your choice.
3. If your API receives a token whose audience is Microsoft Graph rather than your API, reject it. Microsoft's OBO reference says exactly that: the API *"should instead reject the token"*. The fix is on the client side: have it request a token for your API's own scope.
4. Check the middle-tier app has no custom signing key (claims mapping, or an enterprise app configured for SAML SSO). Microsoft says those apps can't be OBO middle tiers. Use a separate app registration for the API.
5. Send a fresh, unexpired access token. Don't cache and replay an old one.
6. Set `requested_token_use` to `on_behalf_of`, as Microsoft requires.

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and the reason, and send both to the app's owner.
2. If an enterprise app with SAML SSO is also used as an API, that is the custom-signing-key case above. The fix is a separate app registration, not a setting.

50020.name: UserUnauthorized
50020.title: AADSTS50020: Account from identity provider not in tenant
50020.description: AADSTS50020: an account from another tenant or IdP isn't a user or guest in yours. Usually a B2B misconfig; can expose orphaned guests. With KQL.
50020.summary: AADSTS50020 means an account from another identity provider or tenant tried to sign in to an app in your tenant, and that account isn't a user or guest there. It is usually a B2B or app misconfiguration: wrong tenant, uninvited guest, single-tenant app. Repeated hits can also reveal orphaned guest accounts that need cleanup.
50020.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserUnauthorized**: Users are unauthorized to call this endpoint. User account '{email}' from identity provider '{idp}' does not exist in tenant '{tenant}' and cannot access the application '{appid}'({appName}) in that tenant. This account needs to be added as an external user in the tenant first. Sign out and sign in again with a different Microsoft Entra user account. If this user should be a member of the tenant, they should be invited via the B2B system.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS50020 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserUnauthorized**: Users are unauthorized to call this endpoint. User account '{email}' from identity provider '{idp}' does not exist in tenant '{tenant}' and cannot access the application '{appid}'({appName}) in that tenant. This account needs to be added as an external user in the tenant first. Sign out and sign in again with a different Microsoft Entra user account. If this user should be a member of the tenant, they should be invited via the B2B system.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Microsoft's troubleshooting article lists these causes:

- A personal Microsoft account used to sign in to an admin portal.
- A single-tenant app (`signInAudience`) being used by accounts from another tenant.
- The app sends users to the wrong authority endpoint (`/common` versus a specific tenant).
- The user is signed in to the wrong tenant in the browser.
- The external user was never invited as a guest.
- The app requires assignment.
- ROPC (username/password flow) used with personal accounts.
- The user was deleted and re-created in their home tenant, which leaves the old guest object in your tenant **orphaned**.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A partner user, first time on an app | Not invited yet, or wrong tenant in the link. Benign. |
| A known guest who used to work, now fails | **Orphaned guest.** Their home account was re-created. Lifecycle cleanup, not an attack. |
| Your own staff on a partner's app | Wrong authority or single-tenant app on the partner side. Benign. |
| Many different external identities you never invited, against one or several of your apps | Someone checking which of your apps accept outside accounts. Investigate. |

The last row is **our reasoning**, not a Microsoft statement. Microsoft documents 50020 as a configuration error. The orphaned-guest case is the more useful finding for most tenants: it shows guest objects whose real-world identity no longer matches.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which external identities hit 50020, against which apps:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == "50020"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            HomeTenants = make_set(HomeTenantId, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by UserPrincipalName
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Possible probing: one IP, many distinct external identities:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50020"
| summarize Identities = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
            Attempts = count()
          by IPAddress
| where Identities >= 5
| sort by Identities desc
```

The `UserPrincipalName` on a 50020 row is the identity that tried to sign in, which by definition isn't a user in your tenant. Check one row in your workspace to see how it is filled before you rely on it; the email in the error message may be hidden or differ. The threshold of 5 is a starting point, not a tested value.

To find orphaned guests, compare the identities above with your guest list. A guest whose email matches a 50020 identity existed in your tenant but no longer matches its home account.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 50020 is not a Conditional Access result. The account isn't in your tenant, so there is no user for your policies to evaluate.
- Once the external user is invited and redeems the invitation, your policies for guests and external users apply to them like any other sign-in. Have those guest policies in place before you invite.
- Cross-tenant access settings decide which outside organisations can collaborate at all. They are the place to limit B2B access, not exclusions in individual apps.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50020?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign out, then sign in again with the account your organisation gave you. If you are a partner, ask your contact to invite you as a guest.

**For admins and developers:**
1. Check the tenant and app in the error. If the user should have access, invite them via B2B.
2. For an orphaned guest (home account re-created), reset the guest's redemption status. Microsoft's article: *"Reset the redemption status of the guest user account in the resource tenant. Then, you can keep the guest user object without having to delete and then re-create the guest account."*
3. For your own app: check `signInAudience` and the authority URL. A multi-tenant app shouldn't send users to a single tenant's endpoint, and a single-tenant app shouldn't be offered to outside users.
4. Review guest accounts on a schedule. Orphaned guests are inactive objects with access rights that nobody uses.

sections.heading: Practice the attack side
sections.text: The [Whose email is it? lab](https://brambrinkmeier.com/labs/tenant-trust/) is a local exercise where a multi-tenant app trusts a token from any tenant and looks users up by email.

50027.name: InvalidJwtToken
50027.title: AADSTS50027: JWT token is invalid or malformed (fix)
50027.description: AADSTS50027: Entra rejected a JWT as invalid or malformed. Client assertions and federated ID tokens are the usual sources. Fix and KQL.
50027.summary: AADSTS50027 means Microsoft Entra ID received a JWT it would not accept: wrong format, missing or duplicated claims, unexpected issuer or audience, outside its valid time range, or a failed signature check on an external ID token. It is usually a developer error. The two common sources are a hand-built client assertion and a federated identity provider's ID token.
50027.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidJwtToken**: Invalid JWT token because of the following reasons:
> - doesn't contain nonce claim, sub claim
> - subject identifier mismatch
> - duplicate claim in idToken claims
> - unexpected issuer
> - unexpected audience
> - not within its valid time range
> - token format isn't proper
> - External ID token from issuer failed signature verification.

That is eight different conditions behind one code, which is why the fix depends entirely on which JWT Entra was looking at. Two kinds of request put a JWT in front of Entra:

- **A client assertion.** An app authenticating with a certificate or a federated credential sends `client_assertion` instead of a secret. Our lab hit 50027 this way.
- **An external ID token.** A federated identity provider returns an ID token to Entra, which validates it. The last bullet in Microsoft's list, *"External ID token from issuer failed signature verification"*, is this case, and so are the `nonce`, `sub` and duplicate-claim bullets, which name `idToken` explicitly.

For the client assertion case, Microsoft's certificate credentials page documents what the JWT must contain. The header:

| Parameter | Microsoft's remark |
|---|---|
| `alg` | Should be **PS256** |
| `typ` | Should be **JWT** |
| `x5t#S256` | Base64url-encoded SHA-256 thumbprint of the X.509 certificate's DER encoding. |

And the claims: `aud` (`https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenantId}/oauth2/v2.0/token`), `iss` and `sub` (both the client ID), `jti`, `nbf`, `exp` and `iat`. On the lifetime, Microsoft says to *"keep it short - 5-10 minutes after `nbf` at most"*. The signature *"is computed by applying the certificate as described in the JSON Web Token RFC7519 specification"*, using PSS padding.

Several of Microsoft's eight bullets map onto that table: `aud` wrong is "unexpected audience", `iss` wrong is "unexpected issuer", and an `exp` in the past is "not within its valid time range".

### Which assertion error you get, and in what order
Our lab separated three of the assertion failures. Entra checks them in this order:

| What is wrong | Code |
|---|---|
| `client_assertion_type` is not the JWT bearer URN | [90023](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90023/) *"Unexpected client assertion type."* |
| The assertion is not a well-formed JWT | **50027** |
| The assertion is a JWT but its validity window has passed or not begun | [700024](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700024/) |
| Nothing was sent at all on a `client_credentials` request | [7000216](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000216/) |

Microsoft's reference also lists **AADSTS700027**, *"Client assertion failed signature validation"*, for a well-formed JWT with a bad signature. So 50027 sits between "wrong kind of parameter" and "right shape, wrong signature": the string reached the JWT parser and the parser rejected it.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a client-credentials token request with the correct `client_assertion_type` and a `client_assertion` that was not a JWT. Entra returned:

> AADSTS50027: JWT token is invalid or malformed.

Both rounds of the run returned the same code and the same one-line message, short enough that the lab's 160-character cut does not truncate it. The run had expected 9002313, 50027 or 700027, and 50027 is the one it got. In the same run, the same request with an unaccepted `client_assertion_type` returned [90023](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90023/), and a syntactically valid assertion whose validity window had passed returned [700024](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700024/) with the current time and the assertion's `nbf` in the message. So the lab confirms the format case specifically, and not the other seven conditions in Microsoft's list.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not, and this is the one code on this page's family where the answer deserves a second look. A malformed JWT is what a developer produces; it is also what someone replaying or editing a captured token produces.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Repeated 50027 for one app from your own build agents or servers | A client assertion implementation under development, or a certificate rotation that went wrong. Benign. |
| 50027 on an app that has worked for months, with no deployment | Look at the certificate. An expired or replaced certificate usually gives a different code, but a half-finished rotation can produce assertions nobody can parse. |
| 50027 for one app from an address you don't own | Someone is sending assertions for your app ID. They do not have a working credential, or you would see a success instead. Check for successes from the same address. |
| 50027 on user sign-ins through a federated identity provider | The identity provider's ID token is being rejected. Check the issuer, the audience and the signing key on the provider, and whether a certificate was rolled. |
| A burst across several apps from one address | Someone is probing with crafted tokens. Nothing is disclosed by this error, but the source is worth a look. |

Our reading on the signal: 50027 means a token was refused, so it is evidence of a failure rather than of a compromise. What makes it worth watching is a success from the same source shortly after.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which table 50027 lands in depends on which JWT failed, and Microsoft doesn't document it for either case. Our reading: a client assertion is an app signing in, so `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`; a federated user's ID token is a user sign-in, so `SigninLogs` or `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`. Start with the union:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50027" or ResultSignature == "50027"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Apps = make_set(AppId, 10)
          by SourceTable
```

The filter covers both columns because the tables describe them differently: in `SigninLogs`, `ResultType` *"provides the 5-6 digit error code that's generated during a sign-in event"*, while `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` describes `ResultType` as *"Success or Failure"* and `ResultSignature` as *"the error code, if any, for the sign-in operation"*.

For the client assertion case, which app and which source:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50027" or ResultSignature == "50027"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            CredentialTypes = make_set(ClientCredentialType, 5),
            Thumbprints = make_set(ServicePrincipalCredentialThumbprint, 5),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 5)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Failures desc
```

`ClientCredentialType` is documented as *"the type of client credential used. Examples include client assertion, client secret, etc."* Whether it and the thumbprint column are filled in when the JWT could not be parsed is not documented: a token Entra cannot read may not identify a credential at all. Check a row before you rely on either column.

The pattern worth alerting on is a refusal followed by a success from the same place:

```kusto
let failedFrom =
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == "50027" or ResultSignature == "50027"
    | summarize FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated) by AppId, IPAddress;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "0" or ResultType =~ "Success"
| join kind=inner failedFrom on AppId, IPAddress
| where TimeGenerated > FirstFail
| project TimeGenerated, AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress, ClientCredentialType, FirstFail
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

Thresholds are a starting point only: for a developer's own address, dozens an hour mean nothing; for an address with no history for that app, one row is enough to look at.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text: Not relevant to the client assertion case: there is no user and no policy evaluation, and the request fails on the credential. For the federated user case, 50027 happens while Entra is validating the incoming token, which is before the point where Conditional Access decides anything. Our reading, by analogy with other first-factor failures; Microsoft doesn't state it for this code.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50027?
sections.text:
**For developers sending a client assertion:**
1. Decode what you are sending. If it isn't three base64url segments separated by dots, it is not a JWT and nothing else matters.
2. Build the header with `alg` PS256, `typ` JWT and `x5t#S256` set to the certificate's SHA-256 thumbprint, and the claims `aud`, `iss`, `sub`, `jti`, `nbf`, `exp` and `iat` as Microsoft's certificate credentials page specifies. `iss` and `sub` are both the client ID.
3. Keep the lifetime short, 5 to 10 minutes after `nbf`. If the window has passed you get [700024](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700024/) rather than 50027.
4. Sign with the private key of a certificate registered on the app registration, using PSS padding.
5. Let a library do it. MSAL builds the assertion from a certificate for you, and most 50027 in this case comes from hand-rolled code.
6. Send it with `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`, or you get [90023](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90023/) first.

**For admins of a federated identity provider:**
1. Work out which of Microsoft's eight conditions applies before changing anything. The `nonce`, `sub`, duplicate-claim and signature-verification bullets are all about an external ID token.
2. Check the issuer and audience values configured on both sides, and that the provider's current signing key is the one Entra is reading. A key rollover on the provider gives *"External ID token from issuer failed signature verification"*.
3. Check clock skew. *"Not within its valid time range"* is a time problem on the provider, not in Entra.

**For admins generally:**
1. Use the queries above to identify the app and its owner, and whether any source that failed also succeeded.
2. If an address with no history for the app is sending assertions, treat the app ID as known to someone outside and review the app's permissions.

50027.kqlSectionText:
Which table 50027 lands in depends on which JWT failed, and Microsoft doesn't document it for either case. Our reading: a client assertion is an app signing in, so `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`; a federated user's ID token is a user sign-in, so `SigninLogs` or `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`. Start with the union:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50027" or ResultSignature == "50027"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Apps = make_set(AppId, 10)
          by SourceTable
```

The filter covers both columns because the tables describe them differently: in `SigninLogs`, `ResultType` *"provides the 5-6 digit error code that's generated during a sign-in event"*, while `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` describes `ResultType` as *"Success or Failure"* and `ResultSignature` as *"the error code, if any, for the sign-in operation"*.

For the client assertion case, which app and which source:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50027" or ResultSignature == "50027"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            CredentialTypes = make_set(ClientCredentialType, 5),
            Thumbprints = make_set(ServicePrincipalCredentialThumbprint, 5),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 5)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Failures desc
```

`ClientCredentialType` is documented as *"the type of client credential used. Examples include client assertion, client secret, etc."* Whether it and the thumbprint column are filled in when the JWT could not be parsed is not documented: a token Entra cannot read may not identify a credential at all. Check a row before you rely on either column.

The pattern worth alerting on is a refusal followed by a success from the same place:

```kusto
let failedFrom =
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == "50027" or ResultSignature == "50027"
    | summarize FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated) by AppId, IPAddress;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "0" or ResultType =~ "Success"
| join kind=inner failedFrom on AppId, IPAddress
| where TimeGenerated > FirstFail
| project TimeGenerated, AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress, ClientCredentialType, FirstFail
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

Thresholds are a starting point only: for a developer's own address, dozens an hour mean nothing; for an address with no history for that app, one row is enough to look at.

fix.short: Developer sending a client assertion: build a real JWT with the header and claims Microsoft documents, signed with the certificate registered on the app. Federation admin: fix the issuer, audience or signing key on the identity provider.
fix.steps:
**For developers sending a client assertion:**
1. Decode what you are sending. If it isn't three base64url segments separated by dots, it is not a JWT and nothing else matters.
2. Build the header with `alg` PS256, `typ` JWT and `x5t#S256` set to the certificate's SHA-256 thumbprint, and the claims `aud`, `iss`, `sub`, `jti`, `nbf`, `exp` and `iat` as Microsoft's certificate credentials page specifies. `iss` and `sub` are both the client ID.
3. Keep the lifetime short, 5 to 10 minutes after `nbf`. If the window has passed you get [700024](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700024/) rather than 50027.
4. Sign with the private key of a certificate registered on the app registration, using PSS padding.
5. Let a library do it. MSAL builds the assertion from a certificate for you, and most 50027 in this case comes from hand-rolled code.
6. Send it with `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`, or you get [90023](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90023/) first.

**For admins of a federated identity provider:**
1. Work out which of Microsoft's eight conditions applies before changing anything. The `nonce`, `sub`, duplicate-claim and signature-verification bullets are all about an external ID token.
2. Check the issuer and audience values configured on both sides, and that the provider's current signing key is the one Entra is reading. A key rollover on the provider gives *"External ID token from issuer failed signature verification"*.
3. Check clock skew. *"Not within its valid time range"* is a time problem on the provider, not in Entra.

**For admins generally:**
1. Use the queries above to identify the app and its owner, and whether any source that failed also succeeded.
2. If an address with no history for the app is sending assertions, treat the app ID as known to someone outside and review the app's permissions.

50027.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a client-credentials token request with the correct `client_assertion_type` and a `client_assertion` that was not a JWT. Entra returned:

> AADSTS50027: JWT token is invalid or malformed.

Both rounds of the run returned the same code and the same one-line message, short enough that the lab's 160-character cut does not truncate it. The run had expected 9002313, 50027 or 700027, and 50027 is the one it got. In the same run, the same request with an unaccepted `client_assertion_type` returned [90023](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90023/), and a syntactically valid assertion whose validity window had passed returned [700024](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700024/) with the current time and the assertion's `nbf` in the message. So the lab confirms the format case specifically, and not the other seven conditions in Microsoft's list.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

50034.name: UserAccountNotFound
50034.title: AADSTS50034 fix: user account not found in the tenant
50034.description: AADSTS50034 means the username does not exist in that Entra tenant. Typo, wrong tenant or guest access, plus KQL for enumeration bursts.
50034.summary: AADSTS50034 means the username doesn't exist in the Microsoft Entra tenant the sign-in went to. Usually it's a typo or the wrong tenant. The security signal is volume from one source: many different non-existent usernames from one IP suggests an attacker testing a guessed or leaked user list. Hunt it with ResultType == "50034".
50034.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserAccountNotFound**: To sign into this application, the account must be added to the directory. This error can occur because the user mis-typed their username, or isn't in the tenant. An application might have chosen the wrong tenant to sign into, and the currently logged in user was prevented from doing so since they did not exist in your tenant. If this user should be able to log in, add them as a guest.

No account with that name exists in the tenant that received the request. No password check happened against a real account.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS50034 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserAccountNotFound**: To sign into this application, the account must be added to the directory. This error can occur because the user mis-typed their username, or isn't in the tenant. An application might have chosen the wrong tenant to sign into, and the currently logged in user was prevented from doing so since they did not exist in your tenant. If this user should be able to log in, add them as a guest.

No account with that name exists in the tenant that received the request. No password check happened against a real account.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request for a user name that doesn't exist in my lab tenant. Entra returned `AADSTS50034` with this first line:

> AADSTS50034: The user account {EUII Hidden} does not exist in the {tenant-id} directory.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint. The sign-in log row and the KQL on this page are not checked against it yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description lists three benign causes: a typo, a user who isn't in the tenant, and an app that picked the wrong tenant. Those explain most rows. The pattern decides:

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One attempt, then a success with the corrected name from the same IP | A typo. Benign. |
| A user from a partner organisation, hitting one specific app | Wrong tenant or a missing guest invitation. Benign. Add them as a guest if they need access. |
| A former employee's name, or a renamed user's old name | Something still uses the old username. Find and update it. |
| Many **different** non-existent names from one IP | Likely an attacker testing a user list (interpretation, not checked against real data): guessed `firstname.lastname` formats or a leaked list (T1087.004). |
| 50034 mixed with 50126 and 50057 from the same IP | A password spray using a list that contains real, disabled and non-existent names (T1110.003). |

Conditional Access does not apply here. There is no user for a policy to match, and CA only runs after the first factor succeeds. Expect `ConditionalAccessStatus` = `notApplied`.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
One IP trying many non-existent usernames:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50034"
| summarize UnknownNames = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Attempts = count(),
            Sample = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 20),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
            Clients = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 5)
          by IPAddress
| where UnknownNames >= 10
| sort by UnknownNames desc
```

The same IPs, across all credential failures: how many real accounts were also hit, and did anything get through?

```kusto
let enumIPs =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50034"
    | summarize UnknownNames = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where UnknownNames >= 10
    | project IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where IPAddress in (enumIPs)
| summarize Attempts = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress, ResultType, ResultDescription
| sort by IPAddress asc, Attempts desc
```

Any `ResultType` of `"0"`, `"50076"`, `"50074"` or `"53003"` in the second result means a password was correct for at least one account. Pivot on that IP and user.

For a non-existent account, check which column holds the name that was typed. It is probably `UserPrincipalName` (an assumption, not yet checked against real data). `SignInIdentifier` is documented as *"populated when a user signs in using other identifiers"*, so look there as well.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- Conditional Access and MFA play no part in a 50034. The request fails before either is evaluated.
- The sign-in itself gives the attacker little, but the different answers do. A non-existent name returns 50034 and a real name with a wrong password returns 50126, so in practice the error alone can tell an attacker which names are real. The risk is the **next step**: the confirmed names get sprayed. Watch the same IPs for 50126 and 50053.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50034?
sections.text:
**For the user:** check the spelling of your username and that you are signing in with your work account. If you are from another organisation, ask the app owner to invite you as a guest.

**For admins:**
1. Single user: check for a typo, a renamed UPN, or an app pointing at the wrong tenant.
2. External user who needs access: add them as a guest (B2B), as Microsoft's description says.
3. Enumeration pattern: you can't block it at the Entra ID layer, because Conditional Access never evaluates a request for a user that doesn't exist. Put the IP on a watchlist or threat-intel feed instead, and watch for follow-up 50126/50053 from the same range. If the names come in a predictable format, that is a hint your UPN convention is public.
4. Make sure every **real** account has MFA, so a list of valid names plus a sprayed password isn't enough.

50052.name: InvalidPasswordExceedsMaxLength
50052.title: AADSTS50052: Password exceeds the maximum length (fix)
50052.description: AADSTS50052: the password is longer than Entra's 256-character limit. Not in Microsoft's error list. What it means, KQL and the fix.
50052.summary: AADSTS50052 means the password sent was longer than Entra's limit of 256 characters. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it, but a Microsoft change notice from 2020 names it InvalidPasswordExceedsMaxLength. Usually a user with an old over-long password, or a tool that sends garbage. Low attack value. Reset the password to 256 characters or fewer.
50052.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS50052 (checked 30 October 2026).

The lab reproduced it. A password-grant token request with a 300-character password returned:

> AADSTS50052: The password entered exceeds the maximum length. Please reach out to your admin to reset the password.

Microsoft documents the code on another page. Its "What's new for authentication?" page has a March 2020 entry, **"User passwords will be restricted to 256 characters"**, effective 13 March 2020, for all endpoints and all user flows:

> Users with passwords longer than 256 characters who sign in directly to Microsoft Entra ID (not a federated IDP, like AD FS) will be asked to change their passwords before they can sign in. Admins may receive requests to help reset the user's password.
>
> The error in the sign-in logs will be similar to *AADSTS 50052: InvalidPasswordExceedsMaxLength*.

That page gives the message as *"The password entered exceeds the maximum length of 256. Please reach out to your admin to reset the password."* The lab got the same text without "of 256".

The limit itself is in Microsoft's password policy: *"A minimum of 8 characters and a maximum of 256 characters."*

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a password-grant (ROPC) token request for a test user in my lab tenant, with a 300-character password. Entra returned `AADSTS50052` with the first line quoted above.

That confirms the code and the current wording at the token endpoint. Our reading: Entra checks the length before it checks the password. The current policy caps passwords at 256 characters, so a 300-character password can't match one set under it. It could only be wrong, yet the answer was the length error and not [AADSTS50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/). We did not test whether a user that doesn't exist gets 50052 too. It lands in **`SigninLogs`**: Status Failure, Conditional Access Not Applied. Entra's explanation on the row reads: *"The user is unable to login because their password exceeds the permitted maximum length. They should contact their admin to reset the password. If SSPR is enabled for their tenant, they can reset their password by following the "Forgot your password" link."* The KQL below was run on these rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). The first two queries found the row. The third returned nothing as written, as expected for one attempt; with its threshold lowered to 1 it found it.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. A real person rarely types 257 characters.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One user, repeated, from their usual devices | A password set before the March 2020 limit, or a sign-in tool or password manager that sends too much. The user needs a reset. |
| One app or service account, every attempt | A script or config sending the wrong value as the password, such as a token, a certificate or a whole file. |
| Many users from one IP, mixed with 50126 | A spray or stuffing tool sending broken or over-long entries from a bad list. Look at the 50126 rows; those are the real attempts. |

The meanings in this table are our reading. Microsoft doesn't describe these patterns. A 50052 is a failed sign-in. No token is issued.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft's 2020 notice says the error shows in the sign-in logs, but doesn't say which table. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50052"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Who hits it, from where, with which app:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50052"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
            Clients = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 5)
          by UserPrincipalName
| sort by Attempts desc
```

IPs that produce 50052 for several users, with their other credential failures next to it. The threshold of 3 users is a starting point:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType in ("50052", "50126", "50034")
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            TooLong = countif(ResultType == "50052"),
            WrongPassword = countif(ResultType == "50126"),
            UnknownUser = countif(ResultType == "50034")
          by IPAddress
| where TooLong > 0 and Users >= 3
| sort by Users desc
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50052?
sections.text:
**For the user:** your password is longer than the 256 characters Entra allows. Ask your admin to reset it, or use "Forgot your password" if your organisation allows self-service reset. Microsoft's notice says: *"If SSPR is enabled for their tenant, they can reset their password by following the "Forgot your password" link."* Pick a new password of 256 characters or fewer.

**For developers:** check what your code sends in the `password` field. If it is longer than 256 characters, it is almost certainly not the password. Probably a secret, token or file read into the wrong variable, though we haven't confirmed that.

**For admins:**
1. Find the user with the queries above.
2. Reset the password to one of 256 characters or fewer. Microsoft's policy allows 8 to 256 characters.
3. If it is a service account used by a script, fix what the script sends, then look at why it uses a password grant at all.

50053.name: IdsLocked
50053.title: AADSTS50053: Account locked or sign-in blocked
50053.description: AADSTS50053: smart lockout locked the account or a risky sign-in was blocked. A burst across many accounts usually means a spray. KQL included.
50053.summary: AADSTS50053 covers two different blocks. Smart lockout locked the account after too many wrong passwords, or Microsoft's built-in protections blocked a high-confidence risky sign-in regardless of the password. The failure reason tells them apart. A burst across many accounts usually means a password spray tripped lockout.
50053.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> This error can result from two different reasons: **IdsLocked** - The account is locked because the user tried to sign in too many times with an incorrect user ID or password. The user is blocked due to repeated sign-in attempts. See Remediate risks and unblock users. Or, sign-in was blocked because it came from an IP address with malicious activity. To determine which failure reason caused this error, sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center … Navigate to … Monitoring & health > Sign-in logs. Find the failed user sign-in with Sign-in error code 50053 and check the Failure reason.

One code, two mechanisms. Read the failure reason before you decide what happened. For the full spray investigation, see [How to detect password spraying in Entra ID](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/detect-password-spray-entra-id/).

**1. Smart lockout.** Too many wrong passwords. Microsoft's smart lockout page:

> By default, smart lockout locks an account from sign-in after: 10 failed attempts in Azure Public and Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet tenants; Three failed attempts for Azure US Government tenants. The account locks again after each subsequent failed sign-in attempt. The lockout period is one minute at first, and longer in subsequent attempts.

Microsoft also says smart lockout *"uses familiar location versus unfamiliar location to differentiate between a bad actor and the genuine user. Both unfamiliar and familiar locations have separate lockout counters."*

**2. Built-in protection block.** The same smart lockout page says Entra ID *"blocks these malicious sign-ins by default and returns AADSTS50053 - IdsLocked error code, regardless of the password validity."* The ID Protection documentation adds:

> Microsoft Entra ID Protection automatically blocks sign-ins that have a very high confidence of being risky. This block most commonly occurs on sign-ins performed using legacy authentication protocols or displaying properties of a malicious attempt. When a user is blocked for either scenario, they receive a 50053 authentication error. The sign-in logs display the following block reason: 'Sign-in was blocked by built-in protections due to high confidence of risk.'

The important phrase is **"regardless of the password validity"**. A 50053 of this kind does not tell you whether the password was right or wrong.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent wrong passwords for one test user, two seconds apart, until Entra stopped accepting them. The eleventh attempt returned `AADSTS50053`:

> AADSTS50053: The account is locked, you've tried to sign in too many times with an incorrect user ID or password.

The run sent up to fifteen attempts and stopped at the first 50053, so the exact lockout threshold isn't recorded here; the earlier attempts returned [50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/). That ordering is the useful part: a spray that stops below the threshold leaves only 50126 rows behind, and 50053 appears only once an account crosses it. The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

In the lab tenant's sign-in logs the 50053 appears under **User sign-ins (interactive)**, Status **Failure**, Conditional Access **Not Applied**, authentication requirement single-factor. The run order is visible in the log and is the useful part: in two separate runs, eleven and thirteen [50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/) rows for the same user and IP appear immediately before the 50053. So the lockout row is the end of a visible run of wrong-password rows, not an isolated event. Microsoft documents the smart lockout threshold as ten failed attempts by default; the counts seen here are the rows the portal showed, which is close to that but not an exact measurement of the threshold.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One user, preceded by a handful of 50126 from their usual IP and device | The user forgot or mistyped the password and tripped smart lockout. Benign. |
| Failure reason "Sign-in was blocked by built-in protections due to high confidence of risk" | Microsoft judged the sign-in malicious. Look at the IP and `ClientAppUsed`. Legacy protocols are the common case. |
| Many **different users** hitting 50053 from one IP or range, after a run of 50126 | A **password spray** (T1110.003) that tripped lockout. |
| Many 50053 against **one user** from unfamiliar IPs | Brute force against that account (T1110.001). |
| 50053 on legacy clients (SMTP, IMAP, POP) for a service account or old device | Often a device or script with a stale password, or a legacy-auth spray. Check the IP. |
| A success, 50076/50074 or 53003 from the same IP for a targeted user | The attacker found a correct password at some point. Treat that account as compromised. |

Conditional Access does not run on a 50053. Microsoft's Conditional Access overview states: *"Conditional Access policies are enforced after first-factor authentication is completed."* So expect `ConditionalAccessStatus` = `notApplied` on these rows.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Split 50053 by mechanism. The built-in protection block is identified by its documented failure reason. Everything else under 50053 is most likely smart lockout (interpretation), but Microsoft does not publish the exact lockout wording, so check the `ResultDescription` values the query returns in your own workspace.

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50053"
| extend FailureReason = tostring(Status.failureReason)
| extend Mechanism = iff(ResultDescription has "built-in protections" or FailureReason has "built-in protections",
                         "Built-in protection block", "Smart lockout (likely)")
| summarize Events = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            Clients = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 5)
          by Mechanism, ResultDescription
| sort by Events desc
```

Spray that tripped lockout: one IP, many locked users, and did that IP ever get further than the password?

```kusto
let lockoutIPs =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50053"
    | summarize LockedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where LockedUsers >= 5
    | project IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where IPAddress in (lockoutIPs)
| where ResultType in ("0", "50076", "50074", "50079", "53003", "50055")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType, ResultDescription,
          ConditionalAccessStatus, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

`ResultType` is a string, so compare with `"50053"`. Legacy clients such as SMTP AUTH can produce 50053 too. If you allow legacy auth, run the first query against `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs` as well. There `Status` is a string, so use `tostring(parse_json(Status).failureReason)`.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- CA can't prevent a 50053. Both mechanisms act at the credential stage, before CA evaluates.
- Smart lockout is always on for every tenant. Changing the threshold or duration needs Entra ID P1.
- **Blocking legacy authentication** with CA removes the protocols where the built-in block most commonly fires, and those protocols can't do MFA.
- MFA does not stop the lockout itself. It decides what happens if the attacker ever gets the password right.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50053?
sections.text:
**For the user:**
- Smart lockout: wait for the lockout period to pass, or reset the password with self-service password reset. Don't keep retrying the old password. Each further failure locks the account again, and later lockouts last longer.
- Built-in block: sign in from a familiar location and a modern client (the browser, current Outlook), not an old mail app.

**For admins:**
1. Check the failure reason first. It decides everything else.
2. Smart lockout on one user: find the source of the bad passwords. A phone or script with an old password keeps re-locking the account. If the source is one of your own servers, rule out a compromise before you assume a stale config: [hunting credential reuse after a web-server breach](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/hunt-credential-reuse-after-web-server-breach/).
3. Built-in block: Microsoft's unblock options are to add the IP to trusted named locations (only if you really own it), or move the client to modern authentication.
4. Spray pattern: use the second query to find any targeted account that got past the password. Reset those passwords and revoke sessions.
5. Block legacy authentication with Conditional Access.

conditionalAccess.text:

- Smart lockout is always on for every tenant. Changing the threshold or duration needs Entra ID P1.
- **Blocking legacy authentication** with CA removes the protocols where the built-in block most commonly fires, and those protocols can't do MFA.
- MFA does not stop the lockout itself. It decides what happens if the attacker ever gets the password right.

kql.leadIn: Split 50053 by mechanism. The built-in protection block is identified by its documented failure reason. Everything else under 50053 is most likely smart lockout (interpretation), but Microsoft does not publish the exact lockout wording, so check the `ResultDescription` values the query returns in your own workspace.
kql.query:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50053"
| extend FailureReason = tostring(Status.failureReason)
| extend Mechanism = iff(ResultDescription has "built-in protections" or FailureReason has "built-in protections",
                         "Built-in protection block", "Smart lockout (likely)")
| summarize Events = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            Clients = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 5)
          by Mechanism, ResultDescription
| sort by Events desc

kql.leadIn: Spray that tripped lockout: one IP, many locked users, and did that IP ever get further than the password?
kql.query:
let lockoutIPs =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50053"
    | summarize LockedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where LockedUsers >= 5
    | project IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where IPAddress in (lockoutIPs)
| where ResultType in ("0", "50076", "50074", "50079", "53003", "50055")
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType, ResultDescription,
          ConditionalAccessStatus, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
