fix.short: User: wait for the lockout to pass or reset your password with self-service reset, and stop retrying the old one. Admin: check the failure reason first. Lockout: find the phone or script sending the old password. Built-in block: move the client to modern authentication.
fix.steps:
**For the user:**
- Smart lockout: wait for the lockout period to pass, or reset the password with self-service password reset. Don't keep retrying the old password. Each further failure locks the account again, and later lockouts last longer.
- Built-in block: sign in from a familiar location and a modern client (the browser, current Outlook), not an old mail app.

**For admins:**
1. Check the failure reason first. It decides everything else.
2. Smart lockout on one user: find the source of the bad passwords. A phone or script with an old password keeps re-locking the account. If the source is one of your own servers, rule out a compromise before you assume a stale config: [hunting credential reuse after a web-server breach](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/hunt-credential-reuse-after-web-server-breach/).
3. Built-in block: Microsoft's unblock options are to add the IP to trusted named locations (only if you really own it), or move the client to modern authentication.
4. Spray pattern: use the second query to find any targeted account that got past the password. Reset those passwords and revoke sessions.
5. Block legacy authentication with Conditional Access.

labReproduced.method: Repeated password-grant (ROPC) token requests against a lab tenant
labReproduced.scenario: Repeated wrong passwords (smart lockout)
labReproduced.message: AADSTS50053: The account is locked, you've tried to sign in too many times with an incorrect user ID or password.

50053.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent wrong passwords for one test user, two seconds apart, until Entra stopped accepting them. The eleventh attempt returned `AADSTS50053`:

> AADSTS50053: The account is locked, you've tried to sign in too many times with an incorrect user ID or password.

The run sent up to fifteen attempts and stopped at the first 50053, so the exact lockout threshold isn't recorded here; the earlier attempts returned [50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/). That ordering is the useful part: a spray that stops below the threshold leaves only 50126 rows behind, and 50053 appears only once an account crosses it. The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

In the lab tenant's sign-in logs the 50053 appears under **User sign-ins (interactive)**, Status **Failure**, Conditional Access **Not Applied**, authentication requirement single-factor. The run order is visible in the log and is the useful part: in two separate runs, eleven and thirteen [50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/) rows for the same user and IP appear immediately before the 50053. So the lockout row is the end of a visible run of wrong-password rows, not an isolated event. Microsoft documents the smart lockout threshold as ten failed attempts by default; the counts seen here are the rows the portal showed, which is close to that but not an exact measurement of the threshold.

50054.title: AADSTS50054: Old password used for sign-in (fix)
50054.description: AADSTS50054: a sign-in used an old password. Unlisted by Microsoft; seen on the Entra Connect Connector account. Fix with PowerShell, plus KQL.
50054.summary: AADSTS50054 means a sign-in used an old password. Microsoft doesn't list the code. Its Entra Connect docs show it for the Connector account, often with AADSTS70002, and fix it with Add-ADSyncAADServiceAccount. For a normal user, our reading is that someone or something still holds a former password; treat repeated rows from unknown IPs like failed passwords.
50054.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS50054 (checked 30 October 2026). It lists 50053 and 50055 but skips 50054.

Microsoft does quote it on another page. [Change the Microsoft Entra Connector account password](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-azureadaccount) lists it under *"errors reported by customers that were fixed by a credentials reset on the Microsoft Entra Connector account"*:

> Event 6900 The server encountered an unexpected error while processing a password change notification:
> AADSTS70002: Error validating credentials. AADSTS50054: Old password is used for authentication.

> Event 659 Error while retrieving password policy sync configuration. Microsoft.IdentityModel.Clients.ActiveDirectory.AdalServiceException: AADSTS70002: Error validating credentials. AADSTS50054: Old password is used for authentication.

The Connector account is the account Entra Connect Sync uses to talk to Entra ID. Microsoft calls it *"supposed to be service free"*. The page gives no cause beyond the message. Our reading: the sync server presented a password the account had before. The account's password changed in Entra ID, but the sync engine kept the old one.

Microsoft documents 50054 only for that account. Whether Entra returns 50054 or [50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/) when a normal user types a former password is not documented. We haven't tested it.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
For the Connector account, no. It is a sync configuration problem that Microsoft fixes with a reset.

For any other account, it may matter, though Microsoft doesn't say so. The message implies the password was right once, so a device, an app or a person likely still holds a password the user used before.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| The Connector account, from your Entra Connect server's IP | The sync engine has a stale password. Reset it as below. |
| A user, from their usual devices, soon after a password change | A phone, mail client or saved credential still uses the old password. |
| A user, from an IP or country they never use | Someone holds a former password, for example from an old leak. Investigate like a failed password from an unknown source. |
| Many accounts from one IP | A list of old passwords being tried. Treat it like a password spray. |

Only the first row comes from Microsoft's documentation. The other three are our reading.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 50054 is logged in. Check all three:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50054"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

Who, from where, and with which app. The Connector account should show your sync server's IP:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50054"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20)
    by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| sort by Rows desc
```

One IP with at least one 50054 row and failed passwords (50054 or 50126) for several accounts. The threshold of 3 is a starting point; tune it to your tenant:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType in ("50054", "50126")
| summarize Accounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName), OldPasswordRows = countif(ResultType == "50054"), Rows = count()
    by IPAddress
| where OldPasswordRows > 0 and Accounts >= 3
| sort by Accounts desc
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50054?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign in with your current password. Update it on every device and app that saved the old one, such as phone mail apps.

**For admins** (Entra Connect Connector account): Microsoft's fix is to reset the account's credentials on the sync server. On the Microsoft Entra Connect Sync server, open PowerShell:

```powershell
$credential = Get-Credential
Add-ADSyncAADServiceAccount -AADCredential $credential
```

Enter Global Administrator credentials when asked. Microsoft says the cmdlet *"resets the password for the service account and updates it both in Microsoft Entra ID and the sync engine."* After that, check that event 6900 or 659 stops.

**For admins** (any other account): find the device or app from the second query. If the IP is unknown to the user, reset the password and revoke the user's sessions, as you would after a failed-password alert you can't explain.

50055.name: InvalidPasswordExpiredPassword
50055.title: AADSTS50055: Password expired
50055.description: AADSTS50055: the password has expired. Routine for users, but during a spray it suggests the attacker may hold a correct password. KQL included.
50055.summary: AADSTS50055 means the user's password has expired, so Microsoft Entra ID ended the sign-in and offers a reset. For a real user it is routine. During a password spray it matters more: the wording implies the password entered was correct, just expired, so the attacker likely holds a valid credential.
50055.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidPasswordExpiredPassword**: The password is expired. The user's password is expired, and therefore their login or session was ended. They will be offered the opportunity to reset it, or can ask an admin to reset it via Reset a user's password using Microsoft Entra ID.

The user is sent to change the password before they can continue.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS50055 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidPasswordExpiredPassword**: The password is expired. The user's password is expired, and therefore their login or session was ended. They will be offered the opportunity to reset it, or can ask an admin to reset it via Reset a user's password using Microsoft Entra ID.

The user is sent to change the password before they can continue.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request with the correct password for a test user who had to change the password at next sign-in. The run accepted 50055, 50144 or 50173 for this case; Entra returned `AADSTS50055` with this first line:

> AADSTS50055: The password is expired.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint.

The same attempt in the lab tenant's sign-in log (Entra admin center, interactive user sign-ins), with identifiers left out:

| Field | Value in the lab row |
|---|---|
| Status | Interrupted |
| Sign-in error code | 50055 |
| Additional details | The user's password is expired, and therefore their login or session was ended. They will be offered the opportunity to reset it, or may ask an admin to reset it. |
| Authentication requirement | Single-factor authentication |
| Conditional Access | Not Applied |
| User type | Member |

The test user had **must change password at next sign-in** set, not an expired password, yet the log row says the password is expired. In the logs the two look the same, so check the user's password policy and `lastPasswordChangeDateTime` before assuming a real expiry. The KQL below was run on the lab rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). The first query found both lab rows. The spray follow-up returned nothing as written, as expected on a lab sample this small; with the spray threshold lowered to 1 it found both rows.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Microsoft's password spray playbook lists *"50055 - Password expired"* among the sign-in events to review in a spray investigation. The playbook doesn't say why. The likely reason is an inference from the description: Entra tells the user the password is **expired**, not **wrong**. In practice that means the password entered was the right one. Compare 50126, where it was wrong.

That changes how you read it:

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A user on their normal device and IP, followed by a password change and success | Routine expiry. Benign. |
| A 50055 from an IP that also produced many 50126 across different users | The spray **found a correct password** for this account. Treat it as a compromised credential. |
| A 50055 from an unfamiliar country or hosting provider for a user who wasn't travelling | Someone else has this user's (old) password. |
| 50055 followed by a success from the same unfamiliar IP | The worst case. The attacker may have changed the password and signed in. Check the audit log for the password change. |

Expect `ConditionalAccessStatus` = `notApplied` on 50055 rows. Conditional Access only runs after the first factor succeeds, and the sign-in stopped at the password stage.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
All 50055 rows, with the source, so you can spot ones that don't fit the user:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50055"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, LocationDetails, AppDisplayName,
          ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

50055 from an IP that was also spraying. These are the rows that matter:

```kusto
let sprayIPs =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50126"
    | summarize FailedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where FailedUsers >= 10
    | project IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50055"
| where IPAddress in (sprayIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultDescription, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

`ResultType` is a string column, so compare it with `"50055"`.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- Conditional Access never ran on the 50055 row itself. It can still matter on the **next** step: if the attacker completes a password change and signs in, CA and MFA apply to that new sign-in.
- That makes MFA the barrier that matters here. In practice, an attacker holding this password still has to pass whatever CA and MFA require on the follow-up sign-in.
- `AuthenticationRequirement` on the 50055 row says nothing about your MFA setup. MFA was never reached.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50055?
sections.text:
**For the user:** change your password when prompted, or ask your admin to reset it. If you weren't trying to sign in at that time, tell your admin.

**For admins:**
1. Routine expiry: let the user reset through the prompt or self-service password reset.
2. 50055 from a spray IP or an unfamiliar location: treat the old password as known to an attacker. Reset it yourself, revoke sessions (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`), and check whether that IP later got a success or an MFA prompt for the user.
3. Make sure the user has MFA registered, so a correct password alone isn't enough.

- `AuthenticationRequirement` on the 50055 row says nothing about your MFA setup. MFA was never reached.

50055.labSectionText:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request with the correct password for a test user who had to change the password at next sign-in. The run accepted 50055, 50144 or 50173 for this case; Entra returned `AADSTS50055` with this first line:

> AADSTS50055: The password is expired.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint.

| Field | Value in the lab row |
|---|---|
| Status | Interrupted |
| Sign-in error code | 50055 |
| Additional details | The user's password is expired, and therefore their login or session was ended. They will be offered the opportunity to reset it, or may ask an admin to reset it. |
| Authentication requirement | Single-factor authentication |
| Conditional Access | Not Applied |
| User type | Member |

The test user had **must change password at next sign-in** set, not an expired password, yet the log row says the password is expired. In the logs the two look the same, so check the user's password policy and `lastPasswordChangeDateTime` before assuming a real expiry. The KQL below was run on the lab rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). The first query found both lab rows. The spray follow-up returned nothing as written, as expected on a lab sample this small; with the spray threshold lowered to 1 it found both rows.

50057.name: UserDisabled
50057.title: AADSTS50057 fix: the user account is disabled
50057.description: AADSTS50057 means the Entra ID account is disabled. How to re-enable a cloud or synced account, and when many 50057s mean a password spray.
50057.summary: AADSTS50057 means the user account is disabled in Microsoft Entra ID, so sign-in was refused. After an offboarding it is expected. The security signal is volume and source: many disabled accounts tried from one IP suggests a password spray working from an old user list. Hunt it with ResultType == "50057".
50057.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserDisabled**: The user account is disabled. The user object in Active Directory backing this account has been disabled. An admin can re-enable this account through PowerShell

The account exists but is switched off (`accountEnabled` = false), so Entra refuses the sign-in. Microsoft's wording mentions the Active Directory object, but the code is the same for a cloud-only account disabled in Entra ID. In hybrid tenants the disable is often done on-premises and synced up, so check both places when re-enabling.

sections.text:

In hybrid tenants the disable is often done on-premises and synced up, so check both places when re-enabling.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request with the correct password for a test user whose account was disabled. Entra returned `AADSTS50057` with this first line:

> AADSTS50057: The user account is disabled.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint.

The same attempt in the lab tenant's sign-in log (Entra admin center, interactive user sign-ins), with identifiers left out:

| Field | Value in the lab row |
|---|---|
| Status | Failure |
| Sign-in error code | 50057 |
| Failure reason | The user account is disabled. |
| Authentication details | Password (password in the cloud), succeeded: false |
| Authentication requirement | Single-factor authentication |
| Conditional Access | Not Applied |
| Client app | Mobile Apps and Desktop clients |
| Resource | Microsoft Graph |
| User type | Member |
| Cross tenant access type | None |

Two things on this page hold in the real row: Conditional Access shows **Not Applied**, because the sign-in stops before policies are evaluated, and the password check itself is recorded as not succeeded. The KQL below was run on the lab rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). The 14-day per-user query found both lab users. The spray query returned nothing as written, as expected for one disabled user per run; with its threshold lowered to 1 it found both source IPs.

sections.heading: What is the quick fix?
sections.text:
If the account should be active, re-enable it. If it was disabled on purpose (leaver, retired service account), nothing is broken and the sign-in attempts are the thing to clean up.

- **Cloud-only user:** Entra admin center > Users > select the user > Edit properties > Account enabled. Or Graph: `Update-MgUser -UserId <id> -AccountEnabled:$true`.
- **Synced user:** enable the account in on-premises Active Directory, then run a sync. A cloud change is overwritten by the next sync.
- **Leaver still trying:** find the device or app retrying and remove the stale profile or token.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Microsoft's password spray playbook lists *"50057 - User account was disabled"* among the sign-in events to review in a spray investigation. Most 50057 rows are still harmless. Read the pattern:

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One recently offboarded user, from their old device or usual IP | A phone, mail client or synced app still trying with the old account. Benign, but clean it up. |
| Rows in the non-interactive log for a leaver | An app still holding a token for that user and retrying silently. Revoke sessions. |
| Many **different disabled accounts** from one IP | In practice, a spray working from an old or leaked user list. Disabled leavers and shared mailboxes are on those lists. (T1110.003) |
| 50057 mixed with 50126 and 50034 from the same IP | The same spray hitting live, disabled and non-existent names. |
| A disabled admin or service account tried from an unfamiliar IP | Someone has a credential for an account you retired. Find out where it came from. |
| A 50057 account that suddenly shows a **success** | The account was re-enabled. Check the audit log for who did it. |

Because the account is disabled, sign-in stops at the credential stage. Expect `ConditionalAccessStatus` = `notApplied` on these rows, as Conditional Access only runs after the first factor succeeds.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
One IP trying several disabled accounts in a day:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50057"
| summarize DisabledUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Attempts = count(),
            Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 20),
            Clients = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 5)
          by IPAddress
| where DisabledUsers >= 3
| sort by DisabledUsers desc
```

What is still trying to use disabled accounts, interactive and non-interactive together:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == "50057"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive
| sort by LastSeen desc
```

The threshold of 3 in the first query is a starting point. Tune it to how many leavers you normally see.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- Conditional Access does not evaluate a 50057. The account is refused before CA runs.
- `AuthenticationRequirement` on these rows says nothing about whether MFA is enforced in your tenant. MFA was never reached.
- Disabling the account blocks **new** sign-ins. It does not by itself cut tokens an app already holds. Microsoft's revoke-access guidance pairs disabling the account with revoking sessions (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`) and already-issued access tokens keep working until they expire: by default 60 to 90 minutes.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50057?
sections.text:
**For the user:** if you still need access, ask your admin. A disabled account is an admin decision, not a password problem. Remove old work accounts from personal phones and mail apps.

**For admins:**
1. If the account should be active, re-enable it. Microsoft's description says an admin can do this through PowerShell. In hybrid tenants, re-enable it in on-premises AD and let it sync.
2. If it is a leaver, find the device or app in the second query and remove the account from it.
3. When you disable an account for offboarding or an incident, also **revoke sessions**.
4. If the first query shows a spray, check whether the same IP produced any success, 50076/50074 or 53003 for **active** accounts. Those accounts had a correct password.

50058.name: UserInformationNotProvided
50058.title: AADSTS50058: Session information isn't sufficient for single sign-on
50058.description: AADSTS50058: silent SSO (prompt=none) found no valid session. A common, expected error with low attack value; the app should prompt. KQL included.
50058.summary: AADSTS50058 means an app tried to sign a user in silently (single sign-on, often with prompt=none) but there was no valid session to use. Microsoft calls it a common, expected error. It is one of the noisiest codes in most tenants and has low attack value. The app should fall back to an interactive sign-in. Filter it out of failure dashboards.
50058.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserInformationNotProvided**: Session information isn't sufficient for single-sign-on. This means that a user isn't signed in. This is a common error that's expected when a user is unauthenticated and hasn't yet signed in. If this error is encountered in an SSO context where the user has previously signed in, this means that the SSO session was either not found or invalid. This error might be returned to the application if prompt=none is specified.

An app asked Microsoft Entra ID to sign the user in **without showing anything** and there was no usable session. The app is expected to catch this and show a normal sign-in.

The usual trigger is `prompt=none`. Microsoft's authorization code flow reference says it *"ensures that the user isn't presented with any interactive prompt. If the request can't be completed silently by using single-sign on, the Microsoft identity platform returns an `interaction_required` error."* The OpenID Connect reference lists the causes: *"no signed-in user, the hinted user isn't signed in, or multiple users are signed in but no hint was provided."* Depending on the flow, the app may get 50058 itself or a protocol error such as `login_required` or `interaction_required`. Our reading is that these are the same event seen from two sides; the sign-in log records the AADSTS code.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS50058 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserInformationNotProvided**: Session information isn't sufficient for single-sign-on. This means that a user isn't signed in. This is a common error that's expected when a user is unauthenticated and hasn't yet signed in. If this error is encountered in an SSO context where the user has previously signed in, this means that the SSO session was either not found or invalid. This error might be returned to the application if prompt=none is specified.

An app asked Microsoft Entra ID to sign the user in **without showing anything** and there was no usable session. The app is expected to catch this and show a normal sign-in.

The usual trigger is `prompt=none`. Microsoft's authorization code flow reference says it *"ensures that the user isn't presented with any interactive prompt. If the request can't be completed silently by using single-sign on, the Microsoft identity platform returns an `interaction_required` error."* The OpenID Connect reference lists the causes: *"no signed-in user, the hinted user isn't signed in, or multiple users are signed in but no hint was provided."* Depending on the flow, the app may get 50058 itself or a protocol error such as `login_required` or `interaction_required`. Our reading is that these are the same event seen from two sides; the sign-in log records the AADSTS code.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Microsoft's description calls it *"a common error that's expected"*. Single-page apps and MSAL.js try silent sign-in first (`ssoSilent`, `acquireTokenSilent`) and Microsoft tells developers to *"handle any login_required or interaction_required errors with an interactive method"*. Every user who opens such an app without a session produces one.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 50058 for many users across Microsoft 365 and line-of-business apps | Normal silent SSO attempts. Benign noise. |
| 50058 followed within seconds by a success for the same user and app | The app fell back to an interactive sign-in. Working as designed. |
| A jump in 50058 for one browser type | Third-party cookie restrictions. Microsoft notes that *"ssoSilent requests will fail despite an active user session"* in some browsers. Our interpretation: that shows up as extra 50058 rows. |
| 50058 for one user, repeating, with no success after | The app keeps retrying silently and never prompts. A bug in the app, not an attack. |

There is no documented attack pattern for 50058. A silent request without a session gets nothing, so it gives an attacker nothing. Exclude it from failure-rate dashboards and spray detections, or it inflates them.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 50058 is logged in. Start by checking where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50058"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which apps generate the noise:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50058"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| sort by Rows desc
```

Users who hit 50058 and never succeed afterwards on the same app the same day, a sign of an app that doesn't fall back to an interactive prompt:

```kusto
let silentFails =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50058"
    | summarize FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated), Fails = count() by UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName;
let successes =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize LastSuccess = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId;
silentFails
| join kind=leftouter successes on UserPrincipalName, AppId
| where isnull(LastSuccess) or LastSuccess < FirstFail
| project UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, Fails, FirstFail
| sort by Fails desc
```

If the first query shows most 50058 in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, run the other two against that table, or both with `union`. Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource match, so row counts there are not request counts. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"50058"`, not `50058`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 50058 happens before Conditional Access. There is no authenticated user yet, so no policy is evaluated.
- The interactive sign-in that follows goes through MFA and your Conditional Access policies as normal.
- Don't confuse it with sign-in frequency. A refresh token refused by a sign-in frequency policy is logged as [70043](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70043/), a different code.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50058?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign in when the app asks. If an app shows this error instead of a sign-in page, the app didn't fall back to an interactive sign-in; report it to whoever runs the app.

**For developers:** treat 50058, `login_required` and `interaction_required` as *"show a sign-in"*, not as a failure. With MSAL.js, catch the error from the silent call and call `loginPopup`, `loginRedirect`, `acquireTokenPopup` or `acquireTokenRedirect`. Pass a `login_hint` with `prompt=none` when you know which user to expect.

**For admins:**
1. Nothing is broken. Exclude `"50058"` from failure counts, password spray rules and alerting thresholds.
2. If the third query returns many users for one app, that app doesn't fall back to an interactive sign-in. Report it to its developer.

microsoftWording.text: **UserInformationNotProvided**: Session information isn't sufficient for single-sign-on. This means that a user isn't signed in. This is a common error that's expected when a user is unauthenticated and hasn't yet signed in. If this error is encountered in an SSO context where the user has previously signed in, this means that the SSO session was either not found or invalid. This error might be returned to the application if prompt=none is specified.

kind.label: Interrupt (an expected extra step, not a failure)

attackSignal.label: Low: usually configuration or user error

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
No. Microsoft's description calls it *"a common error that's expected"*. Single-page apps and MSAL.js try silent sign-in first (`ssoSilent`, `acquireTokenSilent`) and Microsoft tells developers to *"handle any login_required or interaction_required errors with an interactive method"*. Every user who opens such an app without a session produces one.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 50058 for many users across Microsoft 365 and line-of-business apps | Normal silent SSO attempts. Benign noise. |
| 50058 followed within seconds by a success for the same user and app | The app fell back to an interactive sign-in. Working as designed. |
| A jump in 50058 for one browser type | Third-party cookie restrictions. Microsoft notes that *"ssoSilent requests will fail despite an active user session"* in some browsers. Our interpretation: that shows up as extra 50058 rows. |
| 50058 for one user, repeating, with no success after | The app keeps retrying silently and never prompts. A bug in the app, not an attack. |

There is no documented attack pattern for 50058. A silent request without a session gets nothing, so it gives an attacker nothing. Exclude it from failure-rate dashboards and spray detections, or it inflates them.

50059.name: MissingTenantRealmAndNoUserInformationProvided
50059.title: AADSTS50059: No tenant-identifying information in the request (fix)
50059.description: AADSTS50059: the request named no tenant and Entra could not infer one. Common with /common and the device code flow. Fix and KQL.
50059.summary: AADSTS50059 means the request named no tenant and carried nothing Entra could use to work one out. It happens when a single-tenant app calls /common or /organizations without a user hint, for example in the device code flow. It is a configuration error with low attack value. Put your tenant ID or domain in the authority URL.
50059.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **MissingTenantRealmAndNoUserInformationProvided**: Tenant-identifying information wasn't found in either the request or implied by any provided credentials. The user can contact the tenant admin to help resolve the issue.

Every request to the Microsoft identity platform has to resolve to one tenant before anything else can happen. The tenant comes from one of two places: the authority URL, or the credentials in the request. Microsoft's OpenID Connect reference lists what the URL can carry:

| Value | Microsoft's description |
|---|---|
| `common` | Users with both a personal Microsoft account and a work or school account from Microsoft Entra ID can sign in to the application. |
| `organizations` | Only users with work or school accounts from Microsoft Entra ID can sign in to the application. |
| `consumers` | Only users with a personal Microsoft account can sign in to the application. |
| Directory (tenant) ID or `contoso.onmicrosoft.com` | Only users from a specific Microsoft Entra tenant ... can sign in to the application. |

`common` and `organizations` deliberately name no tenant. In an interactive browser sign-in that is fine, because the user types an address and Entra discovers the tenant from it. 50059 is what you get when there is no such step and nothing else in the request implies a tenant either: no username, no credential that belongs to a directory, no tenant in the URL.

Three codes describe tenant problems and are easy to confuse:

- [90002](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90002/) means a tenant *was* named and doesn't exist.
- [900023](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/900023/) means the tenant part of the URL isn't a valid tenant ID or domain at all, for example `undefined`.
- 50059 means nothing was named, and nothing could be inferred.

Microsoft's reference also lists **AADSTS50194** for an overlapping situation: *"Application '{appId}'({appName}) isn't configured as a multitenant application. Usage of the /common endpoint isn't supported for such applications created after '{time}'. Use a tenant-specific endpoint or configure the application to be multitenant."* That error names the app and the endpoint. 50059 is the earlier failure: Entra hadn't resolved a tenant, so it could not get as far as checking the app's supported account types. Our reading, from the lab result below: which of the two you get depends on how far the request gets before the tenant is needed.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run started a device code flow for a single-tenant app registration against `/common`, and separately against `/organizations`. Both returned the same code and message:

> AADSTS50059: No tenant-identifying information found in either the request or implied by any provided credentials.

Both rounds of the run reproduced it, four results in total. The run expected 90133, [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/) or 50194, so the documented multitenant error is not what a device code request gives you here.

The device code request carries only the client ID and the scope, which is exactly the shape 50059 describes: a request with no user and no tenant. Microsoft's device code flow page does allow the endpoint: *"`tenant` | Required | Can be `/common`, `/consumers`, or `/organizations`. It can also be the directory tenant that you want to request permission from in GUID or friendly name format."* Our reading: `/common` is accepted by the protocol and still fails for a single-tenant app, because the tenant can't be inferred from anything in that first call.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is an app or script pointed at a tenant-agnostic endpoint that it can't use.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A CLI or device-code tool fails at the first step | The authority is `/common` or `/organizations` and the app registration is single-tenant. |
| A library default was never changed | Many SDKs default to `common`. For a single-tenant app it has to be set to the tenant. |
| Sample code copied from a multitenant tutorial | The sample's authority was right for its app registration, not for yours. |
| A service-to-service call with no user | There is no user to infer a tenant from, so the URL must name the tenant. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 50059 lands in. Our reading, as with [90002](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90002/): the request did not resolve to a tenant, so your tenant most likely records nothing, and the error is visible to the caller rather than to you. Check anyway; this query is expected to return nothing or very little:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("50059", "50194") or ResultSignature in ("50059", "50194")
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = make_set(AppId, 10), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, ResultType
```

The query includes 50194 because that is the documented error for the same mistake once the app has been resolved, and because a row of either kind points at the same fix.

What your logs can tell you is which tenant the failing app should be using. Find where it signs in successfully:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| where AppId == "<app id of the failing app>"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, AppDisplayName, ResourceTenantId
```

`ResourceTenantId` carries the tenant of the resource in the sign-in. If this returns your tenant ID and the app's configuration says `common`, you have found the change to make.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50059?
sections.text:
**For the user:** nothing to fix on your device. Microsoft's own advice for this code is to contact the tenant admin. Pass on the name of the tool or app that failed.

**For developers:**
1. Put the tenant in the authority URL: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/...`, or your verified domain instead of the GUID.
2. In the device code flow, use the same tenant value in both calls. Microsoft on the token request: *"`tenant` | Required | The same tenant or tenant alias used in the initial request."*
3. Only use `common` or `organizations` when the app registration really is multitenant and the flow has an interactive step where the user's address identifies the tenant.
4. Check the library default. An SDK that defaults to `common` needs the tenant set explicitly for a single-tenant app.

**For admins:**
1. Give the app's owner your tenant ID, from **Entra ID** > **Overview** > **Properties**, or:

```powershell
Connect-AzAccount
Get-AzTenant
```

2. If the app genuinely has to serve several tenants, change **Supported account types** on the registration to a multitenant value rather than leaving the endpoint as `common` against a single-tenant app. Microsoft's signInAudience page maps the portal choices to the manifest values: single tenant is `AzureADMyOrg`, multitenant is `AzureADMultipleOrgs`.
3. For a third-party product, send the vendor the tenant ID and tell them the integration must use a tenant-specific authority.

50072.name: UserStrongAuthEnrollmentRequiredInterrupt
50072.title: AADSTS50072: User needs to enroll for second factor authentication
50072.description: AADSTS50072: user needs to enroll for second factor authentication. Normal for new users; from an unfamiliar IP, check who registers MFA. KQL.
50072.summary: AADSTS50072 is an interrupt: the user must enroll a second factor before the sign-in can finish. For a new user it is expected. Microsoft's password spray playbook lists it among the codes to monitor. From an unfamiliar IP it can mean someone with the correct password is being asked to set up MFA on the account.
50072.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserStrongAuthEnrollmentRequiredInterrupt**: User needs to enroll for second factor authentication (interactive).

Microsoft's password spray playbook lists it among the Entra codes to monitor, worded as *"50072 - User prompted to provide MFA"*. Both texts point to the same moment: the password was accepted, MFA applies, and the sign-in is interrupted for the second factor. The error reference says the user still has to enroll one.

The closely related [50079](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50079/) is the code the playbook describes as *"user needs to register security info"*.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS50072 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserStrongAuthEnrollmentRequiredInterrupt**: User needs to enroll for second factor authentication (interactive).

Microsoft's password spray playbook lists it among the Entra codes to monitor, worded as *"50072 - User prompted to provide MFA"*. Both texts point to the same moment: the password was accepted, MFA applies, and the sign-in is interrupted for the second factor. The error reference says the user still has to enroll one.

The closely related [50079](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50079/) is the code the playbook describes as *"user needs to register security info"*.

sections.heading: What is the quick fix?
sections.text:
Usually nothing is broken. The user has to set up a second factor and then finish signing in.

- **User:** follow the registration prompt from a device and network you trust. If you didn't start this sign-in, stop and contact IT.
- **Admin, new users:** Microsoft's Conditional Access guidance says *"Administrators have to issue Temporary Access Pass credentials to new users so they can satisfy the requirements for multifactor authentication to register"* when registration itself requires MFA. Microsoft also notes *"Temporary Access Pass does not work for guest users."*
- **Admin, unexpected rows:** if the user should already have methods, or the IP is unfamiliar, see the next section.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
For a new hire or a user who just came into scope of an MFA policy, 50072 is the normal path into MFA. It matters when the sign-in isn't the user's: whoever completes enrollment from that session chooses the second factor. This is reasoning from how registration works, not a Microsoft statement. It is the same concern as on the [50079 page](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50079/).

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 50072 for a new or newly in-scope user from a known office or home IP | Expected enrollment. Benign. |
| 50072 from an IP that also produced **50126** failures against other users | A spray found a working password on an account without MFA. |
| 50072 from an unfamiliar IP or country, then a success | Someone may have registered their own method. Check the account's methods. |
| 50072 for a long-standing account that should already be registered | Check whether its methods were removed, and by whom. |

These readings are based on Microsoft's description and the playbook listing. Microsoft doesn't publish a threat pattern for 50072 specifically.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
50072 per user and IP, with whether the same user and IP had a success afterwards:

```kusto
let window = 7d;
let interrupts =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(window)
    | where ResultType == "50072"
    | summarize FirstInterrupt = min(TimeGenerated), Interrupts = count(),
                Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5)
              by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
    | extend Apps = strcat_array(Apps, ", ");
let successes =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(window)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
interrupts
| join kind=leftouter successes on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| summarize SuccessAfter = countif(SuccessTime > FirstInterrupt)
          by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, FirstInterrupt, Interrupts, Apps
| sort by FirstInterrupt desc
```

50072 from IPs that were failing passwords against other users the same day:

```kusto
let sprayIPs =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50126"
    | summarize FailedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where FailedUsers >= 5
    | project IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50072"
| where IPAddress in (sprayIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName,
          ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

The threshold of 5 failed users is a starting point, not a Microsoft number. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"50072"`, not `50072`.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 50072 means an MFA requirement applies and the account can't meet it yet.
- Microsoft documents that an interrupted sign-in *"appears on the logs but shows **Not applied** for Conditional Access."* So `notApplied` on a 50072 row doesn't mean your policies are missing.
- Conditional Access can protect the registration step itself with the **Register security information** user action. Microsoft's template *"requires users who are not on a trusted network to do multifactor authentication"* to register.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50072?
sections.text:
**For the user:** register your second factor when prompted, from a device and network you trust.

**For admins:**
1. For new users, issue a Temporary Access Pass if your registration policy requires MFA.
2. For every 50072 from an IP the user doesn't use, check the account's registered methods and remove any you can't tie to the user.
3. Protect security info registration with a Conditional Access policy on the **Register security information** user action.

50074.name: UserStrongAuthClientAuthNRequiredInterrupt
50074.title: AADSTS50074: strong authentication is required (MFA)
50074.description: AADSTS50074 / UserStrongAuthClientAuthNRequiredInterrupt: the password passed but MFA did not. Fix for users and admins, plus KQL.
50074.summary: AADSTS50074 means MFA was required and the user did not pass the challenge. The first factor (usually the password) had already succeeded. One or two are normal. Many for one user in a short window from an unfamiliar IP is the MFA fatigue pattern: someone with the correct password is pushing prompts and waiting for an approval.
50074.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserStrongAuthClientAuthNRequiredInterrupt**: Strong authentication is required and the user did not pass the MFA challenge.

Microsoft's password spray playbook lists it as *"50074 - MFA required"*. Either way the order of events is the same: the password was accepted, then the MFA step did not complete.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS50074 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserStrongAuthClientAuthNRequiredInterrupt**: Strong authentication is required and the user did not pass the MFA challenge.

Microsoft's password spray playbook lists it as *"50074 - MFA required"*. Either way the order of events is the same: the password was accepted, then the MFA step did not complete.

sections.heading: What is the quick fix?
sections.text:
Usually nothing is broken. In practice this row often appears when MFA is first requested, so the user just needs to finish the prompt.

- **User:** approve the prompt, check the phone has a signal and the Authenticator app is up to date, and retry. If no method is registered, register one at the Security info page.
- **Admin:** check the user's registered methods and the Conditional Access policy that requires MFA on the sign-in's Conditional Access tab.
- **Repeated rows from an unfamiliar IP:** see the next section.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
A single 50074 often just means the sign-in reached the MFA step. It can be logged as an interrupt row before the user finishes MFA, so one row on its own says little. It can also be a user who dismissed a prompt, picked up the wrong phone, or let it time out. **The signal is repetition, and where it comes from.**

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One 50074, then `0` from the same IP and device | The user retried and passed MFA. Benign. |
| Several 50074 for **one user** in minutes, from an IP or country the user doesn't use | **MFA fatigue** (T1621). The attacker has the password and is generating prompts. |
| 50074 burst followed by `0` from the **same unfamiliar IP** | **The user approved a prompt they didn't start.** Treat as account takeover. |
| 50074 from an IP that also produced many **50126** failures | The spray found a correct password and is now stuck at MFA. |
| 50074 alongside **500121** for the same user | Same picture. See [500121](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500121/). |

The playbook's instruction applies directly: *"record successful passwords but failed MFA responses, as this activity indicates that the attacker is getting the password but not passing MFA."*

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Users with repeated 50074 from one IP within an hour:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50074"
| summarize Prompts = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(CreatedDateTime),
            LastSeen = max(CreatedDateTime),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5)
          by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, bin(CreatedDateTime, 1h)
| where Prompts >= 3
| sort by Prompts desc
```

The threshold of 3 is a starting point, not a Microsoft number. Tune it against your own baseline.

The hourly bins use `CreatedDateTime`, not `TimeGenerated`. Microsoft's interactive sign-ins page: *"The `TimeGenerated` field is the time the entry was received and published by Log Analytics, not the time the sign-in occurred. The `CreatedDateTime` field in the logs shows the time the sign-in occurred."* The `TimeGenerated > ago(1d)` filter is fine for picking the time range; for burst windows, use the sign-in time.

What happened at the MFA step. `AuthenticationDetails` is a **string** column holding a JSON array, so parse it first:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50074"
| mv-expand Step = parse_json(AuthenticationDetails)
| extend Method = tostring(Step.authenticationMethod),
         StepResult = tostring(Step.authenticationStepResultDetail),
         Succeeded = tobool(Step.succeeded)
| summarize Steps = count() by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Method, StepResult, Succeeded
| sort by Steps desc
```

The field names inside `AuthenticationDetails` follow the Microsoft Graph `authenticationDetail` object. Check them against a row in your own workspace before relying on this query. Don't use `MfaDetail`; Microsoft marks that column as deprecated.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 50074 is the MFA requirement doing its job. Whatever required MFA (a Conditional Access grant, per-user MFA, security defaults) stopped a sign-in whose first factor (usually the password) had succeeded.
- Microsoft documents that an interrupted sign-in *"appears on the logs but shows **Not applied** for Conditional Access."* Don't conclude from that column that no policy applied.
- Push approval without context is what fatigue attacks rely on. Microsoft enforced number matching for Microsoft Authenticator push in 2023, so the plain "tap Approve" path mostly remains in third-party or NPS-extension MFA. Phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business) remove the push entirely. The [MFA fatigue guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/detect-mfa-fatigue-entra-id/) walks through the investigation.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50074?
sections.text:
**For the user:** if you didn't start the sign-in, deny the prompt and report it. That prompt means someone has your password.

**For admins:**
1. If the 50074 burst came from an IP the user doesn't use, reset the password. The attacker already has it.
2. Check for a later `0` from the same IP. If there is one, revoke sessions (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`) and review what the session accessed.
3. Move users off plain push approval toward phishing-resistant methods.

50076.name: UserStrongAuthClientAuthNRequired
50076.title: AADSTS50076: MFA required to access the resource
50076.description: AADSTS50076: the password was accepted and MFA is now required. An expected interrupt, unless the IP was just failing passwords. KQL included.
50076.summary: AADSTS50076 means the password was accepted but the sign-in now needs multifactor authentication, usually because of a Conditional Access policy, per-user MFA, or a new location. It is an expected interrupt. The signal is who reached it: a 50076 from an IP that was just failing passwords means an attacker has a working password.
50076.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserStrongAuthClientAuthNRequired**: Due to a configuration change made by the admin such as a Conditional Access policy, per-user enforcement, or because you moved to a new location, the user must use multifactor authentication to access the resource. Retry with a new authorize request for the resource.

The first factor passed. Entra ID stopped the sign-in to ask for a second factor. In an interactive browser sign-in the user normally sees the MFA prompt and a follow-up request completes. That is why most 50076 rows are not failures in any practical sense.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
See the [comparison of the codes behind "asked to sign in again"](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/why-user-asked-to-sign-in-again-entra-id/) (70043, 700082, 50173, 50133, 50076).

Usually not. Every MFA prompt in your tenant can produce one. **The value of 50076 is that it shows the first factor (usually the password) succeeded.**

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 50076, then `0` (success) from the same IP and device within minutes | The user completed MFA. Benign. |
| 50076 from an IP that produced many **50126** failures | **The spray found a working password.** MFA is now the only barrier. |
| 50076 followed by repeated **50074** or **500121** for the same user | Someone with the password is pushing MFA prompts the user is not approving. See [50074](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50074/). |
| 50076 in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs` from an IP the user never signed in from | A refresh token being used where a new MFA requirement applies. Could be a user on a new network, could be a replayed token. This reading is reasoning from the mechanism, not a Microsoft statement. |

Microsoft's password spray playbook tells responders to *"record successful passwords but failed MFA responses, as this activity indicates that the attacker is getting the password but not passing MFA."* A 50076 from an attacker IP is that record.

On these rows `AuthenticationRequirement` is `multiFactorAuthentication`. Microsoft documents that a sign-in where primary authentication succeeds and MFA is required carries that value.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Users who hit the MFA step from an IP that was failing passwords for them earlier the same day:

```kusto
let failedPw =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50126"
    | summarize Failures = count(), FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated)
              by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50076"
| join kind=inner failedPw on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| where TimeGenerated > FirstFail
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, Failures,
          AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, AuthenticationRequirement, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

Non-interactive 50076 from IPs the user has had no successful sign-in from, in either table, in the last 14 days. Mobile devices change IPs often, so expect benign rows and check the country and user agent before escalating:

```kusto
let knownIPs =
    union
        (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType)
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50076"
| join kind=leftanti knownIPs on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| summarize Events = count(), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Events desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"50076"`. Non-interactive rows are aggregated by Microsoft when application, user, IP, status and resource match, so `Events` counts log rows, not individual token requests.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 50076 is what a Conditional Access MFA grant, per-user MFA or a location change looks like at the moment it fires. The control is working.
- Microsoft's interactive sign-ins documentation says an interrupted sign-in *"appears on the logs but shows **Not applied** for Conditional Access."* Don't read `notApplied` on a 50076 row as proof that no policy targets the user. Look at the follow-up sign-in.
- If MFA is satisfied by push approval, the password alone gets an attacker to the point where they can generate prompts. Number matching (enforced for Microsoft Authenticator since 2023) and phishing-resistant methods reduce what they can do from there. See the [MFA fatigue guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/detect-mfa-fatigue-entra-id/).

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50076?
sections.text:
**For the user:** complete the MFA prompt. If the app keeps failing silently, sign out and sign in again so it makes a new interactive request, which is what Microsoft's text asks for ("Retry with a new authorize request").

**For admins:**
1. If the 50076 came from an IP you associate with a spray, treat the password as compromised. Reset it and revoke sessions (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`, or **Revoke sessions** on the user in the admin center).
2. Check whether the same IP later produced a `0` for that user. If it did, this is a compromised account, not an attempt.
3. For developers: a daemon or background token refresh can't satisfy MFA. Request the token interactively.

Retry with a new authorize request for the resource.

50079.name: UserStrongAuthEnrollmentRequired
50079.title: AADSTS50079: User must register for MFA
50079.description: AADSTS50079: the user must register for MFA. Normal for new users; from an attacker IP, they could register their own method. KQL included.
50079.summary: AADSTS50079 means MFA is required but the user has not registered security info yet, so Entra ID sends them to register. For a real new user it is expected. If the sign-in came from an attacker IP, the attacker has a correct password and is being invited to register their own MFA method on the account.
50079.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserStrongAuthEnrollmentRequired**: Due to a configuration change made by the admin such as a Conditional Access policy, per-user enforcement, or because the user moved to a new location, the user is required to use multifactor authentication. Either a managed user needs to register security info to complete multifactor authentication, or a federated user needs to get the multifactor claim from the federated identity provider.

Microsoft's password spray playbook lists it as *"50079 - user needs to register security info"*. The password was accepted. The account has no MFA method, so the next screen is registration.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS50079 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserStrongAuthEnrollmentRequired**: Due to a configuration change made by the admin such as a Conditional Access policy, per-user enforcement, or because the user moved to a new location, the user is required to use multifactor authentication. Either a managed user needs to register security info to complete multifactor authentication, or a federated user needs to get the multifactor claim from the federated identity provider.

Microsoft's password spray playbook lists it as *"50079 - user needs to register security info"*. The password was accepted. The account has no MFA method, so the next screen is registration.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
For a new hire, a freshly enabled policy, or a user who never registered, 50079 is the normal path into MFA. **It becomes the most important row in an investigation when the sign-in is not the user's.**

Whoever completes registration from that session chooses the MFA method. If an attacker with a sprayed or phished password lands on an unregistered account, 50079 is the moment they can add their own authenticator app or phone, and from then on MFA protects the attacker, not the user. This is reasoning from how registration works, not a Microsoft statement, but it is why the playbook lists the code.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 50079 for a new or newly in-scope user, from a known office or home IP | Expected registration. Benign. |
| 50079 from an IP that also produced **50126** failures against other users | A spray found a working password on an account with no MFA. |
| 50079 from an unfamiliar IP or country, then a security info registration event, then `0` | **Likely account takeover with attacker-registered MFA** (T1098.005). |
| 50079 for a long-standing account that should already be registered | Check whether its methods were deleted, and by whom. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
50079 from IPs that were failing passwords against other users the same day:

```kusto
let sprayIPs =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50126"
    | summarize FailedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where FailedUsers >= 5
    | project IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "50079"
| where IPAddress in (sprayIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName,
          ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

50079 followed within an hour by a security info registration in `AuditLogs` for the same user:

```kusto
let interrupts =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == "50079"
    | project InterruptTime = TimeGenerated,
              UserPrincipalName = tolower(UserPrincipalName),
              SigninIP = IPAddress;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "security info"
| extend UserPrincipalName = tolower(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)),
         AuditIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| join kind=inner interrupts on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (InterruptTime .. (InterruptTime + 1h))
| project InterruptTime, RegisteredAt = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName,
          SigninIP, AuditIP, OperationName, Result
| sort by RegisteredAt desc
```

Verify the exact `OperationName` values for security info registration in your own workspace before relying on the `has "security info"` filter, and check that `InitiatedBy` carries the user and IP fields for those events. The threshold of 5 failed users is a starting point, not a Microsoft number.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 50079 means an MFA requirement applies but the account can't meet it yet. The requirement is not the problem. Who gets to satisfy it first is.
- Microsoft documents that an interrupted sign-in *"appears on the logs but shows **Not applied** for Conditional Access."*
- Conditional Access can protect the registration step itself, for example by only allowing security info registration from trusted locations or compliant devices. When a policy blocks registration, users see **53010** instead.
- Federated users get this code when the federated identity provider didn't send the MFA claim. In that case registration in Entra ID is not the fix.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50079?
sections.text:
**For the user:** register your MFA method from a device and network you trust. If you get a registration prompt you didn't expect, stop and contact IT.

**For admins:**
1. For every 50079 from an IP the user doesn't use, check the account's registered methods. Remove any you can't tie to the user.
2. If an attacker registered a method, reset the password, remove the method, and revoke sessions (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`).
3. Protect security info registration with Conditional Access so it can only happen from trusted locations or devices.
4. Don't leave accounts unregistered for long. An account with a password and no MFA method is registered by whoever signs in first.

50089.title: AADSTS50089: Flow token expired, sign in again (fix)
50089.description: AADSTS50089: a flow token expired during sign-in. Microsoft calls it expected; the app asks the user to sign in again. Low attack value. KQL.
50089.summary: AADSTS50089 means a sign-in failed because a token that was part of the sign-in had expired. Microsoft calls it expected: auth codes, refresh tokens and sessions expire or get revoked, and the app asks the user to sign in again. It has low attack value. Filter it out of failure dashboards and look only at users who can't get past it.
50089.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> Authentication failed due to flow token expired. Expected - auth codes, refresh tokens, and sessions expire over time or are revoked by the user or an admin. The app will request a new login from the user.

The reference table gives this code no PascalCase name.

Microsoft doesn't define "flow token" anywhere we could find. Our reading is that it refers to the state Entra keeps for a sign-in in progress, so a sign-in page left open too long before the user finishes would produce 50089. The description itself names three things that expire: auth codes, refresh tokens and sessions. Some documented lifetimes:

- **Authorization codes** are short lived. The authorization code flow reference: *"Typically, they expire after about 1 minute."*
- **Refresh tokens** have a default Max Inactive Time of 90 days.
- **Session tokens**: *"Non-persistent session tokens have a Max Inactive Time of 24 hours; persistent session tokens have a Max Inactive Time of 90 days."*

Several close relatives cover specific cases of "your old token or session no longer counts":

- **[50133](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50133/)**: the session is invalid after a password change or expiry.
- **[50173](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50173/)**: the grant was revoked, for example after a password reset.
- **[70043](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70043/)**: a Conditional Access sign-in frequency policy refused the refresh token.

For a comparison of the codes behind repeated sign-in prompts, see [why a user is asked to sign in again](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/why-user-asked-to-sign-in-again-entra-id/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Microsoft's description starts with *"Expected"*. The sign-in fails, nothing is issued, and the app starts over.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A few 50089 rows per user, each followed by a success | A token or sign-in step expired and the user signed in again. Benign. |
| 50089 for many users of one app, all at the same time of day | Our interpretation: users who leave the sign-in page or app open overnight and continue the next morning. Benign. |
| 50089 for one user, repeating several times a day, often with no success after | Something on that device keeps presenting an expired token or session. Clear the app's cached sign-in or browser state. |
| 50089 together with 50133 or 50173 for the same user | A password change or revocation is working its way through the user's sessions. Benign if you know about the change. |

There is no documented attack pattern for 50089. An expired token gets the sender nothing. Keep it out of password spray detections and failure-rate thresholds.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 50089 is logged in. Start by checking where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50089"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which apps and client types produce it:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50089"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| sort by Rows desc
```

Users who hit 50089 again and again without a success afterwards on the same app the same day. These are the ones worth a support ticket:

```kusto
let expired =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50089"
    | summarize FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated), Fails = count() by UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName;
let successes =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize LastSuccess = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId;
expired
| join kind=leftouter successes on UserPrincipalName, AppId
| where isnull(LastSuccess) or LastSuccess < FirstFail
| where Fails >= 5
| project UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, Fails, FirstFail
| sort by Fails desc
```

The threshold of 5 is a starting point; tune it to your tenant. Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource match, so `Fails` counts rows there, not requests. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"50089"`, not `50089`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 50089 is not a Conditional Access block. No policy causes it directly.
- Session lifetime is now controlled with Conditional Access. Microsoft: refresh and session token lifetimes *"are no longer configurable through token lifetime policies"* and *"To control how frequently users are required to sign in, use Conditional Access sign-in frequency instead."*
- A sign-in frequency policy that refuses a refresh token shows up as [70043](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70043/), not 50089. If users complain about frequent prompts, check for 70043 first.
- Microsoft warns that combining **Remember MFA on trusted devices** with sign-in frequency *"might prompt users unexpectedly."*

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50089?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign in again. If it keeps happening, close the app or browser tab completely and start a fresh sign-in instead of continuing an old one.

**For developers:** treat 50089 as "start a new sign-in", not as a fatal error. Microsoft says *"The app will request a new login from the user."* Redeem authorization codes immediately; they typically expire after about a minute. Don't build logic on the code number itself. Microsoft notes that *"Apps that take a dependency on text or error code numbers will be broken over time."* React to the OAuth `error` value instead.

**For admins:**
1. Nothing is broken. Exclude `"50089"` from failure counts and spray detections.
2. Use the third query for users stuck in a loop. Clear the app's cached sign-in on their device or browser.
3. If many users get unexpected sign-in prompts, review your Conditional Access session controls (sign-in frequency, persistent browser session) and turn off **Remember MFA on trusted devices** if you use sign-in frequency.
