securityReading.isItAnAttack:
See the [comparison of the codes behind "asked to sign in again"](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/why-user-asked-to-sign-in-again-entra-id/) (70043, 700082, 50173, 50133, 50076).

Usually not. A password change makes every device the user owns hit 50173 once, and then the user signs in again.

**The security value is during incident response.** When you revoke a compromised user's sessions with `Revoke-MgUserSignInSession` or **Revoke sessions** in the admin center, the Graph call *"Invalidates all the refresh tokens issued to applications for a user (and session cookies in a user's browser), by resetting the signInSessionsValidFromDateTime user property to the current date-time"*, with *"a small delay of a few minutes"* possible. Microsoft's revoke-access procedure (in Microsoft Entra ID: disable the user, revoke refresh tokens, disable devices; in a hybrid environment it first disables the user and resets the password twice in on-premises Active Directory) says that after those steps *"the user can't gain new tokens for any application tied to Microsoft Entra ID."* Revocation on its own doesn't stop someone who still knows the password from signing in again. Every client that still holds a refresh token for that user fails on its next refresh. That includes the attacker's client. Each of those failures should appear as a 50173 row with an IP address, a user agent and device details (my reasoning, not yet checked in a lab).

**IP caveat for confidential clients.** Microsoft's [non-interactive sign-ins page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/concept-noninteractive-sign-ins) says: *"The IP address of non-interactive sign-ins performed by confidential clients doesn't match the actual source IP of where the refresh token request is coming from. Instead, it shows the original IP used for the original token issuance."* So for those apps the IP on a 50173 row may be where the token was first issued, not where the attacker is now. Weigh it with the user agent and device details.

| Pattern after a revocation or password reset | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 50173 from the user's own managed devices and usual IPs | The legitimate user's apps being signed out. Expected. |
| 50173 from an IP, country or device you can't tie to the user | A client you didn't know about was holding a token. Treat it as the attacker's session and pivot on that IP. |
| 50173 rows continue from the same unknown IP, followed by interactive attempts (`SigninLogs`) | The attacker is trying to get back in with credentials. Check the password was actually changed and MFA methods are clean. |
| No 50173 at all after the revocation | Nothing was refreshing a token for that user in the window you looked at. Not proof that nothing was ever stolen. |

Two reading notes:

- The `TokensValidFrom` date in the message is the cut-off set by the revocation or password change. Tokens issued before it are refused.
- Revocation only stops **new** tokens. Microsoft notes that *"By default, access tokens issued by Microsoft Entra ID last for 1 hour."* (Microsoft's token lifetime reference gives the default more precisely as a random value between 60 and 90 minutes.) An attacker can keep using an access token they already have until it expires, and you won't see a 50173 for that period. The exception is Continuous Access Evaluation: Microsoft's CAE page says the implementation *"focuses on Exchange, Teams, and SharePoint Online"* and needs a CAE-capable client. There, an admin revocation or password change is enforced on the access token before it expires, with *"latency of up to 15 minutes"*. CAE access tokens themselves are long-lived, *"up to 28 hours"*, and *"If you aren't using CAE-capable clients, your default access token lifetime remains 1 hour."* The [session revocation guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/revoke-sessions-and-verify-entra-id/) covers this and how to prove the cut-off.

kql.leadIn: Who was still holding a token for this user after you revoked it? Set the user and the time you revoked.
kql.query:
let revokedUser = "{user-principal-name}";
let revokedAt = datetime(2026-10-11T09:00:00Z);
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > revokedAt
| where UserPrincipalName =~ revokedUser
| where ResultType == "50173"
| extend Device = parse_json(DeviceDetail), Location = parse_json(LocationDetails)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Rows = count(),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10)
          by IPAddress,
             Country = tostring(Location.countryOrRegion),
             City = tostring(Location.city),
             OS = tostring(Device.operatingSystem),
             Browser = tostring(Device.browser),
             DeviceId = tostring(Device.deviceId),
             IsManaged = tostring(Device.isManaged),
             IsCompliant = tostring(Device.isCompliant),
             UserAgent
| sort by FirstSeen asc

kql.leadIn: Then take every IP from that result that isn't the user's and see what else it touched, across all users:
kql.query:
let suspectIPs = dynamic(["{ip-address}"]);
union
    (SigninLogs
     | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType, AppDisplayName, Table = "Interactive"),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
     | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType, AppDisplayName, Table = "NonInteractive")
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where IPAddress in (suspectIPs)
| summarize Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 20),
            Results = make_set(ResultType, 20),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)

labReproduced.scenario: Refresh token after the admin revoked sessions

50173.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run did this, in order:

1. Signed a test user in and kept the refresh token.
2. Used that refresh token. **It worked**, and returned a new access token. That is the control.
3. Called `POST /users/{id}/revokeSignInSessions` on Microsoft Graph, which is what the Entra admin center's **Revoke sessions** button does.
4. Waited two minutes, then used a refresh token from before the revocation again.

The fourth step returned `AADSTS50173`:

> AADSTS50173: The provided grant has expired due to it being revoked, a fresh auth token is needed. The user might have changed or reset their password.

Two things that are useful when you are working an incident. The control step matters: the same token worked minutes earlier, so a 50173 is evidence that the revocation reached that token, not that the token was always bad. And the message blames a password change even when the admin only revoked sessions, so **do not read "the user might have changed or reset their password" as proof that a password change happened**. Revocation and password change produce the same wording here.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

In the lab tenant's sign-in logs, the test user's refresh-token activity shows up under **User sign-ins (non-interactive)**, not the interactive table, with the resource **Microsoft Graph** and Conditional Access **Not Applied**. Two grouped rows appeared for that user and resource: one Failure, and one Success with a count of 2. That matches the run (one failed replay after revocation, two successful token uses before it), but the portal's non-interactive view groups rows and doesn't show the error code, so the failure row is consistent with the 50173 rather than confirmed as it from the portal alone.

The grouping is the practical lesson: non-interactive rows are aggregated when user, app, IP, status and resource match, so a row count in that table is not a request count. Use the `# sign ins` value, or the equivalent field in your workspace, before you treat a number as a number of attempts.

50194.title: AADSTS50194 fix: single-tenant app used the /common endpoint
50194.description: AADSTS50194: a single-tenant app signed in through /common. Use your tenant ID in the authority URL; make the app multitenant only if you must.
50194.summary: AADSTS50194 means a single-tenant app registration sent its sign-in to the /common endpoint, which Microsoft Entra ID doesn't allow for single-tenant apps created after a cut-off date. It is a configuration error with low attack value. Fix it by putting your tenant ID in the app's authority URL, or make the app multitenant if it really must serve other tenants.
50194.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> Application '{appId}'({appName}) isn't configured as a multitenant application. Usage of the /common endpoint isn't supported for such applications created after '{time}'. Use a tenant-specific endpoint or configure the application to be multitenant.

The reference table gives this code no PascalCase name.

Every sign-in URL has a tenant part: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<issuer>/oauth2/v2.0/authorize`. Microsoft's protocol overview lists the allowed values: `common` for work, school and personal Microsoft accounts, `organizations` for work or school accounts only, `consumers` for personal accounts only, and *"tenant identifiers such as the tenant ID or domain name"*.

`/common` tells Entra "I don't know the user's tenant yet". That only makes sense for an app that accepts users from any tenant. App registrations are single-tenant by default: Microsoft's conversion guide says *"web app/API registrations in Microsoft Entra ID are single-tenant upon creation"*. When such an app sends its users to `/common`, Entra returns 50194.

The `{time}` placeholder is filled in the real message. Users on the UiPath forum report the text *"created after '10/15/2018'"*. By the message's own wording, single-tenant apps created before that date are not covered. Our reading: that is why an integration that worked for years can fail once someone sets it up again with a new app registration.

Who hits it, from user reports: SaaS connectors and automation tools that default to `/common`, such as WP Mail SMTP's Outlook mailer and the UiPath Microsoft 365 activities, and custom apps that copied a `/common` sample.

Related codes with their own page:

- [90133](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90133/): a device code request on `/common` or `/consumers`. Same family of problem, a specific flow.
- [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/): the app isn't found in the tenant at all. That is what you get when you point the app at the **wrong** tenant ID.
- [90002](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90002/): the tenant name or ID in the URL doesn't exist.

sections.text:
No. The app is set up wrong, and the error is Entra enforcing the app's own setting. A request to `/common` for a single-tenant app gets no token.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Every user of one app, starting the day it went live | The app or connector uses `/common` by default and the app registration is single-tenant. Fix the authority. |
| Started after someone created a new app registration for an existing integration | The new registration falls under the cut-off date in the message, the old one didn't. Likely, but unconfirmed. |
| A few users of a multitenant SaaS app | Not this code's pattern. Look at [50020](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50020/) or [16000](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/16000/) instead. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document whether 50194 is written to the sign-in logs, or in which tenant: the request names no tenant, so it is not obvious whose log would get the row. Check your workspace first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50194"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

If rows exist, find the apps that send `/common` requests. The app ID is in the error text as well as in `AppId`:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50194"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName, ResourceTenantId
| sort by Rows desc
```

If the union returns nothing, take the app ID from the error message the user saw. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"50194"`, not `50194`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50194?
sections.text:
**For the user:** nothing on your side. Send the full error message to whoever runs the app; it names the app ID.

**For developers:**
1. Keep the app single-tenant and use a tenant-specific authority: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/` instead of `.../common/`. The error message offers this first. Microsoft's registration quickstart says *"We recommend Single tenant only - <your tenant> for most applications."*
2. Microsoft's protocol overview accepts either *"the tenant ID or domain name"* there.
3. In third-party tools, look for a "Tenant", "Tenant ID" or "Directory ID" field. A UiPath forum post suggests setting the Tenant parameter of the Microsoft 365 activities; nobody in that thread confirmed it worked.

**For admins:**
1. Only make the app multitenant if people from other organizations really need it. Microsoft's steps: open the app registration, **Authentication**, **Supported account types**, and choose **Accounts in any organizational directory**. In the manifest that is `signInAudience` = `AzureADMultipleOrgs` instead of `AzureADMyOrg`.
2. Know what that switch does. Microsoft describes multitenant as *"when you want users in any Microsoft Entra tenant to be able to use your application"*. Some vendor guides, such as WP Mail SMTP's, tell you to switch to multitenant plus personal accounts. Our view: for an internal mail or automation app, the tenant-ID fix gives the same result without opening the app to other tenants.
3. If the switch fails, check the Application ID URI. Microsoft says that for multitenant apps it must be globally unique, and *"if the App ID URI doesn't follow this pattern, setting an application as multitenant fails."*

union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "50194"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName, ResourceTenantId
| sort by Rows desc
```

If the union returns nothing, take the app ID from the error message the user saw. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"50194"`, not `50194`.

fix.short: Developer or admin: replace `/common` in the app's sign-in URL or tenant setting with your tenant ID or domain. Only switch the app registration to multitenant (Authentication > Supported account types) if users from other organizations must sign in. User: report it to whoever runs the app.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** nothing on your side. Send the full error message to whoever runs the app; it names the app ID.

**For developers:**
1. Keep the app single-tenant and use a tenant-specific authority: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/` instead of `.../common/`. The error message offers this first. Microsoft's registration quickstart says *"We recommend Single tenant only - <your tenant> for most applications."*
2. Microsoft's protocol overview accepts either *"the tenant ID or domain name"* there.
3. In third-party tools, look for a "Tenant", "Tenant ID" or "Directory ID" field. A UiPath forum post suggests setting the Tenant parameter of the Microsoft 365 activities; nobody in that thread confirmed it worked.

**For admins:**
1. Only make the app multitenant if people from other organizations really need it. Microsoft's steps: open the app registration, **Authentication**, **Supported account types**, and choose **Accounts in any organizational directory**. In the manifest that is `signInAudience` = `AzureADMultipleOrgs` instead of `AzureADMyOrg`.
2. Know what that switch does. Microsoft describes multitenant as *"when you want users in any Microsoft Entra tenant to be able to use your application"*. Some vendor guides, such as WP Mail SMTP's, tell you to switch to multitenant plus personal accounts. Our view: for an internal mail or automation app, the tenant-ID fix gives the same result without opening the app to other tenants.
3. If the switch fails, check the Application ID URI. Microsoft says that for multitenant apps it must be globally unique, and *"if the App ID URI doesn't follow this pattern, setting an application as multitenant fails."*

50196.name: LoopDetected
50196.title: AADSTS50196: App is stuck in a sign-in loop (fix)
50196.description: AADSTS50196: Entra detected a client loop, the app repeats the same token request. Usually missing token caching. Fix for apps and KQL.
50196.summary: AADSTS50196 means Entra detected a client loop: the app sent the same request too many times in a short period. Microsoft says the usual cause is missing or broken token caching. It points to a faulty app, not usually to an attacker. The fix is in the app: cache tokens, call the silent method first, and stop retrying on errors.
50196.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **LoopDetected**: A client loop has been detected. Check the app’s logic to ensure that token caching is implemented, and that error conditions are handled correctly. The app has made too many of the same request in too short a period, indicating that it is in a faulty state or is abusively requesting tokens.

Entra is throttling one client. The app asked for the same token over and over, and Entra stopped answering it with tokens.

Microsoft's MSAL.NET throttling page says when this happens: *"Microsoft Entra ID throttles applications when you call the authentication API too frequently. Most often this happens when token caching is not used."* It also says how it shows up. For user-facing calls, the app gets an `invalid_grant` error with the message *"AADSTS50196: The server terminated an operation because it encountered a loop while processing a request"*. For the client credentials grant (app-only tokens), Entra replies with `429 Too Many Requests` and a `Retry-After: 60` header instead. Our reading: an app-only loop may therefore not show up as 50196 at all, but as throttling with no AADSTS code in the client.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Microsoft's description allows two readings: the app *"is in a faulty state or is abusively requesting tokens."* In practice the first is far more common, and the cause sits in the app's code.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One app, many users, starting on the day of a release | A bug in the new version: token cache broken, or a retry loop. |
| One user, one app, one device | That device's token cache is broken or the app is stuck after an error. Often a browser tab or desktop client stuck in a redirect loop. |
| A script or tool (PowerShell, CLI, a sync job) | The script asks for a new token on every call instead of reusing one. |
| One IP, many users, an app you don't recognise | Worth a look, though Microsoft doesn't describe this case. It could be an automated tool replaying tokens at scale. Check what else that IP did. |

Most likely, 50196 is a symptom of request volume, not of a credential being guessed: the user was already signed in.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 50196 is logged in. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50196"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which apps, users and clients loop:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50196"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            Agents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName
| sort by Rows desc
```

A new looping app or a sudden spike. This compares the last day with the 14 days before it:

```kusto
let recent =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50196"
    | summarize RecentRows = count(), RecentUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppId, AppDisplayName;
let baseline =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(15d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ResultType == "50196"
    | summarize BaselineRows = count() by AppId;
recent
| join kind=leftouter baseline on AppId
| extend BaselineRows = coalesce(BaselineRows, 0)
| where BaselineRows == 0 or RecentRows > 3 * (BaselineRows / 14.0)
| project AppDisplayName, AppId, RecentRows, RecentUsers, BaselineRows
| sort by RecentRows desc
```

The factor of 3 is a starting point. Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource ID match, so a single row can stand for many requests. Count rows to compare apps, not to count requests.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS50196?
sections.text:
**For the user:** close the app or browser tab completely and open it again. If that doesn't help, sign out of the app, clear its cached sign-in, and sign in again. If it keeps happening, report it to whoever runs the app; the fix is in the app.

**For developers:** Microsoft's throttling page lists the usual causes:
1. *"Token caching is not setup correctly."*
2. Not calling the silent method (`AcquireTokenSilent`) before an interactive or username/password call.
3. Asking for a scope that doesn't apply to personal Microsoft accounts, such as `User.ReadBasic.All`, *"resulting in cache misses."*

Reuse tokens until they are close to expiry. Don't retry in a tight loop when a call fails. For app-only tokens, honour the `Retry-After` header. MSAL throws `MsalThrottledServiceException` or `MsalThrottledUiRequiredException` when it throttles on the client side; the page notes that *"If MSAL would not apply client-side throttling the application would still not be able to acquire tokens."*

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app, then give its owner the time window and the user agents.
2. If it is a script running under a user account, check that it gets one token and reuses it.
3. If an unknown app or a single IP produces 50196 for many users, look at that IP's other sign-ins before you close it as a bug.

51004.name: UserAccountNotInDirectory
51004.title: AADSTS51004 fix: user account not in the directory
51004.description: AADSTS51004: the user has no account in the tenant the app chose. Wrong tenant, missing guest invite or a federation ID mismatch. Low attack value.
51004.summary: AADSTS51004 means the signing-in user has no account in the tenant the app chose. Microsoft says the app likely picked the wrong tenant; if the user should have access, add them as a guest. Users also report it with federated sign-in (Okta, Google Workspace) when the identity from the IdP matches no Entra user. Low attack value.
51004.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserAccountNotInDirectory**: The user account doesn’t exist in the directory. An application likely chose the wrong tenant to sign into, and the currently logged in user was prevented from doing so since they did not exist in your tenant. If this user should be able to log in, add them as a guest. For further information, please visit add B2B users.

The user is known somewhere, but not in the tenant this sign-in went to. Microsoft's first guess is an app that sent the user to the wrong tenant.

The message users see reads like this example from Microsoft Q&A: *"AADSTS51004: The user account {id} does not exist in the {tenant ID} directory. To sign into this application, the account must be added to the directory."* The tenant ID in the message tells you which directory was asked.

### 51004 or 50034?
The wording is almost the same, so the code is what tells them apart. [50034](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50034/) (*UserAccountNotFound*) is the one Microsoft ties to a mistyped username. When a token request was sent for a username that doesn't exist in a lab tenant, Entra returned 50034, not 51004 (see the 50034 page). Microsoft's 51004 description talks about *"the currently logged in user"*. Our reading: 51004 tends to come after the user has already been identified, by their home tenant or by a federated identity provider, and Entra then can't find a matching account in the target tenant. 50034 is the plain "no such username" answer. Microsoft doesn't document the split in those words.

[50020](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50020/) is a close neighbour too: an account from another identity provider that isn't a user or guest in the tenant. Both point to the same fix for outside users: add them as a guest.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS51004 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserAccountNotInDirectory**: The user account doesn’t exist in the directory. An application likely chose the wrong tenant to sign into, and the currently logged in user was prevented from doing so since they did not exist in your tenant. If this user should be able to log in, add them as a guest. For further information, please visit add B2B users.

The user is known somewhere, but not in the tenant this sign-in went to. Microsoft's first guess is an app that sent the user to the wrong tenant.

The message users see reads like this example from Microsoft Q&A: *"AADSTS51004: The user account {id} does not exist in the {tenant ID} directory. To sign into this application, the account must be added to the directory."* The tenant ID in the message tells you which directory was asked.

### 51004 or 50034?
The wording is almost the same, so the code is what tells them apart. [50034](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50034/) (*UserAccountNotFound*) is the one Microsoft ties to a mistyped username. When a token request was sent for a username that doesn't exist in a lab tenant, Entra returned 50034, not 51004 (see the 50034 page). Microsoft's 51004 description talks about *"the currently logged in user"*. Our reading: 51004 tends to come after the user has already been identified, by their home tenant or by a federated identity provider, and Entra then can't find a matching account in the target tenant. 50034 is the plain "no such username" answer. Microsoft doesn't document the split in those words.

[50020](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50020/) is a close neighbour too: an account from another identity provider that isn't a user or guest in the tenant. Both point to the same fix for outside users: add them as a guest.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Our reading: the user has already proven who they are somewhere; they just aren't in this directory.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A user from another organisation opening your app, or Teams switching into your tenant | Wrong tenant or no guest account. Users report this often in Teams and other Microsoft 365 apps. Benign. Invite them as a guest if they need access. |
| Users of a federated domain (Okta, Google Workspace, other SAML IdP) failing after the IdP login | The IdP authenticated them, but no Entra user matches what the IdP sent. Okta and Microsoft Q&A users report this. A provisioning or ImmutableId problem, not an attack. |
| New hires failing while existing users work, on a federated domain | The account was created at the IdP but never provisioned to Entra ID. |
| A former employee or a renamed user | Something still uses the old identity. Find and update it. |

Unlike [50034](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50034/), there is no documented enumeration pattern for 51004. Our reading is that it has low value for an attacker testing usernames, because it follows a sign-in that already happened somewhere else. A burst of 51004 for many different users from one IP is still worth a look; the KQL below finds it.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 51004 lands in. Check where it lands:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "51004"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which apps send users to a tenant they're not in, and where the users come from:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "51004"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            SampleUsers = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10),
            HomeTenants = make_set(HomeTenantId, 5),
            Protocols = make_set(AuthenticationProtocol, 3)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Users desc
```

Many different accounts from one IP, the shape worth a second look (10 is a starting point; tune it to your tenant):

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "51004"
| summarize Accounts = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Attempts = count(),
            Sample = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 20)
          by IPAddress
| where Accounts >= 10
| sort by Accounts desc
```

For a user who doesn't exist in the tenant, which column holds the name is not documented. `UserPrincipalName` is a reasonable first guess; also check `SignInIdentifier`. A federated domain with many 51004 rows from your own egress IPs points at provisioning, not an attacker. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"51004"`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- Our reading: Conditional Access plays no part, because there is no user object in the tenant for a policy to match.
- If the user is later added as a guest, the target tenant's Conditional Access policies apply to them from then on.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS51004?
sections.text:
**For the user:** check that you are signed in with the right account. In Teams or a browser with several accounts, sign out and sign in again with the account your organisation gave you. If you are from another organisation, ask the app owner to invite you as a guest.

**For developers:** check which tenant your app sends users to. Likely, but not documented: an app hard-wired to one tenant ID sends outside users there, and they fail. Use the tenant the user belongs to, or ask the tenant owner to invite them.

**For admins:**
1. External user who needs access: add them as a guest, as Microsoft's description says. In the Entra admin center (at least User Administrator): **Users** > **New user** > **Invite external user**. Microsoft notes *"The guest user must then redeem their invitation to access resources."*
2. Federated domain (Okta, Google Workspace, other SAML IdP): the user must exist in Entra ID first. Microsoft's federated sign-in docs for Windows devices state that *"each Google Workspace user requires a matching account defined in Microsoft Entra ID"*, and that Entra *"searches for a matching user object in the tenant by using an attribute called ImmutableId"*. The match is case-sensitive. Check the account exists and that its `OnPremisesImmutableId` matches what the IdP sends. Okta's KB describes this exact mismatch as a cause of 51004.
3. New users failing only: check provisioning from the IdP actually created them in Entra ID.
4. Renamed or removed user: find what still uses the old identity and update it.

An application likely chose the wrong tenant to sign into, and the currently logged in user was prevented from doing so since they did not exist in your tenant. If this user should be able to log in, add them as a guest. For further information, please visit add B2B users.

attackSignal.label: Low: usually configuration or user error

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
Usually not. Our reading: the user has already proven who they are somewhere; they just aren't in this directory.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A user from another organisation opening your app, or Teams switching into your tenant | Wrong tenant or no guest account. Users report this often in Teams and other Microsoft 365 apps. Benign. Invite them as a guest if they need access. |
| Users of a federated domain (Okta, Google Workspace, other SAML IdP) failing after the IdP login | The IdP authenticated them, but no Entra user matches what the IdP sent. Okta and Microsoft Q&A users report this. A provisioning or ImmutableId problem, not an attack. |
| New hires failing while existing users work, on a federated domain | The account was created at the IdP but never provisioned to Entra ID. |
| A former employee or a renamed user | Something still uses the old identity. Find and update it. |

Unlike [50034](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50034/), there is no documented enumeration pattern for 51004. Our reading is that it has low value for an attacker testing usernames, because it follows a sign-in that already happened somewhere else. A burst of 51004 for many different users from one IP is still worth a look; the KQL below finds it.

conditionalAccess.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
conditionalAccess.text:
- Our reading: Conditional Access plays no part, because there is no user object in the tenant for a policy to match.

53000.name: DeviceNotCompliant
53000.title: AADSTS53000: Device not compliant
53000.description: AADSTS53000: Conditional Access requires a compliant device and this one isn't. The password worked; on a privileged account, investigate. With KQL.
53000.summary: AADSTS53000 means a Conditional Access policy requires a compliant device and the device signing in isn't compliant. The password was already accepted. Usually it is a user on a personal or unenrolled device. For a privileged account on a new device or IP, treat it as a valid credential in the wrong hands.
53000.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **DeviceNotCompliant**: Conditional Access policy requires a compliant device, and the device isn't compliant. The user must enroll their device with an approved MDM provider like Intune. For additional information, please visit Conditional Access device remediation.

Conditional Access only evaluates after the first factor succeeds. So a 53000 row means the username and password (and any earlier step) were accepted, and the device grant control is what stopped the sign-in. `ConditionalAccessStatus` on these rows is `failure`.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS53000 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **DeviceNotCompliant**: Conditional Access policy requires a compliant device, and the device isn't compliant. The user must enroll their device with an approved MDM provider like Intune. For additional information, please visit Conditional Access device remediation.

Conditional Access only evaluates after the first factor succeeds. So a 53000 row means the username and password (and any earlier step) were accepted, and the device grant control is what stopped the sign-in. `ConditionalAccessStatus` on these rows is `failure`.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Most 53000 rows are users on a personal laptop or phone, a new device that hasn't finished Intune enrollment, or a device that has drifted out of compliance.

The security reading comes from what the code proves: **someone with a working credential tried to use it from a device you don't manage.** That is exactly what an attacker's machine looks like.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Known user, known device, compliance recently lapsed | Benign. Fix the device. |
| New user onboarding, first days | Benign. Device not enrolled yet. |
| Privileged account, device never seen before, unfamiliar IP or country | **Investigate.** The credential works and is being used off-estate. |
| 53000 shortly after a phishing click, or after 50126 failures from the same IP | **Treat the password as compromised.** |
| 53000 in non-interactive logs from an unexpected IP | A refresh token being redeemed from an unmanaged device. Possible token replay (reasoning, not a Microsoft statement). |

Why it matters: an adversary-in-the-middle phishing kit can capture a password, the MFA result and the session cookie, but it runs on the attacker's infrastructure, not on an enrolled device. A compliant-device requirement is one of the controls that still holds after MFA is phished. A 53000 from a source that isn't the user, for an account that otherwise passed MFA, is that control working, and a reason to ask how the earlier layers were passed.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Who is hitting the compliant-device requirement, and from which devices:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "53000"
| extend DeviceId    = tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId),
         DeviceName  = tostring(DeviceDetail.displayName),
         OS          = tostring(DeviceDetail.operatingSystem),
         TrustType   = tostring(DeviceDetail.trustType),
         IsCompliant = tostring(DeviceDetail.isCompliant),
         Country     = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Countries = make_set(Country, 5),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5)
          by UserPrincipalName, DeviceId, DeviceName, OS, TrustType, IsCompliant
| sort by Attempts desc
```

An empty `DeviceId` means the device isn't registered in Entra at all, which is the more interesting case for an attacker machine.

An unregistered device was blocked, then the **same user from the same IP** succeeded somewhere else on the same day. That can mean the credential reached an app or client the device policy doesn't cover:

```kusto
let blocked =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "53000"
    | where isempty(tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId))
    | summarize BlockedIPs = make_set(IPAddress) by UserPrincipalName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=inner blocked on UserPrincipalName
| where set_has_element(BlockedIPs, IPAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed,
          ConditionalAccessStatus, DeviceDetail
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

Run the first query against `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs` as well. There `DeviceDetail` and `LocationDetails` are **string** columns, so wrap them: `parse_json(DeviceDetail).deviceId`.

The `DeviceDetail` property names above (`deviceId`, `displayName`, `operatingSystem`, `trustType`, `isCompliant`) follow the Microsoft Graph `signIn` device detail object. Check them against one row in your own workspace before building a rule on them.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 53000 is produced **by** Conditional Access. Open the sign-in, select the **Conditional Access** tab, and Microsoft's troubleshooting guide says it "shows the specific policy or policies that resulted in the sign-in interruption."
- A policy that requires a compliant device only protects the apps and users it targets. Excluded apps, excluded users and report-only policies are where a stolen credential still works.
- A policy that accepts a compliant device **or** MFA as alternatives lets a phished MFA result satisfy it. For admin accounts, require the device control on its own.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS53000?
sections.text:
**For the user:** enroll the device with your organization's MDM (for example Intune). If it is already enrolled, ask IT which compliance setting is failing.

**For admins:**
1. Open the failed sign-in and confirm which policy and which device it was. Compare the device ID with the user's enrolled devices.
2. If the device is unknown and the account is privileged or the IP is unfamiliar, treat the password as compromised: reset it, revoke sessions (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`) and review recent sign-ins for the same IP.
3. If it is a real user on a real device, fix compliance rather than adding an exclusion. Every exclusion is a path for a stolen credential.

53001.name: DeviceNotDomainJoined
53001.title: AADSTS53001: Device not domain joined
53001.description: AADSTS53001: Conditional Access requires a hybrid joined device and this one isn't. From an unknown IP, check whether a valid password is in use. KQL.
53001.summary: AADSTS53001 means a Conditional Access policy requires a domain-joined (hybrid joined) device and the device signing in isn't one. The password was already accepted. Usually it is a user on a personal or cloud-only device. From an unknown device on an unfamiliar IP, it means a working credential is being used outside your estate.
53001.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **DeviceNotDomainJoined**: Conditional Access policy requires a domain joined device, and the device isn't domain joined. Have the user use a domain joined device.

Most likely (interpretation) this is the Conditional Access grant control that requires a hybrid joined device (on-premises domain joined and registered in Entra ID). Conditional Access only runs after the first factor succeeds, so the credential was accepted before this block. `ConditionalAccessStatus` on these rows is `failure`.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS53001 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **DeviceNotDomainJoined**: Conditional Access policy requires a domain joined device, and the device isn't domain joined. Have the user use a domain joined device.

Most likely (interpretation) this is the Conditional Access grant control that requires a hybrid joined device (on-premises domain joined and registered in Entra ID). Conditional Access only runs after the first factor succeeds, so the credential was accepted before this block. `ConditionalAccessStatus` on these rows is `failure`.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Typical causes are a user on a home PC or phone, an Entra-joined (cloud-only) laptop hitting a policy written for hybrid-joined machines, or a hybrid join that hasn't finished syncing.

The security reading is the same as 53000 (non-compliant device): the code proves **a working credential was used from a device that isn't one of yours.**

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Known user, Entra-joined corporate device | Benign. Policy expects hybrid join; device is cloud-joined. |
| New device, hybrid join pending | Benign. Wait for sync or check the join state. |
| Unregistered device (empty device ID), unfamiliar IP or country | **Investigate.** Someone has the password and is using it off-estate. |
| 53001 after a 50126 run from the same IP | **The spray found a correct password.** The device policy is the only thing that stopped it. |

A device-based grant is a strong control against stolen credentials and against adversary-in-the-middle phishing, because the attacker's machine is not joined to your domain. When a 53001 row shows `AuthenticationRequirement` as `multiFactorAuthentication` and the MFA step as satisfied, the password and MFA layers were already passed and the device requirement was the only layer that held. For a legitimate user on a personal device that is friction; for an unknown device on an unfamiliar IP it means the earlier layers didn't stop whoever holds the credential.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
53001 from devices that aren't registered in Entra at all:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "53001"
| extend DeviceId   = tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId),
         TrustType  = tostring(DeviceDetail.trustType),
         OS         = tostring(DeviceDetail.operatingSystem),
         Country    = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Countries = make_set(Country, 5),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by UserPrincipalName, DeviceId, TrustType, OS
| extend Unregistered = isempty(DeviceId)
| sort by Unregistered desc, Attempts desc
```

Did the same IP fail passwords first? That pattern means a spray succeeded:

```kusto
let deviceBlocked =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType in ("53001", "53000")
    | distinct IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where IPAddress in (deviceBlocked)
| where ResultType in ("50126", "50053", "53000", "53001", "0")
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Results = make_set(ResultType)
          by IPAddress
| where Users > 1
| sort by Users desc
```

For `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, `DeviceDetail` and `LocationDetails` are **string** columns: use `parse_json(DeviceDetail).trustType`. The property names used here follow the Microsoft Graph `signIn` device detail object; check them against one row in your own workspace before building a rule on them.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 53001 is produced **by** Conditional Access. The **Conditional Access** tab on the sign-in shows which policy blocked it.
- If your fleet is moving to Entra-joined devices, a hybrid-join-only policy will produce 53001 for legitimate corporate devices. Combining "hybrid joined" with "compliant device" as alternatives is the common fix.
- As with 53000, pairing the device control with MFA as "require one of" lets a phished MFA result through. Keep a device requirement on its own for admin roles.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS53001?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign in from your corporate, domain-joined computer. If you are already on one, ask IT to check that its join to Entra ID has completed.

**For admins:**
1. Open the sign-in, note the policy and the device. An empty device ID means an unregistered device.
2. If the device is unknown and the IP unfamiliar, treat the password as compromised: reset it, revoke sessions, and check the same IP for other users.
3. If it is a legitimate cloud-joined device, adjust the policy to accept compliant devices too, rather than excluding the user.

A device-based grant is a strong control against stolen credentials and against adversary-in-the-middle phishing, because the attacker's machine is not joined to your domain. When a 53001 row shows `AuthenticationRequirement` as `multiFactorAuthentication` and the MFA step as satisfied, the password and MFA layers were already passed and the device requirement was the only layer that held. For a legitimate user on a personal device that is friction; for an unknown device on an unfamiliar IP it means the earlier layers didn't stop whoever holds the credential.

conditionalAccess.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
conditionalAccess.text:
- 53001 is produced **by** Conditional Access. The **Conditional Access** tab on the sign-in shows which policy blocked it.

- As with 53000, pairing the device control with MFA as "require one of" lets a phished MFA result through. Keep a device requirement on its own for admin roles.

fix.steps:

**For admins:**
1. Open the sign-in, note the policy and the device. An empty device ID means an unregistered device.

53003.name: BlockedByConditionalAccess
53003.title: AADSTS53003: Access blocked by Conditional Access
53003.description: AADSTS53003: Conditional Access blocked the sign-in after the first factor was accepted. From an unknown country, a valid credential was stopped. KQL.
53003.summary: AADSTS53003 means a Conditional Access policy blocked the sign-in or its grant controls weren't met. The first factor was already accepted, because Conditional Access runs after it. From an unknown IP or country, read it as a valid first factor (password or passwordless) in someone else's hands, stopped by policy. The ConditionalAccessPolicies column names the policy.
53003.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **BlockedByConditionalAccess**: Access has been blocked by Conditional Access policies. The access policy does not allow token issuance. If this is unexpected, see the Conditional Access policy that applied to this request or contact your administrator.

The row has `ConditionalAccessStatus` = `failure`. Microsoft defines that as: *"The sign-in satisfied the user and application condition of at least one Conditional Access policy and grant controls are either not satisfied or set to block access."*

sections.heading: What does AADSTS53003 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **BlockedByConditionalAccess**: Access has been blocked by Conditional Access policies. The access policy does not allow token issuance. If this is unexpected, see the Conditional Access policy that applied to this request or contact your administrator.

The row has `ConditionalAccessStatus` = `failure`. Microsoft defines that as: *"The sign-in satisfied the user and application condition of at least one Conditional Access policy and grant controls are either not satisfied or set to block access."*

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
The key fact is the order of evaluation. Microsoft's Conditional Access overview states: *"Conditional Access policies are enforced after first-factor authentication is completed."* So a 53003 means **the password (or other first factor) was correct**. That's why Microsoft's password spray playbook lists *"53003 - User blocked by Conditional Access"* among the events to review.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A user on a new phone, a personal laptop, or travelling | The policy doing its job on a real user. Benign, possibly a support ticket. |
| A block right after a CA policy change, hitting many users | A policy scoped too wide. Configuration, not attack. |
| Non-interactive rows for an app that worked yesterday | A token refresh blocked by a new or changed policy. |
| 53003 from an IP or country the user has never used, with no matching travel | **A valid first factor in someone else's hands**, stopped by policy (T1078.004). Most often a password, but passwordless sign-in (passkey, Windows Hello, certificate) reaches the same point, so check the authentication method in the sign-in log before you assume a password. Treat that credential as compromised. |
| 53003 from an IP that also produced many 50126 across users | The spray found a correct password. CA was the only thing that stopped it. Spray means passwords, so this row does not apply to passwordless users. |
| Repeated 53003 for one user from an attacker IP, with changing clients or user agents | Someone with the password is trying to find a client or app your policies don't cover. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which policies are blocking, and for whom. `ConditionalAccessPolicies` is a dynamic array in `SigninLogs`. Expand it and keep the policies whose result is `failure`:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "53003"
| mv-expand Policy = ConditionalAccessPolicies
| where tostring(Policy.result) == "failure"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed,
          PolicyName = tostring(Policy.displayName)
| summarize Blocks = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10)
          by PolicyName
| sort by Blocks desc
```

53003 from IPs that also sprayed. These users have a known-good password:

```kusto
let sprayIPs =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "50126"
    | summarize FailedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by IPAddress
    | where FailedUsers >= 10
    | project IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "53003"
| where IPAddress in (sprayIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

For token refreshes, run the first query against `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`. There `ConditionalAccessPolicies` is a **string**, so expand `parse_json(ConditionalAccessPolicies)` instead:

```kusto
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "53003"
| mv-expand Policy = parse_json(ConditionalAccessPolicies)
| where tostring(Policy.result) == "failure"
| summarize Blocks = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName)
          by PolicyName = tostring(Policy.displayName), AppDisplayName
| sort by Blocks desc
```

The `displayName` and `result` field names inside each policy entry follow the Microsoft Graph sign-in object. Run the query once without the `where` filter to see the values your workspace holds.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 53003 **is** Conditional Access. The policy either blocks outright or requires something the sign-in couldn't provide.
- Microsoft's troubleshooting guide says the **Conditional Access** tab on the sign-in entry *"shows the specific policy or policies that resulted in the sign-in interruption."* Start there for a single case.
- A 53003 with an unexpected source does not mean you are safe. CA stopped this attempt. The attacker still has the credential and can try other apps, clients and locations.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS53003?
sections.text:
**For the user:** the block is deliberate. Try again from a company device, a supported app, or your usual location. If it still fails, give your admin the time of the attempt and the correlation ID from the error page.

**For admins:**
1. Open the sign-in entry, go to the **Conditional Access** tab, and find the policy with result Failure. Check which condition matched and which grant control failed.
2. If the block was wrong for a real user, fix the policy scope or help the user meet the control. Don't add a broad exclusion to make one ticket go away.
3. If the source is unfamiliar, treat the credential as compromised: reset the password (or remove the passkey), revoke sessions (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`), and look for other sign-ins from the same IP.
4. Look for successful sign-ins from the same IP to apps or clients your policy doesn't cover.

54005.title: AADSTS54005: Authorization code already used (fix)
54005.description: AADSTS54005: an authorization code was redeemed twice. Usually a double callback or retry in the app. Low attack value. Fix and KQL included.
54005.summary: AADSTS54005 means an app tried to redeem an OAuth 2.0 authorization code that had already been redeemed. Usually the app sent the same code twice: a double callback, a retry, or a page reload. It is mostly an app bug with low attack value. The app should get a new code, or use the refresh token it already has.
54005.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> OAuth2 Authorization code was already redeemed, please retry with a new valid code or use an existing refresh token.

In the authorization code flow the app gets a `code` at its redirect URI and then sends it to the `/token` endpoint to get tokens. 54005 means a code reached the token endpoint a second time after it had already been exchanged.

Microsoft's authorization code flow page says *"Authorization codes are short lived"* and lists the generic token-endpoint error for a bad code: `invalid_grant`, *"The authorization code or PKCE code verifier is invalid or has expired."* Our reading: the app sees `invalid_grant`, and `AADSTS54005` is in the error description and `error_codes`. Microsoft's error reference tells developers to branch on the `error` field and not on the AADSTS number.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS54005 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> OAuth2 Authorization code was already redeemed, please retry with a new valid code or use an existing refresh token.

In the authorization code flow the app gets a `code` at its redirect URI and then sends it to the `/token` endpoint to get tokens. 54005 means a code reached the token endpoint a second time after it had already been exchanged.

Microsoft's authorization code flow page says *"Authorization codes are short lived"* and lists the generic token-endpoint error for a bad code: `invalid_grant`, *"The authorization code or PKCE code verifier is invalid or has expired."* Our reading: the app sees `invalid_grant`, and `AADSTS54005` is in the error description and `error_codes`. Microsoft's error reference tells developers to branch on the `error` field and not on the AADSTS number.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. The common causes are in the app:

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A success and a 54005 for the same user and app, seconds apart, same IP | The app redeemed the code twice: two callback handlers, a retry after a slow response, or a framework that runs the callback twice. The first call worked. Benign. |
| 54005 after the user reloads or uses the back button on the callback page | The page sends the old code again. Benign. |
| 54005 for many users of one web app, from your own server's IP | The app's callback code has a bug. Fix the app. |
| 54005 from a different IP than the success, for the same user and app | Our interpretation, not documented: someone else got hold of the code and tried it after the real app. The refusal is the protection working, but find out how the code leaked (logs, referrer headers, a shared proxy). |

Going by Microsoft's description, the second redemption gets nothing: a code that was already used can't be exchanged for tokens again.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 54005 is logged in. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "54005"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which apps produce it, and from how many IPs:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "54005"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            SampleIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

54005 from an IP that is different from the one that signed in successfully to the same app shortly before. This is the pattern from the last table row above, which Microsoft doesn't document as an attack signal:

```kusto
let window = 10m;
let reuse =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "54005"
    | project ReuseTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName, ReuseIP = IPAddress;
let success =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppId, SuccessIP = IPAddress;
reuse
| join kind=inner success on UserPrincipalName, AppId
| where SuccessTime between ((ReuseTime - window) .. ReuseTime)
| where ReuseIP != SuccessIP
| summarize Reuses = count(), ReuseIPs = make_set(ReuseIP, 5), SuccessIPs = make_set(SuccessIP, 5)
          by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| sort by Reuses desc
```

The 10-minute window is a starting point. Expect false positives: a web app redeems the code from its server, so its IP can differ from the browser IP in the user's interactive sign-in. Compare against the app's known server IPs before you treat a hit as suspicious. Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource ID match.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS54005?
sections.text:
**For the user:** start the sign-in again from the app's start page, not by reloading the page you landed on. If it keeps happening, report it to whoever runs the app.

**For developers:**
1. Redeem each code once. Make the callback handler idempotent: if a second request arrives with the same code, don't send it to `/token` again.
2. Don't retry a code redemption automatically after a timeout. Start a new sign-in instead.
3. After the first redemption, use the refresh token, as Microsoft's description says. The auth code flow page: *"Provide the `refresh_token` instead of the `code`."* Also: *"Refresh tokens aren't revoked when used to acquire new access tokens. You're expected to discard the old refresh token."*
4. Use MSAL instead of hand-written token code; it handles the redemption and cache for you.

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and hand the time window to its developer.
2. If the third query shows reuse from IPs that aren't the app's servers, treat it as a possible leak of authorization codes and review where codes could be logged or forwarded.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "54005"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable

```kusto
let window = 10m;
let reuse =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Compare against the app's known server IPs before you treat a hit as suspicious. Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource ID match.

fix.short: Developer: redeem each authorization code once, make the callback handler idempotent, don't retry a redemption after a timeout, and use the refresh token after the first redemption. User: start the sign-in again from the app's start page instead of reloading.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** start the sign-in again from the app's start page, not by reloading the page you landed on. If it keeps happening, report it to whoever runs the app.

**For developers:**
1. Redeem each code once. Make the callback handler idempotent: if a second request arrives with the same code, don't send it to `/token` again.
2. Don't retry a code redemption automatically after a timeout. Start a new sign-in instead.
3. After the first redemption, use the refresh token, as Microsoft's description says. The auth code flow page: *"Provide the `refresh_token` instead of the `code`."* Also: *"Refresh tokens aren't revoked when used to acquire new access tokens. You're expected to discard the old refresh token."*
4. Use MSAL instead of hand-written token code; it handles the redemption and cache for you.

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and hand the time window to its developer.
2. If the third query shows reuse from IPs that aren't the app's servers, treat it as a possible leak of authorization codes and review where codes could be logged or forwarded.

65001.name: DelegationDoesNotExist
65001.title: AADSTS65001: User or admin has not consented to the app
65001.description: AADSTS65001: no user or admin has consented to the permissions an app requested. Consent phishing context: watch apps that flip to success. KQL.
65001.summary: AADSTS65001 means an app asked for a token for permissions that no user or admin has consented to. For a new or misconfigured app it is routine. The security angle is consent phishing: watch for an unfamiliar app that flips from 65001 to success, then check the audit log for "Consent to application" and IsAdminConsent.
65001.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **DelegationDoesNotExist**: The user or administrator hasn't consented to use the application with ID X. Send an interactive authorization request for this user and resource.

The app asked for a token, but the permission grant it needs doesn't exist. The fix Microsoft names is an interactive request, which is where the consent prompt appears.

A sibling: **[65004](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/65004/) UserDeclinedConsent**, *"User declined to consent to access the app."* That is the user saying no at the prompt.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request with the **correct** password for a test user, to a lab app nobody had consented to. The password was right, so the request got past the credential check and stopped at the missing consent. Instead of a token or an MFA prompt, Entra returned `AADSTS65001` with this first line:

> AADSTS65001: The user or administrator has not consented to use the application with ID '{app-id}' named 'lab-signin-client'.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint.

The same attempt in the lab tenant's sign-in log (Entra admin center, interactive user sign-ins), with identifiers left out:

| Field | Value in the lab row |
|---|---|
| Status | Interrupted |
| Sign-in error code | 65001 |
| Application | lab-signin-client |
| Authentication requirement | Single-factor authentication |
| Conditional Access | Not Applied |
| User type | Member |

The row is logged as **Interrupted**, not Failure: the password was right and the sign-in waits for consent. A portal view filtered on Status = Failure misses it; filter on the error code instead. The KQL below was run on the lab rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). Not tested yet: the first query needs a successful sign-in after the consent error and the second needs a consent event in `AuditLogs`, and the exported lab rows have neither.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
On its own, no. 65001 shows up whenever an app is used before anyone has consented to it, or when a developer adds a new permission and forgets the consent step.

The security relevance is **consent phishing** (illicit consent grant). Microsoft describes the attack like this:

> the attacker creates a registered application in Microsoft Entra ID that requests access to data such as contact information, email, or documents. The attacker then tricks an end user into granting that application consent … After the illicit application is granted consent, it has account-level access to data without the need for an organizational account. Normal remediation steps (for example, resetting passwords or requiring multifactor authentication (MFA)) aren't effective against this type of attack

65001 is the state the attacker needs to get past. The interesting moment is when it stops. The [consent phishing guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/investigate-consent-phishing-entra-id/) covers the full investigation and the removal steps.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 65001 for a known, internal app right after a permission change | A developer added a permission and consent wasn't granted yet. Benign. |
| 65001 for an app ID you don't recognise, from several users in a short window | Users were sent a link to an app nobody approved. Look at the app and who published it. |
| An unfamiliar app goes from 65001 to successful sign-ins | **Someone consented.** Find the consent event in the audit log and check whether it was user or admin consent. |
| 65001 for an unknown app in non-interactive or service principal sign-ins | Something is trying to use permissions it was never granted. Identify the app before anyone consents to it. |

The table above is reasoning built on Microsoft's attack description, not a list of Microsoft detections.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Apps that had 65001 and then had successful user sign-ins:

```kusto
let window = 7d;
let missingConsent =
    union
        (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, AppId, AppDisplayName, UserPrincipalName, ResultType),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, AppId, AppDisplayName, UserPrincipalName, ResultType)
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(window)
    | where ResultType == "65001"
    | summarize FirstMissing = min(TimeGenerated), MissingUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName)
              by AppId, AppDisplayName;
union
    (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, AppId, UserPrincipalName, ResultType),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, AppId, UserPrincipalName, ResultType)
| where TimeGenerated > ago(window)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=inner missingConsent on AppId
| where TimeGenerated > FirstMissing
| summarize FirstSuccessAfter = min(TimeGenerated), SuccessUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName, FirstMissing, MissingUsers
| sort by FirstSuccessAfter desc
```

Then find the consent itself. Microsoft's guidance is to search the **Microsoft Purview (unified) audit log** for the activity **"Consent to application"** and check `IsAdminConsent`. The Entra audit log records the same operation; in Log Analytics that is the `AuditLogs` table:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName == "Consent to application"
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
         AppName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
         AppObjectId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id),
         ConsentDetails = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, AppName, AppObjectId, Result, ConsentDetails
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

`ConsentDetails` holds the modified properties of the grant, which is where the admin-consent flag and the granted permissions appear. In the Entra audit log those are the properties named `ConsentContext.IsAdminConsent` and `ConsentAction.Permissions`, not a top-level `IsAdminConsent` field as in Purview. The exact field paths inside `InitiatedBy` and `TargetResources` vary; check them against a real event in your workspace before you build an alert on them.

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"65001"`, not `65001`.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 65001 isn't caused by Conditional Access. It is a missing permission grant.
- MFA does not protect against consent phishing. In Microsoft's words, resetting passwords or requiring MFA *"aren't effective against this type of attack"*, because the app keeps its own access after consent.
- The control that matters is who may consent. Restrict user consent and turn on the admin consent workflow, so a user who hits a consent prompt for a risky app gets [90095](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90095/) and a request goes to a reviewer, instead of granting access themselves.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS65001?
sections.text:
**For developers:** grant consent for the permissions the app requests (admin consent for permissions that need it), then retry the sign-in.

**For admins:**
1. For an app ID you don't recognise, find out who published it and what it asks for **before** anyone consents.
2. If an unknown app flipped from 65001 to success, find the "Consent to application" event, check whether it was admin consent, and review what the app accessed.
3. Remove consent from and disable any app you confirm as malicious. Resetting the user's password alone does not cut off its access.
4. Restrict user consent and enable the admin consent workflow as your standing posture.

65002.title: AADSTS65002 fix: Microsoft app not preauthorized for API
65002.description: AADSTS65002: a Microsoft client app isn't preauthorized for a Microsoft API, and no admin can consent. Use your own app ID. KQL included.
65002.summary: AADSTS65002 means a Microsoft-owned client app asked for a token for a Microsoft-owned API it isn't preauthorized for. Nobody in your tenant can grant that consent. Users hit it from Visual Studio sign-in in the Azure SDK, from scripts that borrow a Microsoft client ID, and from an old Azure Virtual Desktop web client URL. Use your own app registration or the current client.
65002.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> Consent between first party application '{applicationId}' and first party resource '{resourceId}' must be configured via preauthorization - applications owned and operated by Microsoft must get approval from the API owner before requesting tokens for that API. A developer in your tenant might be attempting to reuse an App ID owned by Microsoft. This error prevents them from impersonating a Microsoft application to call other APIs. They must move to another app ID they register.

Both sides of the request are Microsoft apps ("first party"). The client app isn't on the API's preauthorized list, so Entra ID refuses the token. The error names both app IDs, so you can see exactly which pair failed.

The difference from [65001](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/65001/): with 65001 a user or admin in your tenant can grant the missing consent. With 65002 nobody in your tenant can. Microsoft's text says the approval comes from *"the API owner"*, which is Microsoft. A Microsoft moderator's accepted answer in a Q&A thread about Azure Virtual Desktop single sign-on puts it similarly: *"This type of consent is not intended to be granted manually by end users or tenant admins and must be handled via internal preauthorization within Microsoft's platform."*

They must move to another app ID they register.

Both sides of the request are Microsoft apps ("first party"). The client app isn't on the API's preauthorized list, so Entra ID refuses the token. The error names both app IDs, so you can see exactly which pair failed.

The difference from [65001](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/65001/): with 65001 a user or admin in your tenant can grant the missing consent. With 65002 nobody in your tenant can. Microsoft's text says the approval comes from *"the API owner"*, which is Microsoft. A Microsoft moderator's accepted answer in a Q&A thread about Azure Virtual Desktop single sign-on puts it similarly: *"This type of consent is not intended to be granted manually by end users or tenant admins and must be handled via internal preauthorization within Microsoft's platform."*

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Users report three situations:

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Client `{guid}`, from a developer machine | Visual Studio sign-in through the Azure SDK (`VisualStudioCredential`). Microsoft's Azure SDK troubleshooting guide lists this exact error and says the Visual Studio client *"is not yet pre-authorized for the Azure resource mentioned in the error."* |
| A script or integration that sends a Microsoft-owned client ID | A developer copied a Microsoft client ID into their own code. This is the case Microsoft's description warns about. The row rests on Microsoft's description. One Q&A thread is sometimes read as this case, but the poster was using their own client ID and the thread was never resolved, so it doesn't show it. |
| Client `9cdead84-a844-4324-93f2-b2e6bb768d07` (Azure Virtual Desktop) for resource `00000002-0000-0000-c000-000000000000` | An Azure Virtual Desktop user on an old web client URL. The app names come from the poster's Enterprise applications list. The poster fixed it by switching to the current web client. |
| One user or IP hitting 65002 for several **different** Microsoft client IDs in a short time | Our interpretation, not documented: someone is trying Microsoft client IDs one after another to find one that gets a token. Microsoft's text calls 65002 a guard against *"impersonating a Microsoft application"*. Check who and where. |

The error itself gives nothing away: no token is issued.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 65002 lands in. Check all three:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "65002"
| summarize Rows = count(), Clients = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which client and resource pairs fail, and from what. Microsoft's page on verifying first-party apps gives two Microsoft owner tenants: `f8cdef31-a31e-4b4a-93e4-5f571e91255a` (*"the Microsoft Service's Microsoft Entra tenant ID"*) and `72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47`, under which its table lists Microsoft-owned apps. The `IsMicrosoftClient` column checks both:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "65002"
| extend IsMicrosoftClient = AppOwnerTenantId in ("f8cdef31-a31e-4b4a-93e4-5f571e91255a", "72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47")
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, IsMicrosoftClient, ResourceDisplayName, ResourceIdentity
| sort by Rows desc
```

One user or IP trying several different client IDs and getting 65002. A threshold of 3 client IDs in an hour is a starting point; raise it if your developers trigger it:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "65002"
| summarize ClientIds = dcount(AppId), Clients = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
            Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
          by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where ClientIds >= 3
| sort by ClientIds desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"65002"`, not `65002`. If an app in the results is unfamiliar, Microsoft's guide to verifying first-party apps shows how to check its owner: in **Enterprise applications**, filter **Application Type** to **Microsoft Applications**. First-party apps don't always have a service principal in your tenant, so they can appear in sign-in logs without appearing there.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS65002?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this with consent, and neither can your admin. Report the error with both app IDs to whoever runs the app. On Azure Virtual Desktop, a user fixed it by using `https://client.wvd.microsoft.com/arm/webclient` instead of the old `https://rdweb.wvd.microsoft.com/` address.

**For developers:**
1. Look at the client ID your code actually sends. If it belongs to Microsoft, Microsoft's instruction is plain: *"They must move to another app ID they register."*
2. Register your own app, add the API permissions it needs under **API permissions**, and get them consented. Then send that client ID.
3. Azure SDK with `VisualStudioCredential`: the Azure SDK guide points to Visual Studio's pre-authorization guidance. The reporter in the GitHub issue said that didn't help for Azure Monitor Control Service. Our reading: switch to a different credential, or your own app registration, for that resource.

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the client, the resource and the user agent. That tells you whether it is a developer tool, a script or an end-user client.
2. Don't look for a consent button. There isn't one for this error.
3. If the third query returns hits from an unfamiliar IP, treat it like any other suspicious sign-in for that user.
