65004.name: UserDeclinedConsent
65004.title: AADSTS65004: User declined to consent to access the app
65004.description: AADSTS65004: user declined to consent to access the app. Expected after an admin consent request, or the user said no. Fixes and KQL.
65004.summary: AADSTS65004 means the app asked for consent and the user did not give it. Microsoft also documents it as an expected part of the admin consent workflow: after a user submits a request and selects Back to app, the app receives 65004. It has low attack value on its own. Check the app if one unfamiliar app collects declines from many users.
65004.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserDeclinedConsent**: User declined to consent to access the app. Have the user retry the sign-in and consent to the app

The app sent the user to a consent prompt and came back without a grant. In the OAuth authorization code flow, Microsoft lists the matching protocol error as `access_denied`, *"Resource owner denied consent"*, and says *"The client application can notify the user that it can't continue unless the user consents."*

sections.heading: What does AADSTS65004 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **UserDeclinedConsent**: User declined to consent to access the app. Have the user retry the sign-in and consent to the app

The app sent the user to a consent prompt and came back without a grant. In the OAuth authorization code flow, Microsoft lists the matching protocol error as `access_denied`, *"Resource owner denied consent"*, and says *"The client application can notify the user that it can't continue unless the user consents."*

sections.heading: What is the quick fix?
sections.text:
First work out which of two cases you are in:

- **The user just submitted an admin consent request.** Microsoft documents this as expected: *"After a user submits an admin consent approval for an application, another dialog appears with a **Back to app** button. When the user selects the button, Microsoft Entra ID sends an AADSTS65004 error to the redirect URI specified in the original authentication request. This error is an expected part of the admin consent workflow."* Wait for the reviewer. After approval, *"the user needs to begin a new authentication process with the application."*
- **The user said no at the prompt.** If the app is one you trust, have the user sign in again and accept, as Microsoft's description says.

If the user can't accept because the permissions need an admin, that is a different code: [90094](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90094/), or [90095](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90095/) with the admin consent workflow on.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No, not on its own. 65004 is the absence of a grant. The risky moment in consent phishing is a grant that does happen. Microsoft describes the attack: the attacker *"tricks an end user into granting that application consent"*, and after that the app *"has account-level access to data without the need for an organizational account."* The [consent phishing guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/investigate-consent-phishing-entra-id/) covers that investigation.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 65004 shortly after [90095](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90095/) for the same user and app | The admin consent workflow as documented. Benign. |
| 65004 for a known app, then a success after the user retried | The user cancelled once, then accepted. Benign. |
| 65004 for an app ID you don't recognise, from several users | Users were sent to an app nobody approved, and some said no. Check whether others said yes. |

The second and third rows are reasoning from what the code means, not Microsoft detections.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
65004 per app, with how many of those users also hit 90095 (the admin consent workflow) for the same app:

```kusto
let window = 7d;
let declines =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(window)
    | where ResultType == "65004"
    | project DeclineTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName, IPAddress;
let requests =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(window)
    | where ResultType == "90095"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName, AppId
    | extend RequestedAdminConsent = true;
declines
| join kind=leftouter requests on UserPrincipalName, AppId
| summarize Declines = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            UsersWithAdminRequest = dcountif(UserPrincipalName, RequestedAdminConsent == true),
            FirstSeen = min(DeclineTime)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName
| sort by Users desc
```

Apps where `Users` is much larger than `UsersWithAdminRequest` are the ones where people said no at the prompt. For an app you don't know, check the [65001 page](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/65001/) query to see whether anyone later consented.

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"65004"`, not `65004`.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and consent settings affect it?
sections.text:
- 65004 isn't caused by Conditional Access. It is a consent decision.
- With user consent restricted, a user who can't grant the permissions gets [90094](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90094/). With the admin consent workflow on, they get [90095](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90095/), can send a request, and the Back to app step then returns 65004.
- Microsoft notes that users can't grant consent to apps Microsoft detects as risky. Admins can, but Microsoft says they *"should evaluate the app carefully and proceed with caution."*

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS65004?
sections.text:
**For the user:** if you just sent an admin consent request, wait for approval and then sign in to the app again. If you cancelled by mistake and trust the app, sign in again and accept.

**For developers:** handle `access_denied` by telling the user the app can't continue without consent, as Microsoft recommends.

**For admins:**
1. Check whether the 65004 followed a 90095 for the same user and app. If yes, review the pending request.
2. If the app is approved for the organization, grant admin consent so users don't see the prompt.
3. For an app you don't recognise, find who published it and what it asks for before anyone consents.

65005.name: MisconfiguredApplication
65005.title: AADSTS65005 fix: app asks for a resource it didn't register
65005.description: AADSTS65005: the app requested a resource missing from its registered permissions or from the tenant. Fix API permissions or provision the resource.
65005.summary: AADSTS65005 means an app asked for access to a resource (an API) that isn't in the app's registered permissions, or that isn't available in the tenant. For SAML apps it can also mean a wrong Identifier (Entity ID). Users hit it on company apps, scripts and integrations that sign in to Microsoft 365, Intune or Dynamics. It is a configuration error with low attack value.
65005.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **MisconfiguredApplication**: The app required resource access list doesn't contain apps discoverable by the resource, or the client app has requested access to resource, which wasn't specified in its required resource access list or Graph service returned bad request or resource not found. If the app supports SAML, you might have configured the app with the wrong Identifier (Entity). To learn more, see the troubleshooting article for error AADSTS650056.

The "required resource access list" is the list of APIs and permissions in the app's registration (**API permissions** in the portal, `requiredResourceAccess` in the manifest). An older Microsoft KB quotes the message users saw: *"The client application has requested access to resource. This request has failed because the client has not specified this resource in its requiredResourceAccess list."*

Microsoft's consent troubleshooting article shows two other wordings, which point at two different causes:

- **Resource not available in the tenant**: *"`clientAppDisplayName` is requesting access to a resource `resourceAppDisplayName` that isn't available in your organization."*
- **Permissions mismatch**: *"The app requested consent to access resource `resourceAppDisplayName`. This request failed because it doesn't match how the app was preconfigured during app registration."*

How it differs from codes that already have pages:

- [650056](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/650056/) is also "misconfigured application", with missing permissions, missing admin consent or a wrong identifier. The two overlap, and Microsoft's 65005 description sends SAML cases to the 650056 article. Our reading: start with the resource named in the 65005 message.
- [500011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500011/) means the resource has no service principal in the tenant at token time. 65005 can have the same root cause, a missing resource service principal. Our reading is that it tends to show up at consent rather than at token time.

The "required resource access list" is the list of APIs and permissions in the app's registration (**API permissions** in the portal, `requiredResourceAccess` in the manifest). An older Microsoft KB quotes the message users saw: *"The client application has requested access to resource. This request has failed because the client has not specified this resource in its requiredResourceAccess list."*

Microsoft's consent troubleshooting article shows two other wordings, which point at two different causes:

- **Resource not available in the tenant**: *"`clientAppDisplayName` is requesting access to a resource `resourceAppDisplayName` that isn't available in your organization."*
- **Permissions mismatch**: *"The app requested consent to access resource `resourceAppDisplayName`. This request failed because it doesn't match how the app was preconfigured during app registration."*

How it differs from codes that already have pages:

- [650056](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/650056/) is also "misconfigured application", with missing permissions, missing admin consent or a wrong identifier. The two overlap, and Microsoft's 65005 description sends SAML cases to the 650056 article. Our reading: start with the resource named in the 65005 message.
- [500011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500011/) means the resource has no service principal in the tenant at token time. 65005 can have the same root cause, a missing resource service principal. Our reading is that it tends to show up at consent rather than at token time.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. The request fails because the app is set up wrong, and nothing is granted. Users report it in a few typical places:

- Microsoft's KB: *"When you use a company app to sign in to or authenticate to one of the Microsoft Cloud Services, such as Microsoft 365, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Dynamics, Microsoft Power BI, or Microsoft Azure."* The KB's cause: the app *"may not be registered with Microsoft Entra ID, or it may not have the correct permissions applied."*
- A Linux PAM module for Entra ID sign-in (pam_aad): the author found the app's permissions were set on the legacy Windows Azure Active Directory API instead of Microsoft Graph.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One in-house app or script, every user, after a code change | The code asks for an API that isn't in the registration. Developer error. |
| A vendor app fails at the consent screen in your tenant only | The API it needs isn't provisioned in your tenant. Setup step missing. |
| A SAML app fails for everyone | Wrong Identifier (Entity ID). Follow the [650056](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/650056/) fix. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 65005 lands in. Check your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "65005"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which client apps fail, and which resources they asked for:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "65005"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10),
            Protocols = make_set(AuthenticationProtocol, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Users desc
```

The resource in the request may not exist in your tenant, so `ResourceDisplayName` can be empty on these rows. Microsoft doesn't document it either way. If it is empty, read the resource name from the error message the user saw.

Failed consent attempts in the audit log. Microsoft lists **Consent to application** as an `ApplicationManagement` activity. Our assumption: a consent stopped by 65005 is logged there as a failure.

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName == "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "failure"
| project TimeGenerated,
          App = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
          ByUser = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
          ResultReason
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"65005"`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS65005?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this. Send IT the app name and the resource named in the error.

**For developers (you own the app registration):**
1. Open **App registrations** > your app > **API permissions**. Add every API and permission your code requests. Microsoft: *"Compare the resource you're requesting access to in code with the configured permissions in the **Required Resources** tab to make sure you only request resources you've configured."*
2. Check you registered the right API. In the pam_aad report, permissions were on the legacy Windows Azure Active Directory API while the code needed Microsoft Graph.
3. Microsoft's consent article: when the app requests an invalid resource, *"the application developer must update the configuration of the client application to resolve this problem."*

**For admins:**
1. If the resource isn't in your tenant, provision its service principal. Microsoft lists four ways, depending on the app: *"Acquiring a subscription for the resource application (Microsoft-published applications)"*, *"Consenting to the resource application"*, *"Granting the application permissions via the Microsoft Entra admin center"*, and *"Adding the application from the Microsoft Entra application gallery."*
2. For a vendor app you don't own, the fix is on the vendor's side if its registration requests the wrong resource. Microsoft's message says *"Contact the app vendor."*
3. For a SAML app, check that the **Identifier (Entity ID)** in Entra ID matches the Issuer the app sends. See [650056](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/650056/).

microsoftWording.text: **MisconfiguredApplication**: The app required resource access list doesn't contain apps discoverable by the resource, or the client app has requested access to resource, which wasn't specified in its required resource access list or Graph service returned bad request or resource not found. If the app supports SAML, you might have configured the app with the wrong Identifier (Entity). To learn more, see the troubleshooting article for error AADSTS650056.

70002.name: InvalidClient
70002.title: AADSTS70002 fix: error validating client credentials
70002.description: AADSTS70002: Entra couldn't validate an app's credentials. Read the inner code, send the secret Value not its ID, and compare with 7000215.
70002.summary: AADSTS70002 means Microsoft Entra ID couldn't validate the credentials an app sent, typically a client secret that doesn't match. A wrong secret today often comes back as 7000215 instead. 70002 is also seen as an outer code in front of a more specific one, so read the whole message. Usually a setup mistake; repeated failures from IPs you don't own deserve a look.
70002.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidClient**: Error validating the credentials. The specified client_secret does not match the expected value for this client. Correct the client_secret and try again. For more info, see [Use the authorization code to request an access token](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-auth-code-flow#redeem-a-code-for-an-access-token).

A confidential client, such as a web app, a daemon or a connector, proves who it is with a client secret or a certificate. Microsoft's authorization code flow reference says the `client_secret` is *"the application secret that you created in the app registration portal for your app"* and that it *"must be URL-encoded before being sent"*. The SDK does that for you; a hand-built request may not. When Entra can't validate what was sent, the token request fails.

### 70002 or 7000215?
Both are about a bad client secret, and they are easy to confuse.

- [7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/) is *"Invalid client secret is provided"*. Its page records a token request with a wrong secret that came back as 7000215, with Microsoft's current hint to send *"the client secret value, not the client secret ID"*. A Microsoft Q&A thread that people find when searching for 70002, a Postman call with the wrong secret, also shows 7000215.
- 70002 still appears in user reports, often with a second code after it. Quest's knowledge base shows *"AADSTS70002: Error validating credentials. AADSTS50126: Invalid username or password"*. Microsoft's own external MFA provider reference shows *"AADSTS70002: Error validating credentials. AADSTS50012: External ID token from issuer ... failed signature verification"* (Microsoft prints the prefix there as `ENTRA IDSTS`).

Our reading: 70002 works as a general "credential check failed" code, and the code that follows it says what actually failed. If your message has a second AADSTS code, look that one up: [50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/) is a wrong user password, and 50012 is a token whose signature didn't verify. If 70002 stands alone, treat it as a wrong client secret.

Other neighbours:

- [7000222](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000222/): the secret was right but has expired.
- [7000218](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000218/): no secret or assertion was sent at all.
- [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/): the client ID isn't found in the tenant. Check this first if the secret is definitely right.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. The causes users report are setup mistakes: the secret ID pasted instead of the value, an old secret left in a config file after a rotation, or the right secret for the wrong app or tenant. UiPath's documentation, for example, tells users to check the tenant ID and application ID and to *"copy the Secret Value, not the Secret ID"*.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Failures for one app from your own servers, starting at a rotation date | A system still has the old secret. Update it. |
| Failures since day one of a new integration | Secret ID instead of value, or a secret for another app registration. |
| 70002 followed by 50126 | A user's password was wrong. See [50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/), not this page. |
| Repeated failures for one app from IPs you don't own | Someone has an old or leaked secret, or is guessing. Treat it like [7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/) from a foreign IP (T1078.004 if it ever succeeds). |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 70002 lands in. App-only requests would be expected in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`, and requests on behalf of a user in the user tables; that is an assumption. Check, and compare with 7000215 so you see which code your tenant actually returns. One caveat, as on the [7000215 page](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/): the reference for `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` describes `ResultType` as *"Success or Failure"*, so confirm failed rows carry the code; if they don't, filter on `ResultSignature` instead:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("70002", "7000215")
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable, ResultType
```

Which apps fail, from where, and with which key. Microsoft documents `ClientCredentialType` as the type of client credential used (for example client assertion or client secret) and `ServicePrincipalCredentialKeyId` as the key ID of the credential:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType in ("70002", "7000215")
| summarize Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            CredTypes = make_set(ClientCredentialType, 5), KeyIds = make_set(ServicePrincipalCredentialKeyId, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Failures from IPs that have never signed in successfully for that app in the last 30 days. Worth an alert; the 30-day window and a threshold of one are starting points:

```kusto
let knownAppIPs =
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct AppId, IPAddress;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType in ("70002", "7000215")
| join kind=leftanti knownAppIPs on AppId, IPAddress
| summarize Attempts = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType
| sort by Attempts desc
```

If the first query shows 70002 only in the user tables, run the third one against those with `UserPrincipalName` added. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"70002"`, not `70002`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS70002?
sections.text:
**For developers:**
1. Read the full message. If a second AADSTS code follows, fix that one.
2. Send the secret's **Value**, not its ID, for the same app registration as the `client_id`, against the tenant that app lives in.
3. If you build the request by hand, URL-encode the secret, as Microsoft's reference requires.
4. If you can't find the value any more, create a new client secret and use that.

**For admins:**
1. After a rotation, use the second query to find every system still failing, and update it.
2. If failures come from IPs you don't own, treat the app's secrets as exposed: create a new credential, remove the old ones from the app registration, and update your own systems.
3. Move the app to a certificate where it supports one. Microsoft *"recommends that you use a certificate instead of a client secret before moving the application to a production environment."*

fix.steps:
**For developers:**
1. Read the full message. If a second AADSTS code follows, fix that one.
2. Send the secret's **Value**, not its ID, for the same app registration as the `client_id`, against the tenant that app lives in.
3. If you build the request by hand, URL-encode the secret, as Microsoft's reference requires.
4. If you can't find the value any more, create a new client secret and use that.

**For admins:**
1. After a rotation, use the second query to find every system still failing, and update it.
2. If failures come from IPs you don't own, treat the app's secrets as exposed: create a new credential, remove the old ones from the app registration, and update your own systems.
3. Move the app to a certificate where it supports one. Microsoft *"recommends that you use a certificate instead of a client secret before moving the application to a production environment."*

70008.name: ExpiredOrRevokedGrant
70008.title: AADSTS70008: The refresh token has expired or was revoked (fix)
70008.description: AADSTS70008: a refresh token expired from inactivity or was revoked. Usually normal token lifecycle with low attack value; the app must prompt. KQL.
70008.summary: AADSTS70008 means an app tried to use a refresh token or grant that is no longer valid. Microsoft's text names inactivity; the code name also says revoked. It is usually part of the normal token lifecycle and has low attack value. The app should send the user to an interactive sign-in. Hunt it in the non-interactive sign-in logs.
70008.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **ExpiredOrRevokedGrant**: The refresh token has expired due to inactivity. The token was issued on XXX and was inactive for a certain amount of time.

An app presented a refresh token (a "grant") to get a new access token, and Microsoft Entra ID refused it. The description talks about inactivity. The code name, *ExpiredOrRevokedGrant*, also covers revocation. Microsoft doesn't say which cases return 70008 rather than a more specific code.

Two sibling codes in the same reference table are more specific:

- [700082](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700082/) **ExpiredOrRevokedGrantInactiveToken**, with almost the same text, which Microsoft calls an *"Expected part of the token lifecycle"*.
- [50173](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50173/), a grant revoked after a credential change: *"The user might have changed or reset their password."*

Our reading: 70008 is the more generic form of the same event. Treat it like 700082 unless the context points to revocation.

**How long refresh tokens live.** Microsoft's refresh token page gives the defaults: *"24 hours for single-page applications"*, 24 hours for the email one-time passcode flow, and *"90 days for all other scenarios."* The configurable token lifetimes page lists a non-configurable *Refresh Token Max Inactive Time* of 90 days. Tokens *"can be revoked by the sign-in service at any time before their expiration"*, for example when the user changes their password or an admin revokes all refresh tokens for the user.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. A refresh token that expired or was revoked gives nobody access. The common sources are a device or app that wasn't used for a long time, and an app that keeps an old token after a password change or a session revocation.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 70008 from a user's known device, then an interactive success | The user came back after a long break, or after a password change, and signed in again. Benign. |
| 70008 for many users of one app, all at once | Our interpretation: a mass revocation (for example after an incident response) or an app holding tokens far past their lifetime. Check what happened that day. |
| 70008 shortly after you revoked a user's sessions | The revocation is working. The old token was refused. |
| 70008 from an IP or device the user doesn't normally use | Someone presented an old refresh token from an unfamiliar place. Reasoning, not a documented detection: if the token was stolen, expiry or revocation is what stopped it. Worth a short look. |

**IP caveat.** Microsoft's non-interactive sign-ins page says the IP of non-interactive sign-ins by confidential clients *"doesn't match the actual source IP of where the refresh token request is coming from. Instead, it shows the original IP used for the original token issuance."* An unfamiliar IP on a 70008 row is a meaningful signal mainly for public clients (desktop, mobile and browser apps).

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Refresh token redemption is a non-interactive sign-in (*"A client app uses an OAuth 2.0 refresh token to get an access token"* is one of Microsoft's examples), so expect most rows in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`. Microsoft doesn't document the table for this code specifically, so check:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "70008"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Baseline by app and client:

```kusto
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "70008"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed
| sort by Rows desc
```

70008 from an IP the user had no successful sign-in from in the previous 13 days (14 days back up to yesterday). Use it for triage, not as an alert on its own, and keep the confidential-client caveat above in mind:

```kusto
let lookback = 14d;
let knownIPs =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(1d))
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "70008"
| join kind=leftanti knownIPs on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 3)
          by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Rows desc
```

Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource ID match, so `Rows` is not a request count. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"70008"`, not `70008`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- Refresh token lifetimes can't be changed with policy. Microsoft says that *"As of January 30, 2021, refresh and session token lifetimes are no longer configurable through token lifetime policies."*
- To control how often users sign in, Microsoft points to Conditional Access sign-in frequency. A refresh refused because of sign-in frequency is a different code, [70043](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70043/).

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS70008?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign in again when the app asks. If the app keeps failing without asking, sign out of it and back in.

**For developers:** treat 70008 as *"interactive sign-in needed"*. Microsoft's guidance for refresh tokens is that the app *"should handle such revocations gracefully by redirecting the user to an interactive sign-in prompt"*. With MSAL, catch the error from the silent call and fall back to an interactive call. Don't retry the same refresh token. For single-page apps, plan for the 24-hour limit: Microsoft says they *"must be prepared to rerun the authorization code flow using an interactive authentication"*.

**For admins:**
1. Nothing is broken in the normal case. Exclude `"70008"` from failure-rate dashboards.
2. If one app produces most of the rows and users complain, the app probably doesn't fall back to an interactive sign-in. Report it to the developer.
3. If the third query shows rows from unfamiliar public-client IPs, check that user's other sign-ins from the same IP. If anything succeeded there, treat it as a possible token theft and [revoke the user's sessions](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/revoke-sessions-and-verify-entra-id/).

70016.name: AuthorizationPending
70016.title: AADSTS70016: Device code authorization is pending (fix)
70016.description: AADSTS70016: a device code flow is waiting for the user to sign in. Normal, not a failure. Lab-measured code lifetime, KQL and the phishing angle.
70016.summary: AADSTS70016 means a device code flow is waiting for the user to sign in. The app polls the token endpoint, nobody has entered the code yet, and Entra answers with 70016. It is the normal reply while a device code is outstanding, not a failure. For defenders it marks the window in which a device code phishing victim has been shown a code but has not used it.
70016.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **AuthorizationPending**: OAuth 2.0 device flow error. Authorization is pending. The device will retry polling the request.

Nothing is broken. 70016 is the answer the device code flow gives while it waits for a person.

The flow has two halves, described on Microsoft's [device authorization grant page](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-device-code). First the app calls `/devicecode` and gets back a `device_code` (*"A long string used to verify the session between the client and the authorization server"*), a `user_code` (*"A short string shown to the user used to identify the session on a secondary device"*) and a `verification_uri` (*"The URI the user should go to with the `user_code` in order to sign in"*). Then, while the person signs in somewhere else, *"the client should be polling the `/token` endpoint for the requested token using the `device_code`."*

Every poll that happens before the person has finished gets 70016. Microsoft's protocol-level name for the same condition is in its expected-errors table:

| Error | Microsoft's description | Microsoft's client action |
|---|---|---|
| `authorization_pending` | The user hasn't finished authenticating, but hasn't canceled the flow. | Repeat the request after at least `interval` seconds. |

So the correct handling of 70016 is to wait and ask again. An app that treats it as a failure and stops has broken its own sign-in.

Codes that do mean something went wrong sit next to it in Microsoft's reference:

| Code | Microsoft's description | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| **70016** | *"AuthorizationPending - OAuth 2.0 device flow error. Authorization is pending. The device will retry polling the request."* | Still waiting. Keep polling. |
| **70018** | *"BadVerificationCode - Invalid verification code due to User typing in wrong user code for device code flow. Authorization isn't approved."* | The person mistyped the short code. |
| **70019** | *"CodeExpired - Verification code expired. Have the user retry the sign-in."* | Time ran out. Start again. |
| **90119** | *"InvalidUserCode - The user code is null or empty."* | No code was submitted. |
| **90120** | *"InvalidDeviceFlowRequest - The request was already authorized or declined."* | The code was used once already. |
| **65004** | *"UserDeclinedConsent - User declined to consent to access the app."* | The person said no at the consent prompt. |
| [7000014](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000014/) | Not in Microsoft's reference. | The `device_code` value itself isn't recognised. |

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 31 October 2026 an automated lab run requested a device code from a lab tenant and then polled the token endpoint before anyone had signed in. Entra returned:

> AADSTS70016: OAuth 2.0 device flow error. Authorization is pending. Continue polling.

Note the wording. The reference says *"The device will retry polling the request"*; the message the token endpoint actually returns says *"Continue polling."* If you are matching on message text, match on the part both have.

The run then polled again immediately, with no wait. It got the same code and the same message, not a separate too-fast error. That is one observation from one tenant: it does not prove the endpoint never throttles a fast poller, only that an immediate second poll was answered the same way here.

**Measured code lifetime.** The device code in this run was issued with `expires_in` of **900 seconds (15 minutes)** and an `interval` of **5 seconds**. Microsoft documents both fields (`expires_in`: *"The number of seconds before the `device_code` and `user_code` expire"*; `interval`: *"The number of seconds the client should wait between polling requests"*) and its page states the default: *"From the moment the request is sent, the user has 15 minutes to sign in. This is the default value for `expires_in`."* The lab value matches that documented default. The `interval` of 5 seconds is not a number Microsoft publishes anywhere we have found, so treat 5 as what this tenant returned on 31 October 2026, not as a guaranteed constant: read `interval` from the response rather than hard-coding it.

That 15-minute window is also how long 70016 can keep coming back for a single code, which matters for the phishing case below.

No sign-in log row was captured for 70016. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
The code on its own, no. It is the expected reply during a device code sign-in, and a healthy tenant that uses the flow produces it constantly.

The pattern can matter, because 70016 is exactly what device code phishing looks like while the lure is live. Microsoft's [Conditional Access authentication flows page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/concept-authentication-flows) is blunt about the flow: *"Device code flow is a high-risk authentication method that can be part of a phishing attack or used to access corporate resources on unmanaged devices."*

In that attack the attacker, not the victim, runs the client. The attacker requests a device code, sends the `user_code` and the verification URL to the victim in a message that looks like a legitimate prompt, and polls. Each poll returns 70016 until the victim enters the code; then the attacker's poll returns tokens. So:

- **70016 is the lure window.** It is the only part of the attack that is visible before a successful token issue, and it lasts at most the code lifetime measured above.
- **A successful device code sign-in is the damage.** Hunt those, with [the token replay and session hijack guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/detect-token-replay-m365-session-hijack-entra-id/), which covers the device code filters in the sign-in logs and the Conditional Access control that blocks the flow.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Steady 70016 from a tool a user is actively signing into, ending in a success | Normal device code sign-in. |
| 70016 for an app nobody in your tenant should be using device code with | Worth a look. Device code works with public client apps, so the client can be anything, anywhere. |
| A device code success from an IP or country that never appears for that user, shortly after 70016 polling | The shape of a successful device code phish. Treat as a session compromise and revoke. |
| 70016 and nothing else, repeatedly, for the same app | A code was shown and never entered, or a tool that polls and is never completed. Benign on its own. |
| [7000014](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000014/) instead of 70016 | A broken client, not a pending authorization. |

One honest limit: we did not capture a 70016 sign-in log row, so whether the attacker's polling requests appear in your tenant's logs at all is unconfirmed. The poll names a client and a `device_code`, but no user has approved anything yet, so there may be no user and no tenant row to attribute it to. Build detections on the device code **successes**, which definitely are logged, and use 70016 only as context.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which sign-in table 70016 lands in is not documented, and the lab run produced no row to confirm it. Start with a union so you find out for your own tenant:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("70016", "70018", "70019", "90119", "90120")
| summarize Rows = count(),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 5)
          by SourceTable, ResultType
| sort by Rows desc
```

If that returns nothing, 70016 is not surfaced to your tenant, and the next query is the one that matters. `AuthenticationProtocol` is documented with *"deviceCode"* among its possible values, so you can inventory the flow itself rather than its pending state:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode" or OriginalTransferMethod == "deviceCodeFlow"
| summarize Sign_ins = count(),
            Successes = countif(ResultType == "0"),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Codes = make_set(ResultType, 10)
          by SourceTable, AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Sign_ins desc
```

An app in that list that you did not expect is worth a question whatever its result codes. The exact string stored in `OriginalTransferMethod` can differ between tenants, so confirm it on one known device code row before you rely on that half of the filter.

Then look at the successes per user and per location, which is where a phish shows:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == "0"
| summarize Sign_ins = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by UserPrincipalName
| sort by Sign_ins desc
```

As a starting point, treat a user's **first ever** device code success as worth reading in full, and any device code success for a user who does not work with shared or input-constrained devices as suspicious. Tune from your own baseline; a tenant that uses the flow for conference room devices will have a large legitimate one.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- Microsoft says to *"Allow device code flow only where necessary"* and that it *"recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible"*, using a Conditional Access authentication flows policy. Its own example is to allow the flow for conference room devices in one network location and block it everywhere else.
- Our reading: a Conditional Access block does not change 70016. The policy is evaluated when the person signs in at the verification URL, so the polling client keeps getting 70016 until the code expires or the person's sign-in is blocked. That ordering is untested in the lab.
- Blocking the flow stops the attacker's client as well as the user's, which is the point of blocking it.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS70016?
sections.text:
Nothing is wrong. There is no fix, only correct handling.

**For the user:** finish signing in. The device or tool shows a short code and a URL; open the URL, enter the code, and sign in. The tool completes by itself within a few seconds. If you were not expecting a code, and especially if someone sent you one in a message, do not enter it: that is how device code phishing works. Report it instead.

**For developers:**
1. Treat 70016 and `authorization_pending` as "not yet", not as an error. Keep polling.
2. Wait at least `interval` seconds between polls, reading `interval` from the `/devicecode` response.
3. Stop when `expires_in` has passed, and surface the expiry to the user so they can start again.
4. Stop on the terminal errors instead of retrying: `authorization_declined`, `bad_verification_code` and `expired_token`.
5. Use MSAL rather than hand-written polling. It implements the wait, the retry and the terminal cases for you.

**For admins:**
1. Inventory the flow with the second query. Decide which apps and which devices genuinely need it.
2. If nothing needs it, block device code flow with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy. Start in report-only and exclude break-glass accounts.
3. Tell users that a code arriving in a message or an email is a phishing attempt. The legitimate flow starts on a device in front of them.
4. For a device code success you cannot explain, treat it as a compromised session: [revoke sessions and verify](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/revoke-sessions-and-verify-entra-id/).

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
The code on its own, no. It is the expected reply during a device code sign-in, and a healthy tenant that uses the flow produces it constantly.

The pattern can matter, because 70016 is exactly what device code phishing looks like while the lure is live. Microsoft's [Conditional Access authentication flows page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/concept-authentication-flows) is blunt about the flow: *"Device code flow is a high-risk authentication method that can be part of a phishing attack or used to access corporate resources on unmanaged devices."*

In that attack the attacker, not the victim, runs the client. The attacker requests a device code, sends the `user_code` and the verification URL to the victim in a message that looks like a legitimate prompt, and polls. Each poll returns 70016 until the victim enters the code; then the attacker's poll returns tokens. So:

- **70016 is the lure window.** It is the only part of the attack that is visible before a successful token issue, and it lasts at most the code lifetime measured above.
- **A successful device code sign-in is the damage.** Hunt those, with [the token replay and session hijack guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/detect-token-replay-m365-session-hijack-entra-id/), which covers the device code filters in the sign-in logs and the Conditional Access control that blocks the flow.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Steady 70016 from a tool a user is actively signing into, ending in a success | Normal device code sign-in. |
| 70016 for an app nobody in your tenant should be using device code with | Worth a look. Device code works with public client apps, so the client can be anything, anywhere. |
| A device code success from an IP or country that never appears for that user, shortly after 70016 polling | The shape of a successful device code phish. Treat as a session compromise and revoke. |
| 70016 and nothing else, repeatedly, for the same app | A code was shown and never entered, or a tool that polls and is never completed. Benign on its own. |
| [7000014](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000014/) instead of 70016 | A broken client, not a pending authorization. |

One honest limit: we did not capture a 70016 sign-in log row, so whether the attacker's polling requests appear in your tenant's logs at all is unconfirmed. The poll names a client and a `device_code`, but no user has approved anything yet, so there may be no user and no tenant row to attribute it to. Build detections on the device code **successes**, which definitely are logged, and use 70016 only as context.

70016.labSectionText:
On 31 October 2026 an automated lab run requested a device code from a lab tenant and then polled the token endpoint before anyone had signed in. Entra returned:

> AADSTS70016: OAuth 2.0 device flow error. Authorization is pending. Continue polling.

Note the wording. The reference says *"The device will retry polling the request"*; the message the token endpoint actually returns says *"Continue polling."* If you are matching on message text, match on the part both have.

The run then polled again immediately, with no wait. It got the same code and the same message, not a separate too-fast error. That is one observation from one tenant: it does not prove the endpoint never throttles a fast poller, only that an immediate second poll was answered the same way here.

**Measured code lifetime.** The device code in this run was issued with `expires_in` of **900 seconds (15 minutes)** and an `interval` of **5 seconds**. Microsoft documents both fields (`expires_in`: *"The number of seconds before the `device_code` and `user_code` expire"*; `interval`: *"The number of seconds the client should wait between polling requests"*) and its page states the default: *"From the moment the request is sent, the user has 15 minutes to sign in. This is the default value for `expires_in`."* The lab value matches that documented default. The `interval` of 5 seconds is not a number Microsoft publishes anywhere we have found, so treat 5 as what this tenant returned on 31 October 2026, not as a guaranteed constant: read `interval` from the response rather than hard-coding it.

That 15-minute window is also how long 70016 can keep coming back for a single code, which matters for the phishing case below.

No sign-in log row was captured for 70016. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

70021.title: AADSTS70021: No matching federated identity credential (fix)
70021.description: AADSTS70021: no federated identity credential matches the external token. Wrong issuer or subject, or a new credential not yet propagated. Fix and KQL.
70021.summary: AADSTS70021 means a workload sent an external token (from GitHub, Azure DevOps, Kubernetes or another identity provider) and Entra found no federated identity credential on the app or managed identity that matches it. Usually the issuer or subject is wrong, or the credential was created minutes ago and hasn't propagated. It is a configuration error with low attack value.
70021.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS70021 (checked 30 October 2026). Microsoft does document it on two other pages.

Microsoft's page on federated identity credential restrictions quotes the message:

> AADSTS70021: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion.

It gives it in one specific context, propagation after setup:

> It takes time for the federated identity credential to be propagated throughout a region after being initially configured. A token request made several minutes after configuring the federated identity credential may fail because the cache is populated in the directory with old data.

Microsoft's Azure DevOps troubleshooting page lists two longer forms of the same message, with the values from the token appended:

| Message (Azure DevOps doc) | Cause Microsoft gives |
|---|---|
| `No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion. Assertion Issuer: 'https://app.vstoken.visualstudio.com'.` | *"No federated credential was created or the issuer URL isn't correct."* |
| `No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion. Assertion Issuer: 'https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>'. Assertion Subject: 'sc://<org>/<project>/<service-connection>'.` | *"Either the issuer URL or the federation subject doesn't match. The Azure DevOps organization or project was renamed or a manually created service connection was renamed without updating the federation subject on the identity."* |

Background: with workload identity federation, a workload outside Entra (a GitHub Actions job, an Azure DevOps pipeline, a Kubernetes pod) gets a token from its own identity provider and exchanges it for an Entra access token. Microsoft's overview: *"Microsoft identity platform checks the trust relationship on the user-assigned managed identity or app registration and validates the external token against the OpenID Connect (OIDC) issuer URL on the external IdP."* The trust is a federated identity credential with three values. The Graph overview says they *"must match exactly"*, case-sensitively, against the token's `iss`, `sub` and `aud` claims. 70021 means no credential on the app matched.

Our reading: 70021 is the general "no match" code. The more specific codes say which value failed: [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/) (issuer), [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/) (audience), [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) (subject) and [7002138](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002138/) (subject differs only in letter case). If the app has no federated credentials at all, you get [70025](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70025/) instead. Microsoft doesn't document when Entra returns 70021 rather than one of the specific codes.

One related code *is* in the reference: AADSTS700229 ForbiddenTokenType, *"Only app-only tokens can be used as Federated Identity Credentials for Microsoft Entra issuer"*.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Almost never. It is a mismatch between what a workload sends and what the app trusts.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new credential, and the first run fails within minutes | Propagation delay, as Microsoft describes. Retry after a short wait. |
| An Azure DevOps pipeline that worked and now fails | The organization, project or service connection was renamed, so the `sc://` subject changed. Microsoft's cause. |
| A pipeline or workflow that never worked | Wrong issuer or subject on the credential. Microsoft's create-trust page: a wrong subject is saved *"without error. The error does not become apparent until the token exchange fails."* |
| Failures for your app from an IP and identity provider you don't use | Someone presenting a token from their own provider with your app's client ID. Likely it fails exactly because no credential trusts that provider, but we haven't tested this. Worth a look, not an incident. |

Our reading: the attack to watch for is the opposite case. An attacker who can edit your app registration adds a federated credential that trusts their own provider, and then signs in **successfully**. That shows as a success with a new `FederatedCredentialId`, plus an audit event, not as 70021.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 70021 lands in. An app registration's federated sign-in is a service principal sign-in, so the failure probably lands in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`. Microsoft's service principal sign-ins page says managed identity sign-ins are *"included only in the managed identity sign-in log"*, so a failing user-assigned managed identity may log there instead (`AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs`). Check where it lands in your tenant:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "70021" or ResultSignature == "70021"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

The `ResultSignature` check is there because the Azure Monitor reference describes `ResultType` in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` only as *"Success or Failure"*. Look at a failed row to see which column carries the code in your workspace.

For an app that worked before and now fails, find its last successful federated sign-in and which credential it used. The Graph sign-in reference lists `federatedIdentityCredential` as a value of `clientCredentialType`, and describes `federatedCredentialId` as *"the identifier of an application's federated identity credential, if a federated identity credential was used to sign in"*. That the Log Analytics columns carry the same values is our reading:

```kusto
let failing =
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == "70021" or ResultSignature == "70021"
    | distinct AppId;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AppId in (failing)
| where ClientCredentialType == "federatedIdentityCredential"
| where ResultType == "0"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, FederatedCredentialId, IPAddress) by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
```

Then check whether someone changed the app's federated credentials around that time. A third-party write-up (trackr.live) reports that this logs as `Update application` with a modified property named `FederatedIdentityCredentials`. Microsoft doesn't document that property name on the pages we checked, so treat this as a starting point:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName == "Update application"
| mv-expand Target = TargetResources
| mv-expand Prop = Target.modifiedProperties
| where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "FederatedIdentityCredentials"
| project TimeGenerated,
          App = tostring(Target.displayName),
          Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
          OldValue = tostring(Prop.oldValue),
          NewValue = tostring(Prop.newValue)
```

The same write-up says credentials on a user-assigned managed identity are an Azure Resource Manager write and don't appear in the Entra audit log. Look in the Azure activity log for those.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS70021?
sections.text:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. If you created the credential minutes ago, wait and retry. Microsoft: *"wait a short time after adding the federated identity credential before requesting a token"*, and add retry logic to token requests.
2. Read the issuer and subject from the error message (the Azure DevOps forms include them) or from your provider's token, and compare them character by character with the credential. Matching is case-sensitive and *"Wildcard characters aren't supported in any federated identity credential property value."*
3. Check the formats Microsoft gives:
   - GitHub Actions: issuer `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` (Microsoft's page shows it both with and without a trailing slash; match your token's `iss`); subject `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:<name>` for jobs tied to an environment, otherwise `repo:<org>/<repo>:ref:<ref path>`, or `repo:<org>/<repo>:pull-request`.
   - Kubernetes: issuer is the cluster's OIDC issuer URL; subject `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service account>`.
   - Azure DevOps: see the issuer table on Microsoft's troubleshooting page. New service connections use `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0`.
4. Check the audience. Microsoft recommends `api://AzureADTokenExchange`. If only the audience is wrong, you may see [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/).

**For admins:**
1. For Azure DevOps after a rename, Microsoft names the cause but gives no fix. Update the federation subject on the app or managed identity to the new `sc://` value. For a wrong issuer, Microsoft's fix is to edit and save the service connection. If Azure DevOps didn't create the identity, update the issuer yourself.
2. An app or user-assigned managed identity can hold at most 20 federated credentials. If you need one per branch or environment, plan for that limit.
3. If failures come from a provider you don't use, confirm no unexpected federated credential exists on the app, and review who can edit the app registration.

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
Almost never. It is a mismatch between what a workload sends and what the app trusts.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new credential, and the first run fails within minutes | Propagation delay, as Microsoft describes. Retry after a short wait. |
| An Azure DevOps pipeline that worked and now fails | The organization, project or service connection was renamed, so the `sc://` subject changed. Microsoft's cause. |
| A pipeline or workflow that never worked | Wrong issuer or subject on the credential. Microsoft's create-trust page: a wrong subject is saved *"without error. The error does not become apparent until the token exchange fails."* |
| Failures for your app from an IP and identity provider you don't use | Someone presenting a token from their own provider with your app's client ID. Likely it fails exactly because no credential trusts that provider, but we haven't tested this. Worth a look, not an incident. |

Our reading: the attack to watch for is the opposite case. An attacker who can edit your app registration adds a federated credential that trusts their own provider, and then signs in **successfully**. That shows as a success with a new `FederatedCredentialId`, plus an audit event, not as 70021.

fix.short: Developer: if you created the credential minutes ago, wait and retry. Otherwise compare the issuer and subject in the error or token with the federated credential, character by character (case-sensitive, no wildcards), and check the audience. Azure DevOps after a rename: update the sc:// subject.
fix.steps:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. If you created the credential minutes ago, wait and retry. Microsoft: *"wait a short time after adding the federated identity credential before requesting a token"*, and add retry logic to token requests.
2. Read the issuer and subject from the error message (the Azure DevOps forms include them) or from your provider's token, and compare them character by character with the credential. Matching is case-sensitive and *"Wildcard characters aren't supported in any federated identity credential property value."*
3. Check the formats Microsoft gives:
   - GitHub Actions: issuer `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` (Microsoft's page shows it both with and without a trailing slash; match your token's `iss`); subject `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:<name>` for jobs tied to an environment, otherwise `repo:<org>/<repo>:ref:<ref path>`, or `repo:<org>/<repo>:pull-request`.
   - Kubernetes: issuer is the cluster's OIDC issuer URL; subject `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service account>`.
   - Azure DevOps: see the issuer table on Microsoft's troubleshooting page. New service connections use `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0`.
4. Check the audience. Microsoft recommends `api://AzureADTokenExchange`. If only the audience is wrong, you may see [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/).

**For admins:**
1. For Azure DevOps after a rename, Microsoft names the cause but gives no fix. Update the federation subject on the app or managed identity to the new `sc://` value. For a wrong issuer, Microsoft's fix is to edit and save the service connection. If Azure DevOps didn't create the identity, update the issuer yourself.
2. An app or user-assigned managed identity can hold at most 20 federated credentials. If you need one per branch or environment, plan for that limit.
3. If failures come from a provider you don't use, confirm no unexpected federated credential exists on the app, and review who can edit the app registration.

70025.title: AADSTS70025: App has no federated identity credentials (fix)
70025.description: AADSTS70025: an external token was sent for an app or managed identity with no federated identity credentials. Add one or fix the client ID. KQL.
70025.summary: AADSTS70025 means a workload presented an external token for an app registration or managed identity that has no federated identity credentials at all. Usually the credential was never created, was deleted, or the pipeline points at the wrong client ID. Users also report it when a certificate assertion was expected. A configuration error with low attack value.
70025.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS70025 (checked 30 October 2026). Microsoft's Azure DevOps troubleshooting page does:

> **AADSTS70025: Client application has no configured federated identity credentials**
> Make sure federated credentials are configured on the App registration or Managed Identity.

With workload identity federation, the workload sends a token from its own provider (GitHub, Azure DevOps, Kubernetes) as `client_assertion`, and Entra compares it with the federated identity credentials on the app or user-assigned managed identity named by the client ID. 70025 means that list is empty.

Our reading: this is the step before the matching codes. If at least one credential exists but none matches, you get [70021](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70021/), [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/) (issuer), [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/) (audience), [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) (subject) or [7002138](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002138/) (subject case). If the client ID doesn't exist in the tenant at all, you get [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/) instead.

Users also report 70025 in a case Microsoft doesn't describe. On Microsoft Q&A, a user signing in with a **certificate** (a self-signed JWT sent as `client_assertion`, not federation) got *"AADSTS70025: Client application has no configured federated identity credentials."* A second user reported the same with a certificate and a JWT assertion built in Python. The thread doesn't confirm a cause. Our reading, untested: Entra decided the assertion was an external token rather than a certificate assertion, so it looked for federated credentials. If you hit this with a certificate, check that the certificate is uploaded to the same app the client ID names, and how your library builds the assertion.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run set this up in my own tenant: one app registration presents its access token as a client assertion, and a second app carries the federated identity credential that is supposed to accept it. With **no federated credential on the target app at all**, Entra returned `AADSTS70025`:

> AADSTS70025: The client '<app id>'(<app name>) has no configured federated identity credentials.

The message names the client ID and the app's display name, so you can tell straight away which registration is missing the credential. This is the code you get when the credential was never created, or was created on a different app than the one in the request.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new pipeline or workflow fails on its first run | The federated credential was never created on this app or managed identity. |
| A pipeline points at a different app than the one you configured | The client ID in the pipeline or secret is another app registration with no credentials. In AL-Go issue 1147, a preview build of the tool read its credentials from a different GitHub secret than its docs said, and the maintainer called it a bug. |
| It worked before and now fails | Someone deleted the app's last federated credential, or the pipeline now targets another app. Check the audit log (below). |
| A certificate-based app fails with 70025 | Users report this. The cause is unconfirmed; see above. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 70025 lands in. App registration failures probably land in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`; Microsoft says managed identity sign-ins are in the managed identity sign-in log *"only"*, so a user-assigned managed identity may log there instead. Check:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs, AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "70025" or ResultSignature == "70025"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

Failures per app. `ClientCredentialType` is documented as *"The type of client credential used. Examples include client assertion, client secret, etc."* Seeing which type Entra recorded may help with the certificate case; that it is filled in on a failure is our assumption:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "70025" or ResultSignature == "70025"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            CredentialTypes = make_set(ClientCredentialType, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Failures desc
```

If the app had a credential before, look for its removal. A third-party write-up (trackr.live) reports that federated credential changes on an app registration log as `Update application` with a modified property `FederatedIdentityCredentials`; Microsoft doesn't document that name on the pages we checked:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName == "Update application"
| mv-expand Target = TargetResources
| mv-expand Prop = Target.modifiedProperties
| where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "FederatedIdentityCredentials"
| project TimeGenerated,
          App = tostring(Target.displayName),
          Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
          OldValue = tostring(Prop.oldValue),
          NewValue = tostring(Prop.newValue)
```

The same write-up says changes on a user-assigned managed identity are Azure Resource Manager writes and appear in the Azure activity log, not the Entra audit log.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS70025?
sections.text:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. Check which client ID the workload sends, and that it is the app or managed identity you configured.
2. If you meant to use a certificate or secret, check the tool really sends that. In AL-Go issue 1147 the user's workaround was to go back from the preview to the `@main` version of the tool.

**For admins:**
1. Add a federated identity credential on that app registration (**Certificates & secrets** > **Federated credentials**) or on the user-assigned managed identity. Microsoft's create-trust page lists the issuer and subject values for GitHub, Kubernetes and other providers.
2. Wait before the first run. Microsoft's restrictions page says a new credential takes time to propagate and early requests can fail with [70021](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70021/).
3. If a credential was deleted and nobody meant to, find out who did it from the audit log before recreating it.

fix.short: Developer: check that the workload sends the client ID of the app or managed identity you configured. Admin: add a federated identity credential on it (Certificates & secrets > Federated credentials), then wait for it to propagate before the first run.
fix.steps:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. Check which client ID the workload sends, and that it is the app or managed identity you configured.
2. If you meant to use a certificate or secret, check the tool really sends that. In AL-Go issue 1147 the user's workaround was to go back from the preview to the `@main` version of the tool.

**For admins:**
1. Add a federated identity credential on that app registration (**Certificates & secrets** > **Federated credentials**) or on the user-assigned managed identity. Microsoft's create-trust page lists the issuer and subject values for GitHub, Kubernetes and other providers.
2. Wait before the first run. Microsoft's restrictions page says a new credential takes time to propagate and early requests can fail with [70021](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70021/).
3. If a credential was deleted and nobody meant to, find out who did it from the audit log before recreating it.

70025.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run set this up in my own tenant: one app registration presents its access token as a client assertion, and a second app carries the federated identity credential that is supposed to accept it. The message names the client ID and the app's display name, so you can tell straight away which registration is missing the credential. This is the code you get when the credential was never created, or was created on a different app than the one in the request.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).
