70043.name: BadTokenDueToSignInFrequency
70043.title: AADSTS70043: Refresh token expired due to sign-in frequency checks
70043.description: AADSTS70043: a refresh token was refused by a sign-in frequency policy. Session control working as configured, low attack value. KQL included.
70043.summary: AADSTS70043 means a refresh token was refused because a Conditional Access sign-in frequency policy says the user must authenticate again. It is the session control working as configured, so it is expected and has low attack value. Volume tracks how strict your policy is. Hunt it in AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs with ResultType == "70043".
70043.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **BadTokenDueToSignInFrequency**: The refresh token has expired or is invalid due to sign-in frequency checks by Conditional Access. The token was issued on {issueDate} and the maximum allowed lifetime for this request is {time}.

An app tried to use a refresh token silently. A Conditional Access policy with a sign-in frequency session control says the user's last authentication is too old for this request. The app has to send the user to an interactive sign-in.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS70043 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **BadTokenDueToSignInFrequency**: The refresh token has expired or is invalid due to sign-in frequency checks by Conditional Access. The token was issued on {issueDate} and the maximum allowed lifetime for this request is {time}.

An app tried to use a refresh token silently. A Conditional Access policy with a sign-in frequency session control says the user's last authentication is too old for this request. The app has to send the user to an interactive sign-in.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
See the [comparison of the codes behind "asked to sign in again"](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/why-user-asked-to-sign-in-again-entra-id/) (70043, 700082, 50173, 50133, 50076).

No. 70043 is a control you configured doing its job. Expect it wherever you have a sign-in frequency policy, and expect more of it the shorter the interval.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 70043 for a user, followed by an interactive success in `SigninLogs` from the same IP and device | Normal re-authentication. Benign. |
| A jump in 70043 volume on a specific day | Someone created or tightened a sign-in frequency policy. Check your Conditional Access change history. |
| 70043 for a user from an IP or device they don't use, with no interactive sign-in following | An old refresh token being presented from somewhere unexpected. This is reasoning, not a documented detection: the control stopped it, but the token existed somewhere it shouldn't. Investigate as a possible stolen token. |

The message includes the token's issue date and the maximum allowed lifetime, so it tells you how old the token was when it was refused.

**IP caveat for confidential clients.** Microsoft's [non-interactive sign-ins page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/concept-noninteractive-sign-ins) says: *"The IP address of non-interactive sign-ins performed by confidential clients doesn't match the actual source IP of where the refresh token request is coming from. Instead, it shows the original IP used for the original token issuance."* So an unfamiliar IP is a weaker stolen-token signal for confidential clients: it may only show where the token was first issued. The second query below inherits that limit.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which apps and policies generate the volume:

```kusto
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "70043"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress)
          by AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName
| sort by Rows desc
```

The rare case worth a look: 70043 from an IP where the same user had no successful sign-in in the previous 30 days.

```kusto
let lookback = 30d;
let knownUserIPs =
    union
        (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType)
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "70043"
| join kind=leftanti knownUserIPs on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| extend Location = parse_json(LocationDetails)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress,
          Country = tostring(Location.countryOrRegion),
          AppDisplayName, UserAgent, ResultDescription
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"70043"`, not `70043`. `LocationDetails` is a string in this table, hence `parse_json`. Non-interactive rows are aggregated when application, user, IP address, status and resource match, so row counts are not request counts.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- The cause is a Conditional Access **session control**: sign-in frequency. Microsoft's default, with no such policy, is *"a rolling window of 90 days."*
- A shorter interval means more 70043 rows and more prompts. Microsoft warns: *"Triggering reauthentication too frequently can increase security friction to a point that it causes users to experience MFA fatigue and open the door to phishing."*
- The re-authentication after a 70043 is a normal sign-in. It goes through MFA and the rest of your Conditional Access policies.

sections.heading: Why do users keep getting prompted again?
sections.text:
Sign-in frequency applies to most Microsoft native apps, Microsoft web apps (Office.com, Exchange Online, SharePoint and OneDrive, the Teams web client, the Azure portal) and to non-Microsoft SAML and OAuth2/OIDC apps that redirect back to Entra ID regularly. Two device details explain most "I just signed in" complaints:

- On **Microsoft Entra joined and hybrid joined** devices, unlocking the device or signing in interactively refreshes the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) every four hours, and the PRT must fall inside the sign-in frequency window.
- On **Microsoft Entra registered** devices, unlocking the device does not satisfy the policy. The Entra WAM plugin can refresh the PRT while a native app authenticates.

Microsoft also warns that persistent browser cookies ("Stay signed in?") can keep Entra artifacts usable until the token expires, regardless of Conditional Access. Review that setting if you rely on short intervals as a security control.

sections.heading: How is 70043 different from 700082 and 50076?
sections.text:
All three can show up when a user is asked to sign in again, but they have different causes.

| Code | Cause | Attack value |
|---|---|---|
| **70043** | A Conditional Access sign-in frequency policy refused the refresh token | Low |
| [700082](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700082/) | The refresh token sat unused until it expired from inactivity | Low |
| [50076](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50076/) | Microsoft's description: a configuration change by the admin, such as a Conditional Access policy, per-user enforcement, or a new location, means the user must use multifactor authentication | Check the pattern |

The text "Strong Authentication is required" is Microsoft's description for [50074](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50074/), and 50076 has its own wording about a configuration change that requires MFA. The refresh-token text with "sign-in frequency" belongs to 70043. If you searched on either message, match the code in your sign-in log first.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS70043?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign in again when the app asks. This is expected behavior, not an error on your side.

**For admins:**
1. Nothing is broken. If users complain about too many prompts, check which policy sets the interval with the first query and the policy list on the matching interactive sign-in.
2. To change the interval, open the policy in the Microsoft Entra admin center under Conditional Access > Policies, then Session > Sign-in frequency. Microsoft's default with no policy is a rolling 90 days.
3. Reserve short sign-in frequency intervals for high-risk apps, users or unmanaged devices, rather than everyone.
4. If the second query returns a row you can't explain, treat the user's tokens as exposed: revoke the sessions and check the user's recent sign-ins. Microsoft documents `Revoke-MgUserSignInSession` for explicit revocation.

70044.description: AADSTS70044: a Conditional Access sign-in frequency check ended the session. Not in Microsoft's reference. What it means, how to fix it, with KQL.
70044.summary: AADSTS70044 means a Conditional Access sign-in frequency check ended the user's session, so the app must send the user to an interactive sign-in. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it; the wording comes from a Microsoft Q&A answer. It is the session control working, with low attack value. The app should handle it by prompting, not by retrying silently.
70044.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS70044 (checked 30 October 2026).

The wording below comes from a Microsoft Q&A thread, not from a Microsoft documentation page. A Q&A moderator (AmanpreetSingh-MSFT) quoted it in an answer:

> AADSTS70044: The session has expired or is invalid due to sign-in frequency checks by conditional access.

The person who asked quoted the sign-in log failure reason as *"The session has expired or is invalid due to sign-in frequency checks by conditional access. MFA requirement satisfied by claim in the token."*

In that thread, a Conditional Access policy set sign-in frequency to one hour for a VPN app. The moderator said the backend trace showed the credential was authenticated on one day and presented the next, outside the one-hour window, so it was ignored. The same thread says old credentials are usually reused during silent authentication, through a refresh token or a Primary Refresh Token (PRT).

A second Q&A thread describes users with several browsers hitting "error code 70044" under a 30-day sign-in frequency policy. That thread gives no full message text.

Our reading: 70044 is the session-side sibling of [70043](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70043/), which Microsoft does list. 70043 says the **refresh token** is too old for the sign-in frequency policy. 70044 says the **session** is. Both mean the same thing for the user: sign in again. Microsoft doesn't document the difference.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS70044 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS70044 (checked 30 October 2026).

The wording below comes from a Microsoft Q&A thread, not from a Microsoft documentation page. A Q&A moderator (AmanpreetSingh-MSFT) quoted it in an answer:

> AADSTS70044: The session has expired or is invalid due to sign-in frequency checks by conditional access.

The person who asked quoted the sign-in log failure reason as *"The session has expired or is invalid due to sign-in frequency checks by conditional access. MFA requirement satisfied by claim in the token."*

In that thread, a Conditional Access policy set sign-in frequency to one hour for a VPN app. The moderator said the backend trace showed the credential was authenticated on one day and presented the next, outside the one-hour window, so it was ignored. The same thread says old credentials are usually reused during silent authentication, through a refresh token or a Primary Refresh Token (PRT).

A second Q&A thread describes users with several browsers hitting "error code 70044" under a 30-day sign-in frequency policy. That thread gives no full message text.

Our reading: 70044 is the session-side sibling of [70043](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70043/), which Microsoft does list. 70043 says the **refresh token** is too old for the sign-in frequency policy. 70044 says the **session** is. Both mean the same thing for the user: sign in again. Microsoft doesn't document the difference.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Users report it where a sign-in frequency policy exists, and it is the policy doing what it was configured to do.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 70044 for many users shortly after a new or tightened sign-in frequency policy | The policy is now enforced. Expected. |
| 70044 for one user, repeating every few minutes, never followed by a success | The app keeps retrying silently and never prompts. An app bug, not an attack. Our interpretation. |
| 70044 for a user who works in several browsers | Each browser keeps its own cookies and session, so a new browser or cleared cookies starts a new sign-in. This is from a Q&A answer, not from Microsoft documentation. |
| 70044 from an IP or device the user never uses | An old session presented from somewhere unexpected. Our reasoning, not a documented detection: the control stopped it, but check the user's other sign-ins. |

One user report adds a caution. In Q&A 852942, revoking the user's sessions fixed the error only until the next day, and the person who asked later concluded the real cause was AD FS extranet lockout. That is their own conclusion, not a Microsoft answer, but it shows that 70044 can be the visible symptom of a different problem in federated tenants.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 70044 is logged in. Check where it lands in your workspace first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "70044"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

Which apps and session policies produce it. `SessionLifetimePolicies` is documented as *"any conditional access session management policies that were applied during the sign-in event."* It is a string in both tables:

```kusto
union
    (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, SessionLifetimePolicies),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, SessionLifetimePolicies)
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "70044"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, SessionLifetimePolicies
| sort by Rows desc
```

Users stuck in a loop: many 70044 rows in a day and no success on the same app. The threshold of 20 is a starting point; tune it to your volume.

```kusto
let window = 1d;
let fails =
    union
        (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName)
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(window)
    | where ResultType == "70044"
    | summarize Fails = count(), LastFail = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
    | where Fails >= 20;
let successes =
    union
        (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName)
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(window)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName;
fails
| join kind=leftanti successes on UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| sort by Fails desc
```

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- The trigger users report is a Conditional Access **sign-in frequency** session control. Microsoft's default without such a policy is *"a rolling window of 90 days."*
- With **Every time**, Microsoft says the policy *"requires full reauthentication when the session is evaluated"* and *"factors in five minutes of clock skew"*. Microsoft also warns that every-time reauthentication without MFA *"might result in sign-in looping for your users."*
- On Microsoft Entra joined and hybrid joined devices, Microsoft says unlocking the device or signing in interactively refreshes the PRT every four hours, and the PRT's last refresh must fall inside the sign-in frequency window. On Microsoft Entra registered devices, unlocking doesn't satisfy the policy.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS70044?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign in again when the app asks. If the app never shows a sign-in prompt and keeps failing, close it fully, open it again, and sign in. If that doesn't help, tell IT the app name and the time.

**For developers:** treat 70044 like any interaction-required result. Don't retry silently. The Q&A moderator's advice: force an interactive sign-in with `prompt=login` for OAuth and OpenID Connect, or `forceAuthN=true` for SAML. In the thread, `forceAuthN=true` worked but made every user type their username again, so use it only on this error, not on every sign-in.

**For admins:**
1. Find the policy. Open the failed sign-in in the Microsoft Entra admin center and check the Conditional Access tab, or use the second query above.
2. If the interval is shorter than the app can handle, lengthen it or scope the policy to the apps and users that need it. Microsoft advises to *"limit the number of applications that enforce a policy requiring users to reauthenticate every time."*
3. For a single user who keeps failing on a joined device, check that the device's PRT refreshes. The Q&A moderator suggested comparing the event log **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > AAD > Operational** between a working and a failing user.
4. In a federated tenant, rule out AD FS problems such as extranet lockout before you change the policy. That cause comes from one user report.

| 70044 for a user who works in several browsers | Each browser keeps its own cookies and session, so a new browser or cleared cookies starts a new sign-in. This is from a Q&A answer, not from Microsoft documentation. |
| 70044 from an IP or device the user never uses | An old session presented from somewhere unexpected. Our reasoning, not a documented detection: the control stopped it, but check the user's other sign-ins. |

One user report adds a caution. In Q&A 852942, revoking the user's sessions fixed the error only until the next day, and the person who asked later concluded the real cause was AD FS extranet lockout. That is their own conclusion, not a Microsoft answer, but it shows that 70044 can be the visible symptom of a different problem in federated tenants.

conditionalAccess.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
conditionalAccess.text:
- The trigger users report is a Conditional Access **sign-in frequency** session control. Microsoft's default without such a policy is *"a rolling window of 90 days."*
- With **Every time**, Microsoft says the policy *"requires full reauthentication when the session is evaluated"* and *"factors in five minutes of clock skew"*. Microsoft also warns that every-time reauthentication without MFA *"might result in sign-in looping for your users."*
- On Microsoft Entra joined and hybrid joined devices, Microsoft says unlocking the device or signing in interactively refreshes the PRT every four hours, and the PRT's last refresh must fall inside the sign-in frequency window. On Microsoft Entra registered devices, unlocking doesn't satisfy the policy.

fix.steps:
**For the user:** sign in again when the app asks. If the app never shows a sign-in prompt and keeps failing, close it fully, open it again, and sign in. If that doesn't help, tell IT the app name and the time.

**For developers:** treat 70044 like any interaction-required result. Don't retry silently. The Q&A moderator's advice: force an interactive sign-in with `prompt=login` for OAuth and OpenID Connect, or `forceAuthN=true` for SAML. In the thread, `forceAuthN=true` worked but made every user type their username again, so use it only on this error, not on every sign-in.

**For admins:**
1. Find the policy. Open the failed sign-in in the Microsoft Entra admin center and check the Conditional Access tab, or use the second query above.
2. If the interval is shorter than the app can handle, lengthen it or scope the policy to the apps and users that need it. Microsoft advises to *"limit the number of applications that enforce a policy requiring users to reauthenticate every time."*
3. For a single user who keeps failing on a joined device, check that the device's PRT refreshes. The Q&A moderator suggested comparing the event log **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > AAD > Operational** between a working and a failing user.
4. In a federated tenant, rule out AD FS problems such as extranet lockout before you change the policy. That cause comes from one user report.

75011.name: NoMatchedAuthnContextInOutputClaims
75011.title: AADSTS75011: Sign-in method doesn't match what the app asked for (fix)
75011.description: AADSTS75011: a SAML app requested an authentication method the user's session doesn't match. A config issue; remove RequestedAuthnContext or force auth. KQL.
75011.summary: AADSTS75011 means a SAML app asked for a specific authentication method in its request, and the method the user already signed in with is different. Microsoft Entra ID reuses the existing session instead of signing the user in again, so the two don't match. It is a configuration problem with low attack value. Fix it by removing RequestedAuthnContext or adding ForceAuthn.
75011.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **NoMatchedAuthnContextInOutputClaims**: The authentication method by which the user authenticated with the service doesn't match requested authentication method. To learn more, see the troubleshooting article for error [AADSTS75011](https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/azure/active-directory/error-code-aadsts75011-auth-method-mismatch).

This is a SAML single sign-on error. The app put a `RequestedAuthnContext` element in its SAML request. That element names the authentication method the app wants, as an `AuthnContextClassRef` value such as `urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:Password`.

Microsoft's troubleshooting article explains the cause: the user had already signed in before reaching the app, and *"the `AuthnContext` (authentication method) used for that previous authentication is different from the one being requested."* Microsoft Entra ID *"won't perform a fresh authentication request"*. It reuses the authentication context it already has, so the response can't contain the method the app asked for.

Microsoft's example is a federated user who signed in to My Apps with Windows Integrated Authentication through AD FS. The session's `AuthnContextClassRef` is then `urn:federation:authentication:windows`, and *"there will be a mismatch if the app requests other than `urn:federation:authentication:windows`."* The article names a second case: a session where MFA was used.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No documented attack pattern exists for 75011. It is an agreement problem between the app's SAML request and the user's existing session. Our reading: the sign-in fails before the app receives an assertion, so an attacker gains nothing from it.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 75011 for many users of one SAML app, starting on a specific day | The app (or a change to it) started sending `RequestedAuthnContext`. Configuration. |
| 75011 only for federated users | Likely, based on Microsoft's AD FS example: the session came from the federation service with a method the app doesn't accept. |
| 75011 only for users who signed in with MFA or a certificate earlier in the session | The session method (for example a certificate or MFA) is stronger or different from the one the app named. Configuration. |
| 75011 that goes away when the user opens the app in a private window | Likely the same cause: without an existing session, the user authenticates fresh and the method can match. Unconfirmed. |

Exclude it from failure-based attack detections.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 75011 is logged in. Check where it lands in your workspace first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "75011"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which apps cause it, and whether the sessions came from a federation service:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "75011"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            Protocols = make_set(AuthenticationProtocol, 5),
            Issuers = make_set(TokenIssuerType, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

`AuthenticationProtocol` is documented with values including `saml20`. A `FirstSeen` date that lines up with a change to the app is the most useful clue. `TokenIssuerType` is documented with values including `AzureAD` and `ADFederationServices`. If `Issuers` shows `ADFederationServices` rather than `AzureAD`, you are likely in Microsoft's AD FS scenario.

Users who hit 75011 and then succeeded on the same app the same day, a sign that a fresh sign-in (for example a new browser session) works around it:

```kusto
let mismatches =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "75011"
    | summarize FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName;
let successes =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize LastSuccess = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId;
mismatches
| join kind=leftouter successes on UserPrincipalName, AppId
| extend RecoveredLater = isnotnull(LastSuccess) and LastSuccess > FirstFail
| summarize Users = count(), Recovered = countif(RecoveredLater) by AppDisplayName
| sort by Users desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"75011"`, not `75011`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS75011?
sections.text:
**For the user:** close the browser (or open a private window) and open the app again. That may help because there is no earlier session to reuse. This is not a documented fix. If it still fails, report it to the app's owner with the time of the error. It is not something you can fix on your side.

**For developers (the SAML app):**
1. Remove `RequestedAuthnContext` from the `AuthnRequest` if you can. Microsoft calls it *"an optional value"* and its first suggestion is to *"ask the application if the value could be removed"*.
2. If you must keep it, request a fresh sign-in. Microsoft says *"the SAML request must contain the value, `forceAuthn="true"`"*, so the requested method is used. The SAML protocol reference describes `ForceAuthn` as forcing the user *"to reauthenticate, even if they have a valid session with Microsoft Entra ID."*
3. If you keep `RequestedAuthnContext`, set `Comparison` to `exact`. Microsoft's SAML reference says it *"must be set to `exact`"*, and lists the `AuthnContextClassRef` values Microsoft Entra ID supports. Only request one of those.

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and the date it started.
2. Ask the vendor whether the app can stop sending `RequestedAuthnContext`, or send `ForceAuthn="true"` with it. Both changes are made in the app's SAML request, not in Entra ID.
3. If the app needs MFA, enforce that with a Conditional Access policy on the app instead of asking for it in the SAML request. Our recommendation, not a step from Microsoft's article.

76021.name: ApplicationRequiresSignedRequests
76021.title: AADSTS76021 fix: SAML request not signed but required
76021.description: AADSTS76021: the SAML app requires signed requests and got an unsigned one. Fix the signature or the verification certificate. Low attack value.
76021.summary: AADSTS76021 means a SAML app in Microsoft Entra ID is set to require signed authentication requests, and the request it received wasn't signed, or the signature wasn't where the SAML binding expects it. It follows an admin enabling Require verification certificates. It is a configuration error and the check is working as intended. Low attack value.
76021.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **ApplicationRequiresSignedRequests**: The request sent by client is not signed while the application requires signed requests

This is a SAML error. Microsoft's troubleshooting article says it *"indicates that the client didn't sign the request, but the application requires signed requests. Even if the client signs the request, the signature might not be added according to the SAML binding configuration."*

The requirement comes from a setting on the enterprise app. Microsoft: *"To enable the verification of signed requests, select **Require verification certificates** and upload a verification public key that matches with the private key used to sign the request."* Once that is on, Entra ID rejects an `AuthnRequest` it can't verify. Microsoft's list of verification failures includes *"Request not signed, but verification is enabled."*

Where the signature goes depends on the binding:

- **HTTP-Redirect**: *"the signature is included as a query parameter in the URL"* (`SigAlg` and `Signature`).
- **HTTP-POST**: *"the signature is embedded within the XML payload of the SAML message."*

*"If the application expects the signature in one location but the request uses another binding type, Microsoft Entra ID rejects the request."*

sections.heading: What does AADSTS76021 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **ApplicationRequiresSignedRequests**: The request sent by client is not signed while the application requires signed requests

This is a SAML error. Microsoft's troubleshooting article says it *"indicates that the client didn't sign the request, but the application requires signed requests. Even if the client signs the request, the signature might not be added according to the SAML binding configuration."*

The requirement comes from a setting on the enterprise app. Microsoft: *"To enable the verification of signed requests, select **Require verification certificates** and upload a verification public key that matches with the private key used to sign the request."* Once that is on, Entra ID rejects an `AuthnRequest` it can't verify. Microsoft's list of verification failures includes *"Request not signed, but verification is enabled."*

Where the signature goes depends on the binding:

- **HTTP-Redirect**: *"the signature is included as a query parameter in the URL"* (`SigAlg` and `Signature`).
- **HTTP-POST**: *"the signature is embedded within the XML payload of the SAML message."*

*"If the application expects the signature in one location but the request uses another binding type, Microsoft Entra ID rejects the request."*

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. The setting exists so Entra ID only accepts requests the real service provider signed. 76021 is that check refusing a request. Microsoft also notes that *"Requestor verification is provided for by only responding to registered Assertion Consumer Service URLs"*, so an unsigned request can't send the response somewhere new.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Every user of one SAML app fails, starting at a known change | Someone enabled **Require verification certificates** and the app doesn't sign its requests. |
| Failures began when the app or its proxy was updated | The app now signs with a different key, or uses a different binding. |
| Users fail when they open the app from My Apps or the Microsoft 365 app launcher | Microsoft says the setting *"will not allow IDP-initiated authentication requests (like SSO testing feature, MyApps or M365 app launcher) to be validated."* Microsoft doesn't say which error code users see then. Our reading: 76021 is a likely candidate. |

Users report it in exactly this shape. In a Microsoft Q&A thread, sign-in worked until the signature verification feature was turned on, then failed with 76021. The moderator's two causes: the app doesn't send a signed request, or the wrong certificate is uploaded.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 76021 lands in. Check your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "76021"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which apps fail, for how many users, and since when. The first failure time tells you when to look in the audit log:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "76021"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Protocols = make_set(AuthenticationProtocol, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Users desc
```

Who changed the app shortly before the failures began. Microsoft lists **Update service principal** as an audit activity. Our assumption: turning on verification certificates is recorded under it; Microsoft doesn't say so. Set the time window around `FirstSeen`:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName == "Update service principal"
| extend App = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
         ByUser = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, App, ByUser, Result
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS76021?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this. Tell your IT team which app failed and when. If you opened it from My Apps, also try the app's own sign-in page, since requests started from the portal can't be validated with this setting on.

**For the app owner or vendor (service provider):**
1. Sign every SAML `AuthnRequest` with the private key that matches the certificate uploaded in Entra ID.
2. Use RSA-SHA256. Microsoft: *"Only RSA-SHA256 is supported"*, with an admin opt-in for RSA-SHA1.
3. Put the signature where the binding expects it. For HTTP-Redirect it must be in the query string. For HTTP-POST it must be inside the XML `<Signature>` element.

**For admins:**
1. Go to **Entra ID** > **Enterprise apps** > **All applications** > the app > **Single sign-on** > **SAML Certificates** > **Verification certificates** > **Edit**. Check that the uploaded certificate is the one the app signs with and hasn't expired.
2. Check the binding the app uses (HTTP-Redirect or HTTP-POST) matches its SAML configuration, as Microsoft's troubleshooting article says.
3. If the app can't sign requests, clearing **Require verification certificates** removes the requirement. That turns off the protection, so do it only as a deliberate decision.
4. The SSO test button in the admin center doesn't work with this setting on. Microsoft: *"the test experience is disabled as the service provider has to sign the request."* Test from the app's own sign-in page instead.

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
No. The setting exists so Entra ID only accepts requests the real service provider signed. 76021 is that check refusing a request. Microsoft also notes that *"Requestor verification is provided for by only responding to registered Assertion Consumer Service URLs"*, so an unsigned request can't send the response somewhere new.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Every user of one SAML app fails, starting at a known change | Someone enabled **Require verification certificates** and the app doesn't sign its requests. |
| Failures began when the app or its proxy was updated | The app now signs with a different key, or uses a different binding. |
| Users fail when they open the app from My Apps or the Microsoft 365 app launcher | Microsoft says the setting *"will not allow IDP-initiated authentication requests (like SSO testing feature, MyApps or M365 app launcher) to be validated."* Microsoft doesn't say which error code users see then. Our reading: 76021 is a likely candidate. |

90002.name: InvalidTenantName
90002.title: AADSTS90002: Tenant not found (fix)
90002.description: AADSTS90002: the tenant in the sign-in request doesn't exist. Wrong tenant ID, wrong cloud, or unregistered domain. How to fix it, with KQL.
90002.summary: AADSTS90002 means the sign-in request named a tenant that Entra can't find. Usually the tenant ID or domain in the app's settings is wrong, the app talks to the wrong cloud, or the domain was derived from an email address and isn't registered. It is a configuration error with low attack value. Check the tenant ID and the cloud endpoint.
90002.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidTenantName**: The tenant name wasn't found in the data store. Check to make sure you have the correct tenant ID. The application developer will receive this error if their app attempts to sign into a tenant that we cannot find. Often, this is because a cross-cloud app was used against the wrong cloud, or the developer attempted to sign in to a tenant derived from an email address, but the domain isn't registered.

Every sign-in request names a tenant in its URL, as a tenant ID (a GUID) or a domain: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/...`. 90002 means Entra has no tenant by that name in the cloud the request went to.

The "wrong cloud" cause is real because the clouds are separate. Microsoft's national clouds page says *"Each cloud instance is separate from the others and has its own environment and endpoints"* and lists `https://login.microsoftonline.com` (global), `https://login.microsoftonline.us` (US Government) and `https://login.partner.microsoftonline.cn` (China, operated by 21Vianet). A US Government tenant ID sent to the global endpoint is not found, and the other way round.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request to a tenant ID that doesn't exist (a random GUID the script generated). Entra returned `AADSTS90002` with this first line:

> AADSTS90002: Tenant '{tenant-id}' not found. Check to make sure you have the correct tenant ID and are signing into the correct cloud.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint. Note that the returned message mentions the cloud as well as the tenant ID. No sign-in log row was captured. Our reading: there is no tenant to log it in, because the tenant named in the request doesn't exist, and the request never reached the lab tenant either. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a configuration error in the app or script that sent the request.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new app or script fails on its first run | Typo in the tenant ID, or a placeholder value left in the config. |
| An app that works in one environment fails in another | The app points at the wrong cloud endpoint for that tenant. |
| A multi-tenant app that builds the tenant from the user's email domain | The domain isn't a verified domain of any tenant, as Microsoft's description says. |
| An app that worked before and now fails | The tenant was deleted, or the custom domain used as tenant name was removed from it. Our interpretation. |

Our reading: tenant discovery by attackers doesn't need this error and doesn't show up in your logs through it. A request to a tenant that doesn't exist reaches no tenant.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 90002 is logged in. It probably lands in none of yours, for the reason in the lab note above. Check anyway; this query is expected to return nothing:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90002"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

What the logs can do is tell you the right value to configure. For an app that fails with 90002, find where it signs in successfully and which tenant that is. `ResourceTenantId` is documented as *"the tenant identifier of the resource referenced in the sign in"*:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable
    SigninLogs,
    (AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs | extend ResourceTenantId = AADTenantId, AppDisplayName = ServicePrincipalName)
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| where AppId == "<app id of the failing app>"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, ResourceTenantId, AppDisplayName
```

`AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` has no `ResourceTenantId` or `AppDisplayName` column, so the query uses `AADTenantId` and `ServicePrincipalName` there (our choice; the table reference doesn't describe `AADTenantId`). If this returns your tenant ID and the app config holds a different one, you found the cause.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90002?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report the app name to whoever set it up.

**For developers:**
1. Check the tenant ID or domain in the authority URL. Compare it with the real tenant ID; Microsoft's page on finding it says to use **Entra ID** > **Overview** > **Properties** in the Entra admin center, or `Get-AzTenant` in Azure PowerShell.
2. Check the cloud. Microsoft's national clouds page: *"use the endpoints for the cloud instance where you'll deploy the application."* A tenant in US Government or China needs that cloud's login endpoint, not `login.microsoftonline.com`.
3. Don't derive the tenant from the user's email domain unless you handle the case where the domain isn't registered. For a multi-tenant app, sign in through `/organizations` or `/common` and read the tenant from the token instead.

**For admins:**
1. Get the correct tenant ID from the admin center or with PowerShell:

```powershell
Connect-AzAccount
Get-AzTenant
```

2. If the app uses a domain name as tenant, check that the domain is still verified in your tenant.
3. If the app is a third-party product, give the vendor your tenant ID and tell them which cloud your tenant is in.

90009.name: TokenForItselfMissingIdenticalAppIdentifier
90009.title: AADSTS90009 fix: app requests a token for itself
90009.description: AADSTS90009: an app asked for a token for itself without using its GUID app ID. A developer error, no attack value; fix the resource or scope.
90009.summary: AADSTS90009 means an app asked Microsoft Entra ID for a token where the resource is the app itself, but named itself with an App ID URI or other string instead of its GUID application ID. Microsoft supports that only with the GUID. It is a developer error with no attack value. Use the client ID GUID as the resource, or call the right API.
90009.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **TokenForItselfMissingIdenticalAppIdentifier**: The application is requesting a token for itself. This scenario is supported only if the resource that's specified is using the GUID-based application ID.

In a token request the app names two things: itself (the client, by its application ID) and the API it wants a token for (the resource). Here both point at the same app. Entra ID accepts that only if the resource is given as the app's **GUID application ID**. If the resource is given another way, such as the App ID URI, the request fails with 90009.

An app can be named by more than its GUID. Microsoft describes the App ID URI as a string a resource sets *"as its identifier"*, which *"Clients who acquire a token for the API can use … during an OAuth request"*. The service principal's `servicePrincipalNames` hold those URIs. Microsoft recommends `api://<appId>` as the format. So a request with resource `api://<your client ID>` or `https://yourdomain/...` can point back at your own app without containing the bare GUID.

The full message users report reads: *"AADSTS90009: Application '<id>'(<name>) is requesting a token for itself. This scenario is supported only if resource is specified using the GUID based App Identifier."*

sections.heading: What does AADSTS90009 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **TokenForItselfMissingIdenticalAppIdentifier**: The application is requesting a token for itself. This scenario is supported only if the resource that's specified is using the GUID-based application ID.

In a token request the app names two things: itself (the client, by its application ID) and the API it wants a token for (the resource). Here both point at the same app. Entra ID accepts that only if the resource is given as the app's **GUID application ID**. If the resource is given another way, such as the App ID URI, the request fails with 90009.

An app can be named by more than its GUID. Microsoft describes the App ID URI as a string a resource sets *"as its identifier"*, which *"Clients who acquire a token for the API can use … during an OAuth request"*. The service principal's `servicePrincipalNames` hold those URIs. Microsoft recommends `api://<appId>` as the format. So a request with resource `api://<your client ID>` or `https://yourdomain/...` can point back at your own app without containing the bare GUID.

The full message users report reads: *"AADSTS90009: Application '<id>'(<name>) is requesting a token for itself. This scenario is supported only if resource is specified using the GUID based App Identifier."*

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. A request that names itself badly gets nothing. Users report it in three situations:

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| An MSAL.js app gets 90009 from `acquireTokenSilent` when asking for a token for its own App Service API | Reported in Microsoft Q&A. The thread doesn't show the scope used; the error says the app named itself without its GUID. |
| A script or service account asks for a scope with the app's own custom-domain URI | The scope was meant for another API but named the calling app. In one Microsoft Q&A thread a moderator found exactly that: *"the value in scope should be the client-id or application ID URI of your web API"*, not the caller's. |
| A password-grant (ROPC) request through an identity broker such as Auth0 | The broker sends a resource or audience that resolves to its own Entra app. Reported in the Auth0 community. |

None of these is a security signal. In the second row the app didn't mean to ask for itself at all, so check that first.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 90009 lands in, or whether it is logged at all. Our interpretation is that it may be rejected before a sign-in row is written, as a malformed request. Check your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90009"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

If rows exist, which apps request tokens for themselves:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90009"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Resources = make_set(ResourceIdentity, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName = coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName)
| sort by Rows desc
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90009?
sections.text:
**For developers:**
1. Decide which API the token is really for. If it is a **different** API, put that API's identifier in the scope, for example `api://<web API client ID>/.default` or `<web API client ID>/.default`. Then add that API under your app's **API permissions** and get consent.
2. If your app really needs a token for **itself** (one registration for front end and API), give the resource as the GUID application ID, for example a scope of `<your client ID>/.default` or `<your client ID>/<scope>`. Microsoft notes that some APIs *"expect only the app ID (a GUID) and the scope name"* in the scope.
3. With the v1.0 endpoint or a library that sends `resource`, set `resource` to the client ID GUID, not the App ID URI. The Auth0 thread quotes a Stack Overflow answer with this advice; the poster didn't confirm it worked.
4. For app-only tokens, Microsoft's rule is that *"The scope to request for a client credential flow is the name of the resource followed by `/.default`"*.

**For admins:** nothing to change in the tenant. Send the app ID from the error to the developer.

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
No. A request that names itself badly gets nothing. Users report it in three situations:

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| An MSAL.js app gets 90009 from `acquireTokenSilent` when asking for a token for its own App Service API | Reported in Microsoft Q&A. The thread doesn't show the scope used; the error says the app named itself without its GUID. |

| A password-grant (ROPC) request through an identity broker such as Auth0 | The broker sends a resource or audience that resolves to its own Entra app. Reported in the Auth0 community. |

None of these is a security signal. In the second row the app didn't mean to ask for itself at all, so check that first.

90014.name: MissingRequiredField
90014.title: AADSTS90014 fix: required field missing from the request
90014.description: AADSTS90014: Entra expected a field that wasn't in the request. The message names it, often 'scope' or 'request'. Add it or fix the flow; KQL.
90014.summary: AADSTS90014 means Entra expected a field in the request or credential and it wasn't there. The message names the field: users report 'scope' from integrations such as ServiceNow, and 'request' when a browser app navigated back during sign-in. Microsoft gives no more detail. Low attack value. Read the field name and fix the request or the sign-in flow.
90014.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **MissingRequiredField**: This error code might appear in various cases when an expected field isn't present in the credential.

Entra ID expected a field and didn't find it. Microsoft doesn't list the cases, but the message names the field, and that is where to start. Users report two forms:

- *"AADSTS90014: The required field 'scope' is missing from the credential"*, from ServiceNow using OAuth against a Microsoft API.
- *"AADSTS90014: The required field 'request' is missing from the credential"*, from a single-page app signing in through Azure AD B2C, and quoted in a moderator's answer to a user signing in to school or work apps.

Compare [900144](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/900144/), which says *"The request body must contain the following parameter"* and also names what is missing. Microsoft doesn't explain when Entra returns one code and not the other. Either way the fix is to supply what the message names. If the message is about `resource` instead, see [901002](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/901002/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No documented attack pattern exists. The request is incomplete and no token is issued.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Field `scope`, from an integration or service account | A client credentials (or similar) token request without `scope`. Microsoft marks `scope` as **Required** in the client credentials flow. Configuration. |
| Field `request`, from a browser app, now and then | In the B2C thread the accepted answer said it *"can be caused by navigating back after succesfuly loging-in"*, and the developer confirmed the app navigated back right after sign-in. Our reading: the sign-in response was lost because the app left the page before handling it. |
| Field `request`, one user, a third-party app | The user pressed Back or reloaded during sign-in, or the app's flow has the same bug. Not an attack. |
| 90014 from one app, starting right after a release | The new version stopped sending a field. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document whether or where 90014 is logged. Check all three sign-in tables:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "90014"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which app is missing which field. We assume `ResultDescription` carries the message with the field name filled in; we haven't seen a logged row:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "90014"
| extend Field = extract(@"field '([^']+)'", 1, ResultDescription)
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName, AppId, Field
| sort by Rows desc
```

Apps that produced 90014 today but not in the previous 14 days. A `FirstSeen` right after a deployment points at the release:

```kusto
let recent =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "90014"
    | summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by AppId, AppDisplayName;
let before =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(15d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ResultType == "90014"
    | distinct AppId;
recent
| join kind=leftanti before on AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"90014"`, not `90014`. In `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` the app name is in `ServicePrincipalName`, not `AppDisplayName`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90014?
sections.text:
**For the user:**
1. Don't press Back or reload while the sign-in page is working. Close the tab and start again from the app.
2. If it keeps happening, clear the browser's cookies for the site and try again. That was the generic advice in the Q&A thread; one user said it didn't help.
3. Still failing: report it to IT with the full message, including the field name.

**For developers:**
1. Read the field name in the error and add it.
2. `scope` in a client credentials request: send the API's identifier with `.default`, for example `https://graph.microsoft.com/.default`. Microsoft: *"All scopes included must be for a single resource."*
3. `request` in a browser app: let the app finish processing the sign-in response before it routes or navigates anywhere. The accepted answer in the B2C thread recommended a browser trace of the whole flow to see where it breaks.

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and the field, and send both to the app's owner.
2. For ServiceNow or another integration with an OAuth profile, check whether the profile sends a scope. ServiceNow documents the 'scope' form of this error in KB0866332.

90015.name: QueryStringTooLong
90015.title: AADSTS90015 fix: sign-in request URL is too long
90015.description: AADSTS90015: the sign-in request URL was too long for Entra. Shrink state and return URLs, or wait for the app vendor's fix. KQL included.
90015.summary: AADSTS90015 means the sign-in request URL Entra received had a query string that was too long. Sign-in requests travel as URL parameters, so a large state value, a long return URL or a chain of identity providers can push it over the limit. Users report it from Jira Cloud for Outlook, Azure Databricks and chained Okta setups. Low attack value.
90015.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **QueryStringTooLong**: The query string is too long.

The message users see is *"AADSTS90015: Requested query string is too long."*

Sign-in requests to Entra ID are URLs. An OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect sign-in is a request to the `/authorize` endpoint with everything in the query string: `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state` and more. A SAML sign-in works the same way: Microsoft's SAML reference says the app *"uses an HTTP Redirect binding to pass an `AuthnRequest`"* to Entra ID. If that URL gets too long, Entra ID rejects the request with 90015.

Microsoft doesn't publish the limit. Atlassian's support article says Microsoft restricts query parameters *"to a maximum of 2048 characters"*; we haven't found that number in Microsoft's documentation.

What makes a request long, in our reading:
- **The `state` parameter.** Microsoft says it *"can be a string of any content that you wish"* and *"can also encode information about the user's state in the app"*. Apps that pack a lot into it make every sign-in URL longer.
- **Long return or deep-link URLs**, carried inside `redirect_uri`, `state` or a SAML `RelayState`, and URL-encoded on top.
- **Chained identity providers.** Each hop can wrap the previous request in its own. A user on the Okta forum reports the error only with Okta → Okta → Entra ID; single-hop setups worked.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document whether a 90015 is written to the sign-in logs. The request is rejected early, and we don't know whether a row is created. Check all three tables:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "90015"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

If rows exist, find the app, the protocol and the browser. `AuthenticationProtocol` tells SAML (`saml20`) from OAuth (`oAuth2`):

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "90015"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, AuthenticationProtocol
| sort by Users desc
```

Sudden spread across users of one app, the vendor-side pattern. Five users in an hour is a starting point:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "90015"
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Users >= 5
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

If the first query returns nothing while users do see the error, the request probably never produced a sign-in row. Then the browser is your only evidence: ask the user for the Request ID, Correlation ID and timestamp from the error page.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90015?
sections.text:
**For the user:**
1. Open the app from its normal start address, not from an old bookmark or a link deep inside the app.
2. Clear cookies for the site, or use a private window, and keep only one account signed in. These are the steps suggested to Databricks users while the vendor fix was pending.
3. Jira Cloud for Outlook: Atlassian's fix is to sign in to `id.atlassian.com` with Microsoft first, then connect the add-on from Outlook on the web, and then go back to the desktop app.
4. If it still fails, report it with the Request ID, Correlation ID and timestamp from the error page.

**For developers:**
1. Keep `state` short. Microsoft: *"do not put URLs or other sensitive data directly in the state parameter. Instead, use a key or identifier that corresponds to data stored in browser storage"*.
2. Don't carry long deep-link URLs through the sign-in. Store the target and pass a short key.
3. Request only the scopes you need at sign-in. Every scope adds to the URL.
4. For chained identity providers, cut a hop if you can. Our reading is that each hop adds its own wrapped request.

**For admins:**
1. Many users of one app at the same time points to the vendor. Check their status page or support before changing anything in your tenant.
2. For a home-built app, send the second query's result to the developer with the steps above.

90015.kqlSectionText:
Microsoft doesn't document whether a 90015 is written to the sign-in logs. The request is rejected early, and we don't know whether a row is created. Check all three tables:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "90015"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

If rows exist, find the app, the protocol and the browser. `AuthenticationProtocol` tells SAML (`saml20`) from OAuth (`oAuth2`):

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "90015"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, AuthenticationProtocol
| sort by Users desc
```

Sudden spread across users of one app, the vendor-side pattern. Five users in an hour is a starting point:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "90015"
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Users >= 5
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

If the first query returns nothing while users do see the error, the request probably never produced a sign-in row. Then the browser is your only evidence: ask the user for the Request ID, Correlation ID and timestamp from the error page.

fix.short: User: open the app from its normal start URL, not a bookmark or deep link, clear cookies or use a private window, and try again. Developer: keep the request small. Put a short key in `state`, not a URL or app data, and shorten return URLs. Many users at once: it is likely on the app's side.
fix.steps:
**For the user:**
1. Open the app from its normal start address, not from an old bookmark or a link deep inside the app.
2. Clear cookies for the site, or use a private window, and keep only one account signed in. These are the steps suggested to Databricks users while the vendor fix was pending.
3. Jira Cloud for Outlook: Atlassian's fix is to sign in to `id.atlassian.com` with Microsoft first, then connect the add-on from Outlook on the web, and then go back to the desktop app.
4. If it still fails, report it with the Request ID, Correlation ID and timestamp from the error page.

**For developers:**
1. Keep `state` short. Microsoft: *"do not put URLs or other sensitive data directly in the state parameter. Instead, use a key or identifier that corresponds to data stored in browser storage"*.
2. Don't carry long deep-link URLs through the sign-in. Store the target and pass a short key.
3. Request only the scopes you need at sign-in. Every scope adds to the URL.
4. For chained identity providers, cut a hop if you can. Our reading is that each hop adds its own wrapped request.

**For admins:**
1. Many users of one app at the same time points to the vendor. Check their status page or support before changing anything in your tenant.
2. For a home-built app, send the second query's result to the developer with the steps above.

90019.name: MissingTenantRealm
90019.title: AADSTS90019 fix: no tenant found in the sign-in request
90019.description: AADSTS90019: Entra couldn't tell which tenant the sign-in was for. Use the full email address or a tenant-specific authority. Low attack value.
90019.summary: AADSTS90019 means Microsoft Entra ID couldn't work out which tenant a sign-in was for: the request didn't name one and the credentials didn't imply one. Users often see it in Outlook or the browser after typing a short username. Our reading: developers can hit it when an app uses the `common` endpoint with no user or tenant hint. It is a configuration or input error with low attack value.
90019.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **MissingTenantRealm**: Microsoft Entra ID was unable to determine the tenant identifier from the request.

The message users post is longer: *"No tenant-identifying information found in either the request or implied by any provided credentials."* Entra ID didn't know which organisation's directory to use, so, our reading, it stopped before checking anything else.

Entra ID gets the tenant from one of two places:

- **The URL.** In the authority `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/`, Microsoft says *"the `<tenant>` in the URL is the tenant ID of the Microsoft Entra tenant (a GUID), or its tenant domain."*
- **The user.** On the common sign-in page users *"enter a user principal name (UPN). Microsoft Entra ID uses this information to determine the correct sign-in location."* Microsoft calls this Home Realm Discovery.

Our reading: 90019 is what you get when neither source gives an answer. The request went to `common` or `organizations`, and there was no username with a known domain, no hint, and no credential that points at a tenant.

Don't confuse it with two codes that already have pages. [90002](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90002/) means a tenant value was sent but no such tenant exists. [900023](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/900023/) means the tenant value isn't a valid tenant ID or domain at all. With 90019 there was no tenant value to check.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Rarely. Our reading: the request fails before any user, password or app in your tenant is looked at. Users report it in ordinary situations:

- A university helpdesk sees it when students sign in to **Outlook**. Their advice is to enter the full email address, retype saved credentials, and try another browser or a private window.
- TheWindowsClub reports it for Office 365 and Skype for Business sign-ins.
- Quest has a knowledge base entry for it in Essentials for Office 365, a migration tool, which suggests admin tools and integrations hit it too.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One user, one app, then a success | The user typed a short username or a saved credential was wrong. Benign. |
| Every run of a script or service fails | The script sends an app-only request to `common` or `organizations`. A developer error. |
| A third-party federation or migration tool fails for everyone | The tool's tenant or domain setting is empty or wrong. Configuration. |

Our reading: since Entra ID didn't find a tenant, it may not write the failure to your tenant's sign-in log at all. Microsoft doesn't document this. An empty result from the queries below doesn't prove users aren't hitting it; ask them for the error page details.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 90019 lands in, or whether it reaches a tenant's log at all. Check your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90019"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

If rows exist, see which app, client and user agent produce them:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90019"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Clients = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 5),
            Agents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"90019"`, not `90019`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90019?
sections.text:
**For the user:**
1. Sign in with your **full work email address** (for example `{user-principal-name}`), not just your username. Entra ID uses the domain part to find your organisation.
2. If a password manager or the app filled in the name, retype it yourself.
3. Users report that a private browser window, clearing the browser cache, or another browser also helps. If none of that works, send your IT helpdesk the error details.

**For developers:**
1. If your app serves one organisation, put the tenant ID (GUID) or a verified domain in the authority: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/`.
2. For app-only requests (client credentials), the token request needs a tenant. Microsoft's reference marks `tenant` as **Required**: *"The directory tenant the application plans to operate against, in GUID or domain-name format."*
3. For a multitenant app on `common` or `organizations`, give Entra ID a way to find the tenant: a `login_hint` with the user's address, or a domain hint. Microsoft lists the domain hint per protocol: `domain_hint` for OpenID Connect, `whr` for WS-Federation, and a domain hint or `whr` for SAML.

**For admins:**
1. For a third-party tool or federation service (a migration tool, a WS-Federation identity provider), check that its tenant or domain setting is filled in with your tenant ID or a verified domain.
2. Check that users' sign-in names use a domain verified in your tenant. Microsoft notes that sign-in uses *"organization and user settings for the username entered on the sign-in page."*

90023.name: InvalidRequest
90023.title: AADSTS90023: Entra rejected the request as invalid (fix)
90023.description: AADSTS90023: Entra rejected the request as invalid. Two lab-confirmed causes: a wrong client assertion type and a device code client ID mismatch.
90023.summary: AADSTS90023 means Microsoft Entra ID rejected the token request as invalid. Microsoft's reference describes it only as InvalidRequest. The lab has returned it for two different causes with two different messages: a client_assertion_type that is not the JWT bearer URN, and a device code polled with a different client_id than the one that requested it. Read the message, not just the code.
90023.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidRequest**: The authentication service request isn't valid.

That is as much as the reference says, and 90023 is a bucket, not a single fault. It is the code Entra uses when it refuses to process a token request at all, and the lab has produced it from two unrelated causes on two different flows. The code is the same; only the message tells them apart:

| Message returned | Cause | Flow |
|---|---|---|
| *"Unexpected client assertion type."* | `client_assertion_type` is not the JWT bearer URN | Client credentials |
| *"ClientId passed in the request doesn't match the one in cache"* | A device code is polled with a different `client_id` than the one that requested it | Device code |

Both are request-validation failures: something about the shape or the consistency of the request is wrong, so Entra rejects it before doing any real authentication work. Expect other causes to exist that we have not seen. Always read `ResultDescription`, or the `error_description` returned to the caller, before acting on a 90023.

### Cause 1: unexpected client assertion type
> AADSTS90023: Unexpected client assertion type.

An app that authenticates with a certificate or a federated credential sends two parameters instead of a secret: the assertion itself, and a parameter saying what kind of assertion it is. There is exactly one accepted value. Microsoft's certificate credentials page:

| Parameter | Value | Microsoft's description |
|---|---|---|
| `client_assertion_type` | `urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer` | This is a fixed value, indicating that you're using a certificate credential. |
| `client_assertion` | `JWT` | This is the JWT created above. |

The client credentials flow page repeats it: *"The value must be set to `urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`."* Anything else, including a shortened form, a URL-style variant or a double-encoded string, is "unexpected".

Three codes sit close to this one, and the difference is how far the request got:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **90023** | The assertion *type* is not the accepted URN. Entra didn't get as far as reading the assertion. |
| [50027](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50027/) | The type was accepted, but the assertion is not a well-formed JWT. |
| **700027** | *"Client assertion failed signature validation"* in Microsoft's reference. A valid JWT, wrong signature. |
| [7000216](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000216/) | Nothing was sent at all on a `client_credentials` request. |

### Cause 2: device code polled with a different client ID
> AADSTS90023: ClientId passed in the request doesn't match the one in cache

The device code flow spans two requests. The app calls `/devicecode` with its `client_id` and gets a `device_code` back; it then polls `/token` with that `device_code`. Microsoft's [device authorization grant page](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-device-code) requires the second request to carry the same client: the `client_id` on the token request *"Must match the `client_id` used in the initial request."*

The message says what the server is doing. The `device_code` is a handle to state Entra is holding ("the one in cache"), and the client ID that created that state is part of it. Poll with a different client ID and the handle no longer matches its owner, so the request is invalid.

What this means in practice: the `device_code` is not a bearer token you can redeem from anywhere with anything. It is bound to the application that asked for it.

| Code | When you get it in the device code flow |
|---|---|
| **90023** | Right `device_code`, wrong `client_id`. |
| [70016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70016/) | Right `device_code` and `client_id`, but nobody has signed in yet. Normal; keep polling. |
| [7000014](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000014/) | The `device_code` value itself isn't recognised. |

Our reading: this check happens before the "has the user approved yet?" check, because the lab got 90023 rather than [70016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70016/) for a code that was still outstanding. That ordering comes from one run.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
Both causes were reproduced against a lab tenant. The frontmatter records the first one.

### Unexpected client assertion type (30 October 2026)
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a client-credentials token request with a valid `client_assertion` but a `client_assertion_type` that Entra does not accept. Entra returned:

> AADSTS90023: Unexpected client assertion type.

Both rounds of the run returned the same code and the same one-line message, which is short enough that the lab's 160-character cut does not truncate it. The run had expected either 9002313 or 700027, so this is a case where guessing the code from the documentation would have been wrong. In the same run, a `client_assertion` that was not a JWT at all, sent with the correct assertion type, returned [50027](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50027/) instead, so the two checks run in that order: type first, then format.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

### Device code redeemed with a different client ID (31 October 2026)
On 31 October 2026 a later run requested a device code with one application's `client_id` and then polled the token endpoint for that same `device_code` with a different `client_id`. Entra returned:

> AADSTS90023: ClientId passed in the request doesn't match the one in cache

That run had expected 70016, 7000215 or 70002. It got none of them, which is the second time this code has turned up where the documentation gave no reason to expect it. Note the message has no trailing full stop, unlike the assertion-type message, so match on a substring rather than the whole line.

No sign-in log row was captured for this case either, and the message mentions no application, user or tenant, so the attacker's view of it discloses nothing.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not, in either case. A hand-built token request, or a library being driven in a way it wasn't designed for, is the normal cause. The accepted assertion type is long and easy to mistype or to encode twice, and the device code case needs two requests to disagree with each other.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new integration fails on every attempt | The parameter is wrong in the code or the configuration. It has never worked. |
| Started after a library or SDK upgrade | The request is now being assembled differently. Compare the parameters sent before and after. |
