It fails, but device code flow is [a phishing vector](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70016/) and the app's own device code traffic is worth reviewing. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which sign-in table 90023 lands in is undocumented, and the generic description means it can arrive from flows other than client assertions. Start wide and read the descriptions:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90023" or ResultSignature == "90023"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 10)
          by SourceTable
```

`ResultDescription` is documented as *"the error message or the reason for failure for the corresponding sign-in activity"* in `SigninLogs`, and as *"the error description for the sign-in operation"* in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`. The set of descriptions is what tells you which cause your 90023 rows are, and whether there is a third one we have not documented.

Split the two known causes apart. The device code case is a public client flow, so look for it in the user sign-in tables rather than the service principal one:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90023" or ResultSignature == "90023"
| extend Cause = case(ResultDescription has "assertion type", "client assertion type",
                      ResultDescription has "doesn't match the one in cache", "device code client ID mismatch",
                      "other or unknown")
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Apps = make_set(AppId, 10)
          by SourceTable, Cause
| sort by Rows desc
```

Rows landing in `other or unknown` are the interesting ones: a cause of 90023 neither of the lab runs produced.

Narrow to the client assertion case per app:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90023" or ResultSignature == "90023"
| where ResultDescription has "assertion type"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            CredentialTypes = make_set(ClientCredentialType, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Failures desc
```

The `has "assertion type"` filter assumes the message reaches the log. Confirm on one row before building an alert on it; if `ResultDescription` is empty in your workspace, drop that line and separate the cases another way.

Counting all three assertion errors together is often more useful than any one of them, because a developer working on a certificate credential produces a mix:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType in ("90023", "50027", "700027") or ResultSignature in ("90023", "50027", "700027")
| summarize Attempts = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, ResultType, ResultSignature
| sort by Attempts desc
```

As a starting point, a burst over a few minutes for one app is a developer; a slow trickle for weeks is a job nobody has fixed.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90023?
sections.text:
Start by reading the message. The two known causes have nothing to do with each other.

**For developers, "Unexpected client assertion type":**
1. Set `client_assertion_type` to exactly `urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`. Nothing else is accepted.
2. Check the encoding. The value is URL-encoded once as part of the form body. Encoding the colons twice produces a different string, and Entra sees an unexpected type.
3. Send `client_assertion` in the same request. The type parameter alone is not a credential.
4. Prefer a library over hand-built requests. MSAL sets both parameters for you when you configure a certificate credential.
5. If the error changes to [50027](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50027/), the type is now right and the assertion itself needs work: the header needs `alg`, `typ` and `x5t#S256`, and the claims need `aud`, `iss`, `sub`, `jti`, `nbf` and `exp`, as Microsoft's certificate credentials page sets out.

**For developers, "ClientId passed in the request doesn't match the one in cache":**
1. Use one `client_id` for the whole device code flow. The token request must carry the same client ID as the `/devicecode` request that produced the `device_code`.
2. Check for two configurations in one process: a hard-coded default client ID in one code path and a configured one in the other is the usual way the two requests drift apart.
3. Keep the `device_code` with the client ID that obtained it. Do not cache or pass device codes between applications; the binding is enforced.
4. Keep the authority the same across both requests too. A tenant mismatch produces [50059](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50059/) or [90133](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90133/) rather than 90023.
5. Once both requests agree, expect [70016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70016/) until the user signs in. That is the normal reply, not an error.

**For admins:**
1. Nothing to change in the tenant. This is the shape of the request, not a setting on the app or a policy.
2. Use the queries above to find which app and which owner, and pass them Microsoft's certificate credentials page, or its device code page for the device code case.
3. If the device code message appears for apps you do not expect to use the flow, review device code flow in the tenant: see [70016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70016/) for the inventory query and the Conditional Access control.

labReproduced.method: Client-credentials token request against a lab tenant
labReproduced.scenario: Unknown client_assertion_type
labReproduced.message: AADSTS90023: Unexpected client assertion type.

90023.labSectionText:
Both causes were reproduced against a lab tenant. The frontmatter records the first one.

### Unexpected client assertion type (30 October 2026)
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a client-credentials token request with a valid `client_assertion` but a `client_assertion_type` that Entra does not accept. Entra returned:

> AADSTS90023: Unexpected client assertion type.

Both rounds of the run returned the same code and the same one-line message, which is short enough that the lab's 160-character cut does not truncate it. The run had expected either 9002313 or 700027, so this is a case where guessing the code from the documentation would have been wrong. In the same run, a `client_assertion` that was not a JWT at all, sent with the correct assertion type, returned [50027](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50027/) instead, so the two checks run in that order: type first, then format.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

### Device code redeemed with a different client ID (31 October 2026)
On 31 October 2026 a later run requested a device code with one application's `client_id` and then polled the token endpoint for that same `device_code` with a different `client_id`. Entra returned:

> AADSTS90023: ClientId passed in the request doesn't match the one in cache

That run had expected 70016, 7000215 or 70002. It got none of them, which is the second time this code has turned up where the documentation gave no reason to expect it. Note the message has no trailing full stop, unlike the assertion-type message, so match on a substring rather than the whole line.

No sign-in log row was captured for this case either, and the message mentions no application, user or tenant, so the attacker's view of it discloses nothing.

90072.name: PassThroughUserMfaError
90072.title: AADSTS90072: External account doesn't exist in the tenant, MFA can't be satisfied
90072.description: AADSTS90072: an external account isn't in the tenant, or a synced user's ImmutableID doesn't match, so MFA can't be satisfied. Low attack value. KQL.
90072.summary: AADSTS90072 means a user signed in with an external account that doesn't exist in the tenant they tried to reach, so they can't satisfy that tenant's MFA. It also appears for synced users when the ImmutableID (sourceAnchor) in Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID don't match. It is a B2B or sync configuration problem with low attack value.
90072.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **PassThroughUserMfaError**: The external account that the user signs in with doesn't exist on the tenant that they signed into; so the user can't satisfy the MFA requirements for the tenant. This error also might occur if the users are synced, but there is a mismatch in the ImmutableID (sourceAnchor) attribute between Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID. The account must be added as an external user in the tenant first. Sign out and sign in with a different Microsoft Entra user account.

In plain terms, the user authenticated somewhere, but the tenant they are trying to reach has no matching account for them. Without an account there, that tenant can't run its MFA for them, so the sign-in stops.

Microsoft names two causes:

1. **B2B:** an external account that was never added (invited) to the resource tenant.
2. **Directory sync:** a synced user whose ImmutableID (sourceAnchor) in on-premises Active Directory doesn't match the one in Microsoft Entra ID.

It is close to [50020](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50020/), which also means an outside account isn't in the tenant. Microsoft's description of 90072 adds the MFA angle and the sync cause.

sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **PassThroughUserMfaError**: The external account that the user signs in with doesn't exist on the tenant that they signed into; so the user can't satisfy the MFA requirements for the tenant. This error also might occur if the users are synced, but there is a mismatch in the ImmutableID (sourceAnchor) attribute between Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID. The account must be added as an external user in the tenant first. Sign out and sign in with a different Microsoft Entra user account.

In plain terms, the user authenticated somewhere, but the tenant they are trying to reach has no matching account for them. Without an account there, that tenant can't run its MFA for them, so the sign-in stops.

Microsoft names two causes:

1. **B2B:** an external account that was never added (invited) to the resource tenant.
2. **Directory sync:** a synced user whose ImmutableID (sourceAnchor) in on-premises Active Directory doesn't match the one in Microsoft Entra ID.

It is close to [50020](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50020/), which also means an outside account isn't in the tenant. Microsoft's description of 90072 adds the MFA angle and the sync cause.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Both documented causes are configuration problems.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A partner user, first time on one of your apps | Not invited as a guest yet, or the invitation went to a different address. Benign. |
| Your own staff signing in to a partner tenant | Same cause on the partner's side. They need to invite your user. Not your incident. |
| One or a few of your own synced users, starting after an AD change or a sync server rebuild | ImmutableID / sourceAnchor mismatch. A sync problem to fix, not an attack. |
| Many different external identities you never invited | Our interpretation, not a Microsoft statement: someone sending outside accounts at your apps. Same reading as the probing row on [50020](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50020/). Investigate the source. |

The third row is the one that needs real work. An ImmutableID mismatch means on-premises and cloud no longer agree which object is which user, and the affected users can't sign in until it is fixed.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Who hits 90072, against which apps, and whether they are guests or members:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == "90072"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            HomeTenants = make_set(HomeTenantId, 5),
            UserTypes = make_set(UserType, 2),
            CrossTenant = make_set(CrossTenantAccessType, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by UserPrincipalName
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Split the B2B case from the sync case. Rows where the home tenant is your own tenant point to the sync cause; rows from other home tenants point to B2B:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == "90072"
| extend Case = iff(HomeTenantId == ResourceTenantId, "own tenant (check sync)", "external (check B2B)")
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Attempts = count() by Case, AppDisplayName
| sort by Attempts desc
```

That split is our reasoning from the two causes Microsoft lists, not a documented field mapping. Look at one row of each kind in your workspace to see how `HomeTenantId`, `UserType` and `UserPrincipalName` are filled for an account that doesn't exist in the tenant. They may be empty or show the identity from the other side.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- The error is about MFA, but it isn't a Conditional Access block. The tenant has no account for the user, so there is no user object for your MFA policy to work with.
- Once the external user is invited, your guest policies decide how they do MFA. Microsoft: *"If MFA trust is enabled, Microsoft Entra ID checks the user's authentication session for a claim indicating that MFA was fulfilled in the user's home tenant."* *"If MFA trust is disabled, the resource tenant presents the user with a challenge to complete MFA in the resource tenant."*
- Microsoft advises: *"Before you create the Conditional Access policy, check your cross-tenant access settings to make sure your inbound MFA trust settings are configured as intended."*

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90072?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign out and sign in again with the account your organisation gave you for that tenant. If you are a partner, ask your contact to invite you as a guest.

**For admins, B2B case:**
1. Invite the user as a guest (external user) in the resource tenant, using the address they actually sign in with.
2. Check your cross-tenant access settings for that partner, including inbound MFA trust, so the user knows where they will do MFA.

**For admins, sync case:**
1. Compare the user's ImmutableID in Microsoft Entra ID with the sourceAnchor value in on-premises Active Directory. Microsoft names a mismatch in that attribute as the cause.
2. Fix the mapping so both sides refer to the same object, then run a sync and test the sign-in. Our advice, not a Microsoft procedure for this code: find out why the mismatch happened (a re-created AD account, a rebuilt sync server, a changed sourceAnchor attribute) before fixing users one by one.

conditionalAccess.text:
- The error is about MFA, but it isn't a Conditional Access block. The tenant has no account for the user, so there is no user object for your MFA policy to work with.
- Once the external user is invited, your guest policies decide how they do MFA. Microsoft: *"If MFA trust is enabled, Microsoft Entra ID checks the user's authentication session for a claim indicating that MFA was fulfilled in the user's home tenant."* *"If MFA trust is disabled, the resource tenant presents the user with a challenge to complete MFA in the resource tenant."*
- Microsoft advises: *"Before you create the Conditional Access policy, check your cross-tenant access settings to make sure your inbound MFA trust settings are configured as intended."*

fix.short: Admin, B2B case: invite the user as a guest in the resource tenant, using the address they sign in with. Admin, synced user: make the ImmutableID in Entra ID match the sourceAnchor in Active Directory, then sync. User: sign in with your account for that tenant, or ask your contact to invite you.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** sign out and sign in again with the account your organisation gave you for that tenant. If you are a partner, ask your contact to invite you as a guest.

**For admins, B2B case:**
1. Invite the user as a guest (external user) in the resource tenant, using the address they actually sign in with.
2. Check your cross-tenant access settings for that partner, including inbound MFA trust, so the user knows where they will do MFA.

**For admins, sync case:**
1. Compare the user's ImmutableID in Microsoft Entra ID with the sourceAnchor value in on-premises Active Directory. Microsoft names a mismatch in that attribute as the cause.
2. Fix the mapping so both sides refer to the same object, then run a sync and test the sign-in. Our advice, not a Microsoft procedure for this code: find out why the mismatch happened (a re-created AD account, a rebuilt sync server, a changed sourceAnchor attribute) before fixing users one by one.

90094.name: AdminConsentRequired
90094.title: AADSTS90094: "Need admin approval" screen (fix)
90094.description: AADSTS90094 is the error behind the "Need admin approval" screen. What an admin should check before granting, and how to spot consent phishing.
90094.summary: AADSTS90094 means a user tried to consent to an app, but the permissions it asks for need an administrator. Your user-consent restriction is holding. Usually it is a legitimate new app. The security signal is an unfamiliar app hitting 90094 for several users, which fits a consent-phishing attempt. Hunt it in SigninLogs by AppId.
90094.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **AdminConsentRequired**: Administrator consent is required.

**On screen, this is the "Need admin approval" dialog.** Microsoft's guidance on permissions that need admin consent names it as the default experience, shown *"when your app requests a permission that requires admin consent"*. If your users are reporting "Need admin approval", this is the code behind it.

The user reached a consent prompt for an app, and the permissions requested are ones your tenant doesn't let users grant themselves. The user is stopped until an admin consents.

If your tenant has the admin consent workflow turned on, the user sees a different screen, **"Approval required"**, with a box to enter a justification and a **Request approval** button. That screen is [90095](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90095/), not this code.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS90094 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **AdminConsentRequired**: Administrator consent is required.

**On screen, this is the "Need admin approval" dialog.** Microsoft's guidance on permissions that need admin consent names it as the default experience, shown *"when your app requests a permission that requires admin consent"*. If your users are reporting "Need admin approval", this is the code behind it.

The user reached a consent prompt for an app, and the permissions requested are ones your tenant doesn't let users grant themselves. The user is stopped until an admin consents.

If your tenant has the admin consent workflow turned on, the user sees a different screen, **"Approval required"**, with a box to enter a justification and a **Request approval** button. That screen is [90095](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90095/), not this code.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
The code itself means a control worked. Whether there is an attack behind it depends on the app.

Microsoft's illicit-consent guidance describes the attack: an attacker registers an app, tricks a user into consenting, and then *"has account-level access to data without the need for an organizational account"*. The full quote and the investigation are on the [65001 page](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/65001/) and in the [consent phishing guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/investigate-consent-phishing-entra-id/).

Each 90094 is a user who reached a consent prompt and was stopped. That makes it a data point for consent-phishing attempts:

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One or two users, a well-known SaaS app your company is adopting | A legitimate app waiting for admin review. Benign. |
| Many users, one unfamiliar app, within hours | Users were sent a link to that app. That is the shape of a consent-phishing campaign. Look up the app and its publisher. |
| An app name that imitates a Microsoft or internal tool, from an unverified publisher | Treat as phishing until shown otherwise. |
| 90094 for an app, then a "Consent to application" audit event for the same app | Someone with admin rights consented. Confirm that was a deliberate review. |

This reading is built on Microsoft's attack description, not on a Microsoft detection rule.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which apps users are being stopped on:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "90094"
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Attempts = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUsers = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName
| sort by Users desc
```

An app with several users in a short window and no business owner is the one to look at first.

Did anyone grant consent anyway? Microsoft's guidance is to search the **Microsoft Purview (unified) audit log** for **"Consent to application"** and check `IsAdminConsent`. The Entra audit log records the same operation; in Log Analytics:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName == "Consent to application"
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
         AppName = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
         AppObjectId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id),
         ConsentDetails = TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, AppName, AppObjectId, Result, ConsentDetails
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

Compare `AppName` with the apps from the first query. The admin-consent flag sits inside `ConsentDetails` as the property named `ConsentContext.IsAdminConsent` (the granted permissions are in `ConsentAction.Permissions`). Field paths inside `InitiatedBy` and `TargetResources` vary; check them against a real event in your workspace. Note that the audit log identifies the app by its service principal object, while sign-in logs use `AppId`, so match on name or look up the IDs.

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"90094"`, not `90094`.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 90094 isn't a Conditional Access result. It comes from your consent settings.
- MFA doesn't help against consent phishing once consent is granted. Microsoft says password resets and MFA *"aren't effective against this type of attack"*. The consent restriction that produced this 90094 is the control that matters.
- Recommended posture: restrict user consent and turn on the **admin consent workflow**. Users then get [90095](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90095/) and a request goes to reviewers, instead of a dead end that pushes them to find another way.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90094?
sections.text:
**For the user:** ask your IT team to review the app. Don't try other accounts to get past the prompt.

**For admins:**
1. Look up the app from the first query: publisher, requested permissions, and whether anyone in the business asked for it.
2. If it is legitimate, grant admin consent for the permissions it needs, and no more.
3. If it looks like phishing, warn the users who hit it and check the audit query for any consent that did go through.
4. Enable the admin consent workflow so future requests reach a reviewer as 90095.

90095.name: AdminConsentRequiredRequestAccess
90095.title: AADSTS90095: "Approval required" screen (fix)
90095.description: AADSTS90095 is the error behind the "Approval required" screen, where users request admin consent. How to review the request queue safely.
90095.summary: AADSTS90095 is an interrupt: a user hit a consent prompt for permissions that need an admin, and because the admin consent workflow is on, they are told to request approval. This is the recommended setup. The review queue becomes your consent-phishing triage queue. Hunt unfamiliar apps in SigninLogs with ResultType == "90095".
90095.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **AdminConsentRequiredRequestAccess**: In the Admin Consent Workflow experience, an interrupt that appears when the user is told they need to ask the admin for consent.

**On screen, this is the "Approval required" dialog**, with a box to *"Enter justification for requesting this app"* and a **Request approval** button. Microsoft's guidance says it replaces the default screen once an admin turns on *Users can request admin consent to apps they're unable to consent to*.

This is the same situation as [90094](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90094/), a user needing admin consent, but in a tenant where the admin consent workflow is enabled. Instead of a dead end, the user can send a request to the reviewers you designated. Without the workflow, the user gets the **"Need admin approval"** screen instead, which is 90094.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS90095 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **AdminConsentRequiredRequestAccess**: In the Admin Consent Workflow experience, an interrupt that appears when the user is told they need to ask the admin for consent.

**On screen, this is the "Approval required" dialog**, with a box to *"Enter justification for requesting this app"* and a **Request approval** button. Microsoft's guidance says it replaces the default screen once an admin turns on *Users can request admin consent to apps they're unable to consent to*.

This is the same situation as [90094](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90094/), a user needing admin consent, but in a tenant where the admin consent workflow is enabled. Instead of a dead end, the user can send a request to the reviewers you designated. Without the workflow, the user gets the **"Need admin approval"** screen instead, which is 90094.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
The code is an expected step, not a failure. It means your consent controls are set up the way you want them.

The security work is in **what the requests are for**. Microsoft's illicit-consent guidance describes the attack: an attacker registers an app, tricks a user into consenting, and then *"has account-level access to data without the need for an organizational account"*. The full quote and the investigation are on the [65001 page](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/65001/) and in the [consent phishing guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/investigate-consent-phishing-entra-id/).

With the workflow on, an attacker's link ends at a 90095 and a request in your queue. The risk moves to the reviewer: if a reviewer approves a malicious app, the attack succeeds with admin consent.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One user, a known SaaS tool | A normal access request. Review it on its merits. |
| Many users, the same unfamiliar app, in a short window | A link to that app went round, possibly by phishing. Treat the request as suspicious until the app is vetted. |
| An app name imitating a Microsoft or internal tool | Treat as phishing until shown otherwise. Don't approve. |

This reading is built on Microsoft's attack description, not on a Microsoft detection rule.

```kusto
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),

            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName
| sort by Users desc
```

```kusto

| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),

         AppObjectId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id),

| project TimeGenerated, Actor, AppName, AppObjectId, Result, ConsentDetails

```

Field paths inside `InitiatedBy` and `TargetResources` vary; check them against a real event in your workspace before alerting on them.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 90095 isn't a Conditional Access result. It comes from your consent settings and the admin consent workflow.
- MFA doesn't protect against an app that has been granted consent. Microsoft says password resets and MFA *"aren't effective against this type of attack"*. The review step is the control.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90095?
sections.text:
**For the user:** send the request with a short reason, then wait for the reviewer.

**For admins and reviewers:**
1. Before approving, check the app's publisher, the permissions requested, and whether someone in the business actually needs it.
2. Grant only the permissions the app needs.
3. If several users requested the same unfamiliar app at once, treat it as a possible phishing campaign: deny, warn the users, and look for the delivery message.
4. Keep this setup. Restricted user consent plus the admin consent workflow is the recommended posture.

90133.title: AADSTS90133: Device code flow not supported on /common or /consumers (fix)
90133.description: AADSTS90133: device code flow sent to /common or /consumers. Unlisted by Microsoft; its docs say use a tenant-specific authority. Fix and KQL.
90133.summary: AADSTS90133 means a device code request went to the /common or /consumers endpoint, where Entra didn't support it for that app. Microsoft doesn't list the code, but a code comment in its device code docs gives the message and the fix: use a tenant-specific authority. It is a configuration error with low attack value.
90133.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS90133 (checked 30 October 2026). The nearest listed code is AADSTS90130: *"The application isn't supported over the /common or /consumers endpoints."*

Microsoft does mention 90133 elsewhere. The .NET sample in its [device code flow article for desktop apps](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/scenario-desktop-acquire-token-device-code-flow) lists it in a code comment, with the fix:

```csharp
// AADSTS90133: Device Code flow is not supported under /common or /consumers endpoint.
// Mitigation: as explained in the message from Azure AD, the authority needs to be tenanted
```

"Tenanted" means the sign-in URL names your tenant, by ID or domain, instead of `common` or `consumers`. The same sample uses `https://login.microsoftonline.com/contoso.com` as its authority.

This is a code comment, not a reference entry. Microsoft's device code protocol page says something broader. It says the `{tenant}` value *"Can be `/common`, `/consumers`, or `/organizations`"*, or a tenant ID or domain. Our reading: the two pages don't contradict each other if 90133 applies only to some apps, but Microsoft doesn't say which ones. Treat the code comment as the documented trigger and the exact conditions as unknown.

We tried to reproduce it on 30 October 2026. A lab run requested a device code on `/consumers` with an app registered for work accounts only. Entra didn't return 90133. It returned [AADSTS700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/) instead:

> AADSTS700016: Application with identifier '{app-id}' was not found in the directory '{tenant-id}'.

Our reading: on `/consumers` Entra looked for the app in a directory that isn't our lab tenant and didn't find it. In that one run, 700016 came back before any 90133 check. We haven't found the setup that returns 90133. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Microsoft's comment points to a configuration error in the app or script that starts the device code flow. The device code request is the first step of the flow, before any user signs in.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new CLI tool or script fails on its first run | The authority is `/common` or `/consumers`. Use your tenant ID or domain. |
| A tool works for one tenant and fails after a config change | Someone replaced the tenant ID with a generic endpoint. Likely, but unconfirmed. |
| A vendor tool fails for every customer | The vendor's default authority is generic. Ask for a tenant setting. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 90133 is logged in. Probably no row is written in your tenant: the request fails before a user signs in, and `/common` and `/consumers` don't name your tenant. Check anyway; this query is expected to return nothing:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "90133"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS90133?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this. Tell whoever runs the tool that its sign-in setting needs your tenant ID.

**For developers:**
1. Use a tenant-specific authority for device code flow, as Microsoft's comment says: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id or domain>`.
2. Use the same value for the device code request (`/oauth2/v2.0/devicecode`) and the token polling request (`/oauth2/v2.0/token`). Microsoft's protocol page says the polling request must use *"the same tenant or tenant alias used in the initial request."*
3. If the tool serves many tenants, make the tenant a setting instead of hard-coding `common`.

**For admins:** give the tool your tenant ID. Our [AADSTS90002 page](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90002/) shows how to find it.

135011.name: Device disabled
135011.title: AADSTS135011: Device used during authentication is disabled
135011.description: AADSTS135011: the device used to sign in is disabled in Entra ID. After incident response, it shows where a quarantined device reconnects. KQL included.
135011.summary: AADSTS135011 means the device used for the sign-in is disabled in Microsoft Entra ID. Usually an admin disabled it during cleanup or incident response, and something on that device still tries to get tokens. After an incident, these rows show where the quarantined device is and when it reconnects.
135011.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> Device used during the authentication is disabled.

Microsoft's reference table gives no PascalCase name for this code. The device object in Entra ID has its account disabled, so Entra ID won't use it for authentication.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS135011 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> Device used during the authentication is disabled.

Microsoft's reference table gives no PascalCase name for this code. The device object in Entra ID has its account disabled, so Entra ID won't use it for authentication.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
The code itself is not an attack. It is the result of an admin action. The question is **why the device was disabled and what is still trying to use it.**

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Device disabled during stale-device cleanup, user still has it | Benign. The user is on a device you retired. |
| Device disabled during incident response, then 135011 rows appear | **The quarantined device is back online and trying to get tokens.** Note the IP, time and app. |
| 135011 from an IP or country the user never uses | Possible attacker-held device or replayed device-bound session. Investigate (reasoning, not a Microsoft statement). |
| Many users failing with 135011 at once | Bulk disable by a script or policy. Check the audit log for who disabled them. |

Microsoft's own revoke-access procedure disables the user's devices as one of its steps:

```powershell
Update-MgDevice -DeviceId $Device.Id -AccountEnabled:$false
```

So in an incident, 135011 is often the expected aftermath of that step. Its value is forensic: each row tells you when and from where the disabled device reconnected.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Every disabled device still attempting sign-ins, with where it came from:

```kusto
union
    (SigninLogs
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
     | where ResultType == "135011"
     | extend DeviceId = tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId),
              DeviceName = tostring(DeviceDetail.displayName),
              Country = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion),
              Log = "Interactive"),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
     | where ResultType == "135011"
     | extend DeviceId = tostring(parse_json(DeviceDetail).deviceId),
              DeviceName = tostring(parse_json(DeviceDetail).displayName),
              Country = tostring(parse_json(LocationDetails).countryOrRegion),
              Log = "NonInteractive")
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Countries = make_set(Country, 5),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Logs = make_set(Log)
          by UserPrincipalName, DeviceId, DeviceName
| sort by LastSeen desc
```

Focus on one incident: the device you disabled, after the time you disabled it.

```kusto
let incidentDevice = "<device-id>"; // the device ID (deviceId), not the object ID
let disabledAt = datetime(2026-10-01T09:00:00Z);
union
    (SigninLogs
     | where TimeGenerated > disabledAt
     | extend DeviceId = tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId)),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
     | where TimeGenerated > disabledAt
     | extend DeviceId = tostring(parse_json(DeviceDetail).deviceId))
| where DeviceId == incidentDevice
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, ResultType, IPAddress, AppDisplayName,
          ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

`DeviceDetail` is **dynamic** in `SigninLogs` and **string** in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, so each leg of the union extracts the device ID its own way before the tables are combined. The property names follow the Microsoft Graph `signIn` device detail object; check them against a row in your own workspace first.

Which log 135011 lands in is reasoned from the mechanism, not measured: a device-based SSO refresh is non-interactive, a fresh sign-in is interactive. The first query searches both.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 135011 is not a Conditional Access result code. It reports the state of the device object itself.
- Disabling the device removes it as an option for policies that require a compliant or hybrid joined device. If the user's only managed device is disabled, they will start hitting 53000 or 53001 from whatever device they use next.
- Microsoft's revoke-access procedure treats disabling devices and revoking the user's refresh tokens (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`) as separate steps. Do both. By default, Microsoft assigns access tokens a lifetime of 60 to 90 minutes, so already-issued access tokens can keep working until they expire, unless Continuous Access Evaluation applies (Exchange, SharePoint and Teams through CAE-capable clients), where Microsoft says revocation is enforced with *"latency of up to 15 minutes"*. The [session revocation guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/revoke-sessions-and-verify-entra-id/) has the detail.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS135011?
sections.text:
**For the user:** contact IT. The device has been disabled on purpose or by cleanup, and you can't re-enable it yourself.

**For admins:**
1. Check the Entra audit log for who disabled the device and when.
2. If it was disabled during incident response, leave it disabled. Record each 135011 row (IP, time, app) as evidence of where the device is.
3. If it was a mistake or a stale-device cleanup that hit a device still in use, re-enable it:

```powershell
Update-MgDevice -DeviceId $Device.Id -AccountEnabled:$true
```

4. If the device is gone for good, delete the device object and have the user register a new device.

```kusto
          ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

`DeviceDetail` is **dynamic** in `SigninLogs` and **string** in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, so each leg of the union extracts the device ID its own way before the tables are combined. The property names follow the Microsoft Graph `signIn` device detail object; check them against a row in your own workspace first.

Which log 135011 lands in is reasoned from the mechanism, not measured: a device-based SSO refresh is non-interactive, a fresh sign-in is interactive. The first query searches both.

fix.short: Admin: check the audit log for who disabled the device. If it was disabled during incident response, leave it disabled. If it was a mistake, re-enable it with Update-MgDevice -AccountEnabled:$true. If the device is gone, delete it and register a new one. User: contact IT.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** contact IT. The device has been disabled on purpose or by cleanup, and you can't re-enable it yourself.

**For admins:**
1. Check the Entra audit log for who disabled the device and when.
2. If it was disabled during incident response, leave it disabled. Record each 135011 row (IP, time, app) as evidence of where the device is.
3. If it was a mistake or a stale-device cleanup that hit a device still in use, re-enable it:

```powershell
Update-MgDevice -DeviceId $Device.Id -AccountEnabled:$true
```

4. If the device is gone for good, delete the device object and have the user register a new device.

165000.title: AADSTS165000: User session context is missing (fix)
165000.description: AADSTS165000: the browser lost the session cookies mid sign-in. Not in Microsoft's reference. User-reported fix: device clock. Also check cookies. KQL included.
165000.summary: AADSTS165000 means the browser lost or didn't send the cookies, form fields or headers that keep one sign-in together, so the sign-in page stops. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. Users report it on iPads, a Mac and in Edge. Two users fixed it on iPads by setting the device clock to automatic. Low attack value.
165000.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS165000 (checked 30 October 2026).

We found no Microsoft documentation page for it. The wording comes from user reports on Microsoft Q&A. The common part of the message is:

> AADSTS165000: Invalid Request: … One or more of the user context values (cookies; form fields; headers) were not supplied, every request must include these values and maintain them across a complete single user flow.

The first part and the ending vary. Three threads show three versions:

| Thread | Text after "Invalid Request:" and at the end |
|---|---|
| [iPads, school tenant](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/2264720/two-of-our-users-are-getting-the-aadsts165000-erro) | *"The user session context is missing."* |
| [Mac, Microsoft 365 Home](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5643859/aadsts165000-invalid-request-the-user-session-cont) | *"The user session context is missing."* … *"Failure Reasons:[Missing session context cookie;]"* |
| [Edge, Azure Site Recovery appliance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1691539/azure-site-recovery-configuration-gives-aadsts1650) | *"The request did not include the required tokens for the user context."* … *"The request did not return all of the form fields. Failure Reasons:[Token was not provided;]"* |

Our reading of the message: the Microsoft sign-in page tracks one sign-in across several requests with cookies and hidden form fields. When a request in the middle arrives without them, the page can't tie it to the sign-in that started it, and it stops with 165000. The `Failure Reasons` part says which piece was missing. Microsoft hasn't documented this.

What users report as the cause:

- **Wrong device clock.** In the iPad thread, a community member writes that the iPads that failed had the wrong date and time: *"Fixed time zone and set time to automatic, problem solved."* A second user reports the same fix on an iPad.
- **iPad browsers.** The iPad thread saw it in Safari-based and Chrome browsers, after cache clears and even a full wipe.
- **One browser only.** In the Edge thread it happened only in Edge, not in Chrome with the same user, and started after the May 2024 Windows Server updates.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No, as far as any report we found shows. Every case users describe is a browser or device problem.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One or two users, always on the same iPad | The device clock or cookie settings. Check the date and time first. |
| Many users on managed iPads at the same site | A content filter or proxy that changes the sign-in traffic, or a device profile that blocks cookies. The iPad thread used a filtering browser. Our interpretation. |
| One browser on one server fails, another works | A browser issue, as in the Edge thread. Use the other browser or the device code workaround below. |
| A spike for every user at once | Not seen in any report we found. Check for a network change; this is a guess, not a reported cause. |

We found no source that links 165000 to an attack.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document whether or where 165000 is logged. The admin in the iPad thread writes that the sign-in logs showed error code *"399218"*. Our reading: the sign-in log may record these failures under a different code than the one on the user's screen. Search for both:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("165000", "399218")
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable, ResultType, ResultDescription
```

If rows show up, see which devices and browsers they come from. Concentration on one operating system points at the device, not the tenant:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("165000", "399218")
| extend OS = tostring(DeviceDetail.operatingSystem), Browser = tostring(DeviceDetail.browser)
| summarize Attempts = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by OS, Browser, AppDisplayName
| sort by Attempts desc
```

If neither query returns anything, look up the user's failed sign-ins at the time of the error and read `ResultType` and `ResultDescription` from there.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS165000?
sections.text:
**For the user:**
1. Set the device's date and time to automatic, with the right time zone. Two users report this fixed it on iPads.
2. Allow cookies in the browser and don't use private browsing for the sign-in. On Safari, a Q&A answer suggests turning off **Prevent Cross-Site Tracking** and **Block All Cookies**.
3. Try another browser. In the Edge thread, Chrome worked with the same account.
4. On a Mac with Microsoft 365 Home, an Independent Advisor on Q&A suggests that a work or school account used on the device before can get in the way, and points to Microsoft's license removal tool for Office on Mac. This one is a single suggestion, not a confirmed fix.

**For admins:**
1. Ask which device and browser, and check the clock first. It is the only fix that more than one user reports as working.
2. If a content filter sits in front of the devices, a Q&A answer suggests excluding Microsoft sign-in addresses from it, such as `login.microsoftonline.com`, `login.live.com` and `*.office.com`. Users have not confirmed that this fixed it.
3. The same answer suggests checking Conditional Access sign-in frequency and persistent browser session settings for the affected users. Nobody in the thread reports this as the cause.

**For apps that open a browser sign-in (appliances, tools):** the accepted answer in the Edge thread is a workaround: when the error shows, refresh the sign-in tab, or open `https://microsoft.com/devicelogin` in a new tab and enter the device code the app showed. The moderator who posted it said no root cause had been shared yet.

500011.name: InvalidResourceServicePrincipalNotFound
500011.title: AADSTS500011: The resource principal was not found in the tenant
500011.description: AADSTS500011: the API an app asked a token for has no service principal in the tenant. Wrong resource URL, tenant or consent. Low attack value. KQL.
500011.summary: AADSTS500011 means an app asked for a token for an API (the resource) that has no service principal in the tenant the request went to. It is a configuration error: wrong resource URL or scope, wrong tenant, or an API nobody has provisioned or consented to. It has low attack value. Hunt it in SigninLogs and AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs.
500011.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidResourceServicePrincipalNotFound**: The resource principal named {name} wasn't found in the tenant named {tenant}. This can happen if the application hasn't been installed by the administrator of the tenant or consented to by any user in the tenant. You might have sent your authentication request to the wrong tenant. If you expect the app to be installed, you might need to provide administrator permissions to add it. Check with the developers of the resource and application to understand what the right setup for your tenant is.

The full message users see reads *"AADSTS500011 - The resource principal named [resource URL] was not found in the tenant named [tenant ID]"*.

The missing object is the **resource**: the API the app wants a token for. If the missing object is the client app itself, the error is [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/) instead.

Microsoft explains why the object must exist: *"A service principal must be created in each tenant where the application is used."* An API registered in another tenant has no service principal in yours until an admin provisions it or someone consents to it.

> **InvalidResourceServicePrincipalNotFound**: The resource principal named {name} wasn't found in the tenant named {tenant}. sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request for a scope on a resource that doesn't exist in my lab tenant. Entra returned `AADSTS500011` with this first line:

> AADSTS500011: The resource principal named https://does-not-exist.brambrinkmeier.com was not found in the tenant named {tenant-id}.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint.

The same attempt in the lab tenant's sign-in log (Entra admin center, interactive user sign-ins), with identifiers left out:

| Field | Value in the lab row |
|---|---|
| Status | Failure |
| Sign-in error code | 500011 |
| Failure reason | The resource principal named {name} was not found in the tenant named {tenant}. This can happen if the application has not been installed by the administrator of the tenant or consented to by any user in the tenant. |
| Authentication requirement | Single-factor authentication |
| Conditional Access | Not Applied |
| User type | Member |

The log shows Microsoft's template text with placeholders; the actual resource name appears only in the error returned to the client, so keep the client's error message when you troubleshoot. The KQL below was run on the lab rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). The first query found both lab rows. The second query reads `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`, and the lab rows are user sign-ins, so it is not tested yet.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Microsoft's troubleshooting article lists four causes, all configuration:

- *"The resource application isn't provisioned by the administrator in the tenant."*
- *"The resource application isn't consented to by any user in the tenant."*
- *"The resource URL is not configured correctly."*
- *"The tenant ID is not correct."*

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 500011 for one app, every user, starting at a deployment | A typo or wrong value in the resource URL or scope. Developer error. |
| 500011 for a vendor's multitenant app after onboarding | The vendor's API was never provisioned or consented in your tenant. Setup step missing. |
| 500011 naming a resource you don't recognise, from an app or IP you don't recognise | Someone asking your tenant for tokens to an API you never set up. Our interpretation, not a documented detection: the request failed, but the client and IP are worth a look. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
User flows, grouped by client and the resource in the request:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "500011"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Resources = make_set(ResourceIdentity, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Attempts desc
```

App-only flows (client credentials):

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "500011"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            Resources = make_set(ResourceIdentity, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Attempts desc
```

The resource in the error doesn't exist in your tenant, so `ResourceIdentity` and `ResourceDisplayName` may be empty on these rows. That isn't documented either way. If they are, the resource URL is in the error text, so look at `ResultDescription` or open one event in the portal. Silent token requests for a missing resource can also land in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`; swap the table name in the first query to check.

For app-only rows, confirm in your workspace that `ResultType` carries `"500011"` and not *"Failure"*. The Azure Monitor reference for `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` describes it as *"Success or Failure"*. If so, filter on `ResultSignature`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 500011 happens before any Conditional Access decision on the resource. There is no resource in your tenant for a policy to target.
- Once the resource is provisioned, it gets a service principal and appears as a target in Conditional Access like any other app. Check that your policies cover it before users start using it.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500011?
sections.text:
**For developers:**
1. Compare the resource URL or scope in the error with the API's App ID URI or application ID. A wrong value here is the most common cause.
2. Check that the request goes to the right tenant, not a tenant where the API was never set up.

**For admins:**
1. Look under **Enterprise applications** for the resource named in the error. If it isn't there, it was never provisioned in your tenant.
2. If the API should be used, provision it and grant consent. For a vendor app, ask the vendor for their admin consent link. Microsoft documents an admin consent endpoint (`https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0/adminconsent`) that apps use to *"grant permissions to an entire tenant"*.
3. Before consenting, check what the API's permissions allow. Provisioning a resource creates a service principal in your tenant that *"defines what the app can actually do in the specific tenant"*.

500011.labSectionText:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request for a scope on a resource that doesn't exist in my lab tenant. Entra returned `AADSTS500011` with this first line:

> AADSTS500011: The resource principal named https://does-not-exist.brambrinkmeier.com was not found in the tenant named {tenant-id}.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint.

The same attempt in the lab tenant's sign-in log (Entra admin center, interactive user sign-ins), with identifiers left out:

| Field | Value in the lab row |
|---|---|
| Status | Failure |
| Sign-in error code | 500011 |
| Failure reason | The resource principal named {name} was not found in the tenant named {tenant}. This can happen if the application has not been installed by the administrator of the tenant or consented to by any user in the tenant. |
| Authentication requirement | Single-factor authentication |
| Conditional Access | Not Applied |
| User type | Member |

500014.name: InvalidResourceServicePrincipalDisabled
500014.title: AADSTS500014 fix: resource service principal is disabled
500014.description: AADSTS500014: the API's service principal is disabled in your tenant, so no tokens are issued for it. Check the audit log, then re-enable. KQL.
500014.summary: AADSTS500014 means the API a token was requested for (the resource) has a disabled service principal in the tenant, so Microsoft Entra ID won't issue tokens for it. Microsoft gives two causes: a lapsed subscription or an admin who disabled it. If the resource is a Microsoft service such as Exchange Online, sign-ins break for everyone. Find who disabled it before re-enabling.
500014.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidResourceServicePrincipalDisabled**: The service principal for resource '{identifier}' is disabled. This indicates that a subscription within the tenant has lapsed, or that an administrator for this tenant has disabled the application's service principal, preventing tokens from being issued for it. For more information, see Disable user sign-in for application.

The disabled object is the **resource**: the API the token is for, named in the error. The client app the user opened can be perfectly fine.

The switch is the enterprise application's **Enabled for users to sign-in?** property. Microsoft describes what **No** does: *"no users are able to sign in to the application, even if they're assigned to it. Tokens aren't issued for the application. This setting not only prevents users from signing in but also restricts service principals from accessing the application using application permissions."* In Microsoft Graph it is the service principal's `accountEnabled` property.

**How it differs from [7000112](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000112/):** both come from the same switch. Our reading: 7000112 is returned when the disabled app is the **client** being signed in to, and 500014 when it is the **resource** a token is requested for. Microsoft's Exchange Online troubleshooting article shows 7000112 for a disabled Exchange Online service principal on the Microsoft 365 portal. Users report 500014 for the same disabled service principal when Exchange is the resource, for example in Outlook sync tools. Which code you get depends on the request; Microsoft doesn't spell this out. Treat the split as a rough guide: in Microsoft's own Exchange example, Exchange is arguably the resource, and it still shows 7000112.

**How it differs from [500011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500011/):** 500011 means the resource has **no** service principal in the tenant. 500014 means it has one and it is switched off.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS500014 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidResourceServicePrincipalDisabled**: The service principal for resource '{identifier}' is disabled. This indicates that a subscription within the tenant has lapsed, or that an administrator for this tenant has disabled the application's service principal, preventing tokens from being issued for it. For more information, see Disable user sign-in for application.

The disabled object is the **resource**: the API the token is for, named in the error. The client app the user opened can be perfectly fine.

The switch is the enterprise application's **Enabled for users to sign-in?** property. Microsoft describes what **No** does: *"no users are able to sign in to the application, even if they're assigned to it. Tokens aren't issued for the application. This setting not only prevents users from signing in but also restricts service principals from accessing the application using application permissions."* In Microsoft Graph it is the service principal's `accountEnabled` property.

**How it differs from [7000112](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000112/):** both come from the same switch. Our reading: 7000112 is returned when the disabled app is the **client** being signed in to, and 500014 when it is the **resource** a token is requested for. Microsoft's Exchange Online troubleshooting article shows 7000112 for a disabled Exchange Online service principal on the Microsoft 365 portal. Users report 500014 for the same disabled service principal when Exchange is the resource, for example in Outlook sync tools. Which code you get depends on the request; Microsoft doesn't spell this out. Treat the split as a rough guide: in Microsoft's own Exchange example, Exchange is arguably the resource, and it still shows 7000112.

**How it differs from [500011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500011/):** 500011 means the resource has **no** service principal in the tenant. 500014 means it has one and it is switched off.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
The error itself is not. It is a block working. What matters is who disabled the resource, and whether it was a Microsoft service.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 500014 for your own API, after someone disabled it | Working as intended. Clients can no longer get tokens for it. |
| 500014 naming a Microsoft service (Exchange Online, a Microsoft app ID) for many users, or on the Azure portal | Someone disabled a Microsoft service principal in your tenant, or a subscription lapsed. Users report it for the Azure portal, with Microsoft Graph as the resource, and for Dynamics environments. Check the audit log first. |
| 500014 for a Dynamics 365 environment URL with an active subscription | Users report this too. The environment's service principal may be disabled; check its **Enabled for users to sign-in?** setting. |
| 500014 after a licence or trial ended | Microsoft names a lapsed subscription as a cause. |

A disabled Microsoft first-party service principal is worth a second look. Our reading, not a Microsoft statement: if nobody on your team disabled it on purpose, treat the account that did as suspect until you know, because switching off a core service is a quick way to cause a tenant-wide outage.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 500014 lands in. A disabled resource blocks both user and app-only tokens, so it can appear in all three. Check where it lands:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "500014"
| summarize Rows = count(), Resources = dcount(ResourceIdentity) by SourceTable
```

Which resources are disabled, how many users and apps are hitting them, and since when:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "500014"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            ClientApps = make_set(coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName), 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by ResourceIdentity, ResourceDisplayName
| sort by Users desc
```

Who changed a service principal, and when. Microsoft's audit log reference lists **Update service principal** in the ApplicationManagement category. Disabling an enterprise app is likely logged as that activity; Microsoft doesn't say so:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName == "Update service principal"
| mv-expand Target = TargetResources
| mv-expand Prop = Target.modifiedProperties
| where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "AccountEnabled"
| project TimeGenerated,
          App = tostring(Target.displayName),
          ServicePrincipalId = tostring(Target.id),
          OldValue = tostring(Prop.oldValue),
          NewValue = tostring(Prop.newValue),
          ByUser = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
          ByApp = tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

The modified property name `AccountEnabled` is an assumption based on the Graph property, not checked against Microsoft documentation. If the query returns nothing, drop that line and read the `modifiedProperties` of the rows yourself. Non-interactive and service principal sign-in rows are aggregated, so row counts there are not request counts. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"500014"`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 500014 is not a Conditional Access block. A disabled resource gets no tokens, whatever your policies say.
- Don't confuse it with [53003](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/53003/), which is a Conditional Access block. The fix and the owner are different.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500014?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Tell your IT team which resource the error names.

**For developers:** if your API is the resource and a customer gets 500014, the customer's admin disabled your API's service principal in their tenant, or their subscription lapsed. You can't re-enable it from your side.

**For admins:**
1. Read the resource from the error. Find it under **Enterprise applications** (remove the default filters and search by application ID).
2. Find out who disabled it and why with the audit log query, before changing anything. If it was disabled during an incident, leave it.
3. Check that the subscription behind the service is active. Microsoft names a lapsed subscription as the other cause.
4. If it was a mistake: in **Enterprise applications** > the app > **Properties**, set **Enabled for users to sign-in?** to **Yes**. In Microsoft Graph, set `accountEnabled` to `true`. Microsoft documents `accountEnabled` as *"`true` if the service principal account is enabled"*. With Microsoft Graph PowerShell:
   ```powershell
   Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Application.ReadWrite.All"
   $sp = Get-MgServicePrincipal -Filter "appId eq '<resource app ID>'"
   $sp.AccountEnabled
   Update-MgServicePrincipal -ServicePrincipalId $sp.Id -AccountEnabled:$true
   ```
   This mirrors Microsoft's disable command with `$true`. Microsoft's page shows only the disable direction.
5. For Exchange Online, the app ID is `00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000`. Microsoft's article uses the deprecated MSOnline module for this; use Microsoft Graph PowerShell as above.
6. If the app registration was **deactivated** globally by its owner, that is a different switch (`isDisabled`). Microsoft notes that reactivating it *"doesn't enable tenant-local sign-in if a service principal's `accountEnabled` remains `false`"*. Check both.

500021.title: AADSTS500021 fix: tenant blocked by tenant restrictions
500021.description: AADSTS500021: a tenant restrictions v1 proxy header doesn't allow the tenant you tried to reach. Fixed by the network's admin, not the app's.
500021.summary: AADSTS500021 means tenant restrictions (v1) are on in the user's network: a proxy adds a list of allowed tenants to sign-in traffic, and the tenant the user tried to reach isn't on it. It is a control doing its job, with low attack value. The fix is on the side of whoever runs the proxy, usually the user's own organisation, not the app's tenant.
500021.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> Access to '{tenant}' tenant is denied. AADSTS500021 indicates that the tenant restriction feature is configured and that the user is trying to access a tenant that isn't in the list of allowed tenants specified in the header `Restrict-Access-To-Tenant`. For more information, see Use tenant restrictions to manage access to SaaS cloud applications.

Microsoft gives this code no name. The block comes from the **network**, not from the tenant the user is signing in to.

Tenant restrictions (the original version, which Microsoft's v2 page calls *"Tenant restrictions v1"*) work like this. A corporate proxy that does TLS inspection adds two headers to every request to `login.microsoftonline.com`, `login.microsoft.com` and `login.windows.net`:

- `Restrict-Access-To-Tenants`: *"a comma-separated list of tenants you want to allow users to access"*.
- `Restrict-Access-Context`: *"a single directory ID, declaring which tenant is setting the tenant restrictions"*.

If the tenant the user tries to reach isn't on the list, sign-in fails. Microsoft's tenant restrictions page says the user *"sees an access denial message"* about *"a resource that belongs to an organization unapproved by your IT department."* Microsoft's error description writes the header as `Restrict-Access-To-Tenant`; the tenant restrictions page spells it `Restrict-Access-To-Tenants`, with an s. Use the page's spelling on your proxy.

### v1 or v2?
Be precise here, because the two versions use different headers and, as far as Microsoft documents, different codes.

| | Tenant restrictions v1 | Tenant restrictions v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Where the allow list lives | In the proxy header itself | *"moved to the server-side cloud policy"* (cross-tenant access settings) |
| Header | `Restrict-Access-To-Tenants` + `Restrict-Access-Context` | `sec-Restrict-Tenant-Access-Policy: <DirectoryID>:<policyGUID>` |
| Enforcement | Corporate proxy only | Proxy, Windows devices (Group Policy) or Global Secure Access |
| Protects | Authentication plane | Authentication plane, plus data plane with device signalling |
| Code Microsoft shows | **500021** (error reference) | **[5000211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/5000211/)** (v2 setup page) |

So: 500021 points at a v1 allow list on a proxy. If the message says *"A tenant restrictions policy added to this request by a device or network administrator"*, you are looking at v2 and 5000211. Microsoft notes that migrating from v1 to v2 *"is a one-time operation"*.

| Your own users get 500021 for a tenant nobody recognises | The control stopped a sign-in to an unapproved tenant. Our interpretation: worth asking the user why, because this is the data-leak path tenant restrictions are meant to close. |
| 500021 started for many users at once | Someone changed the proxy's allow list, or traffic moved to a proxy with a different list. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft gives the admin of the `Restrict-Access-Context` tenant a dedicated report: **Entra ID** > **Overview** > **Tenant restrictions**. It shows *"sign-ins blocked because of the tenant restrictions policy, including the identity used and the target directory ID."* Microsoft adds that *"Sign-ins are included if the tenant setting the restriction is either the user tenant or resource tenant for the sign-in"*, and that identities from other tenants are masked.

Microsoft doesn't document which Log Analytics table 500021 rows land in, or in which tenant's workspace. Check yours:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "500021"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which target tenants are being blocked, for whom, and from which egress IPs (each egress IP points at a proxy):

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500021"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5),
            EgressIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by HomeTenantId, ResourceTenantId, IsTenantRestricted
| sort by Users desc
```

The `IsTenantRestricted` column is documented as *"Indicates if a signIn is under a tenant restrictions policy or not."* Whether Microsoft sets it on 500021 rows isn't documented. If it does, this finds every sign-in under a restrictions policy, blocked or not:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where IsTenantRestricted == true
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by ResultType, ResourceTenantId
| sort by Rows desc
```

`ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"500021"`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 500021 is not a Conditional Access block. The proxy header decides it, whatever the target tenant's policies say.
- Don't confuse it with [53003](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/53003/), which is a Conditional Access block in the target tenant. The owner of the fix is different.
- Cross-tenant access settings for B2B collaboration are also a different control. One Q&A answer suggests changing outbound B2B settings for this error. Microsoft's description of 500021 points only at the v1 header, so start there.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500021?
sections.text:
**For the user:** the network you are on only allows sign-in to approved tenants. Ask **your own** IT team to allow the tenant you need. If you are a guest on someone else's app, the app's owner can't fix this for you.

**For app owners and B2B hosts:** you can't fix this from your tenant. Tell the guest's IT team your tenant ID or verified domain and ask them to add it to their tenant restrictions list. Users in Microsoft Q&A report this is the step that's missing.

**For admins who run the proxy:**
1. Find the proxy rule that adds `Restrict-Access-To-Tenants` to traffic for the Microsoft sign-in hosts.
2. Add the target tenant. Microsoft says *"Any domain that is registered with a tenant can be used to identify the tenant in this list, and the directory ID itself."* Microsoft's example: `Restrict-Access-To-Tenants: contoso.com,fabrikam.onmicrosoft.com,{guid}`.
3. Keep `Restrict-Access-Context` set to **your own** directory ID. Microsoft warns that with any other ID *"the sign-in logs appear in someone else's tenant, with all personal information removed."*
4. Before you allow a tenant nobody asked for, check why users tried to reach it.
5. If you are moving to tenant restrictions v2, the allow list moves into cross-tenant access settings and the v1 header should be removed from the proxy. Blocks then show as [5000211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/5000211/).

500031.title: AADSTS500031: Signing certificate for the app not found (fix)
500031.description: AADSTS500031: Entra found no signing certificate for the app. Unlisted by Microsoft. Users fixed it by adding a SAML signing certificate. KQL.
500031.summary: AADSTS500031 means Entra couldn't find a signing certificate configured for the app. Microsoft doesn't list the code. The one user report we found was fixed by adding a SAML signing certificate to the enterprise app. It is a configuration error with low attack value. Check the app's SAML Certificates section and make sure a valid certificate is active.
500031.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS500031 (checked 30 October 2026). The wording below comes from a user report.

A user on Microsoft Q&A posted this response from the token endpoint (`/oauth2/v2.0/token`):

```
HttpResponseCode = 400 (BadRequest)
ErrorMsg: AADSTS500031: Cannot find signing certificate configured
```

The user's app was an Angular single-page app using the authorization code flow. It failed with two different client libraries. The user's own accepted answer: *"After adding a missing SAML certificate it works!"* The steps were **Enterprise applications** > the app > **Single sign-on** > **SAML** > add the missing **SAML Signing Certificate**.

That is one report, from 2020. It shows one cause and one fix. It doesn't explain the mechanism.

Our reading: Entra signs the tokens it issues for an app. When an enterprise app has its own signing certificate setting, as SAML apps do, Entra looked for it and found none.

A documented relative exists. [Microsoft's troubleshooting article](https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/azure/active-directory/error-code-aadsts50003-cert-or-key-not-configured) for AADSTS50003, *"No signing key configured"*, covers SAML apps where *"Microsoft Entra ID doesn't recognize the certificate configured for the application."* Its fix is the same: create a new certificate and make it active.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS500031 mean?

A documented relative exists.
