sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. The user report points to a configuration error on the enterprise app. Our reading: the certificate is missing on Entra's side, so a caller can't cause it by changing the request, and everyone who uses the app fails at once.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Every user of one app fails at the same moment | The signing certificate was removed, or never added. Likely, but unconfirmed. |
| A new SAML app fails on its first test | Single sign-on was set up but no certificate was saved. Likely; we haven't tested this. |
| The app worked for years, then failed | Check the certificate's expiry date. Microsoft's certificate tutorial describes rollover and expiry. Whether an expired certificate produces this code is not documented. |
| An OAuth or OpenID Connect app fails with it | The user report above. The enterprise app had SAML settings without a certificate. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table AADSTS500031 is logged in. The user has signed in by then, so `SigninLogs` is the likely table. Check all three:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500031"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

Which apps fail, how many users, and over which protocol:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500031"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by AppId, AppDisplayName, AuthenticationProtocol
| sort by Users desc
```

When the app last worked, which tells you when the certificate went missing:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AppId == "<app id from the query above>"
| summarize LastSuccess = maxif(TimeGenerated, ResultType == "0"), FirstFailure = minif(TimeGenerated, ResultType == "500031")
```

If `LastSuccess` is just before `FirstFailure`, look in the audit log for changes to the app around that time.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500031?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this. Tell IT which app failed. Everyone else is likely affected too.

**For admins:**
1. Open the Microsoft Entra admin center as at least a Cloud Application Administrator. Go to **Entra ID** > **Enterprise apps** > **All applications** and open the app.
2. Go to **Single sign-on**. Under **SAML Certificates**, select **Edit**. The page shows the status (**Active** or **Inactive**), expiry date and thumbprint of each certificate.
3. If there is no certificate, select **New Certificate** and **Save**. A new certificate starts as **Inactive**.
4. On the new row, select **...** > **Make certificate active**.
5. If the app is a SAML app, give the new certificate to the app or its vendor. Microsoft's tutorial says to download it from the **SAML Certificates** section.
6. Watch for the expiry emails. Microsoft says it sends one *"60, 30, and 7 days before the SAML certificate expires."*

**For developers:** if your OAuth or OpenID Connect app gets this error, check whether its enterprise app has single sign-on set to SAML with no certificate. Ask an admin to check the steps above. That is what fixed the user report.

500113.title: AADSTS500113: No reply address is registered for the app (fix)
500113.description: AADSTS500113: the app registration has no redirect URI, so Entra can't return the sign-in. A config error; add the right platform and URI.
500113.summary: AADSTS500113 means a sign-in request went to the authorize endpoint for an app registration that has no redirect URI (reply address) at all. Entra has no allowed place to send the result and refuses the request, even before anyone signs in. It is a configuration error with low attack value. Add the right platform and redirect URI to the app registration.
500113.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS500113 (checked 30 October 2026).

In my lab tenant, an unauthenticated authorize request in a browser, for an app registration with no redirect URI, showed this error on the page:

> AADSTS500113: No reply address is registered for the application.

"Reply address" is the older name for a redirect URI. Microsoft's redirect URI page explains why Entra needs one: *"To sign in a user, your application must send a login request to the Microsoft Entra authorization endpoint, with a redirect URI specified as a parameter. The redirect URI is a critical security feature that ensures the Microsoft Entra authentication server only sends authorization codes and access tokens to the intended recipient."* Our reading: with no redirect URI registered at all, there is no allowed place to send the result, so Entra refuses the request.

A Microsoft moderator on [Microsoft Q&A](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/183594/aadsts500113-no-reply-address-is-registered-for-th) gave the same reading: *"The error states that the reply URL is not available, hence to fix this, you need to add a valid RedirectURI/ReplyURL in your app registration in AAD."*

Don't confuse it with [AADSTS50011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50011/), which Microsoft does list. Our reading of the difference: 50011 means the app has redirect URIs but the one in the request doesn't match; 500113 means the app has none.

sections.text:

"Reply address" is the older name for a redirect URI. Microsoft's redirect URI page explains why Entra needs one: *"To sign in a user, your application must send a login request to the Microsoft Entra authorization endpoint, with a redirect URI specified as a parameter. The redirect URI is a critical security feature that ensures the Microsoft Entra authentication server only sends authorization codes and access tokens to the intended recipient."* Our reading: with no redirect URI registered at all, there is no allowed place to send the result, so Entra refuses the request.

A Microsoft moderator on [Microsoft Q&A](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/183594/aadsts500113-no-reply-address-is-registered-for-th) gave the same reading: *"The error states that the reply URL is not available, hence to fix this, you need to add a valid RedirectURI/ReplyURL in your app registration in AAD."*

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
In a manual lab test on 30 October 2026, an authorize URL for a lab app registration with no redirect URI was opened in a private browser window, without signing in. Entra showed `AADSTS500113` on its error page with this first line:

> AADSTS500113: No reply address is registered for the application.

That confirms the code and its wording at the authorize endpoint. It also shows the error doesn't need a signed-in user: the request was unauthenticated. It lands in **`SigninLogs`**, and the row was logged under the account that was already signed in to that browser (the lab admin), with client app "Browser". So the user on a 500113 row can be whoever had a session, not someone who typed a password. The KQL below was run on these rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). The first query found the row. The `AuditLogs` query isn't tested: the export has no audit rows.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is an app registration that is missing its redirect URI.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new app registration, first test sign-in | The developer created the registration and never added a platform. |
| A desktop or mobile app (for example an Android app) fails on first interactive sign-in | The registration has no **Mobile and desktop applications** platform. Users report this on [Microsoft Q&A](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/183594/aadsts500113-no-reply-address-is-registered-for-th) (Android) and the [Icewolf blog](https://blog.icewolf.ch/archive/2021/07/06/aad-delegated-login-fix-error-aadsts500113-no-reply-address-is/) (delegated login). |
| An app registration made for a background service is now used for user sign-in | Likely: app-only (client credentials) apps don't use the authorize endpoint, so they never needed a redirect URI. Microsoft doesn't say this; a user commenter on the same Q&A thread does. |
| An app that worked and now fails | Someone removed its redirect URIs. Check the audit log (query below). |

An attacker who sends this request probably learns only that the app has no redirect URI. Nobody is signed in and nothing is issued.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 500113 is logged in. The lab run above logged it in `SigninLogs`, under the account that already had a session in the browser. Check both user sign-in tables:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500113"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, AppId, AppDisplayName
```

The audit log is more useful. If the app used to work, find who changed its registration:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where OperationName == "Update application"
| mv-expand Target = TargetResources
| where tostring(Target.displayName) == "<app display name>"
| mv-expand Prop = Target.modifiedProperties
| project TimeGenerated,
    Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
    Property = tostring(Prop.displayName),
    OldValue = tostring(Prop.oldValue),
    NewValue = tostring(Prop.newValue)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

The table reference documents `TargetResources` and `InitiatedBy` only as dynamic columns. The field names inside them (`displayName`, `modifiedProperties`, `user.userPrincipalName`) aren't documented there, and neither is the operation name `Update application`. Look for a property whose old value held URLs and whose new value is empty.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500113?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report the app name to whoever set it up.

**For developers and admins:** add a platform and redirect URI to the app registration. Microsoft's steps:

1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, in **App registrations**, select the application.
2. Under **Manage**, select **Authentication**.
3. Select **Add Redirect URI** (on the **Redirect URI configuration** tab).
4. Pick the platform that matches the app: **Web**, **Single-page application**, **iOS / macOS**, **Android** or **Mobile and desktop applications**.
5. Enter or select the redirect URI, then select **Configure**.

Microsoft: *"For Web and Single-page applications, you specify a redirect URI manually. For Mobile and desktop platforms, you select from generated redirect URIs."* Use the exact URI the app sends. If it then fails with [AADSTS50011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50011/), the URI you added doesn't match the one in the request.

If the app is only meant to run as a background service, it shouldn't be sending users to the authorize endpoint at all. Our reading: switch it to the client credentials flow rather than adding a redirect URI it doesn't need.

500113.labSectionText:
In a manual lab test on 30 October 2026, an authorize URL for a lab app registration with no redirect URI was opened in a private browser window, without signing in. Entra showed `AADSTS500113` on its error page with this first line:

> AADSTS500113: No reply address is registered for the application.

That confirms the code and its wording at the authorize endpoint. It also shows the error doesn't need a signed-in user: the request was unauthenticated. It lands in **`SigninLogs`**, and the row was logged under the account that was already signed in to that browser (the lab admin), with client app "Browser". So the user on a 500113 row can be whoever had a session, not someone who typed a password. The KQL below was run on these rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). The first query found the row. The `AuditLogs` query isn't tested: the export has no audit rows.

500121.name: MFA prompt not completed
500121.title: AADSTS500121: User didn't complete the MFA prompt
500121.description: AADSTS500121: the password worked but the MFA prompt was denied, ignored or timed out. Many for one user is an MFA fatigue signal. KQL included.
500121.summary: AADSTS500121 means the user didn't complete the MFA prompt: it was denied, ignored, timed out, or MFA setup was unfinished. The password had already been accepted. A few are normal. Many for one user in a short window, especially from an unfamiliar IP, is the MFA fatigue pattern.
500121.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **500121**: User didn't complete the MFA prompt.

Microsoft's troubleshooting guide adds that it *"often appears if the user hasn't completed setting up MFA"*.

**Where this is documented:** this code is described in Microsoft's [How to troubleshoot sign-in errors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/howto-troubleshoot-sign-in-errors) guide, not in the main error code reference table. When this page was written (2026-10-11) the reference table had no row for 500121, so there is no PascalCase name to quote.

sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **500121**: User didn't complete the MFA prompt.

**Where this is documented:** this code is described in Microsoft's [How to troubleshoot sign-in errors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/howto-troubleshoot-sign-in-errors) guide, not in the main error code reference table. When this page was written (2026-10-11) the reference table had no row for 500121, so there is no PascalCase name to quote.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Most 500121 rows are users who closed the prompt, had no signal, or hadn't finished setting up MFA. **The security reading is about volume per user and the source IP.** Microsoft frames this code as troubleshooting; the MFA fatigue reading below is reasoning from what the code means, not a Microsoft statement.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One 500121, then `0` from the same IP and device | The user retried. Benign. |
| 500121 for a user who is mid-onboarding | Unfinished MFA setup, as Microsoft describes. |
| Many 500121 for **one user** in a short window from an IP the user doesn't use | **MFA fatigue** (T1621). The first factor (usually the password) succeeded and the attacker is pushing prompts. |
| A 500121 burst followed by `0` from the **same IP** | **The user gave in and approved.** Treat as account takeover. |
| 500121 mixed with **50074** for the same user and IP | Same picture. See [50074](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50074/). |

Microsoft's password spray playbook says to *"record successful passwords but failed MFA responses, as this activity indicates that the attacker is getting the password but not passing MFA."* Every 500121 means the first factor (usually the password) succeeded.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Users with repeated 500121 from one IP within an hour:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "500121"
| summarize NotCompleted = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 5)
          by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where NotCompleted >= 3
| sort by NotCompleted desc
```

Did a fatigued user approve in the end? Successes from the same IP within an hour after the last unfinished prompt:

```kusto
let fatigued =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "500121"
    | summarize NotCompleted = count(), LastNotCompleted = max(TimeGenerated)
              by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
    | where NotCompleted >= 3;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=inner fatigued on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| where TimeGenerated between (LastNotCompleted .. (LastNotCompleted + 1h))
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, NotCompleted,
          AppDisplayName, UserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

The threshold of 3 is a starting point, not a Microsoft number. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"500121"`.

sections.heading: How do Conditional Access and MFA affect it?
sections.text:
- 500121 is the MFA step holding. Whatever required MFA stopped a sign-in whose first factor had succeeded.
- The risk is the user approving on the next attempt. Push approval without context is what fatigue attacks rely on. Number matching is enforced for Microsoft Authenticator push since 2023; phishing-resistant methods remove the push entirely. The [MFA fatigue guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/detect-mfa-fatigue-entra-id/) walks through the investigation.
- Microsoft notes that requiring reauthentication too often *"can increase security friction to a point that it causes users to experience MFA fatigue"*. A user who sees prompts all day is easier to fatigue.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500121?
sections.text:
**For the user:** if you didn't start the sign-in, deny the prompt and report it. If you're setting up MFA, finish registration and sign in again.

**For admins:**
1. For a burst from an unfamiliar IP, reset the user's password. The attacker already has it.
2. Run the second query. If a `0` followed, revoke sessions (`Revoke-MgUserSignInSession`) and review what the session accessed.
3. Move users to phishing-resistant MFA, and check any third-party or NPS-extension MFA path that still allows a plain approve.
4. For onboarding users stuck here, help them finish MFA registration.

500200.title: AADSTS500200: Personal Microsoft account not supported by this app (fix)
500200.description: AADSTS500200: a personal Microsoft account signed in to an app that only takes work or school accounts. Not in Microsoft's reference. Causes, fix, KQL.
500200.summary: AADSTS500200 means someone signed in with a personal Microsoft account (for example Outlook.com, or a Gmail address used as a Microsoft account) to an app or tenant that only accepts work or school accounts. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. It has low attack value. Sign in with a work account, invite the person as a guest, or change the app's supported account types.
500200.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS500200 (checked 30 October 2026).

We found no Microsoft documentation page for it either. The wording below comes from user reports on Microsoft Q&A. Two separate threads quote the same message:

> AADSTS500200: User account '…' is a personal Microsoft account. Personal Microsoft accounts are not supported for this application unless explicitly invited to an organization. Try signing out and signing back in with an organizational account.

A personal Microsoft account (for example Outlook.com, or a Gmail address used as a Microsoft account) tried to sign in to an app that only accepts work or school accounts. The message itself names two ways out: an invitation to the organization, or a work account.

A Microsoft employee answering in the [first thread](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1059353/aadsts500200-user-account-is-a-personal-microsoft) gives the cause as the app's supported account type: *"If your app registration is set to a single-tenant account type, users from other directories or identity providers can't sign into that application."* He says to make sure the user *"was invited to your Azure AD tenant, or that the App you're trying to sign into allows `AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount`."*

That matches what Microsoft documents about account types. An app registration's `signInAudience` decides who can sign in. Microsoft's [supported account types page](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/supported-accounts-validation) lists four values:

| `signInAudience` | Label in the app registration |
|---|---|
| `AzureADMyOrg` | Accounts in this organizational directory only (Single tenant) |
| `AzureADMultipleOrgs` | Accounts in any organizational directory (Multitenant) |
| `AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount` | Accounts in any organizational directory and personal Microsoft accounts (such as Skype, Xbox) |
| `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` | Personal Microsoft accounts only |

Only the last two take a personal account that hasn't been invited. The authority the app signs in through matters too. Microsoft's MSAL configuration page says `/organizations` signs in *"users with work and school accounts"*, a tenant-specific authority signs in *"users of a specific organization only"*, and only `/common` and `/consumers` take personal accounts. Our reading: an app on `/organizations` or a tenant authority gets this error for a personal account even when the registration allows personal accounts. We have not tested that.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is an account-type mismatch. The account is real, but the app doesn't accept that kind of account.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One person, a consumer address (outlook.com, gmail.com) | They used a personal account where a work account is needed. Benign. |
| Users report it on Microsoft 365 apps on a phone while editing their own documents | In the [second thread](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1476251/how-to-fix-error-aadsts500200-user-account-is-a-pe), one user with a Microsoft 365 Family account gets it when editing on Android, and another only in the OneNote Android app. Likely the app was routed to a work-account sign-in, but that is unconfirmed. Not something an admin can fix. |
| Users report it on the Microsoft Learn sandbox | Same thread. The sandbox needs a work account in a tenant. |
| An external partner using a personal address, hitting one of your apps | They were never invited as a guest. Invite them if they need access. |
| A developer's own app, right after registration | The registration is single tenant or multitenant without personal accounts. |

We found no source that links 500200 to an attack pattern. The sign-in fails before any of your resources are reached.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 500200 is logged in, or whether it is logged in your tenant at all. Our reading: a personal account that was never invited has no user object in your tenant, so a row may not appear there. Check first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500200"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

If rows exist, see which apps and which home tenants they come from. `HomeTenantId` is documented as *"the tenant identifier of the user initiating the sign in"*:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500200"
| summarize Attempts = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Sample = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, HomeTenantId
| sort by Attempts desc
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500200?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign out and sign in again with your work or school account, as the message says. If you don't have one for this organization, ask its admin to invite you. Volunteer moderators on Q&A suggest trying a private browser window first, in case the browser keeps signing you in with the personal account. One user in the second thread says that didn't help.

**For developers:**
1. Check **Supported account types** in the app registration, or `signInAudience` in the manifest. If personal accounts must work, use `AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount`. Microsoft warns: *"If you change this property you may need to change other properties first."* Personal-account audiences have extra limits, for example no national clouds and at most two client secrets.
2. Sign in through `/common` (work and personal accounts) or `/consumers` (personal only). `/organizations` and a tenant ID only take work and school accounts.
3. In a comment on the first Q&A thread, one user reports the error with `signInAudience` set to `AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount` and `accessTokenAcceptedVersion` set to 2, on an Azure App Service site. Nobody replied to that comment. If you hit the same, check the authority in the app's configuration (point 2), which is our best guess, not a confirmed cause.

**For admins:**
1. If the person needs access to your app, invite them as a guest. Microsoft says B2B guests *"can use their own personal Microsoft accounts for B2B collaboration without further configuration."*
2. If the app is a third-party product that should accept personal accounts, that is the vendor's registration to change, not yours.

microsoftWording.source: Quoted on the page from the lab or from user reports; the code is not in Microsoft's error code reference

attackSignal.label: Low: usually configuration or user error

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
No. It is an account-type mismatch. The account is real, but the app doesn't accept that kind of account.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| One person, a consumer address (outlook.com, gmail.com) | They used a personal account where a work account is needed. Benign. |
| Users report it on Microsoft 365 apps on a phone while editing their own documents | In the [second thread](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1476251/how-to-fix-error-aadsts500200-user-account-is-a-pe), one user with a Microsoft 365 Family account gets it when editing on Android, and another only in the OneNote Android app. Likely the app was routed to a work-account sign-in, but that is unconfirmed. Not something an admin can fix. |
| Users report it on the Microsoft Learn sandbox | Same thread. The sandbox needs a work account in a tenant. |
| An external partner using a personal address, hitting one of your apps | They were never invited as a guest. Invite them if they need access. |
| A developer's own app, right after registration | The registration is single tenant or multitenant without personal accounts. |

We found no source that links 500200 to an attack pattern. The sign-in fails before any of your resources are reached.

500341.title: AADSTS500341: User account has been deleted from the directory (fix)
500341.description: AADSTS500341: the signing-in account was deleted from the tenant. Not in Microsoft's reference. Restore it within 30 days or reconnect. KQL included.
500341.summary: AADSTS500341 means the account signing in has been deleted from the Microsoft Entra tenant. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it; a Microsoft Viva Goals page does. Something still uses the old account: a saved sign-in, a connection or a script. Restore the user within 30 days if the deletion was a mistake, otherwise reconnect with an active account.
500341.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS500341 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it on a [Viva Goals page about Microsoft Entra errors](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-gb/viva/goals/integration-aad-errors), which gives the message as:

> AADSTS500341: The user account <account ID> has been deleted from the <AAD> directory. To sign into this application, the account must be added to the directory

Its resolution: *"The user account with which this connection was first created is no longer in an active state. Try creating a new connection."*

The same page lists [50034](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50034/) as *"The user account <account ID> doesn't exist in the <AAD> directory."* So the two codes say different things: 50034 is a name that doesn't exist, 500341 an account that existed and was deleted.

Microsoft's page on restoring users explains the deleted state: *"After you delete a user, the account remains in a suspended state for 30 days. During that 30-day window, the user account can be restored, along with all its properties."* After that, *"the permanent deletion process automatically starts and can't be stopped."* Microsoft doesn't say whether 500341 is returned only during those 30 days or also after permanent deletion.

We tried to reproduce it in the lab three times on 30 October 2026 and never got 500341. What we got instead is worth knowing:

| Time between deleting the user and signing in | Result |
|---|---|
| About 30 seconds | [65001](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/65001/), consent not granted: the same answer an active user got in that run |
| About 30 seconds, with consent already granted | **A token was issued.** The sign-in succeeded for a user that no longer existed |
| About 12 minutes | [50034](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50034/), the user account does not exist |

The middle row is the one to take away: a deleted account can still sign in successfully for a short window after deletion. That is a reason to revoke sessions and disable the account before you delete it, rather than relying on the delete alone.

None of the three runs produced 500341, so on this tenant a deleted user ends up at 50034 instead. Microsoft's Viva Goals page gives both codes the same resolution, and we can't tell from here which conditions produce which. The lab tenant's exported sign-in log shows the first attempt in `SigninLogs` under the deleted user's name, as 65001 with status Interrupted.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. It means something still uses an account you deleted.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A connection or integration stops working after an offboarding | It was set up with the deleted user's account, as Microsoft's Viva Goals page describes. Reconnect it with an active account. |
| One device or app keeps failing for a departed employee | A saved sign-in or a mail profile on a device that wasn't wiped. Benign, but find the device. |
| A user deleted by mistake who suddenly can't sign in | Restore them within 30 days. |
| Attempts on a deleted account from IP addresses the person never used | Someone else has the old credentials. The sign-in fails, but check where else those credentials work, for example other accounts with the same password. Our interpretation, not a documented pattern. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 500341 is logged in. Check where it lands:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500341"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

Which deleted accounts are still being used, from where and by what:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500341"
| summarize Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), Agents = make_set(UserAgent, 5)
          by UserPrincipalName, UserId
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Sign-ins for an account after it was deleted, whatever the result. `Delete user` is an activity name in Microsoft's audit activity list. This joins on the object ID; whether `UserId` is still filled for a deleted account is our assumption, not checked:

```kusto
let deletions =
    AuditLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActivityDisplayName == "Delete user"
    | extend UserId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id),
             DeletedBy = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName))
    | project DeletedAt = TimeGenerated, UserId, DeletedBy;
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| join kind=inner deletions on UserId
| where TimeGenerated > DeletedAt
| summarize Attempts = count(), Results = make_set(ResultType, 10), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by UserPrincipalName, UserId, DeletedAt, DeletedBy
| sort by LastSeen desc
```

A `"0"` in `Results` means a sign-in succeeded after the deletion was logged. The lab run above didn't show that: it got 65001, not a success. Look at how long after `DeletedAt` it happened before treating it as a problem.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500341?
sections.text:
**For the user:** your account was removed from the organization. Ask its IT team whether that was intended. If you moved to a new account, sign out of the app and sign in with the new one.

**For developers:** treat 500341 as "this account is gone". Clear the cached account and send the user through an interactive sign-in instead of retrying the same account.

**For admins:**
1. Deleted by mistake: restore the user within 30 days. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, as at least a User Administrator, go to **Entra ID** > **Users** > **Deleted users**. Microsoft says restoring brings back the account's properties and the licenses it had.
2. For a synced user, Microsoft warns that *"if the user still exists in your on-premises directory, the sync engine may restore the user during the next synchronization cycle."* Fix the source object first if the deletion was intended.
3. Deleted on purpose: find what still uses the account with the second query, and reconnect each integration with an active account, as the Viva Goals page says.
4. Unknown IP addresses on a deleted account: treat the old password as known to someone else. If the same person has another account, reset its password and revoke its sessions.

500571.title: AADSTS500571: The guest user account is disabled (fix)
500571.description: AADSTS500571: a guest's account is disabled in the tenant they're signing in to. Not in Microsoft's reference. Who can fix it, plus KQL.
500571.summary: AADSTS500571 means a guest (B2B) user tried to sign in to an app in a tenant where their guest account is disabled. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it, but a Microsoft troubleshooting article does. Their home account can be fine. It has low attack value. The resource tenant decides: leave it blocked, or re-enable the guest object.
500571.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS500571 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it in a [troubleshooting article](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts500571-guest-user-account-is-disabled):

> When a guest user tries to sign in to an application that's integrated into Microsoft Entra ID, they receive an "AADSTS500571" error message ("The guest user account is disabled").

The cause, in Microsoft's words: *"The guest user object is disabled on the resource tenant."*

A user posting on Microsoft Tech Community quotes the full string as returned to Visual Studio:

> V2Error: invalid_grant AADSTS500571: The guest user account is disabled

Background: when you invite a guest, Microsoft says *"an account is created in your tenant. This account doesn't have any credentials associated with it because authentication is performed by the guest user's identity provider."* So there are two accounts. The one in the user's home tenant can be enabled and working while the guest object in the resource tenant is disabled. 500571 is about the second one. If the account in the user's own tenant were disabled, that would be [50057](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50057/).

Microsoft documents it in a [troubleshooting article](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts500571-guest-user-account-is-disabled):

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. A disabled guest object is a deliberate block by the resource tenant, or a mistake.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A partner user who was offboarded or whose project ended | The guest was disabled on purpose. Access is blocked as intended. |
| Many guests from one partner disabled on the same day | A bulk clean-up, an access review, or a script. Check the audit log for who did it. |
| A user who says *"I'm not a guest, I signed in with my own account"* | An admin on Q&A reports this for a Teams user who said he signed in with his own account. Our reading: the app tried to reach another tenant where the user has a disabled guest object, for example a tenant switch in Teams or a link from a partner. |
| Repeated 500571 for a guest who was disabled during an incident | Something still holds that person's sign-in and keeps trying. Worth a look. Our interpretation, not a documented pattern. |

Our reading: the block works. A failed sign-in with 500571 means no token was issued for that guest in your tenant.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 500571 is logged in. Check where it lands:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500571"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

Which guests, from which home tenants, on which apps. `HomeTenantId` is documented as *"the tenant identifier of the user initiating the sign in"* and `UserType` as identifying *"whether the user is a member or guest in the tenant"*:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "500571"
| summarize Attempts = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10)
          by UserPrincipalName, UserId, HomeTenantId, UserType
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Who disabled the guest, and when. `Disable account` and `Update user` are both activity names in Microsoft's audit activity list. Which one a disable produces depends on how it was done, so search for both:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where ActivityDisplayName in ("Disable account", "Update user")
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName),
         TargetId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id),
         Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName))
| where TargetUpn has "#EXT#" or TargetId == "<guest object id>"
| project TimeGenerated, ActivityDisplayName, Actor, TargetUpn, TargetId, Result
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

The `#EXT#` filter is a shortcut for guest UPNs. Microsoft's B2B user properties page says a guest's UPN contains `#EXT#`. Put the `UserId` from the second query in place of `<guest object id>` to be exact. `Update user` also covers changes that have nothing to do with sign-in, so read the modified properties in `TargetResources` before drawing a conclusion.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS500571?
sections.text:
**For the user:** your own organization can't fix this. The block is in the other organization's tenant. Contact whoever invited you there, or their IT. Microsoft says to *"engage the resource tenant owners or sponsor."*

**For admins of the resource tenant:** find out why the guest was disabled, then follow Microsoft's two cases:

| Case | Microsoft's action |
|---|---|
| The guest is supposed to be disabled | *"No actions should be performed. Access is expectedly blocked."* |
| It was disabled by mistake | *"Resource tenant owners should re-enable the account."* |

To re-enable the guest with Microsoft Graph PowerShell, set `accountEnabled` to true. This is the command from Microsoft's page on blocking accounts with PowerShell; `-UserId` takes the UPN or object ID:

```powershell
Connect-Graph -Scopes User.ReadWrite.All
$params = @{
    accountEnabled = $true
}
Update-MgUser -UserId "<guest object id>" -BodyParameter $params
```

Microsoft's troubleshooting article points to `Set-AzureADUser` with `-AccountEnabled $true`, from the AzureAD module. Both set the same `accountEnabled` property, as far as we can tell.

**For admins of the user's home tenant:** nothing to change on your side. Check that the user is trying to reach the tenant they think they are.

501051.title: AADSTS501051: Client app isn't assigned to a role for the API (fix)
501051.description: AADSTS501051: the client app has no app role on an API that requires assignment. Not in Microsoft's error list. Fix and KQL.
501051.summary: AADSTS501051 means a client app asked for an access token to a web API whose enterprise app has "Assignment required" set to Yes, and the client holds no app role on that API. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it, but its protected web API docs do. Low attack value. Assign an app role to the client; don't switch assignment off.
501051.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS501051 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft does document it on another page. Its protected web API guide explains how to restrict token issuance to approved client apps, by setting **Assignment required?** to **Yes** on the API's enterprise application. Then:

> Microsoft Entra ID will now check for app role assignments of client applications that request access tokens for your web API. If a client app hasn't been assigned any app roles, Microsoft Entra ID returns an error message to the client similar to `invalid_client: AADSTS501051: Application <application name> isn't assigned to a role for the <web API>`.

So two things are true at once:
1. The API's enterprise application (its service principal) has **Assignment required?** set to **Yes**.
2. The client app that asked for the token has no app role on that API.

Microsoft's enterprise app properties page describes the switch: *"If this option is set to **Yes**, then users and other applications or services must first be assigned this application before being able to access it."* It applies to *"Applications or services for which other applications or service are requesting access tokens."*

Our reading: 501051 is the app-side twin of [50105](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50105/). 50105 is a user without an assignment. 501051 is a client app without one. Microsoft doesn't say so in those words.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS501051 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS501051 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft does document it on another page. Its protected web API guide explains how to restrict token issuance to approved client apps, by setting **Assignment required?** to **Yes** on the API's enterprise application. Then:

> Microsoft Entra ID will now check for app role assignments of client applications that request access tokens for your web API. If a client app hasn't been assigned any app roles, Microsoft Entra ID returns an error message to the client similar to `invalid_client: AADSTS501051: Application <application name> isn't assigned to a role for the <web API>`.

So two things are true at once:
1. The API's enterprise application (its service principal) has **Assignment required?** set to **Yes**.
2. The client app that asked for the token has no app role on that API.

Microsoft's enterprise app properties page describes the switch: *"If this option is set to **Yes**, then users and other applications or services must first be assigned this application before being able to access it."* It applies to *"Applications or services for which other applications or service are requesting access tokens."*

Our reading: 501051 is the app-side twin of [50105](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50105/). 50105 is a user without an assignment. 501051 is a client app without one. Microsoft doesn't say so in those words.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. It is the assignment check doing what it was set up to do.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new daemon or service fails on its first token request | Nobody assigned it an app role on the API yet. |
| A working client starts failing after a change | Someone turned on **Assignment required?** on the API, or removed the client's app role assignment. Check the audit log. |
| A client you don't recognise hits 501051 against an internal API | Possibly a client with valid credentials trying an API it was never granted (see below). Find out who owns that client. |
| Repeated 501051 from one client, every few minutes | A scheduled job retrying with no fix in sight. Noise until someone assigns the role. |

Microsoft doesn't document this, but the role check probably runs after the client has authenticated, so a 501051 from an unknown client may mean it holds working credentials in your tenant. That deserves a look, even though no token was issued.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 501051 is logged in. App-only requests (client credentials) probably land in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "501051"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

Which clients are refused, and for which API:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "501051"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by ServicePrincipalName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, ResourceIdentity
| sort by Rows desc
```

Service principal sign-in rows are aggregated, so `Rows` is not a request count.

Who changed assignments. Microsoft's audit log reference lists **Add app role assignment to service principal**, **Remove app role assignment from service principal** and **Update service principal** in the ApplicationManagement category:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName in ("Add app role assignment to service principal",
                          "Remove app role assignment from service principal",
                          "Update service principal")
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName,
          Target = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName),
          ByUser = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
          ByApp = tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

Our assumption: turning **Assignment required?** on or off is logged as **Update service principal**. Microsoft's reference lists the activity but not which property changes it covers.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS501051?
sections.text:
**For the user:** this error is between two apps, not about your account. Report it to whoever runs the app.

**For developers:**
1. Make sure the API exposes an app role for applications. Microsoft's guide: in **Create app role**, under **Allowed member types**, select **Applications**.
2. Request the role in the client's app registration: **API permissions** > **Add a permission** > **My APIs** > your API > the role.
3. Get an admin to grant consent. Microsoft: *"Because these are application permissions, not delegated permissions, an admin must grant consent to use the app roles assigned to the application."*
4. Don't branch on the AADSTS code in your code. Microsoft warns that the codes and message strings *"may be changed by Microsoft at any time and without your knowledge."*

**For admins:**
1. Don't fix this by setting **Assignment required?** back to **No**. That opens the API to every client in the tenant again.
2. Grant consent for the app role the client requested, or assign the role directly with Microsoft Graph PowerShell. `-ServicePrincipalId` and `principalId` are the client's service principal. `resourceId` is the API's service principal:

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All"

$client = Get-MgServicePrincipal -Filter "appId eq '<client app id>'"
$api    = Get-MgServicePrincipal -Filter "appId eq '<api app id>'"

$params = @{
    principalId = $client.Id
    resourceId  = $api.Id
    appRoleId   = "<app role id from the API>"
}
New-MgServicePrincipalAppRoleAssignment -ServicePrincipalId $client.Id -BodyParameter $params
```

3. If the API defines no app roles, Microsoft's cmdlet reference says a default ID of `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` *"can be specified to signal that the principal is assigned to the resource app without any specific app roles."* Our reading: a dedicated app role is the better choice, because the API can then check the `roles` claim.
4. If the client is one you don't recognise, don't assign anything. Find its owner first.

530002.title: AADSTS530002: Your device is required to be compliant (fix)
530002.description: AADSTS530002: Conditional Access requires a compliant device and this one isn't. Not in Microsoft's reference. How it differs from 53000, the fix, KQL.
530002.summary: AADSTS530002 means a Conditional Access policy requires a compliant device and the device isn't compliant. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it; a Viva Goals troubleshooting page does, for stored connections whose device fell out of compliance. Most user reports of compliant-device blocks quote the listed code 53000 instead. Usually benign drift out of compliance.
530002.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS530002 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it on another page. The Viva Goals troubleshooting page for integration errors lists it under the heading *"AADSTS530002: Your device is required to be compliant to access this resource"* and says:

> The device on which this connection was first created is no longer in a compliant state. Try reauthenticating or creating a new connection.

That page introduces its list as errors you get *"if you encounter an AAD invalid grant error for an integration"*. So the scenario Microsoft describes is a connection created on a device that was compliant at the time, whose token later fails because the device no longer is.

We found little else. Two web searches for the exact message returned no user thread that quotes 530002. The Q&A and community threads they returned all quote the listed code [53000](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/53000/) instead, for example: *"AADSTS53000: Device is not in required device state: compliant. Conditional Access policy requires a compliant device, and the device is not compliant."*

Our reading: 530002 and 53000 come from the same grant control, **Require device to be marked as compliant**. 53000 is the code people see at sign-in. 530002 shows up, as far as Microsoft's one page says, when a stored grant is used later. Microsoft doesn't document how the two differ, so fix both the same way.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. The common cause is a device that drifted out of compliance: an overdue OS update, a disabled disk encryption setting, or a lapsed Intune check-in.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 530002 for an integration or background sync that worked before | The device the connection was created on is no longer compliant. Microsoft's Viva Goals scenario. |
| 530002 for many users on the same day | A compliance policy changed in Intune and many devices fell out of compliance at once. Likely, but unconfirmed. |
| 530002 for one user on a device with an empty device ID | The device isn't registered, so it can't be compliant. Microsoft says devices *"must be registered in Microsoft Entra ID before they can be marked as compliant."* |
| 530002 for a privileged account from a new IP or country | Our reasoning: a working session or token is being used from a device you don't manage. Check whether it was the user. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 530002 is logged in. The Viva Goals scenario (a refreshed integration token) points to `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs` as the likely place, but check:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("530002", "53000")
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable, ResultType
```

Which devices fail, and what compliance state the sign-in recorded. `DeviceDetail` is dynamic in `SigninLogs` and a string in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, so each leg parses it first. The property names come from the Graph `deviceDetail` resource:

```kusto
let rows =
    union
        (SigninLogs | extend D = parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)) | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, D),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | extend D = parse_json(DeviceDetail) | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, D);
rows
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "530002"
| extend DeviceId = tostring(D.deviceId),
         DeviceName = tostring(D.displayName),
         IsCompliant = tostring(D.isCompliant),
         TrustType = tostring(D.trustType),
         OS = tostring(D.operatingSystem)
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DeviceId, DeviceName, IsCompliant, TrustType, OS
| sort by Rows desc
```

A day with many more devices failing than usual. The factor of 3 is a starting point:

```kusto
let daily =
    union
        (SigninLogs | extend DeviceId = tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId) | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, DeviceId),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | extend DeviceId = tostring(parse_json(DeviceDetail).deviceId) | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, DeviceId)
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ResultType in ("530002", "53000")
    | summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId) by Day = bin(TimeGenerated, 1d);
let baseline = toscalar(daily | summarize avg(Devices));
daily
| where Devices > 3 * baseline
| sort by Day asc
```

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- The control is **Require device to be marked as compliant**. Microsoft says it *"only supports Windows 10+, iOS, Android, macOS, and Linux Ubuntu devices registered with Microsoft Entra ID and enrolled with Intune"*, and that *"Microsoft Edge in InPrivate mode on Windows is considered as a noncompliant device."*
- Compliance comes from Intune or a supported non-Microsoft MDM: *"Intune sends compliance information to Microsoft Entra ID so Conditional Access can decide to grant or block access to resources."* So the fix is usually in Intune, not in Conditional Access.
- By default a policy with several controls requires all of them. With "require one of", hybrid join or MFA can stand in for compliance.
- For guest users, see [530004](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/530004/): the resource tenant has to trust the home tenant's compliance claim.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS530002?
sections.text:
**For the user:** open Company Portal (or your MDM app) on the device, check what it says is wrong, fix it, and sync. Then sign in again. For an integration that stopped working, the Viva Goals advice is to reauthenticate or create the connection again, on a compliant device.

**For admins:**
1. Open the failed sign-in in **Entra ID** > **Monitoring & health** > **Sign-in logs**. The **Conditional Access** tab names the policy; Microsoft says the **Troubleshooting and support** tab may show the reason, *"such as a device that didn't meet compliance requirements."*
2. Look the device up in Intune and read which compliance setting fails.
3. If the second query shows an empty device ID, the device isn't registered. Register or enroll it first.
4. If many devices failed on one day, review the last change to your compliance policies before you touch Conditional Access.

530003.title: AADSTS530003: Your device is required to be managed (fix)
530003.description: AADSTS530003: Conditional Access requires a managed device and this one isn't. Common with Azure CLI and Terraform. Not in Microsoft's reference. KQL.
530003.summary: AADSTS530003 means a Conditional Access policy requires a managed device and the device asking for the token isn't one, or can't prove it. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. Users report it from the Azure CLI, Terraform and Cloud Shell. Usually it is a tool on an unmanaged machine. From a new device or IP, check whether the account is in the right hands.
530003.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS530003 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it on another page. The Viva Goals troubleshooting page for integration errors lists it under the heading *"AADSTS530003: Your device is required to be managed to access this resource"* and says:

> The device on which this connection was first created might not have been in a managed state. Try reauthenticating or creating a new connection.

That page introduces its list as errors you get *"if you encounter an AAD invalid grant error for an integration"*, so it covers a stored connection whose token is refreshed later.

Users report the same message from command-line tools. On HashiCorp Discuss, `terraform plan` on Ubuntu with the azurerm provider failed while reading a token from the Azure CLI:

> ERROR: AADSTS530003: Your device is required to be managed to access this resource.

On Microsoft Q&A, `az account get-access-token --resource https://graph.microsoft.com` in Azure Cloud Shell returned the same text. Neither thread has an answer.

Our reading: a Conditional Access policy requires a managed device (compliant or hybrid joined), and the device asking for the token is not one or can't prove it. Microsoft doesn't publish a name or a precise definition for 530003. The listed codes for the same family are [53000](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/53000/) (device not compliant) and [53001](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/53001/) (device not domain joined).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Most reports come from tools that can't present a device identity: a CLI on Linux, a container, Cloud Shell, or a stored integration.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 530003 from Azure CLI, Terraform or PowerShell on a build agent or Linux machine | The tool runs on a machine that isn't managed by the tenant. Expected under a managed-device policy. |
| 530003 right after `az login --use-device-code` | Microsoft says device code flow can't carry device state (see below), so expect it under a managed-device policy. |
| 530003 from Cloud Shell | Probably because Cloud Shell runs on a Microsoft host, not on the user's device. Unconfirmed; based on one Q&A report. |
| 530003 for a privileged account from a new IP or country | Our reasoning: the account got far enough for a device control to apply. Check whether the sign-in was the user. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 530003 is logged in. Check where it lands first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "530003"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

Which users, apps and device states hit it. `DeviceDetail` is dynamic in `SigninLogs` and a string in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, so each leg parses it before the union. The property names come from the Graph `deviceDetail` resource:

```kusto
let rows =
    union
        (SigninLogs | extend D = parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)) | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IPAddress, D),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | extend D = parse_json(DeviceDetail) | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IPAddress, D);
rows
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "530003"
| extend DeviceId = tostring(D.deviceId),
         TrustType = tostring(D.trustType),
         IsManaged = tostring(D.isManaged),
         IsCompliant = tostring(D.isCompliant),
         OS = tostring(D.operatingSystem)
| summarize Rows = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Agents = make_set(UserAgent, 5)
          by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, DeviceId, TrustType, IsManaged, IsCompliant, OS
| extend Unregistered = isempty(DeviceId)
| sort by Rows desc
```

530003 from an IP where the same user had no successful sign-in in the last 30 days. A starting point for triage, not a detection rule:

```kusto
let lookback = 30d;
let knownUserIPs =
    union
        (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType)
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
union
    (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, UserAgent),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AppDisplayName, UserAgent)
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "530003"
| join kind=leftanti knownUserIPs on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 530003 most likely comes from a device grant control: **Require device to be marked as compliant**, **Require Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device**, or both. The Conditional Access tab on the failed sign-in shows which policy applied.
- Microsoft says device code flow can't satisfy these controls: *"When you use the device-code OAuth flow, the required grant control for the managed device or a device state condition isn't supported. This is because the device that is performing authentication can't provide its device state to the device that is providing a code."* Microsoft's advice there: use **Require multifactor authentication** instead.
- Microsoft also says Edge in InPrivate mode doesn't count as compliant or hybrid joined.
- By default, a policy with several controls requires all of them. With "require one of the selected controls", MFA can stand in for the device.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS530003?
sections.text:
**For the user:** run the tool on your managed work device, or sign in with a browser on that device. If you need the tool somewhere else, such as a build server, ask IT how they want that done.

**For developers:** Microsoft's MSAL.NET page on device authentication says the device must prove its identity, and *"to satisfy this requirement you will have to leverage WAM on Windows or the system browser. On mobile platforms, you'll need to enable the brokers (Microsoft Authenticator and Company portal)."* An embedded web view or a plain HTTP client can't do that. For automation, don't use a user account at all. Use a service principal or managed identity. Our reading is that user device-state controls don't apply to those, but check your own policies.

**For admins:**
1. Open the failed sign-in in **Entra ID** > **Monitoring & health** > **Sign-in logs** and select the **Conditional Access** tab. It names the policy. Microsoft adds that the **Troubleshooting and support** tab may show the reason directly.
2. Check the device in the second query. An empty `DeviceId` means the device isn't registered, so it can't be managed.
3. Decide whether the policy should cover that app. If admins need Azure CLI from unmanaged machines, scope an exception for those users or allow MFA as an alternative. Use the What If tool before you change a production policy.
4. If the device should be managed, enroll or join it and sign in again. The Viva Goals page gives the same advice for stored connections: reauthenticate or create a new connection.

fix.short: User: run the tool on your managed work device, or sign in with a browser there. For automation, use a service principal or managed identity, not a user account. Admin: find the policy on the failed sign-in's Conditional Access tab and decide whether it should cover that app.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** run the tool on your managed work device, or sign in with a browser on that device. If you need the tool somewhere else, such as a build server, ask IT how they want that done.

**For developers:** Microsoft's MSAL.NET page on device authentication says the device must prove its identity, and *"to satisfy this requirement you will have to leverage WAM on Windows or the system browser. On mobile platforms, you'll need to enable the brokers (Microsoft Authenticator and Company portal)."* An embedded web view or a plain HTTP client can't do that. For automation, don't use a user account at all. Use a service principal or managed identity. Our reading is that user device-state controls don't apply to those, but check your own policies.

**For admins:**
1. Open the failed sign-in in **Entra ID** > **Monitoring & health** > **Sign-in logs** and select the **Conditional Access** tab. It names the policy. Microsoft adds that the **Troubleshooting and support** tab may show the reason directly.
2. Check the device in the second query. An empty `DeviceId` means the device isn't registered, so it can't be managed.
3. Decide whether the policy should cover that app. If admins need Azure CLI from unmanaged machines, scope an exception for those users or allow MFA as an alternative. Use the What If tool before you change a production policy.
4. If the device should be managed, enroll or join it and sign in again. The Viva Goals page gives the same advice for stored connections: reauthenticate or create a new connection.

530004.title: AADSTS530004: AcceptCompliantDevice setting isn't configured (fix)
530004.description: AADSTS530004: a guest hit a device-based Conditional Access policy and the resource tenant doesn't trust device claims. Not in Microsoft's reference. Fix, KQL.
530004.summary: AADSTS530004 means a guest user hit a device-based Conditional Access policy in the resource tenant, and that tenant doesn't trust device claims from the guest's home tenant. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it, but a Microsoft troubleshooting article does. It is a B2B configuration gap with low attack value. The fix is the inbound trust settings in cross-tenant access.
530004.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS530004 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it in a troubleshooting article, which quotes the message as:

> AADSTS530004: AcceptCompliantDevice setting isn't configured for this organization. The administrator needs to configure this setting to allow external user access to protected resources.

The article says it happens *"when a guest user tries to access an application or resource in a resource tenant"*, and that *"when an administrator reviews the sign-in logs in the home tenant, the same error code is displayed."*

It names three scenarios, all with a Conditional Access policy in the resource tenant that applies to guests:

| Policy control in the resource tenant | What Microsoft says to do |
|---|---|
| **Require device to be marked as compliant** | Configure cross-tenant access with **Trust compliant devices**, and make sure the guest's device is authenticated, enrolled in Intune or a supported MDM in the home tenant, and compliant. |
| **Require Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device** | Configure cross-tenant access with **Trust Microsoft Entra hybrid joined devices**, and make sure the device is authenticated and hybrid joined in the home tenant. |
| **Require approved client app** | *"This scenario isn't supported. To resolve the error, don't apply this control to guest users."* |

The background is in Microsoft's cross-tenant access overview: by default, *"MFA and device claims from other Microsoft Entra organizations aren't trusted."* Without the trust setting, a guest's compliant or hybrid joined device counts for nothing in your tenant.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS530004 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS530004 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it in a troubleshooting article, which quotes the message as:

The article says it happens *"when a guest user tries to access an application or resource in a resource tenant"*, and that *"when an administrator reviews the sign-in logs in the home tenant, the same error code is displayed."*

It names three scenarios, all with a Conditional Access policy in the resource tenant that applies to guests:

| Policy control in the resource tenant | What Microsoft says to do |
|---|---|
| **Require device to be marked as compliant** | Configure cross-tenant access with **Trust compliant devices**, and make sure the guest's device is authenticated, enrolled in Intune or a supported MDM in the home tenant, and compliant. |
| **Require Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device** | Configure cross-tenant access with **Trust Microsoft Entra hybrid joined devices**, and make sure the device is authenticated and hybrid joined in the home tenant. |
| **Require approved client app** | *"This scenario isn't supported. To resolve the error, don't apply this control to guest users."* |

The background is in Microsoft's cross-tenant access overview: by default, *"MFA and device claims from other Microsoft Entra organizations aren't trusted."* Without the trust setting, a guest's compliant or hybrid joined device counts for nothing in your tenant.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a mismatch between a device policy and the B2B trust settings. A guest who can't pass it is either on a device the home tenant doesn't manage or in a tenant you haven't chosen to trust.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 530004 for every guest from one partner | Your tenant has no trust setting for that partner, or the partner doesn't manage its devices. |
| 530004 for one guest while colleagues from the same partner succeed | That guest's device isn't compliant or registered, or the browser can't send the device claim. |
| 530004 starting on the day a device policy was extended to guests | The policy change, not the guests. Likely, but unconfirmed. |
| 530004 on an approved-client-app policy | Unsupported for guests, per Microsoft. Exclude guests from that control. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft says the error shows up in the home tenant's sign-in logs, and the article's verification steps use the resource tenant's sign-in logs. It doesn't say which table. Check where it lands:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "530004"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

Which partner tenants and devices are affected. In the resource tenant, `HomeTenantId` tells you which partner the guest comes from. In the home tenant, `ResourceTenantId` tells you which external tenant your user was trying to reach. `DeviceDetail` property names come from the Graph `deviceDetail` resource; Microsoft's article says the **Join type** field shows which device claim was passed:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "530004"
| extend TrustType = tostring(DeviceDetail.trustType),
         IsCompliant = tostring(DeviceDetail.isCompliant),
         Browser = tostring(DeviceDetail.browser)
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10)
          by HomeTenantId, ResourceTenantId, CrossTenantAccessType, UserType, TrustType, IsCompliant, Browser
| sort by Rows desc
```

Our reading: an empty `TrustType` means no device claim reached the resource tenant, which points at the "device authentication fails" cases listed below rather than at the trust setting. Compare with a successful guest sign-in from the same partner.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 530004 only appears because a device control in **your** policy applies to guests. Microsoft lists the controls: compliant device, hybrid joined device and approved client app.
- The approved client app control can't be satisfied by guests at all. Microsoft: *"This scenario isn't supported."*
- If you don't want to trust a partner's devices, the alternative is to exclude guests from the device policy and cover them with an MFA policy instead. Our suggestion; weigh it against your own risk.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS530004?
sections.text:
**For the guest user:** sign in from your work device in a normal browser window, not InPrivate or Incognito. If you still get the error, tell your contact in the organization you're visiting. Their admin has to change a setting. Your own IT may need to check that your device is compliant.

**For admins of the resource tenant (where the app lives):**
1. Go to **Entra ID** > **External Identities** > **Cross-tenant access settings**. Edit the **Default settings** inbound defaults, or under **Organizational settings** add the guest's home tenant and open its inbound access.
2. On the **Trust settings** tab (for an organization, choose **Customize settings** first), select **Trust compliant devices**, **Trust Microsoft Entra hybrid joined devices**, or both, to match your policy. Select **Save**.
3. If the failing policy uses **Require approved client app**, exclude guests from it.

Microsoft's troubleshooting article says to create the cross-tenant policy *"in the user's home tenant"*. The cross-tenant documentation describes trust settings as inbound settings that let *your* Conditional Access policies trust claims from an external organization. Our reading: the setting lives in the resource tenant, as a per-organization entry **for** the guest's home tenant. If you are the home tenant's admin, ask the resource tenant to configure it.

**For admins of the guest's home tenant:** make sure the device is actually compliant or hybrid joined in your tenant. Microsoft lists these causes of failed device authentication:
- *"When accessing using a browser in InPrivate or Incognito mode."*
- *"When using unsupported browsers or devices, particularly on mobiles."*
- *"When browser cookies are disabled."*
- *"When a desktop or native application doesn't support device authentication or doesn't use Microsoft Authentication Broker."*

530031.title: AADSTS530031: Access policy does not allow token issuance (fix)
530031.description: AADSTS530031: a tenant policy refused to issue the token. Not in Microsoft's reference; wording from user reports. How it relates to 53003, fix, KQL.
530031.summary: AADSTS530031 means a policy in the tenant refused to issue the token. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it and we found no Microsoft page that does; the wording comes from user reports. Users see it where Conditional Access blocks a sign-in, and the same phrase appears in some 53003 messages. Treat it like 53003: find the policy in the sign-in log.
530031.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS530031 (checked 30 October 2026). We found no other Microsoft page that documents it either. The wording below comes from user reports.

On Microsoft Q&A, a user posted this sign-in log entry:

> Sign-in error code: 530031
> Failure reason: Access policy does not allow token issuance.

The client app was **Browser**. The user said the account was still blocked after being excluded from every Conditional Access policy. The thread's title blames Identity Protection, but nobody in the thread confirmed that. A moderator (not identified as a Microsoft employee) answered that a matching Conditional Access policy was blocking token issuance.

On a Tencent Cloud developer Q&A, a .NET app that requested a SharePoint token with `grant_type=password` got:

> AADSTS530031: Access policy does not allow token issuance.

The same response carried `error: interaction_required` and `suberror: message_only`. The accepted answer there also points at a Conditional Access policy for SharePoint.

The phrase is not unique to 530031. Users quote it as the second sentence of the listed code [53003](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/53003/): *"AADSTS53003: Access has been blocked by Conditional Access policies. The access policy does not allow token issuance."*

Our reading: 530031 is a policy block in the same family as 53003. Microsoft doesn't document which kind of policy produces 530031 instead of 53003, so we can't say whether it is Conditional Access, Identity Protection, or something else. Don't build detections on that distinction until Microsoft documents it.
