700082.name: ExpiredOrRevokedGrantInactiveToken
700082.title: AADSTS700082: The refresh token has expired due to inactivity
700082.description: AADSTS700082: a refresh token expired from inactivity. An expected lifecycle event with low attack value; stolen idle tokens fail here too. KQL.
700082.summary: AADSTS700082 means an app tried to use a refresh token that expired because nobody used it for too long. Microsoft calls it an expected part of the token lifecycle, so it has low attack value. One useful reading: a stolen refresh token that sat unused long enough fails here too. Hunt it in AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs with ResultType == "700082".
700082.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **ExpiredOrRevokedGrantInactiveToken**: The refresh token has expired due to inactivity. The token was issued on {issueDate} and was inactive for {time}. Expected part of the token lifecycle - the user went an extended period of time without using the application, so the token was expired when the app attempted to refresh it.

A sibling in the same table, **70008 ExpiredOrRevokedGrant**, reads *"The refresh token has expired due to inactivity."*

The token wasn't revoked and no policy fired. It sat unused until it expired. The message tells you when it was issued and how long it was inactive.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS700082 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **ExpiredOrRevokedGrantInactiveToken**: The refresh token has expired due to inactivity. The token was issued on {issueDate} and was inactive for {time}. Expected part of the token lifecycle - the user went an extended period of time without using the application, so the token was expired when the app attempted to refresh it.

A sibling in the same table, **70008 ExpiredOrRevokedGrant**, reads *"The refresh token has expired due to inactivity."*

The token wasn't revoked and no policy fired. It sat unused until it expired. The message tells you when it was issued and how long it was inactive.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
See the [comparison of the codes behind "asked to sign in again"](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/why-user-asked-to-sign-in-again-entra-id/) (70043, 700082, 50173, 50133, 50076).

No. Microsoft's own description says it is *"Expected part of the token lifecycle"*. Typical sources are a laptop that was off for weeks, an app the user rarely opens, or a phone that came back from a drawer.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 700082 from a user's known device, then an interactive success | The user came back to an app after a long break. Benign. |
| 700082 from an IP or device the user hasn't used recently | Someone presented an old refresh token from an unfamiliar place. Reasoning, not a documented detection: if that token was stolen, the expiry is what stopped it. Worth a short look. |
| Steady 700082 from a service or shared device | A client that holds tokens but rarely uses them. Configuration, not attack. |

**The useful negative example:** a stolen refresh token is only valuable while it is used. One that the attacker left dormant long enough fails with 700082 rather than giving them access. That is the token lifetime working in your favour, not a detection you can rely on.

**IP caveat for confidential clients.** Microsoft's [non-interactive sign-ins page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/concept-noninteractive-sign-ins) says: *"The IP address of non-interactive sign-ins performed by confidential clients doesn't match the actual source IP of where the refresh token request is coming from. Instead, it shows the original IP used for the original token issuance."* So an unfamiliar IP on a 700082 row is a meaningful signal mainly for public clients (desktop, mobile and browser apps). For confidential clients it may only show where the token was first issued, and the second query below inherits that limit.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Baseline by app:

```kusto
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "700082"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName
| sort by Rows desc
```

700082 from an IP where the same user had no successful sign-in in the previous 30 days:

```kusto
let lookback = 30d;
let knownUserIPs =
    union
        (SigninLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, ResultType)
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "700082"
| join kind=leftanti knownUserIPs on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| extend Device = parse_json(DeviceDetail), Location = parse_json(LocationDetails)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress,
          Country = tostring(Location.countryOrRegion),
          OS = tostring(Device.operatingSystem),
          AppDisplayName, UserAgent, ResultDescription
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

Expect some benign hits here: a user who was away for more than the lookback period has no recent "known" IPs to match. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"700082"`, not `700082`. `DeviceDetail` and `LocationDetails` are strings in this table, hence `parse_json`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- No Conditional Access policy causes 700082. It is token inactivity, not a session control. If a sign-in frequency policy refused the token, you would see [70043](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70043/) instead.
- The interactive sign-in that follows goes through MFA and Conditional Access as normal.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS700082?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign in again.

**For admins:**
1. Nothing to fix. Exclude 700082 from failure-rate dashboards, or it inflates them.
2. If the second query returns an IP you can't explain for a user, check that user's other sign-ins from it. A token that failed here may have a sibling that didn't.

700211.title: AADSTS700211: Federated credential issuer doesn't match (fix)
700211.description: AADSTS700211: the external token's issuer matches no federated identity credential. Wrong issuer URL or no credential for that provider. Fix and KQL.
700211.summary: AADSTS700211 means a workload sent an external token whose issuer matches none of the federated identity credentials on the app or managed identity. Usually the credential has the wrong issuer URL (a typo, a trailing slash, the wrong cluster or Azure DevOps issuer), or no credential exists for that provider. It is a configuration error with low attack value.
700211.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS700211 (checked 30 October 2026). Microsoft's Azure DevOps troubleshooting page does:

> **AADSTS700211: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion issuer**
> No federated credential was created or the issuer URL is not correct.

Users report that the full message names the issuer from the token and adds a hint. From a GitHub issue on the azure-workload-identity project:

> AADSTS700211: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion issuer '`<issuer from the token>`'. Please check your federated identity credential Subject, Audience and Issuer against the presented assertion.

A federated identity credential trusts tokens from one issuer. Microsoft's restrictions page: the issuer *"is the URL of the external identity provider and must match the `issuer` claim of the external token being exchanged"*, and *"If the `issuer` claim has leading or trailing whitespace in the value, the token exchange is blocked."* Microsoft announced case-sensitive matching in August 2024 and rolled it out in stages (see [7002138](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002138/)).

700211 looks like the issuer-specific form of [70021](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70021/); Microsoft doesn't say so. Its siblings are [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/) (audience) and [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) (subject). If the app has no federated credentials at all, you get [70025](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70025/). Microsoft doesn't document the order in which the three values are checked.

Its siblings are [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/) (audience) and [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) (subject). If the app has no federated credentials at all, you get [70025](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70025/). Microsoft doesn't document the order in which the three values are checked.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run set this up in my own tenant: one app registration presents its access token as a client assertion, and a second app carries the federated identity credential that is supposed to accept it. With the credential's **issuer** set to a different URL than the token's, Entra returned `AADSTS700211`:

> AADSTS700211: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion issuer 'https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0'.

The issuer in the message is the one Entra read from the token, not the one on your credential. Compare it character for character with what the credential has.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new federation setup fails on the first run | The issuer on the credential differs from the token's `iss`: a typo, a missing or extra trailing slash, or the wrong URL for the platform. |
| Azure DevOps fails after converting or recreating a service connection | The credential still holds the other Azure DevOps issuer. Microsoft lists two: `https://vstoken.dev.azure.com/<organization id>` and `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0` for new connections. |
| Kubernetes fails after a cluster was rebuilt or the workload moved to another cluster | Each cluster has its own OIDC issuer URL. Likely the credential still points at the old one. |
| Failures for your app from an issuer and IP you don't use | Someone presenting a token from their own provider with your app's client ID. Our reading: it fails because nothing trusts that issuer. Check, but it is not an incident on its own. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 700211 lands in. Our reading: app registration failures land in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`, and a user-assigned managed identity may log in the separate managed identity sign-in log, which Microsoft says holds managed identity sign-ins *"only"*. Check where it lands in your tenant:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "700211" or ResultSignature == "700211"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

Failures per app, with the error text and source IPs. `ResultDescription` is documented as *"the error description for the sign-in operation"*. Whether it carries the issuer the way the returned message does is our assumption; check a row:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "700211" or ResultSignature == "700211"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Failures desc
```

An app that fails from many IPs you don't own, with an issuer you never configured, is the one to look at. That threshold is a judgement call, not a rule.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS700211?
sections.text:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. Get the issuer from the error message, or decode your provider's token and read `iss`.
2. Set the credential's issuer to exactly that string: same case, same trailing slash, no spaces. Microsoft's create-trust page shows the GitHub issuer both as `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` and with a trailing slash, so go by your token.
3. Kubernetes: use the cluster's own OIDC issuer URL. Microsoft's example looks like `https://aksoicwesteurope.blob.core.windows.net/<guid>/`.
4. Azure DevOps: Microsoft says *"You can fix the issuer URL by editing and then saving a service connection. If Azure DevOps didn't create your identity, you must manually update the issuer."* The correct issuer is shown in the service connection's edit dialog.

**For admins:**
1. List the federated credentials on the app or managed identity and compare the issuers with the token. An app can hold at most 20.
2. If the issuer in the failures belongs to a provider you never set up, confirm no credential trusts it and review who can edit the app registration.

700212.description: AADSTS700212: the external token's audience matches no federated identity credential. Usually not api://AzureADTokenExchange. Fix and KQL.
700212.summary: AADSTS700212 means a workload sent an external token whose audience (aud claim) matches none of the federated identity credentials on the app or managed identity. Usually the token was requested for the wrong audience, for example a Kubernetes token not projected for api://AzureADTokenExchange. It is a configuration error with low attack value.
700212.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS700212 (checked 30 October 2026). We found no other Microsoft page that names it either, so the wording below comes from user reports. A user on Microsoft Q&A, running a workload on Azure Kubernetes Service, posted this response (cluster values shortened):

> AADSTS700212: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion audience '`https://uaenorth.oic.prod-aks.azure.com/<tenant>/<guid>/,https://<cluster>.hcp.uaenorth.azmk8s.io,...`'. Please note that the matching is done using a case-sensitive comparison. Please check your federated identity credential Subject, Audience and Issuer against the presented assertion.

The response had `"error":"invalid_client"`. The audience the user's token carried was the cluster's own URLs, not `api://AzureADTokenExchange`.

What Microsoft does document is the audience rule. A federated identity credential lists the audience Entra accepts. Microsoft's Graph overview: it *"says what Microsoft identity platform should accept in the `aud` claim in the incoming token"* and *"should be set to `api://AzureADTokenExchange` for Microsoft Entra ID"*. The restrictions page: *"You must add a single audience value"*. Matching is case-sensitive.

700212 looks like the audience-specific form of [70021](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70021/); Microsoft doesn't say so. Its siblings are [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/) (issuer) and [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) (subject); [70025](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70025/) means the app has no federated credentials at all.

**A lab test on 30 October 2026 returned a different code for this case.** With a federated credential whose audience didn't match the presented token, my lab tenant answered with [`AADSTS7002121`](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002121/), not 700212:

> AADSTS7002121: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion audience '<audience>'. The Audience for the federated identity credential...

In the same run, a wrong issuer gave [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/) and a wrong subject gave [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/), so those two are confirmed. For the audience, 7002121 is what Entra returns today on a current tenant. We can't tell from one tenant whether 700212 is an older code, a different-cloud code, or tied to a particular issuer; the user report above is real and recent, so both appear to exist. If you are writing a detection, match on both. See [7002121](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002121/) for the lab-reproduced page.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It means the workload asked its own provider for a token meant for something else.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Kubernetes pod fails and the audience in the error is the cluster URL | The pod is using its default service account token, not a token projected for `api://AzureADTokenExchange`. Users report this; the Q&A thread above is one case. |
| GitHub Actions fails after changing the `audience` input | The workflow asks GitHub for a token with an audience that the credential doesn't list. The Azure/login README: *"The default `audience` is `api://AzureADTokenExchange`."* |
| A non-public Azure cloud | The Azure/login README notes that for non-public clouds *"the `audience` will also need to be updated."* Presumably the credential and the workflow must agree on the cloud's value. |
| Case differs only (`api://azureadtokenexchange`) | Microsoft has moved to case-sensitive matching in stages since 2024. Fix the case on whichever side is wrong. |

sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 700212 lands in. Our reading: app registration failures land in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`; a user-assigned managed identity may log in the managed identity sign-in log instead. Check:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "700212" or ResultSignature == "700212"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

Failures per app with the error text. Whether `ResultDescription` (documented as *"the error description for the sign-in operation"*) carries the presented audience is our assumption; check a row:

```kusto

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "700212" or ResultSignature == "700212"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Failures desc
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS700212?
sections.text:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. Read the audience from the error message, or decode the token your workload sends and read `aud`.
2. Make the workload request its token for `api://AzureADTokenExchange`, unless you deliberately chose another value. Microsoft: *"For security reasons, you should pick a value that is unique for tokens meant for Microsoft Entra ID."*
3. Kubernetes: the token Entra receives must be a projected service account token with that audience. The answer in the Q&A thread shows a projected volume with `audience: api://AzureADTokenExchange`, mounted at `/var/run/secrets/azure/tokens`. The same answer says the workload identity webhook should inject this when workload identity is enabled. If the mount is missing, check that first.
4. GitHub Actions: leave the `audience` input of `azure/login` at its default unless the credential says otherwise.

**For admins:**
1. Check the credential's audience. It holds exactly one value, and Microsoft recommends `api://AzureADTokenExchange`.
2. If you changed it from the default, make sure every workload that uses the credential requests that same value, in the same case.

700213.description: AADSTS700213: the external token's subject matches no federated identity credential. GitHub environment vs branch, renames, typos. Fix and KQL.
700213.summary: AADSTS700213 means a workload sent an external token whose subject matches none of the federated identity credentials on the app or managed identity. Typical causes: a GitHub job that uses an environment while the credential trusts a branch, a renamed repo or service account, or a typo. Microsoft says the same message is also used for issuer and audience mismatches. Low attack value.
700213.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS700213 (checked 30 October 2026). Microsoft documents it on other pages.

The Azure DevOps troubleshooting page:

> **AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject**
> No federated credential was created or the subject is not correct.

Microsoft's breaking-change notice from August 2024 gives the full message template:

> AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject '{subject}'. Please note that matching is done using a case-sensitive comparison. Check your federated identity credential Subject, Audience, and Issuer against the presented assertion.

It adds two things that matter. First, `'{subject}'` *"provides the value of the subject claim contained in the token being sent from the external IdP"*, so the error tells you what the token said. Second: *"This error template is also used for case-insensitive failures surrounding `issuer` and `audience` validation."* So 700213 doesn't always mean the subject is the problem. Check all three values.

Users see shorter variants too. A Microsoft Q&A post from April 2025 quoted *"…presented assertion subject '103432211958501047059'. Check your federated identity credential Subject, Audience and Issuer against the presented assertion."* without the case-sensitivity sentence.

Background: a federated identity credential trusts one subject from one issuer. The subject identifies the workload: a GitHub repo plus branch, environment or pull request; a Kubernetes service account; an Azure DevOps service connection; a Google service account ID. Microsoft's create-trust page: *"The values must exactly match the configuration"*.

700213 looks like the subject-specific form of [70021](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70021/); Microsoft doesn't say so. Its siblings are [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/) (issuer) and [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/) (audience). When the subject is right apart from letter case, the Azure/login README and user reports show [7002138](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002138/) instead. If the app has no federated credentials at all, you get [70025](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70025/).

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run set this up in my own tenant: one app registration presents its access token as a client assertion, and a second app carries the federated identity credential that is supposed to accept it. With the credential's **subject** set to a value the token doesn't carry, Entra returned `AADSTS700213`:

> AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject '<subject>'.

As with the issuer, the subject printed is the one from the token. Copy it from the message into the credential rather than typing it out.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is almost always a subject that doesn't match.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| GitHub: the subject in the error ends in `:environment:<name>` but the credential trusts a branch | The job declares an `environment`. Microsoft's create-trust page uses `repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:<name>` for jobs tied to an environment, and `:ref:<ref path>` only for jobs that aren't. A Q&A post shows exactly this mismatch (it has no answer). |
| GitHub: the credential was made in the portal and includes `@<number>` after the org or repo | The Azure/login README: portal subjects of the form `repo:<org>@<org-id>/<repo>@<repo-id>:...` never match, because *"The OIDC token GitHub sends does **not** include those numeric IDs"*. |
| GitHub: one credential per branch, and a new branch, tag or pull request fails | Microsoft: *"Pattern matching isn't supported for branches and tags."* Each one needs its own credential, or a flexible credential (preview, below). |
| Azure DevOps: worked before, fails after a rename | Microsoft lists renaming the organization, project or service connection as a cause, for the `sc://` subject. |
| The subject looks identical | Look for an invisible difference. In the April 2025 Q&A case above, a moderator reported that a trailing full stop in the credential's subject was the cause. Letter case gives [7002138](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002138/). |
| Failures for your app with a subject from a repo or account you don't own | Someone presenting their own token with your app's client ID. Our reading: it fails because nothing trusts that subject. Check, but it is not an incident on its own. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 700213 lands in. Our reading: app registration failures land in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`; a user-assigned managed identity may log in the managed identity sign-in log instead. Check:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "700213" or ResultSignature == "700213"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

Failures per app, with the error text. If `ResultDescription` holds the same text as the returned message (our assumption; check a row), it shows the subject the token presented:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "700213" or ResultSignature == "700213"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Failures desc
```

For an app that worked before, check whether its federated credentials were changed. A third-party write-up (trackr.live) reports this logs as `Update application` with a modified property `FederatedIdentityCredentials`; Microsoft doesn't document that name on the pages we checked:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName == "Update application"
| mv-expand Target = TargetResources
| mv-expand Prop = Target.modifiedProperties
| where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "FederatedIdentityCredentials"
| project TimeGenerated,
          App = tostring(Target.displayName),
          Actor = coalesce(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)),
          OldValue = tostring(Prop.oldValue),
          NewValue = tostring(Prop.newValue)
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS700213?
sections.text:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. Copy the subject from the error message. In GitHub Actions, the Azure/login README says the run log shows it under `Federated token details` as `subject claim`.
2. Set the credential's subject to exactly that string. The README: *"set the federated credential Subject to exactly match the `subject claim`"*.
3. Also compare the issuer and audience, because Microsoft uses this message for those failures too.
4. GitHub: pick the entity type that matches the job. A job with `environment:` needs an **Environment** credential. A job without one needs **Branch** or **Tag** with the exact ref. Pull request runs need `repo:<org>/<repo>:pull-request`.
5. Kubernetes: the subject is `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<service account>`. A renamed namespace or service account needs a new credential.

**For admins:**
1. Azure DevOps after a rename: Microsoft names the cause but gives no fix. Update the subject on the identity to the new `sc://` value.
2. Many branches: an app or user-assigned managed identity holds at most 20 federated credentials, and wildcards aren't supported in ordinary credentials. Microsoft's flexible federated identity credential (preview) uses a `claimsMatchingExpression` such as `claims['sub'] matches 'repo:contoso/contoso-repo:ref:refs/heads/*'` and supports issuers *"such as GitHub, GitLab, and Terraform Cloud"*. It is a preview; weigh that before relying on it.
3. Don't widen trust to make an error go away. A subject that matches more branches or environments than needed would let more workflows act as the app.

700226.summary: AADSTS700226 means a federated identity credential whose issuer is a Microsoft Entra tenant was presented with a token that is not a managed identity token. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. The Entra ID issuer exists for the managed identity scenario only, so you can't federate one app registration to another this way. Low attack value.
700226.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS700226 (checked 30 October 2026). The wording below is from a lab run:

> AADSTS700226: Only MSI tokens may be used as Federated Identity Credentials for AAD issuer.

A public repository of federated-credential experiments records the same line, with the trigger: *"AADSTS700226: Only MSI tokens may be used as Federated Identity Credentials for AAD issuer." (when trying to use tokens from app registration to another app registration)*.

"MSI" is managed service identity, the older name for a managed identity. "AAD issuer" means a federated identity credential whose issuer is a Microsoft Entra tenant itself, in the form `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0`, rather than GitHub, Kubernetes or another external provider.

### Why this is worth knowing
Workload identity federation lets an app registration accept a token from somewhere else instead of holding a secret. One of its configurations uses Entra as the issuer. Microsoft documents that configuration for exactly one case: an app registration trusting a **managed identity**. From Microsoft's page on configuring an app to trust a managed identity:

- *"issuer is the URL of the Microsoft Entra tenant's Authority URL in the form `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0`. Both the Microsoft Entra app and managed identity must belong to the same tenant."*
- The issuer field in the portal is described as *"the OAuth 2.0 / OIDC issuer URL of the Microsoft Entra ID authority that issues the managed identity token. This value is automatically populated with the current Entra tenant issuer."*
- *"subject: This is the case-sensitive GUID of the managed identity's Object (Principal) ID assigned to the Azure workload."*
- *"Select managed identity: Click on this link to select the managed identity that will act as the federated identity credential. You can only use User-Assigned Managed Identities as a credential."*

sections.heading: What does AADSTS700226 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS700226 (checked 30 October 2026). The wording below is from a lab run:

> AADSTS700226: Only MSI tokens may be used as Federated Identity Credentials for AAD issuer.

A public repository of federated-credential experiments records the same line, with the trigger: *"AADSTS700226: Only MSI tokens may be used as Federated Identity Credentials for AAD issuer." (when trying to use tokens from app registration to another app registration)*.

"MSI" is managed service identity, the older name for a managed identity. "AAD issuer" means a federated identity credential whose issuer is a Microsoft Entra tenant itself, in the form `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0`, rather than GitHub, Kubernetes or another external provider.

### Why this is worth knowing
Workload identity federation lets an app registration accept a token from somewhere else instead of holding a secret. One of its configurations uses Entra as the issuer. Microsoft documents that configuration for exactly one case: an app registration trusting a **managed identity**. From Microsoft's page on configuring an app to trust a managed identity:

- *"issuer is the URL of the Microsoft Entra tenant's Authority URL in the form `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0`. Both the Microsoft Entra app and managed identity must belong to the same tenant."*
- The issuer field in the portal is described as *"the OAuth 2.0 / OIDC issuer URL of the Microsoft Entra ID authority that issues the managed identity token. This value is automatically populated with the current Entra tenant issuer."*
- *"subject: This is the case-sensitive GUID of the managed identity's Object (Principal) ID assigned to the Azure workload."*
- *"Select managed identity: Click on this link to select the managed identity that will act as the federated identity credential. You can only use User-Assigned Managed Identities as a credential."*

Our reading: 700226 is the runtime half of that restriction. The configuration will accept an Entra issuer and a subject GUID, so nothing stops you entering another app registration's service principal object ID and expecting that app's own token to be exchanged. At token time Entra checks the presented token's type and refuses it. So **app registration to app registration federation through the Entra issuer does not work**, however correct the issuer, subject and audience look. Microsoft's pages describe the managed identity case and do not state the refusal, which is why the error has no documented wording.

This matters if you were planning to give one app registration access to another tenant's or another app's resources without a secret. The supported routes are a client secret, a certificate credential, an external identity provider as the issuer, or on-behalf-of for a user's token.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run configured a federated identity credential on an app registration, using the lab tenant itself as the issuer (`https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0`), and presented a normal app token in a client-credentials request. The run expected a token, because the credential's issuer, subject and audience were the ones the presented token carried. Entra returned:

> AADSTS700226: Only MSI tokens may be used as Federated Identity Credentials for AAD issuer.

The run calls this scenario "Federated credential matches", and that is what makes the code useful: in the same run a mismatch on one of the three values gave [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/), [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) or [7002121](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002121/). 700226 is what Entra returns when those three match and the token is still the wrong kind. The lab did not test the supported arrangement, so it confirms the refusal, not that a managed identity token would have been accepted.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a design limit being hit by a configuration someone built on purpose.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new integration fails on its first run, with issuer, subject and audience all verified correct | Someone federated one app registration to another. That is what 700226 refuses. |
| A workload that used to work starts failing | The workload now presents an app token instead of its managed identity token, for example after moving off an Azure host or switching to a client secret in configuration. |
| The subject in the credential is a service principal object ID rather than a managed identity's Object (Principal) ID | The credential points at the wrong principal. Only a user-assigned managed identity works here. |

Our reading on the security side: 700226 is a refusal, so a row means the exchange did not happen. It is worth noticing if you did not configure an Entra-issuer credential at all, because someone added a federated credential to one of your apps. Credential additions are in the audit log, not the sign-in log.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which table 700226 lands in is undocumented. Our reading: the app registration whose credential was used is the one signing in, so `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` is the likely place. Check with a union first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable
    SigninLogs,
    AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs,
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs,
    AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "700226" or ResultSignature == "700226"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

The filter covers both columns because the tables document them differently: in `SigninLogs`, `ResultType` *"provides the 5-6 digit error code"*, while in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` it is described as *"Success or Failure"* and `ResultSignature` as *"the error code, if any, for the sign-in operation"*.

Which app and which credential:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "700226" or ResultSignature == "700226"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Credentials = make_set(FederatedCredentialId, 5),
            CredentialTypes = make_set(ClientCredentialType, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Failures desc
```

`FederatedCredentialId` is documented as *"Th identifier of an application's federated identity credential if a federated identity credential was used to sign in"* (Microsoft's typo). Whether it is populated on a refusal is not documented, so confirm on a row of your own.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text: Nothing to configure here. The request fails on the token type before any policy decision matters, and a federated credential exchange for an app carries no user and no MFA step.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS700226?
sections.text:
**For developers:**
1. If the workload runs on Azure, give it a **user-assigned managed identity** and present that identity's token. Set the credential's subject to the managed identity's **Object (Principal) ID**, exactly as Microsoft's page requires, and keep both objects in the same tenant.
2. If the caller is an app registration and not a managed identity, stop using the Entra issuer. Use a client secret or a certificate credential on that app, or on-behalf-of when you are acting for a signed-in user.
3. If the caller is outside Azure, use its own provider as the issuer: GitHub, Kubernetes or any OIDC provider that signs with RS256. Microsoft's restrictions page: *"Only issuers that provide tokens signed using the RS256 algorithm are supported for token exchange using workload identity federation."*

**For admins:**
1. Check the federated credential's subject. It must be a user-assigned managed identity's Object (Principal) ID, not an app's service principal object ID.
2. Both objects must be in the same tenant. Microsoft: *"Both the Microsoft Entra app and managed identity must belong to the same tenant."*
3. If you did not expect an Entra-issuer credential on this app, review who added it and why, in the audit log.

750054.title: AADSTS750054 fix: SAML request missing from the sign-in URL
750054.description: AADSTS750054: Entra got a SAML sign-in without a SAMLRequest in the URL. The app must use HTTP Redirect binding and support SP-initiated SSO.
750054.summary: AADSTS750054 means Microsoft Entra ID received a SAML sign-in request without a SAMLRequest or SAMLResponse in the URL query string. The app didn't use the SAML HTTP Redirect binding, or the user landed on Entra's SAML endpoint without a request, for example from a sign-on URL set for an app that only supports IdP-initiated SSO. A configuration error with low attack value.
750054.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> SAMLRequest or SAMLResponse must be present as query string parameters in HTTP request for SAML Redirect binding. To learn more, see the troubleshooting article for error [AADSTS750054](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/azure/active-directory/error-code-aadsts750054-saml-request-not-present).

The reference table gives this code no PascalCase name.

In SAML single sign-on the app (the service provider) sends an authentication request to Entra. Microsoft's SAML protocol page says *"the cloud service (the service provider) uses an HTTP Redirect binding to pass an `AuthnRequest` (authentication request) element to Microsoft Entra ID"*. With that binding the request travels in the URL as a `SAMLRequest` query parameter. If Entra's SAML endpoint is reached and that parameter isn't in the URL, it returns 750054.

Microsoft's troubleshooting article gives the cause: *"Microsoft Entra ID wasn't able to identify the SAML request within the URL parameters in the HTTP request. This can happen if the application is not using HTTP redirect binding when sending the SAML request to Microsoft Entra ID."* It lists three common issues:

1. Single sign-on isn't enabled on the application side.
2. The app only supports IdP-initiated SSO. Microsoft: *"[When] entering a sign-in URL for an application that only supports identity provider-initiated single sign-on can lead to a bounce back from the application without a SAML response."*
3. The sign-on URL is wrong.

What users report: Auth0, set up as the SAML service provider, sends the request with HTTP POST binding when its **Protocol Binding** field is set, and gets 750054 until the field is cleared or set to HTTP-Redirect. A DocuSign SSO setup on Microsoft Q&A hit it during testing.

Related SAML codes with their own page:

- [76021](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/76021/): the request arrived but isn't signed, and the app requires signed requests.
- [75011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/75011/): the request arrived but asks for an authentication method the session doesn't match.

With 750054 the request didn't arrive in the URL at all, so nothing in it was checked yet.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. The request carries no SAML message, so there is nothing to sign anyone in with. It points at a broken SSO setup.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Every user of one SAML app, from the day SSO was set up | Wrong binding in the app (HTTP POST instead of HTTP Redirect), or the wrong sign-on URL. |
| Users who start from the My Apps tile or a bookmark, but not from the app | The **Sign on URL** in Entra points at something that doesn't produce a SAML request, such as an app that only supports IdP-initiated SSO. Our reading of Microsoft's second cause. |
| One user, once | A stale bookmark or a reloaded page on the SAML endpoint. Likely, but unconfirmed. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document whether 750054 is written to the sign-in logs. We assume that without a SAML request Entra may not know which app was meant, so there may be no row, or a row with little app detail. Check first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "750054"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

If rows exist, see which apps and protocols they belong to. Microsoft documents `AuthenticationProtocol` with the possible values *"none, oAuth2, ropc, wsFederation, saml20, deviceCode"*:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "750054"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, AuthenticationProtocol
| sort by Rows desc
```

If nothing comes back, use the correlation ID and timestamp from the user's error page. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"750054"`, not `750054`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS750054?
sections.text:
**For the user:** start the sign-in from the app's own address. If the error comes from a tile in My Apps, tell your IT helpdesk which tile.

**For admins:**
1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open **Enterprise applications**, the app, then **Single sign-on**.
2. Check the **Sign on URL**. It must be a URL in the app that starts SSO and sends a SAML request. If the app only supports IdP-initiated SSO, Microsoft says a sign-on URL can cause the bounce back that ends in 750054.
3. Check with the vendor that SSO is enabled on the app side.
4. Select **Test this application**, paste the error into **Resolving Errors** and choose **Get resolution guidance**, as Microsoft's troubleshooting article describes.

**For developers and app vendors:** send the `AuthnRequest` with HTTP Redirect binding, encoded into the URL as the SAML bindings specification describes, which Microsoft's article links. If your SAML library has a binding setting, set it to HTTP-Redirect. Users report that this is the fix for Auth0.

Microsoft doesn't document whether 750054 is written to the sign-in logs. We assume that without a SAML request Entra may not know which app was meant, so there may be no row, or a row with little app detail. Check first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "750054"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

```kusto

| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "750054"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
```

fix.short: Admin: check that SSO is enabled in the app, that the app supports SP-initiated SSO, and that the Sign on URL in the enterprise app is right. Then run Test this application. Developer: send the AuthnRequest with HTTP Redirect binding, not HTTP POST. User: start sign-in from the app.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** start the sign-in from the app's own address. If the error comes from a tile in My Apps, tell your IT helpdesk which tile.

**For admins:**
1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open **Enterprise applications**, the app, then **Single sign-on**.
2. Check the **Sign on URL**. It must be a URL in the app that starts SSO and sends a SAML request. If the app only supports IdP-initiated SSO, Microsoft says a sign-on URL can cause the bounce back that ends in 750054.
3. Check with the vendor that SSO is enabled on the app side.
4. Select **Test this application**, paste the error into **Resolving Errors** and choose **Get resolution guidance**, as Microsoft's troubleshooting article describes.

**For developers and app vendors:** send the `AuthnRequest` with HTTP Redirect binding, encoded into the URL as the SAML bindings specification describes, which Microsoft's article links. If your SAML library has a binding setting, set it to HTTP-Redirect. Users report that this is the fix for Auth0.

900023.title: AADSTS900023: Tenant identifier is not a valid tenant ID or domain (fix)
900023.description: AADSTS900023: the tenant in the sign-in URL is not a valid tenant ID or domain. Not in Microsoft's error list. Causes and fix.
900023.summary: AADSTS900023 means the tenant part of the sign-in URL isn't a valid tenant ID or domain name at all, for example 'undefined', a stray character or an empty setting. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. It is a configuration error with no attack value. Put the real tenant ID (a GUID) or a verified domain in the app's settings.
900023.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS900023 (checked 30 October 2026).

The lab reproduced it. A token request to the tenant segment `not_a_valid~tenant` returned:

> AADSTS900023: Specified tenant identifier 'not_a_valid~tenant' is neither a valid DNS name, nor a valid external domain.

Every sign-in URL names a tenant: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/...`. Microsoft's MSAL configuration page says that part can be *"A GUID (the ID of your Microsoft Entra instance)"*, *"A domain name associated with your Microsoft Entra instance"*, or one of the placeholders `organizations`, `consumers` or `common`.

900023 means the value matches none of those shapes. Our reading: Entra rejects it on its form, before it looks for a tenant. Compare [AADSTS90002](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90002/): in the same lab run, a well-formed GUID for a tenant that doesn't exist returned 90002 ("Tenant ... not found"), not 900023.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS900023 mean?
sections.text:

> AADSTS900023: Specified tenant identifier 'not_a_valid~tenant' is neither a valid DNS name, nor a valid external domain.

Microsoft's MSAL configuration page says that part can be *"A GUID (the ID of your Microsoft Entra instance)"*, *"A domain name associated with your Microsoft Entra instance"*, or one of the placeholders `organizations`, `consumers` or `common`.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a token request to `https://login.microsoftonline.com/not_a_valid~tenant/...`. Entra returned `AADSTS900023` with the first line quoted above. The message echoes the bad value back, which is the fastest way to see what the app actually sent.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint. No row for it appeared in the lab tenant's exported sign-in logs (interactive, non-interactive and service principal, exported 30 October 2026). Our reading: there is no tenant to write it to, because the request named none; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a broken setting in the app, script or integration that sent the request. Users report these causes:

| Value in the message | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| `'undefined'` | The code built the URL from a variable that was never set. A post on the Auth0 Community forum reports it when the connection has no `domain` and `tenant_domain` set. |
| A value with a stray or wrong character | A typo or copy-paste error. A user on [Microsoft Q&A](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/a/1360543) found *"an incorrect character in the Tenant ID for the integration"*. |
| The tenant field of a third-party integration | A misconfigured tenant value in the product's settings. Okta reports this for its Office 365 integration. |
| Empty, a placeholder, or a whole URL | Probably a config template that was never filled in, or the wrong field pasted (unconfirmed). |

Our reading: an attacker gains nothing from this error. The request never reaches a tenant, so it says nothing about yours.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 900023 is logged in. Likely no row is written in your tenant: the request named no valid tenant, so Entra can't tell whose logs it belongs in. You can check; expect nothing:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "900023"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

Debug from the app side instead: its logs, its config, and the error message, which shows the exact tenant value it sent.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS900023?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report the app name and the full error message to whoever set the app up.

**For developers:**
1. Read the tenant value in the message. That is what your code sent.
2. If it says `undefined` or `null`, find the variable or setting that builds the authority URL and make sure it is set in every environment.
3. Use a tenant GUID, a verified domain such as `contoso.onmicrosoft.com`, or `organizations` / `common` / `consumers`. Those are the values Microsoft documents for the authority.
4. Remove spaces, quotes and other characters that came along in a copy-paste.

**For admins:**
1. Get your tenant ID. Microsoft's page on finding it says to use **Entra ID** > **Overview** > **Properties** in the Entra admin center, or `Get-AzTenant` in Azure PowerShell:

```powershell
Connect-AzAccount
Get-AzTenant
```

2. Paste it into the integration's tenant field again. For Auth0, check the connection's `domain` and `tenant_domain` options; the Auth0 Community post warns that an update to `options` drops values you leave out.
3. If the integration still fails with [AADSTS90002](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/90002/), the value is now well-formed but names the wrong tenant or cloud.

900144.title: AADSTS900144: Request body is missing a required parameter (fix)
900144.description: AADSTS900144: a token or sign-in request is missing a required parameter. A developer error with low attack value; the message names the parameter. KQL.
900144.summary: AADSTS900144 means an app sent a request to Microsoft Entra ID without a parameter the flow requires, such as password, client_id or grant_type. Microsoft calls it a developer error. The error names the missing parameter. It has low attack value; fix the request the app builds. Look for it by app and error text in all three sign-in tables.
900144.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> The request body must contain the following parameter: '{name}'. Developer error - the app is attempting to sign in without the necessary or correct authentication parameters.

The app sent a request to the Microsoft identity platform and left out a parameter that the flow requires. The error replaces `{name}` with the missing parameter, so the message tells you exactly what to add.

Which parameters are required depends on the flow. For the resource owner password credentials (ROPC) flow, for example, Microsoft lists `client_id`, `grant_type` (*"Must be set to `password`"*), `username` and `password` as **Required**. A confidential client must also send `client_secret` or `client_assertion`.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS900144 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> The request body must contain the following parameter: '{name}'. Developer error - the app is attempting to sign in without the necessary or correct authentication parameters.

The app sent a request to the Microsoft identity platform and left out a parameter that the flow requires. The error replaces `{name}` with the missing parameter, so the message tells you exactly what to add.

Which parameters are required depends on the flow. For the resource owner password credentials (ROPC) flow, for example, Microsoft lists `client_id`, `grant_type` (*"Must be set to `password`"*), `username` and `password` as **Required**. A confidential client must also send `client_secret` or `client_assertion`.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 25 October 2026 an automated lab run sent an ROPC token request to my lab tenant without the `password` parameter. Entra returned `AADSTS900144` with this first line:

> AADSTS900144: The request body must contain the following parameter: 'password'.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint, with `{name}` filled in as `password`. The sign-in log row was not captured, and the KQL on this page is not checked against it yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No documented attack pattern exists for 900144. Microsoft calls it a *"Developer error"*. The request is incomplete, so no credential is checked and nothing is issued. Our reading: an attacker learns nothing from it either.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 900144 from one app, starting right after a release | A bug in the new version builds the request without a parameter. Configuration. |
| 900144 naming `client_secret` or `client_assertion` | Our interpretation: a confidential client sent no credential, often an empty secret in the configuration or a missing environment variable. |
| 900144 naming `password` or `username` from a script or tool | A script built an ROPC request with an empty value. Usually a broken automation. |
| 900144 from an unknown IP, for an app ID you don't recognise | Someone is calling the token endpoint with a hand-built request. Not an attack by itself, but worth checking who owns the client. |

Exclude it from failure-based attack detections. A password spray sends a password; it fails with codes such as [50126](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/50126/), not 900144.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document whether or where 900144 is logged, and the lab run above didn't capture a sign-in row, so we can't say yet whether one is written. Check all three sign-in tables:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "900144"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which app is missing which parameter. We assume `ResultDescription` carries the message with the parameter name filled in; we haven't checked that against a logged row:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "900144"
| extend Parameter = extract(@"parameter: '([^']+)'", 1, ResultDescription)
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, Parameter
| sort by Rows desc
```

New sources: apps that produced 900144 today but not in the previous 14 days. A `FirstSeen` right after a deployment points to the release that broke it:

```kusto
let recent =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "900144"
    | summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by AppId, AppDisplayName;
let before =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(15d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ResultType == "900144"
    | distinct AppId;
recent
| join kind=leftanti before on AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

`AppDisplayName` doesn't exist in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`; there, use `ServicePrincipalName`. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"900144"`, not `900144`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS900144?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report the error, with the parameter name from the message, to whoever runs the app.

**For developers:**
1. Read the parameter name in the error and add it to the request.
2. Check the flow's parameter table in Microsoft's documentation. For ROPC, `client_id`, `grant_type`, `username` and `password` are required, and the request is a `POST` with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.
3. Check that the parameter is in the request **body**, not the query string, as the message says. Our reading: a value that is empty or missing in your configuration ends up as no parameter at all.
4. Prefer a Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) over hand-built requests. Microsoft also recommends against ROPC: *"it's incompatible with multifactor authentication (MFA)."*

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and the parameter, and send both to the app's owner.
2. If the app ID is unknown, look it up in Enterprise applications or App registrations. If nobody owns it, treat it like any unknown client calling your tenant.

1. Read the parameter name in the error and add it to the request.
2. Check the flow's parameter table in Microsoft's documentation. For ROPC, `client_id`, `grant_type`, `username` and `password` are required, and the request is a `POST` with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.
3. Check that the parameter is in the request **body**, not the query string, as the message says. Our reading: a value that is empty or missing in your configuration ends up as no parameter at all.
4. Prefer a Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) over hand-built requests. Microsoft also recommends against ROPC: *"it's incompatible with multifactor authentication (MFA)."*

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and the parameter, and send both to the app's owner.
2. If the app ID is unknown, look it up in Enterprise applications or App registrations. If nobody owns it, treat it like any unknown client calling your tenant.

900439.name: USGClientNotSupportedOnPublicEndpoint
900439.title: AADSTS900439: Azure Government app signed in on the public endpoint (fix)
900439.description: AADSTS900439: an Azure Government app used a public-cloud sign-in endpoint. Not in Microsoft's reference. Use login.microsoftonline.us instead.
900439.summary: AADSTS900439 means an app registered in the Azure Government cloud tried to sign in through a public-cloud endpoint. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it; a Microsoft troubleshooting article does. It also covers Microsoft 365 GCC High and DoD. It is a configuration error with no attack value. Point the app at login.microsoftonline.us.
900439.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS900439 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it in a [troubleshooting article](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-aadsts900439-usgclientnotsupportedonpublicendpoint), which names it **USGClientNotSupportedOnPublicEndpoint**:

> When trying to sign in to an application registered in the Azure Government cloud using a public endpoint, the sign-in fails, and you receive the AADSTS900439 (USGClientNotSupportedOnPublicEndpoint) error.

The article gives the code and name but not the full message text, and we found no user report that quotes it in full.

Microsoft's cause:

> Microsoft Entra authority for Azure Government has been updated from `https://login-us.microsoftonline.com` to `https://login.microsoftonline.us`. This change also applies to Microsoft 365 GCC High and Microsoft 365 DoD environments, which Microsoft Entra authority for Azure Government also services. Microsoft Entra ID enforces the correct endpoint for sign-in operations.

The article adds: *"You can no longer sign in to an application registered in the Azure Government cloud using the public endpoint `https://login-us.microsoftonline.com`."* The clouds are separate. Microsoft's national clouds page: *"Each cloud instance is separate from the others and has its own environment and endpoints."* It lists `https://login.microsoftonline.us` for US Government and `https://login.microsoftonline.com` for the global service.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a configuration error in the app or its SDK settings.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| An older app or script for a GCC High, DoD or Azure Government tenant fails | It still uses `login-us.microsoftonline.com`. |
| A tool that works for commercial tenants fails for a government tenant | The tool is hard-coded to a public-cloud endpoint. Our interpretation; the article only names `login-us.microsoftonline.com`. |
| A third-party product fails for your government tenant only | The vendor has no setting for the US Government cloud, or it isn't set. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document where 900439 is logged. Our reading: the request reaches a public-cloud endpoint, not your Azure Government tenant, so a row in your tenant's logs is unlikely. Check anyway; this is expected to return nothing:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "900439"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS900439?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Tell whoever runs the app that it uses the wrong sign-in endpoint for a US Government tenant.

**For developers:** use the Azure Government endpoints. Microsoft's article lists:

| Name | Azure Government endpoint |
|---|---|
| Portal | `https://portal.azure.us` |
| Microsoft Graph API | `https://graph.microsoft.us` |
| Active Directory endpoint and authority | `https://login.microsoftonline.us` |

Change the authority, and the Graph base URL too if the app calls Graph. Microsoft's national clouds page: *"use the endpoints for the cloud instance where you'll deploy the application."*

**For admins:**
1. Search app configs, scripts and connection settings for `login-us.microsoftonline.com` and replace it with `https://login.microsoftonline.us`.
2. For third-party products, tell the vendor your tenant is in the US Government cloud (GCC High, DoD or Azure Government) and ask for their setting for it.

900561.name: BadResourceRequestInvalidRequest
900561.title: AADSTS900561 fix: endpoint only accepts POST, got GET
900561.description: AADSTS900561: an Entra endpoint got a GET where it needs a POST. Usually a replayed URL, the back button or a broken MFA provider hand-off. Low risk.
900561.summary: AADSTS900561 means a Microsoft Entra endpoint that only takes POST requests received a GET. Microsoft says it can come from a developer error or from a user pressing the browser back button, and that it can be ignored. Users also report it with external MFA providers. It has low attack value.
900561.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **BadResourceRequestInvalidRequest**: The endpoint only accepts {valid_verbs} requests. Received a {invalid_verb} request. {valid_verbs} represents a list of HTTP verbs supported by the endpoint (for example, POST), {invalid_verb} is an HTTP verb used in the current request (for example, GET). This can be due to developer error, or due to users pressing the back button in their browser, triggering a bad request. It can be ignored.

Some Entra endpoints only take data in the body of a POST request. A browser that opens such a URL directly, from the address bar, a bookmark or the back button, sends a GET instead. Entra refuses it. The real message fills in the verbs, for example *"The endpoint only accepts POST, OPTIONS requests. Received a GET request."*

Two Microsoft-documented places where a POST is expected:

- **The token endpoint.** Microsoft's authorization code flow reference shows the code redemption as `POST /{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token` with a form-encoded body. Pasting a token request into a browser sends a GET. A user on Microsoft Q&A did exactly that with a device code token request and got 900561; the same request worked from curl.
- **External authentication methods (EAM).** Microsoft's provider reference says the call to the provider *"is made through a `POST` request because a large list of parameters gets passed to the provider"*, and that *"the provider needs to use `POST` to send a response back to the `redirect_uri`"*. Our reading: a provider that returns to `https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/federation/externalauthprovider` with a GET, or a user who reloads that step, gets 900561. SecureAuth's knowledge base describes intermittent 900561 errors with its product set up as an EAM.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Microsoft says it *"can be ignored"*. It is a malformed request, and a malformed request gets nothing back.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A single 900561 for a user, then a normal sign-in | Back button, a reloaded page or an old tab. Benign. |
| Users who open a saved login.microsoftonline.com URL | Our reading: a bookmark of a mid-sign-in URL would send a GET in the same way. Replace it with the app's own start URL. |
| Every user of an external MFA provider, or many of them | The hand-off between Entra and the provider is broken. Users report this with third-party EAM providers. An integration fault, not an attack. |
| One developer or script, repeatedly | A token request sent as GET, or a test pasted into a browser. Fix the client. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document whether 900561 is written to the sign-in logs. We assume the request often fails before Entra knows which user or app it belongs to, so there may be no row at all. SecureAuth's knowledge base says that for its EAM case the error is not recorded in the Entra sign-in or audit logs. Check whether your workspace has any:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "900561"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

If rows exist, see which apps and clients produce them. `UserAgent` shows whether it is a browser or a script:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "900561"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Messages = make_set(ResultDescription, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, UserAgent
| sort by Rows desc
```

If the union returns nothing, rely on what the user sees: the error page shows a correlation ID and a timestamp. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"900561"`, not `900561`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS900561?
sections.text:
**For the user:** close the tab and start again from the app's own address, not from a bookmark, the browser history or the back button. If it happens at the MFA step every time, tell your IT helpdesk.

**For developers:**
1. Send token requests to `/oauth2/v2.0/token` as a POST with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, as in Microsoft's examples. A browser address bar can't do that.
2. If you build an external authentication method provider, return the response to the `redirect_uri` with a POST, as Microsoft's provider reference requires.

**For admins:**
1. A one-off is noise. Microsoft says it can be ignored.
2. Users who keep hitting it from a bookmark: give them the app's start URL instead.
3. Repeated errors at the MFA step with an external authentication method: collect the correlation ID and timestamp from the error page and raise it with the provider. SecureAuth's knowledge base suggests a HAR trace and comparing the `kid` of the `id_token_hint` with your tenant's published keys; if they don't match, it advises a Microsoft support case.

901002.title: AADSTS901002 fix: resource parameter sent to v2.0 endpoint
901002.description: AADSTS901002: an app sent the v1.0 resource parameter to the v2.0 endpoint. Use scope=<API>/.default or the v1.0 URLs. KQL included.
901002.summary: AADSTS901002 means an app sent the v1.0 `resource` parameter to the Microsoft identity platform (v2.0) endpoint, which only takes `scope`. It is a configuration mismatch, often in third-party products set up with v2.0 URLs. Low attack value. Replace `resource=<API>` with `scope=<API>/.default`, or point the app at the v1.0 endpoints it was built for.
901002.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> AADSTS901002: The 'resource' request parameter isn't supported.

The app talks to the Microsoft identity platform endpoint (URLs containing `/oauth2/v2.0/`) but builds its request the v1.0 way, with a `resource` parameter.

The two endpoints name the target API differently. Microsoft's v1.0-to-v2.0 comparison shows a v1.0 request with `&resource=https://graph.microsoft.com/` and the v2.0 equivalent with `&scope=https://graph.microsoft.com/directory.read%20...`. On v2.0, *"the **scope** parameter indicates which resource and permissions the app is requesting authorization. The desired resource is still present in the request - it's encompassed in each of the values of the scope parameter."*

There is a direct translation. Microsoft's scopes reference: *"Using `scope={resource-identifier}/.default` is functionally the same as `resource={resource-identifier}` on the v1.0 endpoint."* Neither the authorization code flow nor the client credentials flow reference lists a `resource` parameter for v2.0.

Not the same as [500011](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/500011/). 500011 means the API you named doesn't exist in the tenant. 901002 means you named it with a parameter the endpoint doesn't accept.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document whether or where 901002 is logged. The request is invalid, so a sign-in row may not exist. Check all three tables:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "901002"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which apps send the v1.0 parameter, and since when:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == "901002"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 5)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Rows desc
```

`AppDisplayName` is empty for rows from `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`, which uses `ServicePrincipalName`. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"901002"`, not `901002`. A `FirstSeen` that matches the day a product was configured confirms the cause.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS901002?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report it to IT, with the name of the app.

**For developers:**
1. Remove `resource` from requests to `/oauth2/v2.0/authorize` and `/oauth2/v2.0/token`.
2. Put the API in `scope` instead. For the same access as `resource=https://graph.microsoft.com`, send `scope=https://graph.microsoft.com/.default`. For specific delegated permissions, append them to the API identifier, as in Microsoft's example `https://graph.microsoft.com/Calendars.Read`.
3. For the client credentials flow, `scope` is required and must be *"the resource identifier (application ID URI) of the resource you want, suffixed with `.default`"*.

**For admins of a third-party product:**
1. Check which endpoint the product expects. If its documentation asks for a "resource" or "resource URI", it is built for v1.0.
2. Then configure the v1.0 URLs, without `v2.0` in the path. Microsoft's comparison page shows the v1.0 authorize request as `https://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/authorize`. It doesn't show the token URL; our reading is that it is `.../oauth2/token` on the same pattern.
3. If the product supports v2.0, switch its setting from resource to scope instead. Follow the vendor's guide; IBM's Cognos article is behind a login, so we couldn't read its exact steps.

1002016.title: AADSTS1002016: Client uses TLS 1.0, 1.1 or 3DES (fix)
1002016.description: AADSTS1002016: the client uses TLS 1.0, 1.1 or 3DES, which Entra retired. Unlisted by Microsoft. Enable TLS 1.2; KQL to find old clients.
1002016.summary: AADSTS1002016 means the client connected to Entra with TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 or the 3DES cipher, which Entra no longer accepts. Microsoft doesn't list the code; a user reports it from an older .NET app. Microsoft retired legacy TLS for public Entra instances on 31 January 2022. It is a client configuration error with low attack value. Enable TLS 1.2.
1002016.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS1002016 (checked 30 October 2026). The wording below comes from user reports.

A user on Microsoft Q&A posted this message from a VB.NET desktop app using MSAL.NET:

> AADSTS1002016: You are using TLS version 1.0, 1.1 and/or 3DES cipher which are deprecated to improve the security posture of Azure AD.

TheWindowsClub quotes the same text.

The message matches Microsoft's documented TLS change. Microsoft's [TLS 1.2 guidance for Entra](https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/azure/active-directory/enable-support-tls-environment) says Entra stops supporting TLS 1.1, TLS 1.0 and the 3DES cipher suite (`TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA`). The dates on that page:

| Instance | Deprecation date | Status |
|---|---|---|
| U.S. government | 31 March 2021 | Completed |
| Public | 31 January 2022 | Completed |
| Operated by 21Vianet in China | 31 January 2025 | Ongoing |

The page we opened doesn't quote AADSTS1002016 itself. Our reading: this is the error Entra returns to a client that still negotiates one of the retired protocols.

**In the lab, you no longer get this far.** On 30 October 2026 a lab run sent a token request to `login.microsoftonline.com` with the client pinned to TLS 1.0. The connection was reset during the TLS handshake (`ECONNRESET`), with no HTTP response and no AADSTS code. So on the public cloud today, a TLS 1.0 client fails before Entra can answer, and the symptom is a connection error in your application, not this error code. Treat AADSTS1002016 as a code from the deprecation window, or from an instance that still accepts the old protocol long enough to reply.
