sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. The client is old or badly configured. Microsoft's page names components that may be affected: Microsoft Entra Connect, Microsoft Graph PowerShell, application proxy connectors, PTA agents, legacy browsers and apps integrated with Entra ID.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A PowerShell script or .NET Framework app fails | Our reading: the .NET Framework runtime isn't using TLS 1.2. The Q&A user fixed it by forcing TLS 1.2 in code. |
| A server older than Windows Server 2012 R2 fails | Microsoft says only Windows 8.1, Windows Server 2012 R2 and later support TLS 1.2 natively over WinHTTP. Earlier versions need an update and registry values. |
| One old browser or device fails | Microsoft lists browsers without TLS 1.2, such as Internet Explorer 8 to 10 on Windows 7. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table AADSTS1002016 is logged in. Check all three:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "1002016"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20) by SourceTable, AppId, UserAgent
```

Microsoft documents a second signal: *"For clients or apps that sign in over legacy TLS, Microsoft Entra ID marks the Legacy TLS field in Additional Details with True."* Its page gives a query per table. This version runs it over all three at once and adds the result code (our adaptation of Microsoft's query):

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Legacy TLS" and AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "True"
| extend JsonAuthProcDetails = parse_json(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| mv-apply JsonAuthProcDetails on (
    where JsonAuthProcDetails.key startswith "Legacy TLS"
    | project HasLegacyTls = JsonAuthProcDetails.value
  )
| where HasLegacyTls == true
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, AppId, AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName, UserAgent, ResultType
| sort by Rows desc
```

`UserAgent` often names the client, for example a PowerShell or .NET version. Our reading: if this returns nothing but the first query does, the failed rows don't carry the Legacy TLS flag.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS1002016?
sections.text:
**For the user:** update the app or browser. If it's a company tool, report the error and the tool name to IT.

**For developers:** make the client use TLS 1.2.
- Microsoft says *".NET Framework 4.6.2 and later versions support TLS 1.2"* once the registry is set, and that 4.6 and earlier need an update.
- The Q&A user fixed a .NET Framework app with one line before calling MSAL: `ServicePointManager.SecurityProtocol = SecurityProtocolType.Tls12`.
- In Windows PowerShell 5.1, the same .NET setting is (our translation of that line):

```powershell
[Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12
```

Setting it in code fixes one process. The registry settings below fix the machine.

**For admins:** on the affected Windows machine, set the values Microsoft lists. These two make .NET Framework use the OS's TLS versions and strong cryptography:

```powershell
$paths = @(
  'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\.NETFramework\v2.0.50727',
  'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\.NETFramework\v4.0.30319',
  'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\.NETFramework\v2.0.50727',
  'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\.NETFramework\v4.0.30319'
)
foreach ($p in $paths) {
  if (-not (Test-Path $p)) { New-Item -Path $p -Force | Out-Null }
  New-ItemProperty -Path $p -Name SystemDefaultTlsVersions -Value 1 -PropertyType DWord -Force | Out-Null
  New-ItemProperty -Path $p -Name SchUseStrongCrypto -Value 1 -PropertyType DWord -Force | Out-Null
}
```

The script is ours; the keys and values are from Microsoft's page. Restart the app or service afterwards. Microsoft also lists the SCHANNEL `TLS 1.2\Client` and `TLS 1.2\Server` keys (`Enabled` = 1, `DisabledByDefault` = 0). Windows 8.1, Windows Server 2012 R2 and later support TLS 1.2 natively over WinHTTP. Earlier versions need update 3140245.

Then run the second query again to find any other clients still on legacy TLS.

1003031.title: AADSTS1003031: Admin consent failed, app lists no API permissions (fix)
1003031.description: AADSTS1003031: admin consent failed because the app registration lists no API permissions. Unlisted by Microsoft. Cause, fix and KQL.
1003031.summary: AADSTS1003031 means admin consent failed because the app registration's required resource access is misconfigured. Microsoft doesn't list the code. Users report it on the tenant-wide /adminconsent URL, and a Microsoft employee says the app registration had no API permissions. It is a configuration error with low attack value. Add at least one API permission to the app.
1003031.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS1003031 (checked 30 October 2026). The wording below comes from user reports.

A user on Microsoft Q&A posted this message after opening the tenant-wide admin consent URL for an external tenant:

> AADSTS1003031: Misconfigured required resource access in client application registration.

A second Q&A user got the same text back on the redirect URI, as `error=access_denied` with `admin_consent=True` in the query string. A third got it when an admin in another organization opened an admin consent link for a multi-tenant Teams bot.

The accepted answer on the first thread comes from a Microsoft employee (Q&A moderator). It says the error occurs *"when the Tenant-Wide Admin Consent URL ... is used to add a multi-tenant application to a tenant, but the application registration in the resource tenant lacks API permissions."* And: *"If no API permissions are defined in the app registration, the consent flow fails with the error AADSTS1003031."* This is a forum answer, not a documentation page.

The URL in question is the one Microsoft documents for tenant-wide admin consent:

```http
https://login.microsoftonline.com/{organization}/adminconsent?client_id={client-id}
```

A volunteer moderator on the same thread points to the `requiredResourceAccess` section of the app manifest, where API permissions are declared. Our reading: the message says that list is empty or unusable for consent, which matches the employee's answer.

On the second thread, an answerer wrote that the code *"doesn't exist in our public docs"* and *"does seem to match the AADSTS650056 error"*. [AADSTS650056](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/650056/) looks like the documented, closest relative. It also covers a client that *"has not listed any permissions"*.

The accepted answer on the first thread comes from a Microsoft employee (Q&A moderator). It says the error occurs *"when the Tenant-Wide Admin Consent URL ... is used to add a multi-tenant application to a tenant, but the application registration in the resource tenant lacks API permissions."* And: *"If no API permissions are defined in the app registration, the consent flow fails with the error AADSTS1003031."* This is a forum answer, not a documentation page.

The URL in question is the one Microsoft documents for tenant-wide admin consent:

```http
https://login.microsoftonline.com/{organization}/adminconsent?client_id={client-id}
```

A volunteer moderator on the same thread points to the `requiredResourceAccess` section of the app manifest, where API permissions are declared. Our reading: the message says that list is empty or unusable for consent, which matches the employee's answer.

On the second thread, an answerer wrote that the code *"doesn't exist in our public docs"* and *"does seem to match the AADSTS650056 error"*. [AADSTS650056](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/650056/) looks like the documented, closest relative. It also covers a client that *"has not listed any permissions"*.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Users report it as a setup error in an app registration. The person who hits it is an admin trying to grant consent, so the attempt is deliberate and visible.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| An admin hits it once while onboarding a new multi-tenant app | The app registration has no API permissions, as the Microsoft employee describes. |
| It happens with the client ID of a backend API | Users report passing the API's client ID instead of the client app's. A Q&A volunteer moderator suggests using the frontend client ID that holds the permissions. Likely because an API registration often lists no permissions of its own (unconfirmed). |
| It keeps happening after permissions were added | Possibly the consent URL still uses another app's client ID. Check the `client_id` value. |

As far as we can tell, the error stops consent from being granted, so nobody gains access through it. Still review any app you didn't expect an admin to consent to.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table AADSTS1003031 is logged in. Our reading: the admin signs in interactively before consent, so the row, if any, is most likely in `SigninLogs` of the tenant where consent was attempted. Check all three tables first:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "1003031"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

Which app and which admin:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "1003031"
| summarize Attempts = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName, HomeTenantId, ResourceTenantId
| sort by LastSeen desc
```

`AppId` is the client ID to check. If `HomeTenantId` differs from your tenant, the admin was a guest. In the external-tenant case the row likely belongs to the tenant the admin consented in (unconfirmed), so the app developer's tenant may see nothing.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS1003031?
sections.text:
**For the user:** if you are an admin granting consent, stop and tell the app's developer or vendor. The fix is in their app registration. If you are not an admin, pass the error and the app name to your IT team.

**For developers:**
1. Open the app registration in the developer's (home) tenant. Go to **API permissions**.
2. Add at least one permission. The Microsoft employee's answer gives Microsoft Graph, delegated `User.Read`, as an example. Add the permissions the app really needs.
3. Check that the admin consent URL uses the client ID of this app. If the app calls your own API, the client app needs a permission on that API in its own registration.
4. If external tenants must use the app, the volunteer moderator's answer says to set **Supported account types** to accounts in any organizational directory, on both the client and the API registration.

**For admins** (in the tenant granting consent):
1. Check the client ID in the consent URL and the permissions the app requests. Microsoft says to *"carefully review the permissions an application requests before granting consent."*
2. Tenant-wide admin consent needs a role such as Cloud Application Administrator, Application Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator. Privileged Role Administrator is needed for Microsoft Graph application permissions.
3. If the developer can't fix the registration quickly, the Microsoft employee's answer gives a workaround: create the service principal yourself.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes Application.ReadWrite.All
New-MgServicePrincipal -BodyParameter @{ AppId = "<client id of the app>" }
```

Our reading: this only adds the app to your tenant. Any permissions still need consent once the developer has added them.

5000211.title: AADSTS5000211: Blocked by a tenant restrictions policy (fix)
5000211.description: AADSTS5000211: a tenant restrictions v2 policy from your proxy or device blocked sign-in to another tenant. Not in Microsoft's reference. Fix and KQL.
5000211.summary: AADSTS5000211 means a tenant restrictions v2 policy, added to the request by a corporate proxy, a managed Windows device or Global Secure Access, doesn't allow sign-in to the tenant the request was for. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it; Microsoft's tenant restrictions v2 page shows it. It is a control doing its job. Use an allowed tenant or change the policy.
5000211.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS5000211 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft shows it on its page [Set up tenant restrictions v2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/external-id/tenant-restrictions-v2), as the result of a blocked service principal sign-in with Microsoft Graph PowerShell:

> Connect-MgGraph : ClientSecretCredential authentication failed: AADSTS5000211: A tenant restrictions policy added to this request by a device or network administrator does not allow access to 'tenant'.

Tenant restrictions v2 (TRv2) is a policy an organization sets on which other tenants may be signed in to from its network and devices. The policy travels with the request. On a corporate proxy, Microsoft says to send this header to the Microsoft sign-in domains (`login.live.com`, `login.microsoft.com`, `login.microsoftonline.com`, `login.windows.net`):

```text
sec-Restrict-Tenant-Access-Policy: <DirectoryID>:<policyGUID>
```

`<DirectoryID>` is the tenant ID of the organization that set the policy and `<policyGUID>` *"the object ID for your cross-tenant access policy"*. So the error doesn't come from the tenant you are signing in to. It comes from the policy of the organization whose network or device you are on.

Microsoft names three ways the policy gets added:

| Where | What Microsoft says |
|---|---|
| Corporate proxy | *"This header enforces your tenant restrictions v2 policy on all sign-ins on your network."* |
| Managed Windows devices | *"Tenant restrictions are enforced upon resource access to provide data path coverage and protection against token infiltration. A corporate proxy isn't required for policy enforcement."* |
| Global Secure Access | Universal tenant restrictions *"tag all traffic no matter the operating system, browser, or device form factor."* |

In Microsoft's Chrome example, the browser shows a page saying internet access is blocked rather than this text. Our reading: the 5000211 string is what you see in scripts, SDKs and command-line tools.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS5000211 mean?
sections.text:

|---|---|

| Global Secure Access | Universal tenant restrictions *"tag all traffic no matter the operating system, browser, or device form factor."* |

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. The policy blocked a sign-in it was set up to block. The question is whether that sign-in was legitimate work.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A script or tool on the corporate network fails to reach a customer's or partner's tenant | That tenant isn't on your TRv2 allow list. The policy needs an exception, or the work happens elsewhere. |
| A user tries to sign in to a personal or unknown tenant from a managed device | The policy did its job. Whether that needs a follow-up depends on what they were trying to do. |
| It starts for many people on the same day | A TRv2 policy was just turned on, or the header was added to the proxy. |
| It happens on the corporate network but not at home | The header is added by the proxy, not the device. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Where the row lands depends on who you are. For service principals Microsoft is explicit: *"If a service principal sign-in is blocked by tenant restrictions v2, the sign-in log will only appear in the tenant that received the sign-in request. No sign-in log will be generated in the tenant where the tenant restrictions v2 policy is configured."* For user sign-ins Microsoft doesn't say. Our reading: the organization that set the policy may see nothing of its own blocks in its own sign-in logs.

Check where 5000211 lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "5000211"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

If you are the tenant receiving the sign-ins, for example a customer tenant that a partner's staff can't reach, see whose policy blocks them. `IsTenantRestricted` is documented as *"Indicates if a signIn is under a tenant restrictions policy or not"*, and `HomeTenantId` as *"the tenant identifier of the user initiating the sign in"*:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "5000211" or IsTenantRestricted == true
| summarize Attempts = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Results = make_set(ResultType, 10),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10)
          by HomeTenantId, IPAddress
| sort by Attempts desc
```

`IsTenantRestricted == true` also catches sign-ins that were under a policy and allowed, which is why `Results` is there. Not checked against real data yet.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS5000211?
sections.text:
**For the user:** your organization's network or device doesn't allow sign-in to that tenant. Use an account in an allowed tenant, or ask your IT team to allow the one you need. Signing in from another network may work if the block comes from the proxy, but check your organization's rules first.

**For developers and script owners:**
1. Check whether the request goes through a proxy or runs on a managed device. The error means the header or device policy was added, not that your app or secret is wrong.
2. Ask the team that owns the TRv2 policy to allow the target tenant for your app, or run the job from an environment the policy doesn't cover, if your organization allows that.

**For admins of the organization that set the policy:**
1. Find where the policy is added: proxy header, Windows device policy, or Global Secure Access. The `<policyGUID>` in the header is the object ID of your cross-tenant access policy.
2. Review the tenant restrictions settings in that cross-tenant access policy. If the access is legitimate, allow the external tenant there. Our reading of the setup page; we have not tested a policy change.
3. If you previously set up tenant restrictions v1 to block consumer sign-ins, Microsoft says *"you need to stop sending `restrict-msa` to login.live.com"* once you move to v2.

**For admins of the tenant being signed in to:** you can't fix it on your side. The block is the other organization's policy. Tell them which tenant ID and app their people need.

5000224.name: NotAllowedTenantBlockedTenantFraud
5000224.title: AADSTS5000224 fix: tenant blocked for suspected fraud
5000224.description: AADSTS5000224: Microsoft blocked the tenant, apparently for fraud. Admins can't undo it; only a Microsoft support case can. What to do and what to check.
5000224.summary: AADSTS5000224 means the Microsoft Entra tenant is blocked, and Microsoft's internal name points to fraud. Nobody can sign in to it. Microsoft documents no setting an admin can change to undo it: the error text says to contact Microsoft support. If you see it for a foreign tenant in your own logs, check which tenant and app your users were reaching.
5000224.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **NotAllowedTenantBlockedTenantFraud**: We are sorry, this resource is not available. If you are seeing this message by mistake, please contact Microsoft support.

The message the user sees says only that the resource isn't available. The internal name says more: the tenant is not allowed because it was blocked, and the block is tagged as fraud. Microsoft doesn't publish the criteria, how the block is decided, or how long it lasts. Its own text gives one remedy: contact Microsoft support.

In the Microsoft Q&A threads about this code, Microsoft moderators describe it as the tenant's authentication being *"temporarily disabled due to a recent security incident"*, and in one thread say it is not caused by a subscription expiring. Those are forum answers, not documentation. In one thread the product group later reported that the tenant the user named was not blocked at all, and the error came from a different tenant.

Don't confuse it with [5000225](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/5000225/), a tenant made inaccessible because it was **inactive**. That one has a documented reactivation process and a 20-day deadline. For 5000224, Microsoft documents neither.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |

| One person, in the Azure portal only, with an old demo or trial tenant | The portal opened a blocked directory. Their own fix, not Microsoft guidance, and a Microsoft moderator in the same thread said expiry was not the cause. |

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

```kusto
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS5000224?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix it. If it is your organization's tenant, tell your IT team. If you see it in the Azure portal and you have more than one directory, one user reports that signing in directly to their own tenant (`https://portal.azure.com/<your-tenant-ID>`) and changing the startup directory got them past it.

**For admins of the blocked tenant:**
1. Microsoft documents no admin setting that lifts this block. The error text sends you to Microsoft support, and that is the only route.
2. The normal route is a support request in the Microsoft Entra admin center, as at least a **Service Support Administrator**. If any admin account can still sign in, use it.
3. Microsoft's support page also lists two other routes: a request through your Azure support plan, or [Microsoft Support for business](https://support.serviceshub.microsoft.com/supportforbusiness) if you are not an Azure customer. Microsoft says support *"is available online and by phone for Microsoft paid and trial subscriptions"*. It doesn't document a route specific to blocked tenants.
4. Have the tenant ID, the full error, the correlation ID and the timestamp from the error page ready. Microsoft moderators on Q&A asked for the tenant's onmicrosoft.com domain and the Global Administrator's UPN, sent privately.
5. Expect it to take time. One user on Q&A reported a case running for about seven weeks without a public resolution.

**For admins who see it for another tenant:** you can't and shouldn't fix it. Run the second query, identify the tenant and app, and decide whether to block that app or domain in your own tenant.

5000225.title: AADSTS5000225: Tenant blocked due to inactivity (fix)
5000225.description: AADSTS5000225: Microsoft blocked the tenant for inactivity. Reactivation is possible for 20 days, then the tenant is deleted. What to do now.
5000225.summary: AADSTS5000225 means Microsoft made the whole Microsoft Entra tenant inaccessible because it was inactive. Nobody can sign in to it, admins included. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it; Microsoft's inactive-tenant page does. An admin can ask Microsoft to reactivate it within 20 days. After that the tenant is deleted and can't be recovered.
5000225.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS5000225 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it on its page [Tenant inaccessible due to inactivity](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/fundamentals/inaccessible-tenant):

> Error message `Error message: AADSTS5000225: This tenant has been blocked due to inactivity. To learn more about ...` is expected for tenants inaccessible due to inactivity.

Users on Microsoft Q&A quote the full text:

> AADSTS5000225: This tenant has been blocked due to inactivity. To learn more about tenant lifecycle policies, see https://aka.ms/TenantLifecycle

The block is on the tenant, not on a user. Microsoft's reason: *"Configured tenants no longer in use might still generate costs for your organization. Making a tenant inaccessible due to inactivity helps reduce unnecessary expenses."*

The deadline is short. Microsoft: *"Administrators can request a tenant to be reactivated within 20 days of the tenant entering an inactive state. Tenants that remain in this state for longer than 20 days are deleted."* And: *"The tenant is deleted after 20 days of being inaccessible due to inactivity and it isn't recoverable."*

Microsoft's page doesn't say what counts as inactive. Moderators on Q&A marked as Microsoft External Staff write that the tenant *"has been inactive for over 200 days past the billing cycle"*. That figure is not on Microsoft's documentation page, so treat it as a support answer, not a documented rule.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Microsoft blocked the tenant. Nobody did it to you.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A test, trial or developer tenant nobody used for months | The normal case. If you still need it, act within 20 days. |
| A personal Microsoft account that still belongs to a former employer's tenant | A user on Q&A reports this when trying to leave the organization so they could delete their account. Their own account isn't blocked; the old tenant is. |
| An app that signs in to a customer's or partner's tenant suddenly gets this | That tenant was blocked. It is their admin's problem, not yours. |
| A production tenant you use every day | Unexpected. Open a case with Microsoft straight away. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document where 5000225 is logged. Our reading: if your own tenant is blocked you can't sign in to read its logs, and a sign-in to someone else's blocked tenant is logged there if anywhere, not in yours. If your workspace still receives data, this check is expected to return nothing:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "5000225"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10) by SourceTable
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS5000225?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix it. If the tenant belongs to your organization, tell an admin now, because of the 20-day limit. If it belongs to a former employer or a test you no longer need, you can ignore it. A user on Q&A who wanted to leave such a tenant was advised by another user, not by Microsoft, to contact Microsoft support.

**For developers and app owners:** Microsoft says to *"minimize the number of authentication requests sent to this deactivated tenant until the tenant is reactivated."* Stop retry loops against it. Don't open more than one support request; Microsoft says it contacts you once a decision is made.

**For admins:**
1. Decide quickly whether you need the tenant. After 20 days it is deleted and can't be recovered.
2. To reactivate, contact Microsoft through the global support phone numbers linked from Microsoft's inactive-tenant page. Microsoft asks you to *"refrain from submitting another assistance request while your existing case is in process and until you receive a response with a decision on this case."*
3. Have the details ready. A Microsoft External Staff moderator on Q&A asked for the tenant ID, the error code, the correlation ID and timestamp of a recent failure, and a business justification.
4. If it was only a test tenant, the same moderator's advice is to create a new one instead.
5. If you don't plan to reactivate it, review Microsoft's data protection policies, which the page links to.

5000611.title: AADSTS5000611: Key Derivation Function version 1 is invalid (fix)
5000611.description: AADSTS5000611: an unpatched Windows device used the retired KDFv1 algorithm. Not in Microsoft's reference. Which devices, the fix, and KQL to find them.
5000611.summary: AADSTS5000611 means a Windows device tried to authenticate with the retired KDFv1 algorithm, which Microsoft Entra ID now blocks because of CVE-2021-33781. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it, but a Microsoft deprecation notice does. It hits joined and hybrid joined devices on Windows builds without the July 2021 fix. Low attack value; update the device.
5000611.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS5000611 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it in a deprecation notice for the Key Derivation Function version 1 (KDFv1) algorithm. The notice gives the sign-in log entry as:

> Sign-in error code: 5000611
> Failure reason: Symmetric Key Derivation Function version '1' is invalid. Update the device with the latest updates.

Microsoft's background, from the same notice:

- KDFv1 was *"used for the authentication of Microsoft Entra joined or Microsoft Entra hybrid joined devices in builds of Windows released before July 2021."*
- A flaw that *"allowed unauthorized authentication"* is tracked as CVE-2021-33781. Microsoft fixed it in a Windows security update in July 2021, and *"all Windows builds released after July 2021 no longer use the KDFv1 algorithm."*
- Microsoft is *"incrementally rolling out a security update that blocks the use of the KDFv1 algorithm."* *"Unpatched Windows devices won't authenticate with Microsoft Entra once the rollout of this change completes."* *"Early in the rollout retrying authentication will likely succeed."*

The notice gives no enforcement dates and no KB numbers.

Users quote the message with slightly different wording. On Microsoft Q&A, a user on Windows 10 who couldn't open Microsoft 365 mail or a company intranet site posted this message:

> AADSTS5000611: Symmetric Key Derivation Function version 'KDFV1' is invalid. Update the device for the latest updates.

The version appears as `'KDFV1'` there and as `'1'` in Microsoft's notice. Match on the code, not on the text.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is an outdated Windows device failing a check that protects against a known vulnerability. The block is the fix working.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 5000611 from a few Windows 10 devices | Devices missing security updates since mid-2021. Update them. |
| 5000611 that sometimes succeeds on retry | Microsoft says retries likely succeed early in the rollout. Expect that to stop. |
| 5000611 that persists after "all updates are installed" | Users report this on Windows 10 builds that couldn't move to a newer feature release. Check the build, not just the update status. |
| 5000611 only in older Office apps | Users report it in Office 2016 and Outlook 2019, and report working around it by moving to Microsoft 365 apps. User reports only; Microsoft doesn't say this. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft says *"this error message is also present in the Microsoft Entra sign-in logs"*, but not in which table. Check where it lands:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "5000611"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

The list of affected devices, which is what Microsoft's notice asks you to build. `DeviceDetail` is dynamic in `SigninLogs` and a string in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, so each leg parses it first. Property names come from the Graph `deviceDetail` resource; `operatingSystem` is documented as *"the OS name and version used in the sign-in"*:

```kusto
let rows =
    union
        (SigninLogs | extend D = parse_json(tostring(DeviceDetail)) | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, D),
        (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | extend D = parse_json(DeviceDetail) | project TimeGenerated, ResultType, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, D);
rows
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "5000611"
| extend DeviceId = tostring(D.deviceId), DeviceName = tostring(D.displayName),
         OS = tostring(D.operatingSystem), TrustType = tostring(D.trustType)
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 10), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by DeviceId, DeviceName, OS, TrustType
| sort by LastSeen desc
```

Hand the `DeviceName` list to whoever runs patching. Our reading is that a device stops appearing here once it is updated; if it keeps appearing, the update didn't take.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS5000611?
sections.text:
**For the user:** install all pending Windows updates, restart, and sign in again. If Windows can't install the updates (for example, not enough disk space), tell IT. Retrying may work for a while, but Microsoft says it will stop working.

**For admins:**
1. Build the device list with the second query.
2. Update those devices. Microsoft: *"All Windows devices that authenticate using Microsoft Entra must have the security patch applied or be running builds of Windows released after July 2021."*
3. If a device stays on the list after updating, check its Windows build. In Q&A 5491800, installing the latest updates for an older Windows 10 build didn't help. A volunteer moderator suggested upgrading to 22H2; the thread doesn't confirm that it worked. Microsoft doesn't name a standalone patch.
4. Microsoft also recommends looking for affected builds proactively, using the guidance in CVE-2021-33781, and setting automated update policies.
5. If only an old Office version fails on an updated device, users report working around it by moving to Microsoft 365 apps. Treat that as a user report, not a documented fix.

fix.short: User: install all pending Windows updates, restart and sign in again; tell IT if updates won't install. Admin: find the affected devices with the second query and update them. If a device stays on the list after updating, check its Windows build; an older Windows 10 build may need a feature upgrade.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** install all pending Windows updates, restart, and sign in again. If Windows can't install the updates (for example, not enough disk space), tell IT. Retrying may work for a while, but Microsoft says it will stop working.

**For admins:**
1. Build the device list with the second query.
2. Update those devices. Microsoft: *"All Windows devices that authenticate using Microsoft Entra must have the security patch applied or be running builds of Windows released after July 2021."*
3. If a device stays on the list after updating, check its Windows build. In Q&A 5491800, installing the latest updates for an older Windows 10 build didn't help. A volunteer moderator suggested upgrading to 22H2; the thread doesn't confirm that it worked. Microsoft doesn't name a standalone patch.
4. Microsoft also recommends looking for affected builds proactively, using the guidance in CVE-2021-33781, and setting automated update policies.

5002730.title: AADSTS5002730: Unsupported key for the JWT signing algorithm (fix)
5002730.description: AADSTS5002730: Entra rejected a JWT whose signing algorithm doesn't fit its key. Unlisted by Microsoft. Seen with MSAL.NET 4.60.0. Fix and KQL.
5002730.summary: AADSTS5002730 means Entra rejected a JWT because its signing algorithm doesn't fit the key. Microsoft doesn't list the code. The MSAL.NET 4.60.1 release notes tie it to certificate sign-in with SHA2 and PSS signing and an Entra bug; the fix was to upgrade MSAL.NET. Users also report it for OBO with an HS256 token. Low attack value.
5002730.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS5002730 (checked 30 October 2026). The closest listed code is AADSTS50027, `InvalidJwtToken`.

Microsoft's MSAL.NET team describes it in the [4.60.1 release notes](https://github.com/AzureAD/microsoft-authentication-library-for-dotnet/releases/tag/4.60.1). The fix addressed:

> an issue where attempts to acquire a token via certificate authentication resulted in a Microsoft.Identity.Client.MsalServiceException (Error code: AADSTS5002730), signaling an "Invalid JWT token. Unsupported key for the signing algorithm." This was due to a known bug in Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) that affects the handling of JWT tokens signed with certain algorithms, specifically SHA2 and PSS.

The bug report behind it, [MSAL.NET issue 4690](https://github.com/AzureAD/microsoft-authentication-library-for-dotnet/issues/4690), shows the full message:

> AADSTS5002730: Invalid JWT token. Unsupported key for the signing algorithm.

That report used a confidential client with a PEM certificate and `AcquireTokenForClient`, on MSAL.NET 4.60.0. A maintainer said a partner team's first look suggested *"an external issue (AAD)"*. The workaround in the thread was to stay on 4.59.0.

So the documented trigger is a client assertion: the signed JWT an app sends instead of a client secret when it signs in with a certificate. Microsoft's certificate credentials page now says the assertion's `alg` *"Should be **PS256**"* and to *"Use PSS padding."* Our reading: the 4.60.0 failure was on the Entra side, and PS256 itself is the recommended algorithm. Microsoft doesn't say whether or when the Entra bug was fixed.

A second trigger comes from a user report. A user on Microsoft Q&A got the same message in an on-behalf-of (OBO) exchange from a Teams tab app. The user believed the token they exchanged was signed with **HS256**. They said the same code got an RS256 token in another tenant. A volunteer moderator, an MVP and not Microsoft staff, answered with "I think": such a token can't be exchanged, and an Entra-issued token is needed. Our reading: here the JWT is the incoming user token, not a client assertion, and HS256 is a shared-secret algorithm that Entra doesn't accept for it.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Not on the evidence available. Both reports are apps with a signing or library problem.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A service or daemon fails right after a library upgrade | The MSAL.NET 4.60.0 case. Upgrade to 4.60.1 or later. |
| One app fails, others with certificates work | Probably the app builds its own client assertion with an `alg` that doesn't match its key (unconfirmed). |
| An OBO call fails in a Teams or custom app | The incoming token isn't an Entra-issued, RS256-signed token. Users report this. |
| Your app IDs, from IPs you don't recognise | We found no report of this. Possibly someone sending hand-built assertions for your app. Check the app's credentials and sign-ins. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table AADSTS5002730 is logged in. Our reading: the certificate case is an app signing in as itself, so `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` is the likely table; the OBO case involves a user, so it may land in a user table. Check all three:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "5002730"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, AppId
```

For apps signing in as themselves, see which credential was used:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "5002730"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20)
    by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, ClientCredentialType, ServicePrincipalCredentialThumbprint
| sort by Rows desc
```

If `FirstSeen` lines up with a deployment, check which MSAL version that deployment shipped.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS5002730?
sections.text:
**For developers:**
1. On MSAL.NET 4.60.0, upgrade to 4.60.1 or later. The release notes say 4.60.1 addressed this error.
2. If you build the client assertion yourself, follow Microsoft's certificate credentials page: `alg` PS256, `typ` JWT, a `x5t#S256` thumbprint header, PSS padding.
3. For OBO, exchange an Entra-issued access token for your API. Don't pass a token signed with a shared secret (HS256). The Q&A answer recommends the Teams SSO flow or MSAL to get it.

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and certificate thumbprint. Give them to the app's owner.
2. Ask the owner which MSAL version and signing settings the app uses. Nothing in Entra needs changing for the MSAL.NET case.

7000014.title: AADSTS7000014: Device code value isn't valid (fix)
7000014.description: AADSTS7000014: the device_code in a device code token request isn't valid. Undocumented by Microsoft; reproduced in the lab. Cause, fix, KQL.
7000014.summary: AADSTS7000014 means a device code token request carried a device_code value that Entra doesn't accept. In the lab it came back for a device_code that was never issued. Microsoft doesn't document the code; most likely the app sent a wrong, cut-off or made-up value, not an expired one (that is 70020, per user reports). It has low attack value. Fix how the app stores and sends the code.
7000014.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS7000014 (checked 30 October 2026). I found no other Microsoft page that documents it either.

My lab tenant returned this message for a device code token request whose `device_code` value had never been issued:

> AADSTS7000014: The provided value for the input parameter 'device_code' is not valid.

How the device code flow works, from Microsoft's device code page: the app first calls `/devicecode` and gets back a `device_code`, *"A long string used to verify the session between the client and the authorization server."* The app then polls `/token` with `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`, the same `client_id` (*"Must match the `client_id` used in the initial request"*) and that `device_code`. 7000014 is a rejection of the `device_code` value in that second step.

Microsoft's page lists the protocol errors an app can get while polling. One of them fits this case:

> `bad_verification_code`: The `device_code` sent to the `/token` endpoint wasn't recognized. Verify that the client is sending the correct `device_code` in the request.

Our reading: 7000014 is the AADSTS code behind an unrecognised `device_code`. The lab run recorded only the message line, not the `error` field, so which protocol error comes with it is not confirmed.

Two sibling codes have nearly the same wording. Neither is in Microsoft's reference either, and the wording below comes from user reports:

| Code | Message as users posted it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 70020 | *"The provided value for the input parameter 'device_code' is not valid. This device code has expired."* ([azure-cli issue 22251](https://github.com/Azure/azure-cli/issues/22251)) | The code was real but its time ran out. |
| 90132 | *"The provided value for the input parameter 'device_code' is not valid. Device codes supporting the personal Microsoft Account sign-in audience can only be used for v2 common or consumers tenants."* ([Microsoft Q&A 929217](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/929217/oauth2-error-aadsts90132-device-code-is-not-valid)) | A personal account was used with a tenant-specific endpoint. |

7000014 carries no such second sentence. It looks like the general "this value isn't one we recognise" case.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a device code token request to my lab tenant with a `device_code` that the tenant had never issued. Entra returned `AADSTS7000014` with this first line:

> AADSTS7000014: The provided value for the input parameter 'device_code' is not valid.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint. Note what the run expected: 70020, 70000 or 9002313. It got none of those. No row for it appeared in the lab tenant's exported sign-in logs (interactive, non-interactive and service principal, exported 30 October 2026). Likely a device code that was never issued is rejected before any sign-in is recorded, but that is unconfirmed. The KQL on this page returns nothing on the lab rows, as expected.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. It points to an app that sends a broken `device_code`.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A CLI, script or tool fails right after it shows the "enter the code" message | The app stores or sends the `device_code` wrongly: cut off, double-encoded, or from a different request. Likely, but unconfirmed. |
| A home-grown device code script that never worked | The script polls with the `user_code` (the short code the user types) instead of the `device_code`. A guess; not tested. |
| Failures after a long wait | Expect 70020 (expired) rather than 7000014, based on user reports of 70020. |
| Polling with a different `client_id` or tenant than the `/devicecode` call | Microsoft requires the same `client_id`. Which code this returns is untested. |

Device code phishing is a real attack: Microsoft's Conditional Access page calls the flow *"a high-risk authentication method that can be part of a phishing attack."* Our reading is that 7000014 is not a sign of it. In that attack the attacker requests a real code and polls with it, so their requests carry a valid `device_code`. A burst of 7000014 from one IP is more likely a broken tool than a phishing kit.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 7000014 is logged in. The request likely names a client and a tenant but no user, because no user ever approved a code that was never issued. A row may not exist at all. Check anyway:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("7000014", "70020", "90132")
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, ResultType, AppId
```

More useful in practice: see which apps use the device code flow in your tenant and how they fare. `AuthenticationProtocol` lists `deviceCode` among its documented values:

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Failures = countif(ResultType != "0") by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

An app that shows up here and that you don't expect is worth a look whatever its error code.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- Microsoft *"recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible"* with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy.
- Our reading: 7000014 is not that block. The value is rejected before any user is known, so there is nothing for a policy to evaluate. A user blocked by such a policy gets a Conditional Access failure on the sign-in, which you investigate on the sign-in's **Conditional Access** tab, as Microsoft's page describes.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7000014?
sections.text:
**For the user:** start the sign-in again so the app gets a fresh code. If it fails again straight away, report the tool and its version to whoever maintains it.

**For developers:**
1. Poll `/token` with the exact `device_code` string from the `/devicecode` response. Don't trim, re-encode or truncate it; it is long.
2. Send the `device_code`, not the `user_code`.
3. Use the same `client_id` and the same tenant endpoint for both calls.
4. Handle the documented polling errors: repeat on `authorization_pending` after `interval` seconds; stop on `authorization_declined`, `bad_verification_code` and `expired_token`.
5. Prefer a library (MSAL) over hand-written polling.

**For admins:**
1. Find the app with the first query, then ask its owner which tool and version it is.
2. If nobody should use device code flow, block it with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy. That stops the flow for real attackers too.

```kusto
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, ResultType, AppId
```

```kusto
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Failures = countif(ResultType != "0") by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

An app that shows up here and that you don't expect is worth a look whatever its error code.

fix.short: User: start the sign-in again so the app gets a fresh code; if it fails again, report the tool and version to its maintainer. Developer: poll `/token` with the exact `device_code` string from `/devicecode` (not the `user_code`), using the same `client_id` and tenant endpoint for both calls.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** start the sign-in again so the app gets a fresh code. If it fails again straight away, report the tool and its version to whoever maintains it.

**For developers:**
1. Poll `/token` with the exact `device_code` string from the `/devicecode` response. Don't trim, re-encode or truncate it; it is long.
2. Send the `device_code`, not the `user_code`.
3. Use the same `client_id` and the same tenant endpoint for both calls.
4. Handle the documented polling errors: repeat on `authorization_pending` after `interval` seconds; stop on `authorization_declined`, `bad_verification_code` and `expired_token`.
5. Prefer a library (MSAL) over hand-written polling.

**For admins:**
1. Find the app with the first query, then ask its owner which tool and version it is.
2. If nobody should use device code flow, block it with a Conditional Access authentication flows policy. That stops the flow for real attackers too.

7000014.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a device code token request to my lab tenant with a `device_code` that the tenant had never issued. Entra returned `AADSTS7000014` with this first line:

Likely a device code that was never issued is rejected before any sign-in is recorded, but that is unconfirmed. The KQL on this page returns nothing on the lab rows, as expected.

7000110.title: AADSTS7000110: Code or refresh token used by a different app (fix)
7000110.description: AADSTS7000110: a code or refresh token was redeemed with the wrong client ID. Not in Microsoft's error list. Cause, fix and KQL.
7000110.summary: AADSTS7000110 means an authorization code or refresh token was redeemed with a client ID other than the one it was issued to. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it, but a Microsoft troubleshooting article does. Usually a config mix-up between two app registrations. Low attack value, but check unfamiliar IPs. Use the same client ID.
7000110.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS7000110 (checked 30 October 2026).

Microsoft documents it in a troubleshooting article. The message:

> Request is ambiguous, multiple application identifiers found. The client ID used to obtain the grant (e.g. refresh token or authorization code) might not match the client ID passed in this request or client credential.

Microsoft's cause: the application tried to

> - Redeem an OAuth2 authorization code to get an access token or a refresh token that has the wrong application ID (`client_id` parameter).
> - Use a refresh token that was initially issued to the application ID of a different caller.

An authorization code or refresh token belongs to the app that requested it. If the token request names another app, Entra sees two app IDs and refuses. The "client credential" part of the message suggests a third variant. Our reading: a confidential client whose secret or certificate belongs to a different app registration than the `client_id`. Microsoft's article doesn't list that case.

sections.text:

> Request is ambiguous, multiple application identifiers found. The client ID used to obtain the grant (e.g. refresh token or authorization code) might not match the client ID passed in this request or client credential.

> - Redeem an OAuth2 authorization code to get an access token or a refresh token that has the wrong application ID (`client_id` parameter).
> - Use a refresh token that was initially issued to the application ID of a different caller.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. It is a config mix-up.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Fails right after a code is returned to the app | The authorize request and the token request use different client IDs. Common when an app has separate dev and prod registrations. |
| A refresh token stored by one app is reused by another | Probably two apps share a token cache or a database table (unconfirmed). |
| Fails after an app registration was replaced | Stored refresh tokens still belong to the old app ID. Users have to sign in again. |
| Refresh tokens for your users presented from IPs and user agents your apps don't use | Our interpretation: someone may be replaying a token captured from one app under another client ID. Check the IPs before dismissing it. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 7000110 is logged in. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "7000110"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

Which apps, and from where. Many users on one app is a config bug. One user from an unfamiliar IP is worth a closer look:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "7000110"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Users asc
```

Our reading: the `AppId` in the row is probably the client ID that was sent in the token request, not the one the token was issued to. That isn't documented. Non-interactive rows are aggregated, so counts are not request counts.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7000110?
sections.text:
**For the user:** sign out of the app and sign in again. If it keeps happening, report it to the app's owner.

**For developers:**
1. Microsoft's fix: *"Use an OAuth2 authorization code or a refresh token that's from the same application ID (`client_id` parameter)."*
2. Check that the authorize request and the token request read the client ID from the same setting. Look for a dev client ID in one place and a prod one in another.
3. Keep refresh tokens per app. Don't share a token cache between two app registrations.
4. For a confidential client, check that the secret or certificate belongs to the same app registration as the `client_id`. This step comes from the message's "client credential" wording, which Microsoft doesn't explain.
5. After replacing an app registration, clear the stored refresh tokens and send users through sign-in. Microsoft's refresh token page says apps should handle revoked tokens *"by redirecting the user to an interactive sign-in prompt"*.

**For admins:**
1. Find the app in the second query and give the developer its `AppId`, plus the app ID they expected.
2. If the rows come from IPs or user agents that none of your apps use, treat it like a suspicious token use. Look at the same user's successful non-interactive sign-ins from those IPs.

7000112.name: UnauthorizedClientApplicationDisabled
7000112.title: AADSTS7000112: The application is disabled (fix)
7000112.description: AADSTS7000112: the app's service principal is disabled, so no tokens are issued. Find who disabled it in the audit log before re-enabling. KQL.
7000112.summary: AADSTS7000112 means the app's service principal is disabled in the tenant, so Microsoft Entra ID won't issue tokens for it. Often an admin did it on purpose, for example to cut off a suspicious app. If it hits a Microsoft app such as Exchange Online, sign-ins break tenant-wide. Find who disabled it in the audit log and re-enable it only if that was a mistake.
7000112.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **UnauthorizedClientApplicationDisabled**: The application is disabled.

The app has a service principal (an enterprise application) in the tenant, and that service principal is switched off. In the Entra admin center this is the **Enabled for users to sign-in?** property. Microsoft describes what **No** does:

> If this option is set to No, then no users are able to sign in to the application, even if they're assigned to it. Tokens aren't issued for the application. This setting not only prevents users from signing in but also restricts service principals from accessing the application using application permissions.

In Microsoft Graph the same switch is the service principal's `accountEnabled` property: *"If set to `false`, then no users are able to sign in to this app, even if they're assigned to it."* Our reading is that 7000112 is what a client sees when it hits that switch. Microsoft's description doesn't say so in those words.

The error message usually names the app. Microsoft's Exchange Online troubleshooting article shows this example: *"AADSTS7000112: Application '00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000'(Office 365 Exchange Online) is disabled."*

### Disabled by Microsoft
An app can also be disabled from Microsoft's side. Graph has a separate property, `disabledByMicrosoftStatus`, which *"Specifies whether Microsoft has disabled the registered application"*, with the value `DisabledDueToViolationOfServicesAgreement` for *"suspicious, abusive, or malicious activity, or a violation of the Microsoft Services Agreement"*. That property sits on the app registration, in the publisher's tenant. Whether a Microsoft-disabled app returns 7000112 or a different code in your tenant isn't documented.

sections.text:

The app has a service principal (an enterprise application) in the tenant, and that service principal is switched off. In the Entra admin center this is the **Enabled for users to sign-in?** property. Microsoft describes what **No** does:

> If this option is set to No, then no users are able to sign in to the application, even if they're assigned to it. Tokens aren't issued for the application. This setting not only prevents users from signing in but also restricts service principals from accessing the application using application permissions.

In Microsoft Graph the same switch is the service principal's `accountEnabled` property: *"If set to `false`, then no users are able to sign in to this app, even if they're assigned to it."* Our reading is that 7000112 is what a client sees when it hits that switch. Microsoft's description doesn't say so in those words.

The error message usually names the app. Microsoft's Exchange Online troubleshooting article shows this example: *"AADSTS7000112: Application '00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000'(Office 365 Exchange Online) is disabled."*

### Disabled by Microsoft
An app can also be disabled from Microsoft's side. Graph has a separate property, `disabledByMicrosoftStatus`, which *"Specifies whether Microsoft has disabled the registered application"*, with the value `DisabledDueToViolationOfServicesAgreement` for *"suspicious, abusive, or malicious activity, or a violation of the Microsoft Services Agreement"*. That property sits on the app registration, in the publisher's tenant. Whether a Microsoft-disabled app returns 7000112 or a different code in your tenant isn't documented.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run registered an app, created its service principal, set `accountEnabled` to `false` on that service principal, and then signed a test user in through it. Entra returned `AADSTS7000112`:

> AADSTS7000112: Application '<app id>'(<app name>) is disabled.

That confirms the cause directly: the **service principal**, the enterprise application object in your tenant, is the thing that is disabled. The app registration itself was untouched and still existed. The message names the application ID and the display name, so you can go straight to Enterprise applications and look at that object's **Enabled for users to sign-in?** setting.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

In the lab tenant's sign-in logs the row appears under **User sign-ins (interactive)**, Status **Failure**, Conditional Access **Not Applied**. The **Application** column shows the disabled app's own display name, not the sign-in client, so the row points straight at the application you need to re-enable.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
The error itself is not. It is a block working. What matters is who disabled the app and why.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 7000112 for an app an admin disabled during an incident | Working as intended. The app is cut off. |
| 7000112 for a suspicious app after you disabled it, from IPs you don't own | Possibly the app's operator, or tooling using its tokens, is still trying (unconfirmed). Each row gives you an IP and a time. Worth recording, not worth re-enabling. |
| 7000112 for a Microsoft first-party app (Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint) | Someone disabled a Microsoft service principal in your tenant. Microsoft's Exchange Online article shows this breaks Microsoft 365 sign-in with *"Sorry, but we're having trouble signing you in."* Check the audit log for who did it. |
| 7000112 for a line-of-business app nobody remembers disabling | A clean-up job, a script, or an admin who thought the app was unused. Check the audit log before re-enabling. |

A disabled Microsoft first-party service principal is worth a second look. Our reading, not a Microsoft statement: disabling Exchange Online or another core service principal is a quick way to cause a tenant-wide outage, so if nobody on your team did it on purpose, treat the account that did as suspect until you know.

If you disabled an app as part of a consent phishing response, see the [consent phishing investigation guide](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/investigate-consent-phishing-entra-id/), which treats 7000112 as one of the codes to watch afterwards.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 7000112 lands in. A disabled app blocks both users and app-only access, so it can appear in all three. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000112"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which disabled apps are still being used, by how many users, and from where:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000112"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            SampleIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName = coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName)
| sort by Users desc
```

Who changed a service principal, and when. Microsoft's audit log reference lists **Update service principal** in the ApplicationManagement category. Disabling an enterprise app is likely logged as that activity; Microsoft doesn't say so:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName == "Update service principal"
| mv-expand Target = TargetResources
| mv-expand Prop = Target.modifiedProperties
| where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "AccountEnabled"
| project TimeGenerated,
          App = tostring(Target.displayName),
          ServicePrincipalId = tostring(Target.id),
          OldValue = tostring(Prop.oldValue),
          NewValue = tostring(Prop.newValue),
          ByUser = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
          ByApp = tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

The audit activity name comes from Microsoft's audit log reference. The modified property name `AccountEnabled` is our assumption based on the Graph property, not checked against Microsoft documentation. If the query returns nothing, drop the `AccountEnabled` line and read the `modifiedProperties` of the rows yourself. Non-interactive and service principal sign-in rows are aggregated, so row counts there are not request counts. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"7000112"`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 7000112 is not a Conditional Access block. A disabled app gets no tokens at all, whatever your policies say.
- Don't confuse it with [53003](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/53003/), which is a Conditional Access block. The fix and the owner are different.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7000112?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. The app is turned off in your organisation. Tell your IT team which app showed the error.

**For developers:** if your app is multi-tenant and a customer gets 7000112, the customer's admin disabled your app's service principal in their tenant. You can't re-enable it from your side. Ask them to.

**For admins:**
1. Find out who disabled it and why with the audit log query, before changing anything. If it was disabled during an incident, leave it disabled.
2. If it was a mistake: in **Enterprise applications** > the app > **Properties**, set **Enabled for users to sign-in?** to **Yes**. In Microsoft Graph, set `accountEnabled` to `true` on the service principal.
3. For Exchange Online, Microsoft's article gives the steps with the old MSOnline module (`Set-MsolServicePrincipal -AccountEnabled $true` on app ID `00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000`). That article notes the MSOnline and Azure AD modules are deprecated and points to Microsoft Graph PowerShell instead.
4. If the account that disabled a Microsoft first-party app can't explain it, investigate that account like any other suspicious admin action.
5. If you want to block an app permanently, disabling is fine. Remove it later once nothing legitimate depends on it. After removal the code a client gets will probably change, to [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/) or 700011; which one isn't documented.

7000112.kqlSectionText:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 7000112 lands in. A disabled app blocks both users and app-only access, so it can appear in all three. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000112"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which disabled apps are still being used, by how many users, and from where:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000112"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            SampleIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName = coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName)
| sort by Users desc
```

Who changed a service principal, and when. Microsoft's audit log reference lists **Update service principal** in the ApplicationManagement category. Disabling an enterprise app is likely logged as that activity; Microsoft doesn't say so:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName == "Update service principal"
| mv-expand Target = TargetResources
| mv-expand Prop = Target.modifiedProperties
| where tostring(Prop.displayName) == "AccountEnabled"
| project TimeGenerated,
          App = tostring(Target.displayName),
          ServicePrincipalId = tostring(Target.id),
          OldValue = tostring(Prop.oldValue),
          NewValue = tostring(Prop.newValue),
          ByUser = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
          ByApp = tostring(InitiatedBy.app.displayName)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

The audit activity name comes from Microsoft's audit log reference. The modified property name `AccountEnabled` is our assumption based on the Graph property, not checked against Microsoft documentation. If the query returns nothing, drop the `AccountEnabled` line and read the `modifiedProperties` of the rows yourself. Non-interactive and service principal sign-in rows are aggregated, so row counts there are not request counts. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"7000112"`.

fix.short: Admin: first find who disabled the app and why in the audit log; leave it disabled if that was during an incident. If it was a mistake, set Enterprise applications > the app > Properties > Enabled for users to sign-in? to Yes. User: tell your IT team which app showed the error.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. The app is turned off in your organisation. Tell your IT team which app showed the error.

**For developers:** if your app is multi-tenant and a customer gets 7000112, the customer's admin disabled your app's service principal in their tenant. You can't re-enable it from your side. Ask them to.

**For admins:**
1. Find out who disabled it and why with the audit log query, before changing anything. If it was disabled during an incident, leave it disabled.
2. If it was a mistake: in **Enterprise applications** > the app > **Properties**, set **Enabled for users to sign-in?** to **Yes**. In Microsoft Graph, set `accountEnabled` to `true` on the service principal.
3. For Exchange Online, Microsoft's article gives the steps with the old MSOnline module (`Set-MsolServicePrincipal -AccountEnabled $true` on app ID `00000002-0000-0ff1-ce00-000000000000`). That article notes the MSOnline and Azure AD modules are deprecated and points to Microsoft Graph PowerShell instead.
4. If the account that disabled a Microsoft first-party app can't explain it, investigate that account like any other suspicious admin action.
5. If you want to block an app permanently, disabling is fine. Remove it later once nothing legitimate depends on it. After removal the code a client gets will probably change, to [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/) or 700011; which one isn't documented.

7000112.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run registered an app, created its service principal, set `accountEnabled` to `false` on that service principal, and then signed a test user in through it. Entra returned `AADSTS7000112`:

> AADSTS7000112: Application '<app id>'(<app name>) is disabled.

That confirms the cause directly: the **service principal**, the enterprise application object in your tenant, is the thing that is disabled. The app registration itself was untouched and still existed. The message names the application ID and the display name, so you can go straight to Enterprise applications and look at that object's **Enabled for users to sign-in?** setting.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

In the lab tenant's sign-in logs the row appears under **User sign-ins (interactive)**, Status **Failure**, Conditional Access **Not Applied**. The **Application** column shows the disabled app's own display name, not the sign-in client, so the row points straight at the application you need to re-enable.
