7000215.name: Invalid client secret
7000215.title: AADSTS7000215: Invalid client secret is provided
7000215.description: AADSTS7000215: an app sent an invalid client secret. Usually a rotation mistake; repeated failures from foreign IPs suggest a leaked secret. KQL.
7000215.summary: AADSTS7000215 means an app or service principal sent a client secret that Microsoft Entra ID didn't accept. Usually it is a developer or rotation mistake. The security signal is repeated failures for one app ID from an IP you don't own, which suggests someone trying a leaked or old secret. Hunt it in AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs.
7000215.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> Invalid client secret is provided. Developer error - the app is attempting to sign in without the necessary or correct authentication parameters.

The reference table gives this code no PascalCase name. Two siblings help you tell the cases apart:

- **[7000222](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000222/) InvalidClientSecretExpiredKeysProvided**: *"The provided client secret keys are expired. Create new keys for your app, or consider using certificate credentials for added security"*
- **7000218**: *"The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'."*

So 7000222 means the secret was right but expired, 7000218 means no secret or assertion was sent at all, and 7000215 means a secret was sent and it was wrong.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS7000215 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> Invalid client secret is provided. Developer error - the app is attempting to sign in without the necessary or correct authentication parameters.

The reference table gives this code no PascalCase name. Two siblings help you tell the cases apart:

- **[7000222](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000222/) InvalidClientSecretExpiredKeysProvided**: *"The provided client secret keys are expired. Create new keys for your app, or consider using certificate credentials for added security"*
- **7000218**: *"The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'."*

So 7000222 means the secret was right but expired, 7000218 means no secret or assertion was sent at all, and 7000215 means a secret was sent and it was wrong.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run created an app registration with a client secret, then sent a client-credentials request with a made-up secret. Entra returned `AADSTS7000215`:

> AADSTS7000215: Invalid client secret provided. Ensure the secret being sent in the request is the client secret value, not the client secret ID, for a secret added to app '<app id>'.

A control request in the same run, with the real secret, returned a token. So this code means the secret itself is wrong, not that the app or the tenant is misconfigured.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. Microsoft labels it a developer error, and most 7000215 comes from a typo in configuration or a system that still holds a secret you rotated. The security reading depends on where the requests come from.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 7000215 for one app from your own servers or build agents, starting right after a secret rotation | A system still holding the old secret. Benign, but it tells you exactly which systems to update. |
| 7000215 for one app from an IP you don't own and have never seen succeed for that app | Someone trying a secret for your app from outside. A leaked or old secret is the likely source. Investigate. |
| 7000215 followed by a success (`ResultType` `"0"`) for the same app from the same unknown IP | The attacker found a working secret. Treat the app as compromised. |
| 7000215 spread across many app IDs from one IP | Someone testing a set of credentials against your tenant. Investigate the source. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Failures by app and source IP:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000215"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            KeyIds = make_set(ServicePrincipalCredentialKeyId, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Failures from IPs that never had a success for the same app in the last 30 days:

```kusto
let knownAppIPs =
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct AppId, IPAddress;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "7000215"
| join kind=leftanti knownAppIPs on AppId, IPAddress
| summarize Attempts = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Any IP from that list that later succeeds for the same app:

```kusto
let failedFrom =
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == "7000215"
    | summarize FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated) by AppId, IPAddress;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=inner failedFrom on AppId, IPAddress
| where TimeGenerated > FirstFail
| project TimeGenerated, AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress, ServicePrincipalCredentialKeyId, FirstFail
| sort by TimeGenerated asc
```

Check two things in your own workspace before relying on these queries:

- The Azure Monitor reference for `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` describes `ResultType` as *"Success or Failure"*, while the user sign-in tables document it as the numeric error code as a string. Look at a few failed rows and confirm they carry `"7000215"` and that successes carry `"0"`. If they don't, filter on `ResultSignature` (*"Contains the error code, if any, for the sign-in operation"*) instead.
- Whether `ServicePrincipalCredentialKeyId` is filled in on a **failed** secret isn't documented. A wrong secret may not match any key, so the column may be empty. On successes it tells you which credential was used.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- A service principal using a client secret has no MFA step.
- 7000215 is a failed credential check. For user sign-ins, Conditional Access only evaluates after the first factor succeeds; the same logic suggests no policy was evaluated here. That is reasoning from the user case, not a documented statement for service principals.
- So the controls that matter are on the credential itself: who can read it, where it is stored, and whether it is a secret at all.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7000215?
sections.text:
**For developers:** check that the app sends the current secret for the right app registration and tenant. If the secret expired, you get [7000222](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000222/), not 7000215.

**For admins:**
1. After a rotation, use the first query to list every IP still failing for that app, and update those systems.
2. If failures come from an IP you don't own, treat the app's existing secrets as exposed: create a new credential, remove the old ones from the app registration, and update your own systems.
3. If the third query returns a row, the app was used by someone else. Review what the app's permissions allow and what it accessed after that time.
4. Follow Microsoft's own hint in the 7000222 message and *"consider using certificate credentials for added security"*.

7000216.title: AADSTS7000216: No client credential in a client_credentials request (fix)
7000216.description: AADSTS7000216: a client_credentials token request carried no secret or assertion. Not in Microsoft's error list. How to fix it, with KQL.
7000216.summary: AADSTS7000216 means a token request used grant_type=client_credentials but carried no client_secret, no client_assertion and no request parameter, so Entra had nothing to authenticate the app with. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. It is a developer error with low attack value. Send the app's secret or a signed client assertion.
7000216.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS7000216 (checked 30 October 2026). We found no other Microsoft page that names it. The wording below is from a lab run:

> AADSTS7000216: 'client_assertion', 'client_secret' or 'request' is required for the 'client_credentials' grant type.

A client-credentials request is an app signing in as itself, so the only thing proving who it is, is the credential in the POST body. 7000216 means there wasn't one.

Microsoft's client credentials flow page gives three shapes of that request, and each needs a credential:

| Credential | Parameters Microsoft lists |
|---|---|
| Shared secret | `client_id`, `scope`, `client_secret`, `grant_type=client_credentials` |
| Certificate | `client_id`, `scope`, `client_assertion_type`, `client_assertion`, `grant_type=client_credentials` |
| Federated credential | `client_assertion` from an external identity provider |

Microsoft's own note on the certificate form: *"The parameters for the certificate-based request differ in only one way from the shared secret-based request: the `client_secret` parameter is replaced by the `client_assertion_type` and `client_assertion` parameters."* `client_assertion_type` has one accepted value, `urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`.

The error message also names a third option, `request`. That parameter is not in any of the three tables on Microsoft's client credentials page, so we can't tell you from Microsoft's documentation what Entra accepts in it. Our reading, from the name and the company it keeps in the message, is that it is a signed request object carrying the parameters as a JWT. Unverified, and not something you need in order to fix this error.

### 7000216 against 7000218
[7000218](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000218/) is the same mistake on a different grant. Microsoft lists it as *"The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'."* In our lab the two separated cleanly:

| Request | Code |
|---|---|
| `grant_type=client_credentials`, no credential | **7000216** |
| Password grant (ROPC) by a confidential client, no credential | [7000218](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000218/) |

So if you are reading a log and want to know which flow failed, 7000216 says the caller was doing client credentials. The rest of the family tells you what happened once a secret *was* sent: [7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/) means the secret was wrong, [7000222](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000222/) means it had expired, and [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/) means the app ID isn't in that tenant at all.

Whether Entra treats the caller as a confidential client matters for 7000218 and is explained in Microsoft's troubleshooting article for that code: a **Web** redirect URI makes the app confidential, a **Mobile and desktop applications** redirect URI makes it public, and with no redirect URI in the request the **Allow public client flows** setting decides. sections.heading: What does AADSTS7000216 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS7000216 (checked 30 October 2026). We found no other Microsoft page that names it. The wording below is from a lab run:

> AADSTS7000216: 'client_assertion', 'client_secret' or 'request' is required for the 'client_credentials' grant type.

A client-credentials request is an app signing in as itself, so the only thing proving who it is, is the credential in the POST body. 7000216 means there wasn't one.

Microsoft's client credentials flow page gives three shapes of that request, and each needs a credential:

| Credential | Parameters Microsoft lists |
|---|---|
| Shared secret | `client_id`, `scope`, `client_secret`, `grant_type=client_credentials` |
| Certificate | `client_id`, `scope`, `client_assertion_type`, `client_assertion`, `grant_type=client_credentials` |
| Federated credential | `client_assertion` from an external identity provider |

Microsoft's own note on the certificate form: *"The parameters for the certificate-based request differ in only one way from the shared secret-based request: the `client_secret` parameter is replaced by the `client_assertion_type` and `client_assertion` parameters."* `client_assertion_type` has one accepted value, `urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`.

The error message also names a third option, `request`. That parameter is not in any of the three tables on Microsoft's client credentials page, so we can't tell you from Microsoft's documentation what Entra accepts in it. Our reading, from the name and the company it keeps in the message, is that it is a signed request object carrying the parameters as a JWT. Unverified, and not something you need in order to fix this error.

### 7000216 against 7000218
[7000218](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000218/) is the same mistake on a different grant. Microsoft lists it as *"The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'."* In our lab the two separated cleanly:

| Request | Code |
|---|---|
| `grant_type=client_credentials`, no credential | **7000216** |
| Password grant (ROPC) by a confidential client, no credential | [7000218](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000218/) |

So if you are reading a log and want to know which flow failed, 7000216 says the caller was doing client credentials. The rest of the family tells you what happened once a secret *was* sent: [7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/) means the secret was wrong, [7000222](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000222/) means it had expired, and [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/) means the app ID isn't in that tenant at all.

Whether Entra treats the caller as a confidential client matters for 7000218 and is explained in Microsoft's troubleshooting article for that code: a **Web** redirect URI makes the app confidential, a **Mobile and desktop applications** redirect URI makes it public, and with no redirect URI in the request the **Allow public client flows** setting decides. The client-credentials grant has no public-client variant, so 7000216 doesn't depend on that setting.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a client-credentials token request with `client_id`, `scope` and `grant_type=client_credentials`, and no credential of any kind. Entra returned:

> AADSTS7000216: 'client_assertion', 'client_secret' or 'request' is required for the 'client_credentials' grant type.

Two rounds of the run produced the same code and the same text, and the run had expected [7000218](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000218/). In the same run a correct secret on the same app returned a token, a wrong secret returned [7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/), and a password grant with no secret returned [7000218](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000218/). The message is also complete rather than truncated, which is worth noting because the lab records only the first 160 characters of a message.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Usually not. It is a request that was never going to work, so it is most often a developer or deployment mistake: an empty secret variable, a configuration file that didn't load, or a secret read from a store the process can't reach.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new job or container fails every run, for one app | The secret is missing from the environment or the config file. Nothing was ever sent. |
| Started right after a deployment, for an app that worked before | The secret variable lost its value, or the key vault reference is unresolved. |
| For one app ID, from an IP you don't own | Someone is probing with your app ID. On its own this reveals nothing to them, but check whether that IP also produced [7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/) or a success. |
| Across many app IDs from one IP | Someone enumerating app IDs. Our reading: 7000216 tells the caller nothing about whether an app exists, since the credential check never runs. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which sign-in table 7000216 lands in is undocumented. Our reading: an app signing in as itself belongs in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`, but since the request has no credential the service principal may not be resolved at all and nothing may be written. Check both possibilities:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("7000216", "7000218") or ResultSignature in ("7000216", "7000218")
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, ResultType
```

The filter covers `ResultSignature` as well, because the two tables document the columns differently: for `SigninLogs`, `ResultType` *"provides the 5-6 digit error code that's generated during a sign-in event"*, while `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` describes `ResultType` as *"Success or Failure"* and `ResultSignature` as *"the error code, if any, for the sign-in operation"*.

Which app and which source, so you know what to repair:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000216" or ResultSignature == "7000216"
| summarize Failures = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            CredentialTypes = make_set(ClientCredentialType, 5),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 3)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Failures desc
```

`ClientCredentialType` is documented as *"the type of client credential used. Examples include client assertion, client secret, etc."* On a request with no credential it is likely empty or absent; that is not documented, so check a row.

Pair it with successes to tell a broken deployment from an unknown caller. An IP that never succeeds for the app is the one to look at:

```kusto
let knownAppIPs =
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ResultType == "0" or ResultType =~ "Success"
    | distinct AppId, IPAddress;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000216" or ResultSignature == "7000216"
| join kind=leftanti knownAppIPs on AppId, IPAddress
| summarize Attempts = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Attempts desc
```

A starting threshold: a handful an hour from your own build agents is a configuration bug; a steady stream from an address you don't recognise is worth an investigation.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7000216?
sections.text:
**For developers:**
1. Put the credential in the POST body. With a secret: `client_secret=<the secret value>`, URL-encoded. Microsoft: *"The client secret must be URL-encoded before being sent."* Basic authentication in the `Authorization` header is also supported.
2. With a certificate or a federated credential: send `client_assertion=<the JWT>` and `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`.
3. Check the request really carries what you think. An empty environment variable produces an empty `client_secret`, which Entra reads as absent. Log the parameter names you send, never the values.
4. Keep `grant_type=client_credentials` and a `scope` that is one resource ending in `/.default`.
5. If the next error is [7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/), the credential is now arriving and is wrong, which is progress.

**For admins:**
1. Identify the app from the query above and tell its owner which credential is missing.
2. If the app has no usable credential at all, add one: a certificate is preferable to a secret.
3. If the failures come from an address you don't own, nothing leaked here, but treat it as probing of that app ID and check for [7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/) or successes from the same address.

7000218.title: AADSTS7000218: Client secret or assertion missing from the request (fix)
7000218.description: AADSTS7000218: a confidential client sent no client secret or assertion. Usually a missing credential or a public-client flow setting. KQL.
7000218.summary: AADSTS7000218 means a token request reached Microsoft Entra ID as a confidential client but carried no client secret and no client assertion. Usually the app forgot the credential, or it uses ROPC, device code or IWA while the app registration is still set to confidential. Low attack value. The fix is to send the credential or, only when it fits, allow public client flows.
7000218.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'.

The reference table gives this code no PascalCase name.

A token request arrived for an app that Microsoft Entra ID treats as a **confidential client**, and it carried no proof of the app's identity. Microsoft's troubleshooting article says the request fails with `invalid_client` and that confidential clients must supply a client secret or a client assertion.

Two siblings help you tell the cases apart:

- **[7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/)**: *"Invalid client secret is provided."* A secret was sent and it was wrong.
- **[7000222](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000222/)**: *"The provided client secret keys are expired."* The secret was right but expired.

So 7000218 means nothing was sent at all.

### How Entra decides the client is confidential
This is the part that catches most people. According to Microsoft's troubleshooting article:

1. If the request has a redirect URI, the **platform type** of that redirect URI decides. A **Web** redirect URI makes the app a confidential client. A **Mobile and desktop applications** redirect URI makes it a public client.
2. If the request has no redirect URI (ROPC, device code, Integrated Windows Authentication), Entra uses the **Allow public client flows** setting on the app registration. Yes means public, No means confidential.

So a desktop tool that uses device code flow, registered with the default setting, gets 7000218 even though it was never meant to have a secret.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run created an app registration **without** public client flows enabled, then sent a password-grant (ROPC) request with no credential. Entra returned `AADSTS7000218`:

> AADSTS7000218: The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'.

The same run also sent a client-credentials request with no credential, and that returned a different code, `AADSTS7000216` ("'client_assertion', 'client_secret' or 'request' is required for the 'client_credentials' grant type"). So the code depends on the grant type: 7000218 comes from a user-credential flow, 7000216 from client credentials.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

In the lab tenant's sign-in logs the row appears under **User sign-ins (interactive)**, Status **Failure**, Conditional Access **Not Applied**, with the Application column naming the confidential app that sent the request without a credential.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Almost never. 7000218 is a configuration mismatch between the app and its registration. The request carried no credential, so it can't have succeeded.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 7000218 for a new app during testing | The developer hasn't added the secret or certificate yet, or registered the wrong platform type. |
| 7000218 for a desktop script or CLI tool using device code or ROPC | The registration is confidential (public client flows set to No). Fix the registration or the flow. |
| 7000218 for an app that worked yesterday | Someone changed the redirect URI platform or the public client setting, or a deployment dropped the secret from its configuration. Check the audit log for **Update application**. |
| 7000218 from an IP you don't own, for your app ID | Someone outside is trying your app ID without a credential. Our interpretation: they have the client ID, which is public by design, but not the secret. Low risk on its own. |

Microsoft notes that *"The client ID is a public value that identifies the application, while the client secret is a confidential value."* Knowing a client ID is not a compromise.

The real security question is the fix, not the error. See the admin steps below before switching an app to a public client.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 7000218 lands in. Our reading: an app-only request (client credentials) would be a service principal sign-in, and a delegated request (device code, ROPC, authorization code) would be a user sign-in. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000218"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which apps hit it, from where, and since when:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "7000218"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName = coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName)
| sort by Rows desc
```

If an app moved from 7000218 to success, check whether it got there by adding a secret or by being switched to a public client. The audit log shows the change to the app registration:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName startswith "Update application"
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, InitiatedBy, TargetResources
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

Microsoft's audit activity reference lists both **Update application** and **Update application - Certificates and secrets management** in the ApplicationManagement category. The query uses `startswith` so it catches both; the exact punctuation in the stored `OperationName` may differ from the reference. `TargetResources` holds the changed properties, but which property names a public client switch writes isn't documented, so read the rows rather than filter on them. Service principal rows are aggregated when the service principal, status, IP address and resource match, so row counts there are not request counts. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"7000218"`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7000218?
sections.text:
**For developers:**
1. If your app is a confidential client (web app, web API, daemon), send the credential. Add `client_secret`, or a `client_assertion` signed with a certificate, to the token request. Microsoft's authorization code reference says the client secret *"is required for web apps and web APIs, which can store the `client_secret` securely on the server side."*
2. If your app runs on a user's device (desktop, mobile, CLI, script), it is a public client and must not carry a secret. Microsoft: public clients *"can't be trusted to safely keep application secrets"*. Register a **Mobile and desktop applications** redirect URI, or for flows without a redirect URI, ask an admin to turn on public client flows.
3. To find out which flow your code uses, look at `grant_type` in the token request (in code or a Fiddler trace). Microsoft's article lists `password` for ROPC, `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code` for device code, `authorization_code`, `client_credentials`, and `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer` for on-behalf-of.

**For admins:**
1. For a confidential app, the fix is a credential, not a setting. Prefer a certificate or managed identity over a secret.
2. Only for a real public client flow: in **App registrations** > the app > **Authentication** > **Advanced settings**, set **Allow public client flows** to **Yes**. Microsoft warns that this changes the client type from confidential to public, with security implications.
3. Our reading of those implications, not Microsoft's wording: once public client flows are on, anyone who knows the client ID can start ROPC or device code flows for that app without a secret. The client ID is public, so the secret no longer stands between an attacker and those flows. Don't flip the setting just to make the error go away, and don't flip it on an app that also uses a secret for server-side work.
4. If you do allow public client flows, make sure MFA and Conditional Access cover the users who sign in through that app.

attackSignal.label: Low: usually configuration or user error

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
Almost never. 7000218 is a configuration mismatch between the app and its registration. The request carried no credential, so it can't have succeeded.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 7000218 for a new app during testing | The developer hasn't added the secret or certificate yet, or registered the wrong platform type. |
| 7000218 for a desktop script or CLI tool using device code or ROPC | The registration is confidential (public client flows set to No). Fix the registration or the flow. |
| 7000218 for an app that worked yesterday | Someone changed the redirect URI platform or the public client setting, or a deployment dropped the secret from its configuration. Check the audit log for **Update application**. |
| 7000218 from an IP you don't own, for your app ID | Someone outside is trying your app ID without a credential. Our interpretation: they have the client ID, which is public by design, but not the secret. Low risk on its own. |

Microsoft notes that *"The client ID is a public value that identifies the application, while the client secret is a confidential value."* Knowing a client ID is not a compromise.

The real security question is the fix, not the error. See the admin steps below before switching an app to a public client.

kql.leadIn: Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 7000218 lands in. Our reading: an app-only request (client credentials) would be a service principal sign-in, and a delegated request (device code, ROPC, authorization code) would be a user sign-in. Check where it lands in your workspace:
kql.query:
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000218"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable

kql.leadIn: Which apps hit it, from where, and since when:
kql.query:
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "7000218"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName = coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName)
| sort by Rows desc

kql.leadIn: If an app moved from 7000218 to success, check whether it got there by adding a secret or by being switched to a public client. The audit log shows the change to the app registration:
kql.query:
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName startswith "Update application"
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, InitiatedBy, TargetResources
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000218"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which apps hit it, from where, and since when:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "7000218"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName = coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName)
| sort by Rows desc
```

If an app moved from 7000218 to success, check whether it got there by adding a secret or by being switched to a public client. The audit log shows the change to the app registration:

```kusto
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Category == "ApplicationManagement"
| where OperationName startswith "Update application"
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, InitiatedBy, TargetResources
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
```

Microsoft's audit activity reference lists both **Update application** and **Update application - Certificates and secrets management** in the ApplicationManagement category. The query uses `startswith` so it catches both; the exact punctuation in the stored `OperationName` may differ from the reference. `TargetResources` holds the changed properties, but which property names a public client switch writes isn't documented, so read the rows rather than filter on them. Service principal rows are aggregated when the service principal, status, IP address and resource match, so row counts there are not request counts. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"7000218"`.

labReproduced.method: Password-grant (ROPC) token request against a lab tenant
labReproduced.scenario: Confidential client does ROPC without a secret
labReproduced.message: AADSTS7000218: The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'.

7000218.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run created an app registration **without** public client flows enabled, then sent a password-grant (ROPC) request with no credential. Entra returned `AADSTS7000218`:

> AADSTS7000218: The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'.

The same run also sent a client-credentials request with no credential, and that returned a different code, `AADSTS7000216` ("'client_assertion', 'client_secret' or 'request' is required for the 'client_credentials' grant type"). So the code depends on the grant type: 7000218 comes from a user-credential flow, 7000216 from client credentials.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

In the lab tenant's sign-in logs the row appears under **User sign-ins (interactive)**, Status **Failure**, Conditional Access **Not Applied**, with the Application column naming the confidential app that sent the request without a credential.

7000222.name: InvalidClientSecretExpiredKeysProvided
7000222.title: AADSTS7000222: The provided client secret keys are expired
7000222.description: AADSTS7000222: an app sent an expired client secret. A missed rotation, low attack value; a cue to move to certificates or managed identity. KQL.
7000222.summary: AADSTS7000222 means an app or service principal sent a client secret that has passed its expiry date. It is almost always a missed rotation, not an attack. The security angle is secret hygiene: an expired secret still sitting in config files shows where secrets live. Microsoft recommends managed identities or certificates instead. Hunt it in AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs.
7000222.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidClientSecretExpiredKeysProvided**: The provided client secret keys are expired. Create new keys for your app, or consider using certificate credentials for added security

An app tried to get a token with a client secret that was valid once but has passed its end date. The secret itself was right. Nobody replaced it in time.

Two siblings help you tell the cases apart:

- **[7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/)**: *"Invalid client secret is provided."* A secret was sent and it was wrong.
- **7000218**: *"The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'."* No secret or assertion was sent at all.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS7000222 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidClientSecretExpiredKeysProvided**: The provided client secret keys are expired. Create new keys for your app, or consider using certificate credentials for added security

An app tried to get a token with a client secret that was valid once but has passed its end date. The secret itself was right. Nobody replaced it in time.

Two siblings help you tell the cases apart:

- **[7000215](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7000215/)**: *"Invalid client secret is provided."* A secret was sent and it was wrong.
- **7000218**: *"The request body must contain the following parameter: 'client_assertion' or 'client_secret'."* No secret or assertion was sent at all.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Almost never. 7000222 is what a missed rotation looks like: a script, scheduled job or integration still holds a secret that expired. It usually shows up as a sudden outage of that integration.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 7000222 for one app from your own servers, starting on a specific day | The secret expired that day and nobody rotated it. Benign, but the integration is broken. |
| 7000222 from your own servers after you created a new secret | You added a new secret but missed one system that still holds the old one. |
| 7000222 for an app from an IP you don't own | Someone outside holds a copy of an old secret for your app. Our interpretation, not a Microsoft statement: the expiry stopped them, but the secret leaked at some point. Find out where it was stored. |

The useful security reading is the third row and the inventory it gives you. Every IP that sends an expired secret is a place where that secret was stored. If one of those systems was compromised, read [hunting credential reuse after a web-server breach](https://brambrinkmeier.com/guides/hunt-credential-reuse-after-web-server-breach/) for which other secrets to rotate.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which apps are failing, and from where:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000222"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            KeyIds = make_set(ServicePrincipalCredentialKeyId, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Expired-secret attempts from IPs that never had a success for the same app in the last 30 days:

```kusto
let knownAppIPs =
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | distinct AppId, IPAddress;
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "7000222"
| join kind=leftanti knownAppIPs on AppId, IPAddress
| summarize Attempts = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AppId, ServicePrincipalName, IPAddress
| sort by Attempts desc
```

Check two things in your own workspace before relying on these queries:

- The Azure Monitor reference for `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` describes `ResultType` as *"Success or Failure"*, while the user sign-in tables document it as the numeric error code as a string. Look at a few failed rows and confirm they carry `"7000222"` and that successes carry `"0"`. If they don't, filter on `ResultSignature` instead.
- Whether `ServicePrincipalCredentialKeyId` is filled in on an expired-secret failure isn't documented. If it is, it tells you exactly which secret is still in use, which makes cleanup easy.

A secret used by a confidential client in a delegated (user) flow may surface in the user sign-in tables instead. That is our reading of how the flows work, not a documented statement. If the first query returns nothing but users report the error, search `SigninLogs` for the same `ResultType`.

sections.heading: How does Conditional Access affect it?
sections.text:
- 7000222 is a failed credential check, so no policy grants or blocks it. Conditional Access for workload identities can't fix an expired secret.
- Microsoft notes that workload identities *"Can't perform multifactor authentication"* and *"Need to store their credentials or secrets somewhere."* The control that matters is the credential type.
- Conditional Access for workload identities can add location and risk conditions to single-tenant service principals, which limits where a leaked secret works. It needs Workload Identities Premium licenses.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7000222?
sections.text:
**For developers:** create a new credential on the app registration's **Certificates and secrets** page and update every system that uses it. Don't stop at the first system that works again.

**For admins:**
1. Use the first query to list every IP still sending the expired secret, and update or retire each of those systems.
2. Remove the expired secret from the app registration once nothing uses it. Microsoft: *"An unused credential on an application can result in a security breach."*
3. Move away from secrets. Microsoft's order of preference is a managed identity first, then certificate credentials: *"Don't use password credentials, also known as secrets."* Certificate credentials work *"anywhere a client secret could be used"*, including the client credentials flow.
4. Use application management policies to limit secret lifetimes or block new secrets, so the next rotation is planned rather than an outage.
5. If the second query returns an IP you don't own, treat every credential that was stored alongside that secret as exposed.

7002121.title: AADSTS7002121: Federated credential audience doesn't match the assertion (fix)
7002121.description: AADSTS7002121: the external token's audience matches no federated identity credential. Not in Microsoft's error list. Fix and KQL.
7002121.summary: AADSTS7002121 means a workload presented an external token whose aud claim matches no federated identity credential on the app or managed identity. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. Usually the token was requested for the wrong audience instead of api://AzureADTokenExchange, or the case differs. It is a configuration error with low attack value.
7002121.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS7002121 (checked 30 October 2026). We found no other Microsoft page that names it either. The wording below is from a lab run, not from a Microsoft page.

A federated identity credential on an app registration or a user-assigned managed identity says which external token Entra will exchange for an access token. It pins three values: issuer, subject and audience. 7002121 is the audience failing to match.

Microsoft's Graph overview describes the property: **audiences** is *"the audience that can appear in the external token"*, it *"says what Microsoft identity platform should accept in the `aud` claim in the incoming token"*, and it *"should be set to `api://AzureADTokenExchange` for Microsoft Entra ID"*. The restrictions page adds *"You must add a single audience value, which has a limit of 600 characters"*, and lists the error a wrong count gives at configuration time: *"Federated identity credentials must have exactly one audience."*

The accepted value depends on the cloud. For a managed identity acting as the credential, Microsoft lists:

| Cloud | Audience value |
|---|---|
| Microsoft Entra ID global service | `api://AzureADTokenExchange` |
| Microsoft Entra ID for US Government | `api://AzureADTokenExchangeUSGov` |
| Microsoft Entra China operated by 21Vianet | `api://AzureADTokenExchangeChina` |

Matching is case-sensitive. - [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) subject doesn't match
- [7002138](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002138/) subject matches except for case

sections.heading: What does AADSTS7002121 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS7002121 (checked 30 October 2026). We found no other Microsoft page that names it either. The wording below is from a lab run, not from a Microsoft page.

A federated identity credential on an app registration or a user-assigned managed identity says which external token Entra will exchange for an access token. It pins three values: issuer, subject and audience. 7002121 is the audience failing to match.

Microsoft's Graph overview describes the property: **audiences** is *"the audience that can appear in the external token"*, it *"says what Microsoft identity platform should accept in the `aud` claim in the incoming token"*, and it *"should be set to `api://AzureADTokenExchange` for Microsoft Entra ID"*. The restrictions page adds *"You must add a single audience value, which has a limit of 600 characters"*, and lists the error a wrong count gives at configuration time: *"Federated identity credentials must have exactly one audience."*

The accepted value depends on the cloud. For a managed identity acting as the credential, Microsoft lists:

| Cloud | Audience value |
|---|---|
| Microsoft Entra ID global service | `api://AzureADTokenExchange` |
| Microsoft Entra ID for US Government | `api://AzureADTokenExchangeUSGov` |
| Microsoft Entra China operated by 21Vianet | `api://AzureADTokenExchangeChina` |

Matching is case-sensitive. Microsoft's breaking-changes page, under *"Federated Identity Credentials now use case-sensitive matching"* with an effective date of September 2024: *"Previously, when matching the Federated Identity Credential (FIC) `issuer`, `subject`, and `audience` values against the corresponding `issuer`, `subject`, and `audience` values contained in the token sent to Microsoft Entra ID by an external IdP, case-insensitive matching was used. To provide more fine-grained control to customers, we're switching to enforcing case-sensitive matching."*

The siblings tell you which of the three values failed:

- [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/) issuer doesn't match
- [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) subject doesn't match
- [7002138](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002138/) subject matches except for case
- [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/) audience doesn't match, in user reports
- [70025](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70025/) the app has no federated credentials at all

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run created an app registration with a federated identity credential, then presented a token whose `aud` claim was a GUID rather than the credential's configured audience. Entra returned `AADSTS7002121`:

> AADSTS7002121: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion audience '\<audience>'. The Audience for the federat...

The lab records only the first line of `error_description`, cut at about 160 characters, so the sentence about the configured audience is truncated. The same run confirmed the siblings on the same app: a wrong issuer gave [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/), a wrong subject gave [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/), a subject differing only in case gave [7002138](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/7002138/), and an app with no credential at all gave [70025](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70025/). So Entra does distinguish the three fields, and 7002121 is specifically the audience.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. The workload asked its own identity provider for a token meant for something else, or the credential and the workload disagree about the audience string.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A new pipeline or workload fails on its first federated run | The token is requested for the provider's default audience rather than `api://AzureADTokenExchange`. |
| Kubernetes pod fails and the audience in the error is a cluster URL | The pod is using its default service account token, not one projected for the credential's audience. |
| Works in the commercial cloud, fails in US Government or China | The audience must be that cloud's value from the table above. |
| Only the case differs | Matching has been case-sensitive since the September 2024 change. Fix the case on whichever side is wrong. |
| The error appears right after someone edited the credential | The audience was changed on one side only. A credential holds exactly one audience value. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which sign-in table 7002121 lands in is undocumented. Our reading: an app registration's token request lands in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`, and a user-assigned managed identity presenting the token may land in the managed identity sign-in log instead. Start with a union so you don't miss it:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable
    SigninLogs,
    AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs,
    AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs,
    AADManagedIdentitySignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("7002121", "700212") or ResultSignature in ("7002121", "700212")
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, ResultType
```

The query filters `ResultSignature` as well as `ResultType` because the two tables document the column differently. For `SigninLogs`, `ResultType` *"provides the 5-6 digit error code that's generated during a sign-in event"*; for `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs` it is described only as *"Success or Failure"*, with `ResultSignature` holding *"the error code, if any, for the sign-in operation"*. Look at one failed row in your own workspace and keep the filter that matches.

Which app and which credential, with the error text:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType in ("7002121", "700212") or ResultSignature in ("7002121", "700212")
| summarize Failures = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            Credentials = make_set(FederatedCredentialId, 5),
            CredentialTypes = make_set(ClientCredentialType, 5),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 5),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppId, ServicePrincipalName
| sort by Failures desc
```

`FederatedCredentialId` is documented as *"Th identifier of an application's federated identity credential if a federated identity credential was used to sign in"* (the typo is Microsoft's), and `ClientCredentialType` as *"the type of client credential used"*. Whether either column is filled in when the match fails is not documented; check a row before building a rule on it. The same goes for whether `ResultDescription` carries the presented audience.

A failing workload that also succeeds tells you the audience it should be sending. Compare the two:

```kusto
AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AppId == "<app id of the failing app>"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by ResultType, ResultSignature, FederatedCredentialId, ClientCredentialType
| sort by LastSeen desc
```

A starting point for alerting: more than about 20 of these in an hour for one app usually means a deployment went out with the wrong audience, not an attack.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7002121?
sections.text:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. Read the audience out of the error message, or decode the token your workload presents and read its `aud` claim.
2. Request the token for `api://AzureADTokenExchange`, in that exact case, unless your credential deliberately uses another value. Use the cloud-specific value from the table above outside the commercial cloud.
3. Kubernetes: mount a projected service account token with that audience instead of the pod's default token.
4. GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps: leave the audience input of the login step at its default unless the credential says otherwise.
5. If the issuer or the subject is also wrong, you will see [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/) or [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/) next. Fix all three against the values in the error messages.

**For admins:**
1. Open the app registration or managed identity, **Certificates & secrets** > **Federated credentials**, and read the audience. It holds exactly one value.
2. If you changed it from `api://AzureADTokenExchange`, every workload using that credential must request the same string, in the same case.
3. Don't fix a case mismatch by recreating the credential with a different case. Fix whichever side is wrong and leave the other alone, so the other workloads using it keep working.

7002138.summary: AADSTS7002138 means the subject in a workload's external token matches a federated identity credential only when letter case is ignored. Since Microsoft's 2024 change, matching is case-sensitive, so the exchange fails. Typical case: a GitHub environment named Production while the credential says production. 7002138.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS7002138 (checked 30 October 2026). The README of Microsoft's `Azure/login` GitHub Action documents it in its troubleshooting section:

> Error: AADSTS7002138: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject 'repo:<org>/<repo>:ref:refs/heads/main'. The subject matches with case-insensitive comparison, but not with case-sensitive comparison.

A user on Microsoft Q&A posted the full response, which goes on:

> …Check your federated identity credential Subject, Audience and Issuer against the presented assertion. See documentation at: https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/workload-id/workload-identity-federation. See breaking change notification and remediation at: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/reference-breaking-changes#august-2024.

The breaking change it points to: in August 2024 Microsoft announced that federated identity credential `issuer`, `subject` and `audience` values are matched case-sensitively, where they used to be matched case-insensitively. Microsoft's invalid example:

- Token subject: `repo:contoso/contoso-org:ref:refs/heads/main`
- FIC subject: `repo:Contoso/Contoso-Org:ref:refs/heads/main`

The notice rolled the change out in stages: first to apps and managed identities created after 14 August 2024, then to inactive ones from 27 September 2024, and *"For active applications, case-sensitive matching comes at a later date to be communicated."* That explains setups that ran for years and then broke with no change on your side.

Our reading: 7002138 is a more specific form of [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/). The notice itself said the 700213 message would be revamped to mention case. 7002138 goes further and tells you case is the *only* difference. Microsoft doesn't document whether there are matching codes for issuer or audience that differ only in case; the case-only codes we found all concern the subject. See [70021](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/70021/) for the general no-match code and [700211](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700211/) and [700212](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700212/) for issuer and audience.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run set this up in my own tenant: one app registration presents its access token as a client assertion, and a second app carries the federated identity credential that is supposed to accept it. With the credential's subject set to the **same value in different capitals**, Entra returned `AADSTS7002138` rather than 700213:

> AADSTS7002138: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject '<subject>'. The subject matches with case-insensitive comparison, but not with case-sensitive comparison.

That confirms the split in practice: a subject that is wrong gives [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/), and a subject that is right apart from capitals gives this code. If you see 7002138, the value is correct and only the case is off, which is usually an environment name such as `Production` against `production`.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. Entra found a credential that would have matched before the 2024 change. The fix is the casing.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A GitHub workflow uses `environment: Production` and the error shows `:environment:Production` | The credential says `production`, or the other way round. On the Q&A thread, the top answer fixed it by renaming the environment to lowercase. Microsoft's notice gives the same advice for Azure App Service users. |
| The org or repo name has capitals | GitHub sends the casing it holds. The README: uppercase characters in the org, repo, branch or environment name must match the `subject claim` in the run log. |
| Deployments broke without anyone changing the workflow | The staged rollout above reached your app. |
| It still fails after "fixing" the case | Users report puzzling cases where the subject looks identical (Azure/login issue 573). Copy the subject from the log rather than retyping it. |

sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 7002138 lands in. Our reading: app registration failures land in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`; a user-assigned managed identity may log in the managed identity sign-in log instead. Check:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "7002138" or ResultSignature == "7002138"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable
```

To catch every app hit by the case change, list both codes together. If `ResultDescription` holds the returned message (our assumption; check a row), it shows the subject with the casing the token used:


sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS7002138?
sections.text:
**For developers and pipeline owners:**
1. Copy the subject from the error or from the run log (`Federated token details`, `subject claim`).
2. Either update the credential's subject to that exact string, or change the workflow so the token carries the credential's casing. Microsoft's notice: *"replace the current `issuer`, `subject`, or `audience` value in the FIC with the `issuer`, `subject`, or `audience` value that was contained in the error message."*
3. For a GitHub environment, renaming it in the workflow (for example `Production` to `production`) is the fix users report and Microsoft suggests for App Service.

**For admins:**
1. Use the query above to find every app still failing, and fix the credentials in one go.
2. Microsoft's overview now states the rule plainly: the values *"must case-sensitively match"*. Copy values from tokens or logs, never type them by hand.

attackSignal.label: Low: usually configuration or user error

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
No. Entra found a credential that would have matched before the 2024 change. The fix is the casing.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A GitHub workflow uses `environment: Production` and the error shows `:environment:Production` | The credential says `production`, or the other way round. On the Q&A thread, the top answer fixed it by renaming the environment to lowercase. Microsoft's notice gives the same advice for Azure App Service users. |
| The org or repo name has capitals | GitHub sends the casing it holds. The README: uppercase characters in the org, repo, branch or environment name must match the `subject claim` in the run log. |
| Deployments broke without anyone changing the workflow | The staged rollout above reached your app. |
| It still fails after "fixing" the case | Users report puzzling cases where the subject looks identical (Azure/login issue 573). Copy the subject from the log rather than retyping it. |

7002138.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run set this up in my own tenant: one app registration presents its access token as a client assertion, and a second app carries the federated identity credential that is supposed to accept it. With the credential's subject set to the **same value in different capitals**, Entra returned `AADSTS7002138` rather than 700213:

> AADSTS7002138: No matching federated identity record found for presented assertion subject '<subject>'. The subject matches with case-insensitive comparison, but not with case-sensitive comparison.

That confirms the split in practice: a subject that is wrong gives [700213](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700213/), and a subject that is right apart from capitals gives this code. If you see 7002138, the value is correct and only the case is off, which is usually an environment name such as `Production` against `production`.

The sign-in log row isn't captured yet; see [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

9002313.name: InvalidRequest
9002313.title: AADSTS9002313: Request is malformed or invalid (fix)
9002313.description: AADSTS9002313: the sign-in or token request was malformed. A developer error with low attack value; capture a trace and fix the request. KQL.
9002313.summary: AADSTS9002313 means Microsoft Entra ID couldn't process a sign-in or token request because the request itself was malformed. It is a developer or integration error, not a credential failure. Microsoft's own advice is to capture a Fiddler trace and check how the request is built. It has low attack value. Find which app sends the bad requests and fix the request.
9002313.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> **InvalidRequest**: Request is malformed or invalid. - The issue arises because there was something wrong with the request to a certain endpoint. The suggestion to this issue is to get a fiddler trace of the error occurring and looking to see if the request is properly formatted or not.

The request never got as far as checking a password or a secret. Something in how it was built was wrong, so Microsoft Entra ID rejected it as a request.

Microsoft's description doesn't say which part of the request is wrong. That is the hard part of this code: it is generic. The OAuth 2.0 protocol error that goes with this kind of problem is `invalid_request`, which the authorization code flow reference describes as a *"Protocol error, such as a missing required parameter."* Its advice for the client: *"Fix and resubmit the request. This error is a development error typically caught during initial testing."* Our reading is that 9002313 is the AADSTS code behind many of those `invalid_request` responses, but Microsoft doesn't publish that mapping.

The OAuth 2.0 protocol error that goes with this kind of problem is `invalid_request`, which the authorization code flow reference describes as a *"Protocol error, such as a missing required parameter."* Its advice for the client: *"Fix and resubmit the request. This error is a development error typically caught during initial testing."* Our reading is that 9002313 is the AADSTS code behind many of those `invalid_request` responses, but Microsoft doesn't publish that mapping.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Almost never. A malformed request gets the sender nothing, and Microsoft treats the code as a request-formatting problem.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 9002313 for one app, starting right after a deployment or library update | The new version builds its requests differently. A regression in the app. |
| 9002313 for every user of one app, from the start | The integration was never built correctly. Common with hand-written OAuth code. |
| 9002313 for one user only | Something specific to that user's request, such as a stale bookmark to a sign-in URL or a broken browser extension. Likely, but unconfirmed. |
| 9002313 from an IP you don't know, for an app ID you don't recognise | Someone's tooling is building bad requests against your tenant. Our interpretation: it is worth a look at what else that IP did, but the 9002313 itself is not harmful. |

There is no documented attack pattern for 9002313. Keep it out of password spray detections, because it says nothing about credentials.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 9002313 is logged in, or whether every malformed request produces a sign-in log row at all. Start by checking where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "9002313"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = dcount(AppId) by SourceTable
```

Which apps send the malformed requests, and since when. A sudden start date usually points at a release:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "9002313"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 5)
          by AppId, AppDisplayName = coalesce(AppDisplayName, ServicePrincipalName)
| sort by Rows desc
```

Check `ResultDescription` in the output. It may carry more detail than the generic reference text, such as the name of the parameter that was wrong. Whether it does isn't documented, so treat it as a bonus if it's there.

Non-interactive and service principal rows are aggregated when application, user (or service principal), IP address, status and resource match, so row counts in those tables are not request counts. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"9002313"`, not `9002313`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS9002313?
sections.text:
**For the user:** this isn't something you caused with your password. If an old bookmark or saved link starts the sign-in, open the app from its normal start page instead. If the error stays, report it to whoever runs the app with the time it happened.

**For developers:**
1. Do what Microsoft suggests: capture the failing request with Fiddler (or your browser's developer tools) and check it parameter by parameter against the protocol reference for that endpoint.
2. Check that the request goes to the right endpoint for its parameters. A v2.0 parameter such as `scope` sent to a v1 endpoint, or the reverse, is a typical way to build an invalid request. That is our example, not one Microsoft lists for this code.
3. Check encoding. Values in a token request body must be form-encoded; a raw `+`, `&` or space in a secret or redirect URI breaks the request. Again our example, not a Microsoft statement.
4. Prefer a Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL) over hand-written requests. It builds the protocol messages for you.

**For admins:**
1. Use the second query to find the app and the date it started. Hand both to the app owner or vendor.
2. If the app is a third-party SaaS integration, the request is built on the vendor side. Open a ticket with them and include the correlation ID and timestamp from the sign-in log row.
3. If the app ID is unknown to you, check whether it has a service principal in your tenant before deciding it is harmless. A related code for an app that isn't there is [700016](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/700016/).

9002326.title: AADSTS9002326: Cross-origin token request from a non-SPA app (fix)
9002326.description: AADSTS9002326: a browser token request for an app not registered as an SPA. Not in Microsoft's error list. Causes, fixes and KQL.
9002326.summary: AADSTS9002326 means a browser sent a token request (it carried an Origin header) for an app that isn't registered as a single-page application. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. Typical causes: client credentials or a secret called from JavaScript, or an SPA whose redirect URI isn't the spa type. Low attack value. Fix the app registration or move the call to a backend.
9002326.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS9002326 (checked 30 October 2026).

The lab reproduced it. A password-grant token request from a public client, sent with the header `Origin: https://lab.brambrinkmeier.com`, returned:

> AADSTS9002326: Cross-origin token redemption is permitted only for the 'Single-Page Application' client-type. Request origin: 'https://lab.brambrinkmeier.com'.

Entra treats a token request that carries an `Origin` header as one made from a browser. It accepts such a request only when the app is set up as a single-page application (SPA). Microsoft's wording below links the header to the browser.

Microsoft describes the message, without the code number, in its authorization code flow reference:

> Single page apps may receive an `invalid_request` error indicating that cross-origin token redemption is permitted only for the 'Single-Page Application' client-type. This indicates that the redirect URI used to request the token has not been marked as a `spa` redirect URI.

The same page explains why the check exists:

> Applications can't use a `spa` redirect URI with non-SPA flows, for example, native applications or client credential flows. [...] the Microsoft identity platform also prevents the use of client credentials in all flows in the presence of an `Origin` header, to ensure that secrets aren't used from within the browser.

Our reading of the lab result: the check is not only about secrets. The lab request used the password grant from a public client, with no secret, and still got 9002326. So any token request with an `Origin` header from an app that isn't an SPA can hit it.

Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS9002326 (checked 30 October 2026).

The lab reproduced it. A password-grant token request from a public client, sent with the header `Origin: https://lab.brambrinkmeier.com`, returned:

> AADSTS9002326: Cross-origin token redemption is permitted only for the 'Single-Page Application' client-type. Request origin: 'https://lab.brambrinkmeier.com'.

Entra treats a token request that carries an `Origin` header as one made from a browser. It accepts such a request only when the app is set up as a single-page application (SPA). Microsoft's wording below links the header to the browser.

Microsoft describes the message, without the code number, in its authorization code flow reference:

> Single page apps may receive an `invalid_request` error indicating that cross-origin token redemption is permitted only for the 'Single-Page Application' client-type. This indicates that the redirect URI used to request the token has not been marked as a `spa` redirect URI.

The same page explains why the check exists:

> Applications can't use a `spa` redirect URI with non-SPA flows, for example, native applications or client credential flows. [...] the Microsoft identity platform also prevents the use of client credentials in all flows in the presence of an `Origin` header, to ensure that secrets aren't used from within the browser.

Our reading of the lab result: the check is not only about secrets. The lab request used the password grant from a public client, with no secret, and still got 9002326. So any token request with an `Origin` header from an app that isn't an SPA can hit it.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a password-grant (ROPC) token request from a public client app in my lab tenant. The request carried the header `Origin: https://lab.brambrinkmeier.com`. Entra returned `AADSTS9002326` with the first line quoted above.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint. The message names the origin it saw, which helps you find the page that sent the call. It lands in **`SigninLogs`** (interactive user sign-ins): one row per lab run, Status Failure, Conditional Access Not Applied, client app "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients". Entra's explanation on the row (the "additional details" field) reads: *"The application must fix either the reply URIs registered on the application registration to include a unique reply address of type "spa", or they must fix the token request to not include an Origin header, if being sent from a non-browser client."* That is Microsoft's own description of the fix, which its error reference doesn't carry. The KQL below was run on these rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). Both queries found the lab rows.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
Almost always no. It is a mismatch between where the code runs (a browser) and how the app is registered.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| Works in Postman, fails from the web page | Users report exactly this ([Q&A 1534740](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1534740/cross-origin-token-redemption-is-permitted-only-fo), [Q&A 1608608](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1608608/cross-origin-token-redemption-is-permitted-only-fo)). Our reading: Postman sends no `Origin` header; the browser does. |
| A script on a SharePoint page or a front end calls `client_credentials` with a secret | Users report it on this call (Q&A 1534740). The secret is in browser code, which Microsoft blocks on purpose. Treat the secret as exposed. |
| An SPA using MSAL.js fails on the code redemption step | The redirect URI is registered as **Web**, not **Single-page application**. This is the cause Microsoft describes. |
| A hybrid mobile app (Ionic/Capacitor) fails with origin `capacitor://localhost` | Users report it ([Ionic forum](https://forum.ionicframework.com/t/capacitor-msal-azure-b2c-ios-not-working-aadsts9002326/240436)). Likely the app's web view sends an `Origin` header, so Entra treats it as a browser (unconfirmed). |

As far as we can tell, the error gives an attacker nothing. The request fails before a token is issued. The one security point is the second row. If a client secret sits in JavaScript, anyone who opens the page can read it. Rotate it.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 9002326 is logged in. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "9002326"
| summarize Rows = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, AppId
```

Which apps fail, and from which clients. `UserAgent` often tells you it is a browser:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "9002326"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            IPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            Agents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            Descriptions = make_set(ResultDescription, 3)
          by SourceTable, AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

If both queries return nothing, the rows may not be written to your tenant's logs at all. That is also undocumented. The message itself, with its `Request origin`, is then your best evidence.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS9002326?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report the app name, the page you were on and the time to whoever runs the app.

**For developers:**
1. **If the app is an SPA**, register the redirect URI under **Authentication** > **Add a platform** > **Single-page application**, not under **Web**. Microsoft's auth code flow page says to *"update the redirect URI for your app to use the `spa` type"*. Use the authorization code flow with PKCE, for example with MSAL.js. Microsoft notes PKCE is *"required by the Microsoft identity platform for single page apps using the authorization code flow"*.
2. **If browser code calls `client_credentials` or sends a client secret**, move that call to a backend. Microsoft's guidance is plain: *"Don't use the application secret in a native app or single page app because a `client_secret` can't be reliably stored on devices or web pages."* The browser then calls your backend, and the backend calls Entra.
3. **If browser code uses the password grant**, stop. Use an interactive sign-in with MSAL.js instead.
4. **For hybrid mobile apps**, our reading is that the web view counts as a browser. Either register the app as an SPA and use a browser-style flow, or use a native MSAL library so the token request doesn't come from the web view. Test both; the Ionic thread has no replies and no confirmed fix.

**For admins:**
1. Look up the app by the `AppId` from the queries, or by the client ID in the error.
2. In **App registrations** > the app > **Authentication**, check which platform the redirect URI is under.
3. If the app had a secret in browser code, create a new secret, update the backend that should hold it, and delete the old one.
