9002327.title: AADSTS9002327: SPA token redeemed without a browser Origin (fix)
9002327.description: AADSTS9002327: an SPA's code or refresh token was redeemed without a browser Origin header. Not in Microsoft's error list. Fixes and KQL.
9002327.summary: AADSTS9002327 means a token request used an authorization code or refresh token issued to a single-page app, but the request had no Origin header, so it didn't come from a browser. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. A Q&A answerer links it to redemption from server-side code. Low attack value. Redeem in the browser, or register a Web platform.
9002327.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS9002327 (checked 30 October 2026).

The wording below comes from user reports. A user on Microsoft Q&A posted this token endpoint response (`400 Bad Request`, `invalid_request`):

> AADSTS9002327: Tokens issued for the 'Single-Page Application' client-type may only be redeemed via cross-origin requests.

The app was registered with the **Single-page application** platform and used the authorization code flow with PKCE. A Microsoft moderator answered that the error is thrown *"due to your token requests missing the Origin header"*, and gave two fixes: add the header, or change the redirect URI platform to **Web** or **Native/Desktop**. Another answerer, not marked as Microsoft staff, wrote: *"Usually, you get the AADSTS9002327 error when trying to exchange a refresh token from server-side code."*. The thread doesn't confirm which applied.

Microsoft documents the rule, without the code number, in its authorization code flow reference:

> Applications can't use a `spa` redirect URI with non-SPA flows, for example, native applications or client credential flows. To ensure security and best practices, the Microsoft identity platform returns an error if you attempt to use a `spa` redirect URI without an `Origin` header.

Our reading: 9002327 is that error. A code or refresh token issued through a `spa` redirect URI can only be redeemed by a request that carries an `Origin` header, which is what a browser sends. It is the mirror of [9002326](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/9002326/), where a request with an `Origin` header hits an app that isn't an SPA.

sections.heading: What does AADSTS9002327 mean?
sections.text:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS9002327 (checked 30 October 2026).

The wording below comes from user reports. A user on Microsoft Q&A posted this token endpoint response (`400 Bad Request`, `invalid_request`):

> AADSTS9002327: Tokens issued for the 'Single-Page Application' client-type may only be redeemed via cross-origin requests.

The app was registered with the **Single-page application** platform and used the authorization code flow with PKCE. A Microsoft moderator answered that the error is thrown *"due to your token requests missing the Origin header"*, and gave two fixes: add the header, or change the redirect URI platform to **Web** or **Native/Desktop**. Another answerer, not marked as Microsoft staff, wrote: *"Usually, you get the AADSTS9002327 error when trying to exchange a refresh token from server-side code."*. The thread doesn't confirm which applied.

Microsoft documents the rule, without the code number, in its authorization code flow reference:

> Applications can't use a `spa` redirect URI with non-SPA flows, for example, native applications or client credential flows. To ensure security and best practices, the Microsoft identity platform returns an error if you attempt to use a `spa` redirect URI without an `Origin` header.

Our reading: 9002327 is that error. A code or refresh token issued through a `spa` redirect URI can only be redeemed by a request that carries an `Origin` header, which is what a browser sends. It is the mirror of [9002326](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/9002326/), where a request with an `Origin` header hits an app that isn't an SPA.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a mismatch between how the app is registered and where it redeems tokens.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A developer testing the token call in Postman or curl | No `Origin` header is sent. The SPA registration rejects it. Likely, but unconfirmed. |
| An app that renders on the server (SSR, Blazor Server, MVC) registered as SPA | One Q&A answerer suggests this: the code is redeemed by server code, not the browser. |
| A backend that takes the SPA's refresh token and refreshes it itself | One Q&A answerer calls this the usual cause. The refresh token stays bound to the browser. |
| A sudden spike after a deployment | Probably token redemption moved from the browser to a backend or proxy (unconfirmed). |

Our reading: the check is a defence. A code or refresh token issued to a browser app can't simply be redeemed from a script without the `Origin` header. Anyone can set that header in a script, though, so it is not a strong barrier. Don't treat it as one.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 9002327 is logged in, or whether it is logged at all. Check where it lands in your workspace:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "9002327"
| summarize Rows = count() by SourceTable
```

If it does land in a user sign-in table, find the apps and the clients behind it. A server or tool user agent instead of a browser points at server-side redemption:

```kusto
union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "9002327"
| summarize Rows = count(),
            Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10)
          by AppDisplayName, AppId
| sort by Rows desc
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS9002327?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report the app name to whoever runs it.

**For developers:**
1. Decide where tokens should be redeemed. If the browser does it, use MSAL.js in the browser and let it make the token call. The browser sends the `Origin` header.
2. If your server redeems the code or refreshes tokens, the app isn't an SPA. Register a **Web** redirect URI and authenticate the server as a confidential client. That is one of the two fixes the Microsoft moderator gave.
3. The moderator's other fix was to add the `Origin` header. Our reading: fine for a test in Postman or curl. Don't ship a backend that fakes a browser header to get around the SPA rules.
4. Don't mix flows on one redirect URI. Microsoft: *"Applications can't use a `spa` redirect URI with non-SPA flows."*

**For admins:**
1. Look at the app registration's **Authentication** page. Check which platform the failing redirect URI is under: **Single-page application**, **Web**, or **Mobile and desktop applications**.
2. If the app's backend does the redemption, move that redirect URI to **Web**, with the developer's agreement. Moving it changes how the app must authenticate.

1. Look at the app registration's **Authentication** page. Check which platform the failing redirect URI is under: **Single-page application**, **Web**, or **Mobile and desktop applications**.
2. If the app's backend does the redemption, move that redirect URI to **Web**, with the developer's agreement. Moving it changes how the app must authenticate.

9002331.title: AADSTS9002331: App is for personal Microsoft accounts only (fix)
9002331.description: AADSTS9002331: the app is for personal Microsoft accounts only and the request didn't use /consumers. Not in Microsoft's error list. Fixes and KQL.
9002331.summary: AADSTS9002331 means the app is registered for personal Microsoft accounts only, but the sign-in didn't use the /consumers endpoint, or a work account tried to use it. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. Low attack value. Use the /consumers endpoint, or change the app's supported account types.
9002331.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS9002331 (checked 30 October 2026).

The wording below comes from a user report on Microsoft Q&A. The user posted a screenshot; a Microsoft moderator quoted the text as:

> AADSTS9002331: Application '...73f'(...Demo) is configured for use by Microsoft Account users only. Please use the /consumers endpoint to serve this request.

The moderator's explanation: the app registration allows only personal Microsoft accounts (`PersonalMicrosoftAccount`), and the error happens when a user from a Microsoft Entra tenant or another identity provider tries to sign in. The fix given was to change the app's supported account types. The thread doesn't confirm the fix.

The app setting behind it is **Supported account types**. Microsoft's signInAudience page maps **Personal Microsoft accounts only** to `signInAudience` value `PersonalMicrosoftAccount`.

**A lab test on 30 October 2026 returned a different code for this case.** I registered an app with Supported account types set to personal Microsoft accounts only, then sent a password-grant request to my tenant's own endpoint. Entra answered with `AADSTS9002346`, not 9002331:

> AADSTS9002346: Application '<app id>'(<app name>) is configured for use by Microsoft Account users only. Please use the /consumers endpoint to serve this request.

The wording is the same apart from the number. So on a current tenant this condition produces 9002346, while the user report above shows 9002331 for the same situation. Match on both if you are writing a rule, and see [9002346](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/9002346/) for the lab-reproduced page.

The endpoint matters too. Microsoft's OpenID Connect reference describes the `{tenant}` values in the sign-in URL:

| Value | Microsoft's description |
|---|---|
| `common` | Users with both a personal Microsoft account and a work or school account from Microsoft Entra ID can sign in to the application. |
| `organizations` | Only users with work or school accounts from Microsoft Entra ID can sign in to the application. |
| `consumers` | Only users with a personal Microsoft account can sign in to the application. |
| tenant ID or domain | Only users from a specific Microsoft Entra tenant [...] can sign in to the application. |

Microsoft's error reference does list the reverse case, AADSTS9002332: *"Application '{principalId}'({principalName}) is configured for use by Microsoft Entra users only. Please do not use the /consumers endpoint to serve this request."* Our reading: 9002331 is its mirror. A personal-accounts-only app was called on an endpoint other than `/consumers`.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a mismatch between the app's supported account types and the sign-in endpoint or the account used.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A sample or tutorial app fails on first run | The app was registered as **Personal Microsoft accounts only** but the code uses a tenant ID, `/organizations` or `/common`. Our interpretation. |
| A work account user can't sign in to an app that works for a personal account | The app was never meant for work accounts, or was registered with the wrong account type. |
| A third-party product fails for your staff | The vendor's app is registered for personal accounts only. Only the vendor can change that. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which table 9002331 is logged in. Our reading: an app registered for personal accounts only usually has no service principal in your tenant, and a request on `/consumers` or `/common` may never reach your tenant at all. Expect few or no rows. Check anyway:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "9002331"
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = make_set(AppId, 10) by SourceTable
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS9002331?
sections.text:
**For the user:** if you have a personal Microsoft account (Outlook.com, Hotmail, Xbox), try that one. If the app should work with your work account, report it to the app's owner.

**For developers:**
1. Decide who the app is for. Personal accounts only: sign in through `https://login.microsoftonline.com/consumers/`. That is what the error message asks for.
2. If work or school accounts must sign in too, change **Supported account types** on the app registration. The Microsoft moderator's fix was exactly this. Microsoft's signInAudience page lists the options and the validation rules that differ between them.
3. For both personal and work accounts, use `AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount` and the `/common` endpoint. Microsoft notes that with `common` or `consumers` *"the consuming resource application must be configured to support such type of accounts"*.

**For admins:**
1. If this is your own app registration, check **Supported account types** under the app's **Authentication** page, and agree the change with the developer.
2. If it is a vendor's app, you can't change it. Ask the vendor for a version registered for work accounts.

9002341.title: AADSTS9002341: User must allow Windows single sign-on (fix)
9002341.description: AADSTS9002341: the user hasn't allowed an app to use their Windows sign-in for SSO (EEA consent prompt). Low attack value; how to auto-accept. KQL.
9002341.summary: AADSTS9002341 means the user hasn't given permission for an app to use their Windows sign-in for single sign-on. Microsoft links it to the Windows SSO change in the European Economic Area, where Windows asks before reusing the Windows account in other apps. It has low attack value. Users accept the prompt; admins can auto-accept it on managed Windows 11 devices.
9002341.meaningText:
Microsoft's description:

> V2Error: `invalid_grant` - The user is required to permit single sign-On (SSO). This error occurs when the user has not granted the necessary permissions for the application to perform SSO. The user should be redirected to the consent screen to grant the necessary permissions. Refer to [this announcement](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/windows-it-pro-blog/upcoming-changes-to-windows-single-sign-on/ba-p/4008151) for more information.

The app tried to sign the user in with the credentials from their Windows sign-in. The user hadn't said yes to that, so the request failed with `invalid_grant`.

The announcement Microsoft links to is the December 2023 Windows IT Pro post *Upcoming changes to Windows single sign-on*. It opens: *"Microsoft has been working to ensure compliance with the Digital Markets Act (DMA) in the European Economic Area (EEA)."*

Microsoft's current Learn page on the change describes the behaviour. In the EEA, users *"are not automatically signed in to other Microsoft applications and services after signing in to Windows. Instead, Windows asks users whether they want to use the same credentials to sign in to additional apps or services."* The notice *"appears the first time a user uses an app that enables sign-in with a personal Microsoft account, or work or school Entra ID, after signing in to Windows. If the user chooses to use the same credentials they used to sign in to Windows, this notice will not appear again."*

This is not the app consent you know from [65001](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/65001/). Nobody grants API permissions here. The question is whether Windows may reuse the Windows account for single sign-on in this app.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a permission prompt on the user's own device, and the failure means no token was issued. There is no documented attack pattern.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| 9002341 for users in the EEA on Windows, often the first time they open an app | The Windows SSO prompt hasn't been accepted yet. Benign. |
| 9002341 followed by a success for the same user and app | The user accepted the prompt, or signed in another way. Working as designed. |
| 9002341 repeating for one user and app, with no success | Our reading: the user declined the prompt (the screenshot on Microsoft's page shows a *Don't sign in* button) or the app doesn't send them to it. |
| A drop in 9002341 after you deploy the admin setting | The auto-accept setting is in effect on those devices. |

Exclude it from failure-rate dashboards and spray detections.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 9002341 is logged in. Check where it lands:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "9002341"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which apps and operating systems hit it. `DeviceDetail` is `dynamic` in `SigninLogs` and `string` in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, so normalise it first:

```kusto
union
    (SigninLogs | extend Dev = todynamic(DeviceDetail)),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | extend Dev = todynamic(DeviceDetail))
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "9002341"
| extend OS = tostring(Dev.operatingSystem)
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName, OS
| sort by Users desc
```

Users who keep hitting it on the same app and don't succeed there after their first failure that day. These are the people to contact, or the devices to cover with the admin setting:

```kusto
let prompts =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "9002341"
    | summarize Fails = count(), FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName;
let successes =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize LastSuccess = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId;
prompts
| join kind=leftouter successes on UserPrincipalName, AppId
| where isnull(LastSuccess) or LastSuccess < FirstFail
| project UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, Fails, FirstFail
| sort by Fails desc
```

The threshold is up to you; start with users who have more than a handful of `Fails`. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"9002341"`, not `9002341`.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS9002341?
sections.text:
**For the user:** when Windows asks whether to use your Windows account to sign in to the app, choose to continue. Microsoft says the notice then *"will not appear again"* for that app.

**For developers:** Microsoft's description says *"The user should be redirected to the consent screen to grant the necessary permissions."* Treat 9002341 like other interaction-required errors: catch it on the silent call and start an interactive sign-in, so the user sees the prompt.

**For admins:**
1. On managed Windows devices you can accept the prompt for your users. Microsoft documents a registry policy: path `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AAD`, value `AutoAcceptSsoPermission` (DWORD) = `1`.
2. Requirements, per Microsoft: Windows 11, version 24H2 or 25H2, with the July 2026 security update (KB5101650) or later. It *"Applies only to Windows managed enterprise devices with Microsoft Entra ID accounts."*
3. Deploy it with Group Policy, Intune or another MDM, Configuration Manager, or *"Any management tool that supports registry policy deployment."*
4. Personal Microsoft accounts and unmanaged devices have no admin control. Those users still see the prompt.
5. Run the third query again after the rollout and check that the remaining users are on unmanaged or older devices.

9002341.kqlSectionText:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 9002341 is logged in. Check where it lands:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "9002341"
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by SourceTable
```

Which apps and operating systems hit it. `DeviceDetail` is `dynamic` in `SigninLogs` and `string` in `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, so normalise it first:

```kusto
union
    (SigninLogs | extend Dev = todynamic(DeviceDetail)),
    (AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | extend Dev = todynamic(DeviceDetail))
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "9002341"
| extend OS = tostring(Dev.operatingSystem)
| summarize Rows = count(), Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName) by AppDisplayName, OS
| sort by Users desc
```

Users who keep hitting it on the same app and don't succeed there after their first failure that day. These are the people to contact, or the devices to cover with the admin setting:

```kusto
let prompts =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "9002341"
    | summarize Fails = count(), FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId, AppDisplayName;
let successes =
    union SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == "0"
    | summarize LastSuccess = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, AppId;
prompts
| join kind=leftouter successes on UserPrincipalName, AppId
| where isnull(LastSuccess) or LastSuccess < FirstFail
| project UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, Fails, FirstFail
| sort by Fails desc
```

The threshold is up to you; start with users who have more than a handful of `Fails`. `ResultType` is a **string** column, so compare it with `"9002341"`, not `9002341`.

fix.short: User: when Windows asks to use your Windows account, choose to continue. Developer: catch it on the silent call and start an interactive sign-in. Admin: on managed Windows 11 24H2/25H2 devices, set `AutoAcceptSsoPermission` (DWORD) to `1` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AAD`.
fix.steps:
**For the user:** when Windows asks whether to use your Windows account to sign in to the app, choose to continue. Microsoft says the notice then *"will not appear again"* for that app.

**For developers:** Microsoft's description says *"The user should be redirected to the consent screen to grant the necessary permissions."* Treat 9002341 like other interaction-required errors: catch it on the silent call and start an interactive sign-in, so the user sees the prompt.

**For admins:**
1. On managed Windows devices you can accept the prompt for your users. Microsoft documents a registry policy: path `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\AAD`, value `AutoAcceptSsoPermission` (DWORD) = `1`.
2. Requirements, per Microsoft: Windows 11, version 24H2 or 25H2, with the July 2026 security update (KB5101650) or later. It *"Applies only to Windows managed enterprise devices with Microsoft Entra ID accounts."*
3. Deploy it with Group Policy, Intune or another MDM, Configuration Manager, or *"Any management tool that supports registry policy deployment."*
4. Personal Microsoft accounts and unmanaged devices have no admin control. Those users still see the prompt.
5. Run the third query again after the rollout and check that the remaining users are on unmanaged or older devices.

9002346.title: AADSTS9002346: App is for personal Microsoft accounts only (fix)
9002346.description: AADSTS9002346: the app is for personal Microsoft accounts only and the request used a tenant endpoint. Not in Microsoft's error list. Fix and KQL.
9002346.summary: AADSTS9002346 means the app registration is set to personal Microsoft accounts only, and the request went to a tenant endpoint instead of /consumers. Microsoft's error reference doesn't list it. It is a configuration error with low attack value. Either call /consumers, or change Supported account types on the app registration.
9002346.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS9002346 (checked 30 October 2026). We found no other Microsoft page that names it. The wording below is from a lab run:

> AADSTS9002346: Application '\<app id>'(\<app name>) is configured for use by Microsoft Account users only. Please use th...

The lab records only the first line of `error_description`, cut at about 160 characters. The sentence completes as *"Please use the /consumers endpoint to serve this request"*, which is how the same message appears in a user report for the near-identical code [9002331](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/9002331/).

The setting behind it is **Supported account types** on the app registration. Microsoft's signInAudience page maps the portal choices to manifest values:

| Supported account types | `signInAudience` |
|---|---|
| Accounts in this organizational directory only (Single tenant) | `AzureADMyOrg` |
| Accounts in any organizational directory (Any Microsoft Entra directory - Multitenant) | `AzureADMultipleOrgs` |
| Accounts in any organizational directory ... and personal Microsoft accounts (such as Skype, Xbox) | `AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount` |
| Personal Microsoft accounts only | `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` |

An app at `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` exists only for consumer accounts, and consumer accounts sign in through `/consumers`. Microsoft's OpenID Connect reference describes the endpoint values:

| Value | Microsoft's description |
|---|---|
| `common` | Users with both a personal Microsoft account and a work or school account from Microsoft Entra ID can sign in to the application. |
| `organizations` | Only users with work or school accounts from Microsoft Entra ID can sign in to the application. |
| `consumers` | Only users with a personal Microsoft account can sign in to the application. |
| Directory (tenant) ID or domain | Only users from a specific Microsoft Entra tenant ... can sign in to the application. |

So the request named a tenant that the app does not serve. Microsoft's reference does list the mirror case, **AADSTS9002332**: *"Application '{principalId}'({principalName}) is configured for use by Microsoft Entra users only. Please do not use the /consumers endpoint to serve this request."* 9002346 is the same check in the other direction.

### 9002346 and 9002331
[9002331](https://brambrinkmeier.com/entra/aadsts/9002331/) carries the same sentence with a different number. A Microsoft Q&A thread quotes it as *"AADSTS9002331: Application '...73f'(...Demo) is configured for use by Microsoft Account users only. Please use the /consumers endpoint to serve this request."*, and a Microsoft moderator answers: *"From your error message, it looks like your App Registration is set for users to sign-in using their `PersonalMicrosoftAccount` only."*

On a current tenant, the lab run below produced 9002346 for that condition, not 9002331. We can't tell from one tenant whether 9002331 is older, path-specific or flow-specific, so treat them as one condition and match on both in a detection rule.

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run registered an app with **Supported account types** set to personal Microsoft accounts only, then sent a password-grant (ROPC) token request to the lab tenant's own endpoint, with a user from that tenant. Entra returned `AADSTS9002346`:

> AADSTS9002346: Application '\<app id>'(\<app name>) is configured for use by Microsoft Account users only. Please use th...

Control requests in the same run, using an ordinary single-tenant app on the same endpoint with the same user, reached the credential check and returned either a token or a credential error. So 9002346 is about the app's supported account types and the endpoint, not about the user or the password.

No sign-in log row was captured. See [how pages are checked](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/).

In the lab tenant's sign-in logs the row appears under **User sign-ins (interactive)**, Status **Failure**, Conditional Access **Not Applied**, with the Application column naming the personal-accounts-only app.

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. The app's supported account types and the endpoint the code calls disagree.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| A sample or tutorial app fails on the first run | Registered as **Personal Microsoft accounts only** while the code uses a tenant ID, `/organizations` or `/common`. |
| Work account users can't sign in to an app that works with a personal account | The app was never meant for work accounts, or the account type was set wrongly at registration. |
| A third-party product fails for all your staff | The vendor's app registration is consumer-only. Only the vendor can change that. |
| It appears right after someone edited the app registration | **Supported account types** was narrowed to personal accounts only. Check the audit log. |

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Which sign-in table 9002346 lands in is undocumented, and our reading is that most of these never reach your tenant's logs at all: a consumer-only app usually has no service principal in your tenant, and the refusal happens at the endpoint. Expect few or no rows, and check with a union rather than guessing one table:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType in ("9002346", "9002331") or ResultSignature in ("9002346", "9002331")
| summarize Rows = count(), Apps = make_set(AppId, 10), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, ResultType
```

If you do get rows, the faster question is which account types your own app registrations use. That is a Graph or PowerShell query against the directory, not a log query:

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Application.Read.All"
Get-MgApplication -All |
    Where-Object { $_.SignInAudience -eq "PersonalMicrosoftAccount" } |
    Select-Object DisplayName, AppId, SignInAudience
```

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS9002346?
sections.text:
**For the user:** if you have a personal Microsoft account (Outlook.com, Hotmail, Xbox), try signing in with that one. If the app is meant for your work account, report it to whoever owns the app.

**For developers:**
1. Decide who the app is for. Personal accounts only: send the request to `https://login.microsoftonline.com/consumers/`, which is what the error message asks for.
2. If work or school accounts must sign in too, change **Supported account types** on the app registration. For both kinds of account, use `AzureADandPersonalMicrosoftAccount` and the `/common` endpoint.
3. Don't hardcode a tenant ID in an app registered for personal accounts only. The two settings contradict each other.

**For admins:**
1. For your own app registration, check **Supported account types** on the app's **Authentication** page, and agree any change with the developer. Microsoft's signInAudience page lists the validation rules that differ between the account types, so a change can also require edits elsewhere in the registration.
2. For a vendor's app, you cannot change it. Ask the vendor for a registration that supports work accounts.

9010010.title: AADSTS9010010: Resource parameter doesn't match the requested scopes (fix)
9010010.description: AADSTS9010010: the resource parameter doesn't match the requested scopes. Common with MCP clients and trailing slashes. Cause, fix and KQL.
9010010.summary: AADSTS9010010 means a token request carried a resource parameter that doesn't match the resource named in its scopes. Microsoft documents it for MCP clients: the resource value must exactly match the Application ID URI, and the scopes must belong to that same app. A trailing slash is a common cause. It is a client configuration error with low attack value.
9010010.meaningText:
Microsoft's [error code reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity-platform/reference-error-codes) doesn't list AADSTS9010010 (checked 30 October 2026).

My lab tenant returned this message for a client-credentials token request that carried both `scope=https://graph.microsoft.com/.default` and `resource=https://management.azure.com/`:

> AADSTS9010010: The resource parameter provided in the request doesn't match with the requested scopes.

Microsoft does explain the code, on its page about securing an MCP server with Entra ID:

> `AADSTS9010010` means the **Application ID URI configured on your app registration doesn't exactly match the value of the `resource` parameter** in the client's OAuth request.

The same page gives a second cause: *"This error also occurs when the client sends a scope that's defined on a different app registration than the one referenced by the `resource` parameter. Microsoft Entra ID resolves the `resource` and the scope to the same resource app; if they point at different app registrations, the request fails."* That second cause is what the lab request did: the scope names Microsoft Graph, the resource names Azure Resource Manager.

Background. On the v2.0 endpoint the resource is normally named inside the scope. Microsoft's scopes page: *"Using `scope={resource-identifier}/.default` is functionally the same as `resource={resource-identifier}` on the v1.0 endpoint."* The `resource` parameter comes back through RFC 8707 (Resource Indicators), which the MCP authorization spec requires. Microsoft's MCP page: *"The MCP specification requires the client to identify the protected resource it wants a token for by sending the `resource` parameter (from RFC 8707) in its token request."* So a request now carries the resource twice, and the two must agree.

The match is exact. Microsoft: *"The `resource` value the client sends must match the Application ID URI character for character, including the scheme (`https://`), casing of the host, and path. A trailing slash is a common culprit: because an Application ID URI can't end with a slash, a client that sends `resource=https://mcp.contoso.com/` never matches the registered `https://mcp.contoso.com`."*

sections.heading: Reproduced in the lab
sections.text:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a client-credentials request to the token endpoint with `scope=https://graph.microsoft.com/.default` and `resource=https://management.azure.com/`. Entra returned `AADSTS9010010` with this first line:

> AADSTS9010010: The resource parameter provided in the request doesn't match with the requested scopes.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint for an app (not a user) request. It lands in **`AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`** for an app-only request: one row, Failure, client credential type "federatedIdentityCredential", resource Microsoft Graph. The KQL below was run on these rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). Both queries found the row (the second with its app ID placeholder replaced).

sections.heading: Is it an attack?
sections.text:
No. It is a mismatch in how the client builds its token request. No token is issued.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| An MCP client (Claude Code, an IDE, an agent) fails to connect to an Entra-protected MCP server | The client sends `resource` with a trailing slash, or a URL that differs from the Application ID URI. Users report exactly this in [claude-code issue 52871](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/52871), where `resource=https://mcp.businesscentral.dynamics.com/` was sent while the server's metadata declared it without the slash. |
| A script or daemon sends `resource` and `scope` for two different APIs | The scope belongs to another app registration, as in the lab request. |
| A broker or identity provider in front of Entra forwards `resource` with only OIDC scopes (`openid profile`) | Users report this with Auth0 federated to Entra in the same GitHub issue. Our reading: no resource-prefixed scope exists to match. |
| Your own MCP server app is still on v1 access tokens | Microsoft: if `requestedAccessTokenVersion` isn't `2`, *"you can't register an HTTPS Application ID URI that matches your MCP server URL, so the `resource` value can never match."* |

Our reading: the request fails before a token is issued, and only the app's own owner can make it match. There is nothing an attacker gains from triggering it.

sections.heading: How do I find it in my logs (KQL)?
sections.text:
Microsoft doesn't document which sign-in table 9010010 is logged in. Our reading: user-delegated requests (MCP clients signing in a user) would land in `SigninLogs` or `AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs`, and app-only requests like the lab one in `AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`. That is not verified. Check all three:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "9010010"
| summarize Rows = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceTable, AppId, ResourceDisplayName
| sort by Rows desc
```

To fix the request you need the right resource. For an app that fails with 9010010, see which resources it does get tokens for:

```kusto
union withsource=SourceTable SigninLogs, AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AppId == "<app id of the failing client>"
| summarize Successes = countif(ResultType == "0"), Failures9010010 = countif(ResultType == "9010010") by SourceTable, ResourceDisplayName, ResourceIdentity
| sort by Failures9010010 desc
```

A resource with failures and no successes is the one whose `resource` value or scope is wrong. Both queries are starting points; adjust the time window to your retention.

sections.heading: How do I fix AADSTS9010010?
sections.text:
**For the user:** you can't fix this yourself. Report the app or MCP server name to whoever set it up, and include the full error.

**For developers (client side):**
1. If you talk to the v2.0 endpoint and don't need RFC 8707, drop `resource` and name the API only in `scope`, for example `scope=https://graph.microsoft.com/.default`. Microsoft's scopes page says the two are functionally the same.
2. If you must send `resource` (MCP clients do), send it verbatim from the server's protected resource metadata. Don't normalise it; the reporter of [claude-code issue 52871](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/52871) suspects that round-tripping it through a URL parser added the trailing slash. Nobody in the thread confirmed that.
3. Make every scope in the request belong to the same API as `resource`. Remove scopes from other APIs and request them in a separate token request.

**For developers (MCP server side), from Microsoft's MCP page:**
1. Set the app registration to v2 access tokens (`requestedAccessTokenVersion` = `2`).
2. Set the Application ID URI to the exact canonical URL of your MCP server, with no trailing slash.
3. Publish that same value as `resource` in your protected resource metadata, so clients send what Entra expects.

**For admins:** compare the failing app's `resource` value with the Application ID URI of the API's app registration. If they differ by a slash, a case or a path, that is the cause.

microsoftWording.source: Quoted on the page from the lab or from user reports; the code is not in Microsoft's error code reference

attackSignal.label: Low: usually configuration or user error

securityReading.isItAnAttack:
No. It is a mismatch in how the client builds its token request. No token is issued.

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---|---|
| An MCP client (Claude Code, an IDE, an agent) fails to connect to an Entra-protected MCP server | The client sends `resource` with a trailing slash, or a URL that differs from the Application ID URI. Users report exactly this in [claude-code issue 52871](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/52871), where `resource=https://mcp.businesscentral.dynamics.com/` was sent while the server's metadata declared it without the slash. |
| A script or daemon sends `resource` and `scope` for two different APIs | The scope belongs to another app registration, as in the lab request. |
| A broker or identity provider in front of Entra forwards `resource` with only OIDC scopes (`openid profile`) | Users report this with Auth0 federated to Entra in the same GitHub issue. Our reading: no resource-prefixed scope exists to match. |
| Your own MCP server app is still on v1 access tokens | Microsoft: if `requestedAccessTokenVersion` isn't `2`, *"you can't register an HTTPS Application ID URI that matches your MCP server URL, so the `resource` value can never match."* |

Our reading: the request fails before a token is issued, and only the app's own owner can make it match. There is nothing an attacker gains from triggering it.

9010010.labSectionText:
On 30 October 2026 an automated lab run sent a client-credentials request to the token endpoint with `scope=https://graph.microsoft.com/.default` and `resource=https://management.azure.com/`. Entra returned `AADSTS9010010` with this first line:

> AADSTS9010010: The resource parameter provided in the request doesn't match with the requested scopes.

That confirms the code and its wording at the token endpoint for an app (not a user) request. It lands in **`AADServicePrincipalSignInLogs`** for an app-only request: one row, Failure, client credential type "federatedIdentityCredential", resource Microsoft Graph. The KQL below was run on these rows ([how](https://brambrinkmeier.com/methodology/)). Both queries found the row (the second with its app ID placeholder replaced).
